derivation: Name fact anchored to Caesar and the legion among the Eburones; two named answers supported verbatim by 'Quintum Titurium Sabinum et Lucium Aurunculeium Cottam legatos praeesse iussit'. These are the two legates destroyed in Ambiorix's ambush; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ex quibus unam in Morinos ducendam Gaio Fabio legato dedit, alteram in Nervios Quinto Ciceroni, tertiam in Esubios Lucio Roscio.
question: Cui legato Caesar legionem in Nervios ducendam dedit?
question_en: To which legate did Caesar give the legion to lead among the Nervii?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Caesar and the Nervii; single named answer supported verbatim by 'alteram in Nervios Quinto Ciceroni'. Quintus Cicero (brother of the orator), whose winter camp among the Nervii was besieged and relieved by Caesar, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Diebus circiter XV, quibus in hiberna ventum est, initium repentini tumultus ac defectionis ortum est ab Ambiorige et Catuvolco.
question: A quibus ducibus Eburonum initium repentini tumultus ac defectionis ortum est?
question_en: From which leaders of the Eburones did the sudden uprising and revolt begin?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Eburones (whose chiefs they are, 5.24); two named answers supported verbatim by 'initium repentini tumultus ac defectionis ortum est ab Ambiorige et Catuvolco'. Ambiorix's revolt is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Erant in ea legione fortissimi viri, centuriones, qui primis ordinibus appropinquarent, Titus Pullo et Lucius Vorenus. Hi perpetuas inter se controversias habebant, quinam anteferretur, omnibusque annis de locis summis simultatibus contendebant.
question: Qui duo fortissimi centuriones in legione Ciceronis de locis summis perpetuo inter se contendebant?
question_en: Which two very brave centurions in Cicero's legion perpetually competed with each other for the top ranks?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Cicero's besieged legion (the 'ea legio' of 5.39-44); two named answers supported verbatim by 'centuriones ... Titus Pullo et Lucius Vorenus. Hi perpetuas inter se controversias habebant'. The rival centurions are a celebrated closed-book episode.

author: Caesar
source_text: Comprobat hominis consilium fortuna, et cum unum omnes peterent, in ipso fluminis vado deprehensus Indutiomarus interficitur, caputque eius refertur in castra.
question: Quis Trevirorum princeps in ipso fluminis vado ab equitibus Labieni deprehensus et interfectus est?
question_en: Which chief of the Treveri was caught in the very ford of the river by Labienus's cavalry and killed?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Treveri and Labienus; single named answer supported verbatim by 'in ipso fluminis vado deprehensus Indutiomarus interficitur'. The killing of Indutiomarus, instigator of the revolt, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Sed de his duobus generibus alterum est druidum, alterum equitum.
question: Quae duo genera hominum honoratorum apud Gallos esse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which two classes of honored men does Caesar report exist among the Gauls?
derivation: The famous fact that among Gauls of rank there are two privileged orders. Anchored to Caesar + the Gauls; single, verifiable two-name answer supported verbatim (alterum druidum, alterum equitum). Indirect statement (genera... esse) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Disciplina in Britannia reperta atque inde in Galliam translata esse existimatur, et nunc, qui diligentius eam rem cognoscere volunt, plerumque illo discendi causa proficiscuntur.
question: Ubi disciplinam druidum repertam esse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Where does Caesar report that the discipline of the druids was discovered?
derivation: Caesar's claim about the origin of druidic disciplina. Anchored to the druids; single place-name answer supported verbatim (in Britannia reperta). Indirect statement (disciplinam... repertam esse) under tradit; closed-book, oft-cited.

author: Caesar
source_text: Tantis excitati praemiis et sua sponte multi in disciplinam conveniunt et a parentibus propinquisque mittuntur. Magnum ibi numerum versuum ediscere dicuntur. Itaque annos nonnulli vicenos in disciplina permanent.
question: Quot annos nonnulli in druidum disciplina permaneant Caesar tradit?
question_en: How many years does Caesar report that some remain in the druids' training?
derivation: Length-of-training number fact. Anchored to the druidic disciplina; single number answer supported verbatim (annos... vicenos). Indirect question (permaneant, subj.) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Neque fas esse existimant ea litteris mandare, cum in reliquis fere rebus, publicis privatisque rationibus Graecis litteris utantur.
question: Quibus litteris Galli in publicis privatisque rationibus utantur Caesar scribit?
question_en: Which script does Caesar say the Gauls used for their public and private accounts?
derivation: Notable fact that, while not committing druidic lore to writing, the Gauls used Greek script for records. Anchored to the Gauls + accounts; verifiable answer supported verbatim (Graecis litteris utantur). Indirect question (utantur, subj.) under scribit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Deum maxime Mercurium colunt. Huius sunt plurima simulacra: hunc omnium inventorem artium ferunt, hunc viarum atque itinerum ducem, hunc ad quaestus pecuniae mercaturasque habere vim maximam arbitrantur.
question: Quem deum Gallos maxime colere Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which god does Caesar report the Gauls worship most?
derivation: The most-cited fact of the Gallic pantheon section. Anchored to Caesar + the Gauls; single name answer supported verbatim (Deum maxime Mercurium colunt). Indirect statement (Gallos colere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Galli se omnes ab Dite patre prognatos praedicant idque ab druidibus proditum dicunt.
question: A quo deo Galli se omnes prognatos esse praedicant, ut Caesar scribit?
question_en: From which god do the Gauls proclaim they are all descended, as Caesar writes?
derivation: Iconic claim of Gallic descent. Anchored to the Gauls; single divine-name answer supported verbatim (ab Dite patre prognatos). Direct question with the source's acc.+inf. (se prognatos esse) plus parenthetical attribution.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ob eam causam spatia omnis temporis non numero dierum sed noctium finiunt; dies natales et mensum et annorum initia sic observant ut noctem dies subsequatur.
question: Utrum numero dierum an noctium Galli omnia temporis spatia finire soleant Caesar tradit?
question_en: Does Caesar report that the Gauls reckon all spans of time by the count of days or of nights?
derivation: The well-known Celtic night-reckoning custom. Anchored to the Gauls; disjunctive question with a single verifiable answer supported verbatim (non numero dierum sed noctium). Indirect question (soleant, subj.) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Germani multum ab hac consuetudine differunt. Nam neque druides habent, qui rebus divinis praesint, neque sacrificiis student. Deorum numero eos solos ducunt, quos cernunt et quorum aperte opibus iuvantur, Solem et Vulcanum et Lunam, reliquos ne fama quidem acceperunt.
question: Quos solos deorum numero Germanos ducere Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which gods alone does Caesar report the Germani count among the gods?
answer_en: The Sun, Vulcan, and the Moon.
derivation: Specific German religious custom (contrast with the Gauls). Anchored to the Germani; complete three-name enumeration supported verbatim (Solem et Vulcanum et Lunam). Indirect statement (Germanos ducere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Agriculturae non student, maiorque pars eorum victus in lacte, caseo, carne consistit.
question: In quibus rebus maiorem partem victus Germanorum consistere Caesar scribit?
question_en: In what does Caesar say the greater part of the Germani's food consists?
derivation: Specific German dietary custom. Anchored to the Germani; complete three-item enumeration supported verbatim (in lacte, caseo, carne consistit). Indirect statement (maiorem partem... consistere) under scribit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Itaque ea quae fertilissima Germaniae sunt loca circum Hercyniam silvam, quam Eratostheni et quibusdam Graecis fama notam esse video, quam illi Orcyniam appellant, Volcae Tectosages occupaverunt atque ibi consederunt.
question: Quam gentem Gallorum loca circum Hercyniam silvam occupavisse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which Gallic people, according to Caesar, occupied the lands around the Hercynian forest?
derivation: Named-people fact about settlement around the Hercynian forest. Anchored to the Hercynian forest; single people-name answer supported verbatim (Volcae Tectosages occupaverunt). Indirect statement (gentem... occupavisse) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Huius Hercyniae silvae, quae supra demonstrata est, latitudo novem dierum iter expedito patet.
question: Quot dierum iter in latitudinem Hercyniam silvam patere Caesar tradit?
question_en: How many days' journey wide does Caesar report the Hercynian forest to be?
derivation: Measure fact for the Hercynian forest's breadth. Anchored to the Hercynian forest; single number answer supported verbatim (latitudo novem dierum iter ... patet). Indirect statement (silvam patere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Sunt item, quae appellantur alces. Harum est consimilis capris figura et varietas pellium, sed magnitudine paulo antecedunt mutilaeque sunt cornibus et crura sine nodis articulisque habent neque quietis causa procumbunt.
question: Quas feras Hercyniae silvae crura sine nodis articulisque habere Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which beasts of the Hercynian forest does Caesar report have legs without knots or joints?
derivation: Named animal of the Hercynian forest with its signature feature (jointless legs). Anchored to the forest; single animal-name answer supported verbatim (alces ... crura sine nodis articulisque habent). Indirect statement (feras habere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Tertium est genus eorum, qui uri appellantur. Hi sunt magnitudine paulo infra elephantos, specie et colore et figura tauri.
question: Quo animali uros magnitudine paulo inferiores esse Caesar scribit?
question_en: To which animal does Caesar report the uri (aurochs) are slightly inferior in size?
answer_en: Elephants (the uri are a little smaller than elephants).
derivation: Named animal of the Hercynian forest with a comparative-size fact. Anchored to the uri; single answer supported verbatim (magnitudine paulo infra elephantos). Indirect statement (uros inferiores esse) under scribit; abl. of comparison.

author: Caesar
source_text: per Arduennam silvam, quae est totius Galliae maxima atque ab ripis Rheni finibusque Treverorum ad Nervios pertinet milibusque amplius quingentis in longitudinem patet
question: Quam silvam totius Galliae maximam esse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which forest does Caesar report is the largest in all Gaul?
derivation: Superlative geography fact. Anchored to Gaul; single place-name answer supported verbatim (quae est totius Galliae maxima). Indirect statement (silvam... esse) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Catuvolcus, rex dimidiae partis Eburonum, qui una cum Ambiorige consilium inierat, aetate iam confectus, cum laborem aut belli aut fugae ferre non posset, omnibus precibus detestatus Ambiorigem, qui eius consilii auctor fuisset, taxo, cuius magna in Gallia Germaniaque copia est, se exanimavit.
question: Qua re Catuvolcus, dimidiae partis Eburonum rex, se exanimaverit Caesar tradit?
question_en: With what did Catuvolcus, king of half the Eburones, kill himself, according to Caesar?
derivation: Named-person fact: the manner of Catuvolcus' suicide. Anchored to Catuvolcus + the Eburones; single answer supported verbatim (taxo ... se exanimavit). Indirect question (exanimaverit, subj.) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Simili ratione ibi Vercingetorix, Celtilli filius, Arvernus, summae potentiae adulescens, cuius pater principatum Galliae totius obtinuerat et ob eam causam, quod regnum appetebat, ab civitate erat interfectus, convocatis suis clientibus facile incendit.
question: Cuius gentis fuit Vercingetorix, dux Gallorum, secundum Caesarem?
question_en: Of what people was Vercingetorix, the leader of the Gauls, according to Caesar?
derivation: Name/ethnicity fact for the central figure of Book 7. Anchored to Vercingetorix; predicate 'Arvernus' supported verbatim. Vercingetorix the Arvernian is closed-book staple history; single short answer.

author: Caesar
source_text: Simili ratione ibi Vercingetorix, Celtilli filius, Arvernus, summae potentiae adulescens, cuius pater principatum Galliae totius obtinuerat et ob eam causam, quod regnum appetebat, ab civitate erat interfectus, convocatis suis clientibus facile incendit.
question: Cuius filius fuit Vercingetorix Arvernus?
question_en: Whose son was Vercingetorix the Arvernian?
derivation: Relation fact anchored to Vercingetorix; single named answer 'Celtilli' supported verbatim by 'Celtilli filius'. The father Celtillus (who sought kingship and was killed) is a fixed genealogical fact; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Totius Galliae concilium Bibracte indicitur. Eodem conveniunt undique frequentes. Multitudinis suffragiis res permittitur: ad unum omnes Vercingetorigem probant imperatorem.
question: Quem totius Galliae concilium Bibracte habitum imperatorem belli ad unum probavit?
question_en: Whom did the council of all Gaul held at Bibracte unanimously approve as commander of the war?
derivation: Office/election fact anchored to the council at Bibracte; single named answer supported verbatim by 'ad unum omnes Vercingetorigem probant imperatorem'. The choice of Vercingetorix as leader of the revolt is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Vbi ea dies venit, Carnutes Cotuato et Conconnetodumno ducibus, desperatis hominibus, Cenabum signo dato concurrunt civesque Romanos, qui negotiandi causa ibi constiterant, in his Gaium Fufium Citam, honestum equitem Romanum, qui rei frumentariae iussu Caesaris praeerat, interficiunt bonaque eorum diripiunt.
question: In quo oppido Carnutes, caede civium Romanorum facta, Gallici belli initium fecerunt?
question_en: In what town did the Carnutes, by massacring Roman citizens, make the beginning of the Gallic war?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the Carnutes; single town answer supported verbatim by 'Carnutes ... Cenabum ... civesque Romanos ... interficiunt'. The massacre at Cenabum, the spark of the revolt, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Caesar ad oppidum Avaricum, quod erat maximum munitissimumque in finibus Biturigum atque agri fertilissima regione, profectus est, quod eo oppido recepto civitatem Biturigum se in potestatem redacturum confidebat.
question: Quod oppidum maximum munitissimumque in finibus Biturigum fuisse Caesar scribit?
question_en: Which town does Caesar write was the largest and most fortified in the territory of the Bituriges?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the Bituriges and Caesar; single town answer supported verbatim by 'Avaricum, quod erat maximum munitissimumque in finibus Biturigum'. Indirect statement (fuisse) under scribit; the storming of Avaricum is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Denique ex omni numero, qui fuit circiter milium XL, vix DCCC, qui primo clamore audito se ex oppido eiecerunt, incolumes ad Vercingetorigem pervenerunt.
question: Cum Avaricum a Romanis expugnatum esset, ex circiter quadraginta milibus hominum quot vix incolumes ad Vercingetorigem pervenerunt?
question_en: When Avaricum was stormed by the Romans, out of about forty thousand people how many scarcely reached Vercingetorix safely?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Avaricum and Vercingetorix; the count (vix DCCC out of circiter milium XL) supported verbatim. The slaughter at Avaricum, with barely 800 of 40,000 surviving, is the iconic figure Caesar gives; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Omnium consensu hac sententia probata uno die amplius XX urbes Biturigum incenduntur.
question: Quot urbes Biturigum uno die, Vercingetorige suadente, a Gallis incensae sunt?
question_en: How many towns of the Bituriges were burned by the Gauls in one day, on Vercingetorix's plan?
derivation: Number fact anchored to the Bituriges and Vercingetorix's scorched-earth policy; answer 'amplius XX' supported verbatim. Distinctive count; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Exercitum in duas partes divisit: quattuor legiones in Senones Parisiosque Labieno ducendas dedit, sex ipse in Arvernos ad oppidum Gergoviam secundum flumen Elaver duxit.
question: Ad quod Arvernorum oppidum Caesar sex legiones secundum flumen Elaver duxit?
question_en: To which town of the Arverni did Caesar lead six legions along the river Elaver (Allier)?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the Arverni, Caesar, six legions and the Elaver; single town answer supported verbatim by 'sex ipse in Arvernos ad oppidum Gergoviam secundum flumen Elaver duxit'. Gergovia, the Arvernian stronghold, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Nostri, cum undique premerentur, XLVI centurionibus amissis deiecti sunt loco.
question: Quot centuriones Caesaris in proelio ad Gergoviam adverso amissi sunt?
question_en: How many of Caesar's centurions were lost in the unsuccessful battle at Gergovia?
derivation: Number fact anchored to the repulse at Gergovia; answer (XLVI = 46) supported verbatim by 'XLVI centurionibus amissis'. The loss of officers at Gergovia is the distinctive figure of Caesar's one defeat in the campaign; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Fugato omni equitatu Vercingetorix copias, ut pro castris collocaverat, reduxit protinusque Alesiam, quod est oppidum Mandubiorum, iter facere coepit.
question: Cuius gentis oppidum erat Alesia, quo Vercingetorix victus se recepit?
question_en: Of what people was Alesia the town, to which Vercingetorix withdrew after defeat?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Alesia and Vercingetorix; single answer supported verbatim by 'Alesiam, quod est oppidum Mandubiorum'. Alesia of the Mandubii, site of the final siege, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Coactis equitum VIII milibus et peditum circiter CCL haec in Aeduorum finibus recensebantur, numerusque inibatur, praefecti constituebantur.
question: Quantae copiae equitum peditumque coactae sunt, ut Gallis Alesiae obsessis subsidio venirent?
answer: Octo milia equitum et circiter ducenta quinquaginta milia peditum.
question_en: How large a force of cavalry and infantry was raised to relieve the Gauls besieged at Alesia?
answer_en: Eight thousand cavalry and about two hundred fifty thousand infantry.
derivation: Number fact anchored to the relief army for Alesia; counts (VIII milibus equitum, circiter CCL [milia] peditum) supported verbatim. The size of the Gallic relief army is the iconic figure of the siege; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Commio Atrebati, Viridomaro et Eporedorigi Aeduis, Vercassivellauno Arverno, consobrino Vercingetorigis, summa imperi traditur.
question: Quis Arvernus, Vercingetorigis consobrinus, inter quattuor duces auxiliaribus copiis ad Alesiam praefuit?
question_en: Which Arvernian, cousin of Vercingetorix, was among the four leaders set over the relief forces at Alesia?
derivation: Name/relation fact anchored to the relief army and to Vercingetorix; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Vercassivellauno Arverno, consobrino Vercingetorigis'. Anchored as the Arvernian cousin to give a single referent among the four joint commanders; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Quod si indiligentiores fuerint, milia hominum delecta octoginta una secum interitura demonstrat.
question: Quot milia hominum delecta una cum Vercingetorige Alesiae obsidebantur?
question_en: How many thousand chosen men were besieged at Alesia together with Vercingetorix?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Vercingetorix and Alesia; answer 'octoginta milia' supported verbatim ('milia hominum delecta octoginta una secum interitura'), echoed by Critognatus' 'hominum milibus LXXX' (7.77). Closed-book count of the Alesia garrison.

author: Caesar
source_text: Mittuntur de his rebus ad Caesarem legati. Iubet arma tradi, principes produci. Ipse in munitione pro castris consedit: eo duces producuntur; Vercingetorix deditur, arma proiciuntur.
question: Quis dux Gallorum post Alesiae obsidionem Caesari deditus est, armis proiectis?
question_en: Which leader of the Gauls was surrendered to Caesar after the siege of Alesia, his arms thrown down?
derivation: Event fact anchored to Alesia and Caesar; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Vercingetorix deditur, arma proiciuntur'. The surrender of Vercingetorix at Alesia is among the most famous events in Roman history; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Labienus eo supplemento, quod nuper ex Italia venerat, relicto Agedinci, ut esset impedimentis praesidio, cum quattuor legionibus Lutetiam proficiscitur. Id est oppidum Parisiorum, quod positum est in insula fluminis Sequanae.
question: Cuius gentis oppidum erat Lutetia, in insula fluminis Sequanae positum, quod Labienus petivit?
question_en: Of what people was Lutetia the town, set on an island of the river Sequana (Seine), to which Labienus marched?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Lutetia, the Seine, and Labienus; single answer supported verbatim by 'Lutetiam ... Id est oppidum Parisiorum, quod positum est in insula fluminis Sequanae'. Lutetia of the Parisii (Paris) is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: His litteris cognitis Romae dierum viginti supplicatio redditur.
question: Quot dierum supplicatio Romae decreta est, cum de Caesaris rebus ad Alesiam gestis cognitum esset?
question_en: A thanksgiving of how many days was decreed at Rome when Caesar's deeds at Alesia became known?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Rome and the close of the Alesia campaign; answer 'viginti dierum' supported verbatim by 'dierum viginti supplicatio redditur'. The twenty-day thanksgiving is the iconic closing fact of Book 7; closed-book.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Caesaris nostri commentarios rerum gestarum Galliae, non comparantibus superioribus atque insequentibus eius scriptis, contexui novissimumque imperfectum ab rebus gestis Alexandriae confeci usque ad exitum non quidem civilis dissensionis, cuius finem nullum videmus, sed vitae Caesaris.
question: Quis octavum De Bello Gallico librum scripsit, ut Caesaris commentarios imperfectos conficeret?
question_en: Who wrote the eighth book of De Bello Gallico, in order to complete Caesar's unfinished commentaries?
derivation: Authorship fact: Book 8 is not by Caesar but by his officer Aulus Hirtius, who in the preface (first person, 'contexui ... confeci') states he wove together and completed Caesar's unfinished Commentarii on the Gallic War. The author's identity (Hirtius) is the manuscript heading and a standard fact of literary history; the substance (a continuator completed the imperfect last commentary) is verbatim in the source. Closed-book, entity-anchored to the eighth book and Caesar's commentaries.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Coactus assiduis tuis vocibus, Balbe, cum cotidiana mea recusatio non difficultatis excusationem, sed inertiae videretur deprecationem habere, rem difficillimam suscepi.
question: Quem Hirtius in prooemio octavi De Bello Gallico libri alloquitur?
question_en: Whom does Hirtius address in the preface of the eighth book of De Bello Gallico?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Hirtius's preface; the addressee is named in the vocative 'Balbe' (Cornelius Balbus, Caesar's confidant), supported verbatim. Single named answer; closed-book detail of literary history.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Ibi cum Lucterius apud suos cives quondam integris rebus multum potuisset, semperque auctor novorum consiliorum magnam apud barbaros auctoritatem haberet, oppidum Uxellodunum, quod in clientela fuerat eius, egregie natura loci munitum, occupat suis et Drappetis copiis oppidanosque sibi coniungit.
question: Quod oppidum Lucterius et Drappes copiis suis occupaverunt, ubi ultima Gallorum defensio facta est?
question_en: Which town did Lucterius and Drappes seize with their forces, where the last Gallic resistance was made?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Lucterius and Drappes; the town Uxellodunum supported verbatim ('oppidum Uxellodunum ... occupat suis et Drappetis copiis'). Uxellodunum, the last great stronghold of Gallic resistance, is closed-book; single named answer.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Cum contra exspectationem omnium Caesar Uxellodunum venisset oppidumque operibus clausum animadverteret neque ab oppugnatione recedi videret ulla condicione posse, magna autem copia frumenti abundare oppidanos ex perfugis cognosset, aqua prohibere hostem temptare coepit.
question: Cum oppidani Uxelloduni frumento abundarent, qua re Caesar eos ad deditionem coegit?
question_en: Since the townsmen of Uxellodunum had abundant grain, by what means did Caesar force them to surrender?
answer_en: By cutting off their water supply.
derivation: Method fact anchored to Caesar and Uxellodunum; since the town had ample grain, Caesar cut off its water ('aqua prohibere hostem temptare coepit'), supported verbatim. The water-deprivation of Uxellodunum is the defining feature of the siege; closed-book, short answer.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Itaque omnibus qui arma tulerant manus praecidit vitamque concessit, quo testatior esset poena improborum.
question: Quam poenam Caesar Uxelloduno capto eis qui arma tulerant inflixit?
question_en: What punishment did Caesar inflict on those who had borne arms when Uxellodunum was captured?
derivation: Distinctive event fact anchored to Caesar and the captured Uxellodunum; 'omnibus qui arma tulerant manus praecidit vitamque concessit' supported verbatim — he cut off the hands of all who had borne arms but spared their lives, as a deterrent. A notorious episode of the campaign; closed-book.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: unaque consilium cum eo Lucterium Cadurcum cepisse, quem superiore commentario prima defectione Galliae facere in provinciam voluisse impetum cognitum est
question: Cuius gentis fuit Lucterius, qui cum Drappete Uxellodunum tenuit?
question_en: Of what people was Lucterius, who held Uxellodunum together with Drappes?
derivation: Ethnicity fact anchored to Lucterius; 'Lucterium Cadurcum' supported verbatim. Lucterius the Cadurcan, a leader of the final revolt and of the Uxellodunum holdout, is closed-book; single short answer.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Qua ex fuga cum constaret Drappetem Senonem, qui, ut primum defecerat Gallia, collectis undique perditis hominibus, servis ad libertatem vocatis, exulibus omnium civitatum adscitis, receptis latronibus impedimenta et commeatus Romanorum interceperat, non amplius hominum duobus milibus ex fuga collectis provinciam petere
question: Cuius gentis fuit Drappes, socius Lucterii apud Uxellodunum?
question_en: Of what people was Drappes, Lucterius's ally at Uxellodunum?
derivation: Ethnicity fact anchored to Drappes; 'Drappetem Senonem' supported verbatim. Drappes the Senonian, who with Lucterius held Uxellodunum, is entity-anchored and verifiable; single short answer.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Eodem tempore Lacterius, quem profugisse ex proelio scripsi, cum in potestatem venisset Epasnacti Arverni (crebro enim mutandis locis multorum fidei se committebat, quod nusquam diutius sine periculo commoraturus videbatur, cum sibi conscius esset, quam inimicum deberet Caesarem habere), hunc Epasnactus Arvernus, amicissimus populi Romani, sine dubitatione ulla vinctum ad Caesarem deduxit.
question: Quis Arvernus, amicus populi Romani, Lucterium vinctum ad Caesarem deduxit?
question_en: Which Arvernian, a friend of the Roman people, brought Lucterius in chains to Caesar?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Lucterius; 'Epasnactus Arvernus, amicissimus populi Romani, ... vinctum ad Caesarem deduxit' supported verbatim. Epasnactus the Arvernian handed Lucterius over to Caesar. Note the text spells the name here as 'Lacterius' (i.e. Lucterius). Entity-anchored; single named answer.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Bellovacos, qui belli gloria Gallos omnes Belgasque praestabant, finitimasque his civitates duce Correo Bellovaco et Commio Atrebate exercitus comparare atque in unum locum cogere, ut omni multitudine in fines Suessionum, qui Remis erant attributi, facerent impressionem
question: Quibus ducibus Bellovaci finitimaeque civitates contra Romanos arma comparaverunt?
question_en: Under what leaders did the Bellovaci and neighboring states raise arms against the Romans?
answer_en: Under Correus the Bellovacan and Commius the Atrebatian.
derivation: Leaders fact anchored to the Bellovaci; the two named leaders 'duce Correo Bellovaco et Commio Atrebate' supported verbatim. Correus the Bellovacan and Commius the Atrebatian, heads of the Belgic revolt, are entity-anchored; closed-book.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Commius incensum calcaribus equum coniungit equo Quadrati lanceaque infesta magnis viribus medium femur traicit Voluseni.
question: Quem Commius Atrebas lancea per medium femur vulneravit?
question_en: Whom did Commius the Atrebatian wound with a lance through the middle of the thigh?
derivation: Name/event fact anchored to Commius the Atrebatian; 'lanceaque infesta ... medium femur traicit Voluseni' supported verbatim. Commius wounded the cavalry prefect Gaius Volusenus Quadratus in the thigh; entity-anchored, single named answer; closed-book episode of Commius's feud with the Romans.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Cum in Carnutes venisset, quorum in civitate superiore commentario Caesar exposuit initium belli esse ortum, quod praecipue eos propter conscientiam facti timere animadvertebat, quo celerius civitatem timore liberaret, principem sceleris illius et concitatorem belli, Gutruatum, ad supplicium depoposcit.
question: Quem virum Caesar apud Carnutes, ut belli concitatorem, ad supplicium depoposcit?
question_en: Which man did Caesar demand for execution among the Carnutes as the rouser of the war?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Carnutes and Caesar; 'concitatorem belli, Gutruatum, ad supplicium depoposcit' supported verbatim. Gutruatus, the instigator of the Carnutian revolt that began the war, was handed over and put to death; entity-anchored, single named answer.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Scio Caesarem singulorum annorum singulos commentarios confecisse; quod ego non existimavi mihi esse faciendum, propterea quod insequens annus, L. Paulo C. Marcello consulibus, nullas habet magnopere Galliae res gestas.
question: Quibus consulibus fuit insequens annus, quo, ut Hirtius scribit, nullae magnae in Gallia res gestae sunt?
question_en: In whose consulship was the following year, in which, as Hirtius writes, no great deeds were done in Gaul?
derivation: Date/office fact anchored to Hirtius's authorial note; the consuls L. Aemilius Paulus and C. Claudius Marcellus (50 BC) supported verbatim. Also records Hirtius's remark that, unlike Caesar (one commentary per year), he combined the quiet year. Closed-book Roman fasti; named answer.

author: Aulus Hirtius
work: De Bello Gallico, liber VIII (auctore Hirtio)
source_text: Labienus interim in Treveris equestre proelium facit secundum compluribusque Treveris interfectis et Germanis, qui nullis adversus Romanos auxilia denegabant, principes eorum vivos redigit in suam potestatem atque in his Surum Aeduum, qui et virtutis et generis summam nobilitatem habebat solusque ex Aeduis ad id tempus permanserat in armis.
question: Quis solus ex Aeduis ad id tempus in armis permanserat, qui a Labieno captus est?
question_en: Who alone of the Aedui had up to that time remained in arms, and was captured by Labienus?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Aedui and Labienus; 'Surum Aeduum ... solusque ex Aeduis ad id tempus permanserat in armis' supported verbatim. Surus, the last Aeduan still in arms, captured by Labienus among the Treveri; entity-anchored, single named answer.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Hinc itinere facto in campum Mundensem cum esset ventum, castra contra Pompeium constituit.
question: In quo campo Caesar contra Cn. Pompeium castra constituit, ubi postremum magnumque proelium belli Hispaniensis commissum est?
question_en: In which plain did Caesar pitch camp opposite Gnaeus Pompeius, where the last great battle of the Spanish war was fought?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Caesar against Cn. Pompeius (Pompey the Great's elder son). Supported verbatim by 'in campum Mundensem cum esset ventum, castra contra Pompeium constituit'. The campus Mundensis is Munda, site of Caesar's decisive final pitched battle of the civil war (45 BC); closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: In quo proelio ceciderunt milia hominum circiter XXX et siquid amplius, praeterea Labienus, Attius Varus, quibus occisis utrisque funus est factum, itemque equites Romani partim ex urbe, partim ex provincia ad milia III.
question: Quis dux Pompeianus, olim Caesaris in Gallia legatus, in proelio Mundensi una cum Attio Varo cecidit?
question_en: Which Pompeian commander, once Caesar's legate in Gaul, fell in the battle of Munda together with Attius Varus?
derivation: Name fact anchored to T. Labienus and the battle of Munda. Supported verbatim by 'praeterea Labienus, Attius Varus, quibus occisis utrisque funus est factum'. The death of Labienus, Caesar's former chief legate in Gaul who defected to Pompey, at Munda is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: In quo proelio ceciderunt milia hominum circiter XXX et siquid amplius, praeterea Labienus, Attius Varus, quibus occisis utrisque funus est factum, itemque equites Romani partim ex urbe, partim ex provincia ad milia III.
question: Quot fere hominum milia ex adversariis in proelio Mundensi ceciderunt?
question_en: About how many thousands of the enemy fell in the battle of Munda?
derivation: Number fact anchored to the battle of Munda. Supported verbatim by 'ceciderunt milia hominum circiter XXX et siquid amplius'; 'fere' mirrors the source's approximative 'circiter'. The roughly thirty thousand Pompeian dead at Munda are closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Ita ipsis Liberalibus fusi fugatique non superfuissent, nisi in eum locum confugissent, ex quo erant egressi.
question: Quo die festo Cn. Pompei copiae in proelio Mundensi fusae fugataeque sunt?
question_en: On what festival day were Pompeius's forces routed in the battle of Munda?
derivation: Date fact anchored to the battle of Munda. Supported verbatim by 'ipsis Liberalibus fusi fugatique'. Munda was fought on the Liberalia, 17 March 45 BC; the festival dating of the battle is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Aquilas et signa habuit XIII legionum; sed ex quibus aliquid firmamenti se existimabat habere duae fuerunt vernaculae, quae a Trebonio transfugerant
question: Quot legionum aquilas et signa Cn. Pompeius in bello Hispaniensi habuit?
question_en: The eagles and standards of how many legions did Gnaeus Pompeius have in the Spanish war?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Cn. Pompeius's army. Supported verbatim by 'Aquilas et signa habuit XIII legionum'. The thirteen-legion Pompeian army Caesar faced at Munda is closed-book for this campaign; the same thirteen eagles are later reported captured.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Erat idem temporis Sex. Pompeius frater qui cum praesidio Cordubam tenebat, quod eius provinciae caput esse existimabatur
question: Quod oppidum, a Sex. Pompeio cum praesidio tentum, caput Hispaniae ulterioris esse existimabatur?
question_en: Which town, held with a garrison by Sextus Pompeius, was considered the capital of Further Spain?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Sextus Pompeius (Pompey the Great's younger son) and the province. Supported verbatim by 'Cordubam tenebat, quod eius provinciae caput esse existimabatur'. That Corduba was the capital of Hispania Ulterior, garrisoned by Sextus, is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Cn. Pompeius cum equitibus paucis nonnullisque peditibus ad navale praesidium Carteiam contendit, quod oppidum abest ab Corduba milia passuum CLXX.
question: Ad quod oppidum maritimum Cn. Pompeius adulescens post cladem Mundensem cum paucis confugit?
question_en: To which coastal town did Gnaeus Pompeius the younger flee with a few men after the disaster at Munda?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Cn. Pompeius and the aftermath of Munda. Supported verbatim by 'ad navale praesidium Carteiam contendit'. That the defeated elder son of Pompey fled to the naval base of Carteia is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Cn. Pompeius cum equitibus paucis nonnullisque peditibus ad navale praesidium Carteiam contendit, quod oppidum abest ab Corduba milia passuum CLXX.
question: Quot milia passuum oppidum Carteia ab Corduba abesse auctor tradit?
question_en: How many miles does the author record that the town of Carteia is distant from Corduba?
derivation: Distance fact anchored to two named towns, Carteia and Corduba. Supported verbatim by 'abest ab Corduba milia passuum CLXX'; framed with 'auctor tradit' as the author's own datum (CLXX = 170).

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Exclusus a munitione amissisque auxiliis ad convallem exesumque locum in speluncam Pompeius se occultare coepit, ut a nostris non facile inveniretur nisi captivorum indicio. Ita ibi interficitur. Cum Caesar Gadibus fuisset, Hispalim pridie Idus Apriles caput adlatum et populo datum est in conspectum.
question: In quam urbem caput Cn. Pompei adulescentis interfecti adlatum et populo in conspectum datum est?
question_en: Into which city was the head of the slain Gnaeus Pompeius the younger brought and shown to the people?
derivation: Place and name fact anchored to Cn. Pompeius. After Munda he was hunted down, hid in a cave, and was killed; supported verbatim by 'in speluncam Pompeius se occultare coepit ... Ita ibi interficitur. ... Hispalim ... caput adlatum et populo datum est in conspectum'. The killing of Pompey the Great's elder son and the display of his head at Hispalis is closed-book.

author: Cato
source_text: Et virum bonum quom laudabant, ita laudabant: bonum agricolam bonumque colonum; amplissime laudari existimabatur qui ita laudabatur.
question: Quibus verbis maiores, ut Cato scribit, virum bonum amplissime laudabant?
question_en: With what words, as Cato writes, did the ancestors most highly praise a good man?
answer_en: A good farmer and a good husbandman.
derivation: The famous claim of the praefatio: the highest praise for a man was to call him 'bonum agricolam bonumque colonum.' Anchored to Cato + the maiores; the answer is the exact predicate phrase, supported verbatim. Closed-book: one of the most-quoted lines of Cato. Imperfect 'laudabant' kept indicative; 'ut Cato scribit' is a parenthetical author-frame.

author: Cato
source_text: At ex agricolis et viri fortissimi et milites strenuissimi gignuntur, maximeque pius quaestus stabilissimusque consequitur minimeque invidiosus, minimeque male cogitantes sunt qui in eo studio occupati sunt.
question: Ex quibus hominibus et viros fortissimos et milites strenuissimos gigni Cato adfirmat?
question_en: From which men does Cato assert that both the bravest men and the most vigorous soldiers are born?
derivation: Cato's celebrated claim that farmers are the source of the bravest men and most vigorous soldiers. Anchored to Cato + agricolae; single answer 'ex agricolis,' supported verbatim. Closed-book and widely quoted. Indirect statement: passive infinitive 'gigni' with accusative subjects under 'adfirmat.'

author: Cato
source_text: Maiores nostri sic habuerunt et ita in legibus posiverunt: furem dupli condemnari, foeneratorem quadrupli.
question: Quanti, ut Cato refert, maiores in legibus foeneratorem condemnari iusserunt?
question_en: For how much, as Cato reports, did the ancestors order in their laws that a usurer be condemned?
derivation: Preface's comparison: the laws condemned a thief to double, a usurer to quadruple — Cato's point that usury was judged worse than theft. Anchored to Cato + the maiores' laws; genitive-of-penalty answer 'quadrupli' supported verbatim ('foeneratorem quadrupli'). Closed-book datum on Roman attitudes to usury. 'condemnari' passive inf. with acc. subject under 'iusserunt.'

author: Cato
source_text: Praedium quod primum siet, si me rogabis, sic dicam: de omnibus agris optimoque loco iugera agri centum, vinea est prima, vel si vino multo est; secundo loco hortus irriguus; tertio salictum; quarto oletum; quinto pratum; sexto campus frumentarius; septimo silva caedua; octavo arbustum; nono glandaria silva.
question: Quod agri genus Cato inter omnia primo loco numerat?
question_en: Which kind of farmland does Cato rank first among all?
derivation: Cato's well-known ranking of the nine kinds of farmland, with the vineyard (vinea) first. Anchored to Cato; single answer 'vineam,' supported verbatim by 'vinea est prima.' Closed-book: a standard datum in discussions of Roman agronomy. Only the first place is asked (the full list would fail short-answer).

author: Cato
source_text: Quid est agrum bene colere? Bene arare. Quid secundum? Arare. Quid tertium? Stercorare.
question: Quid Cato primum esse dicit in agro bene colendo?
question_en: What does Cato say is the first thing in cultivating a field well?
derivation: Cato's celebrated catechism on good husbandry: first to plow well, second to plow, third to manure ('arare, arare, stercorare'). Anchored to Cato; single answer 'bene arare,' supported verbatim. Closed-book: among the most-quoted lines of Cato. Indirect statement under 'dicit.'

author: Cato
source_text: Brassica est quae omnibus holeribus antistat.
question: Quod holus Cato omnibus holeribus antistare scribit?
question_en: Which vegetable does Cato write surpasses all other vegetables?
derivation: Cato's famous superlative praise of the cabbage as the best of all vegetables, opening his cabbage-chapter. Anchored to Cato; single answer 'brassicam,' supported verbatim. Closed-book: Cato's enthusiasm for cabbage is well-known trivia (discussed e.g. by Pliny). 'antistare' + dative; acc. subject 'brassicam' under 'scribit.'

author: Catullus
source_text: CVI dono lepidum nouum libellum arida modo pumice expolitum? Corneli, tibi: namque tu solebas meas esse aliquid putare nugas iam tum, cum ausus es unus Italorum omne aeuum tribus explicare cartis doctis, Iuppiter, et laboriosis.
question: Cui Catullus lepidum novum libellum suum dedicavit?
question_en: To whom did Catullus dedicate his charming new little book?
derivation: The dedication of the libellus, named in the poem ('Corneli, tibi') — one of the most famous dedications in Latin poetry; the addressee is canonically Cornelius Nepos. Entity-anchored to Catullus + his libellus; single named answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: namque tu solebas meas esse aliquid putare nugas iam tum, cum ausus es unus Italorum omne aeuum tribus explicare cartis doctis, Iuppiter, et laboriosis.
question: Quot cartis Cornelius, cui Catullus libellum dedicavit, omne aevum explicare ausus est?
question_en: In how many volumes did Cornelius, to whom Catullus dedicated his book, dare to unfold all of time?
derivation: Nepos' universal history (the Chronica) in three volumes — 'omne aevum tribus explicare cartis', a celebrated fact of Roman literary history. Number answer, verbatim in the source.

author: Catullus
source_text: PASSER, deliciae meae puellae, quicum ludere, quem in sinu tenere, cui primum digitum dare appetenti et acris solet incitare morsus
question: Quod animal in deliciis habuit puella Catulli?
question_en: What animal did Catullus' girl keep as her darling pet?
derivation: Lesbia's pet sparrow — the most famous pet in Latin literature, and evidence of Roman pet-keeping. Anchored to Catullus' puella (Lesbia); one-word answer stated verbatim ('passer, deliciae meae puellae').

author: Catullus
source_text: TAM gratum est mihi quam ferunt puellae pernici aureolum fuisse malum, quod zonam soluit diu ligatam.
question: Quid zonam Atalantae, puellae pernicis, diu ligatam solvisse ferunt?
question_en: What is said to have loosed the long-tied girdle of Atalanta, the swift girl?
derivation: The golden apple that ended Atalanta's race and virginity — myth as shared story; the text's 'puella pernix' is the canonical Atalanta. 'ferunt' keeps the traditional frame; the apple and girdle are verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: LVGETE, o Veneres Cupidinesque, et quantum est hominum uenustiorum: passer mortuus est meae puellae, passer, deliciae meae puellae, quem plus illa oculis suis amabat.
question: Quos deos Catullus lugere iubet, cum passer puellae suae mortuus est?
question_en: Which gods does Catullus command to mourn when his girl's sparrow has died?
derivation: The mock-dirge for the sparrow opens by summoning the Veneres Cupidinesque — a proverbially famous invocation, parodying Roman mourning. Anchored to Catullus + the dead passer; short named answer, verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: qui nunc it per iter tenebricosum illuc, unde negant redire quemquam. at uobis male sit, malae tenebrae Orci, quae omnia bella deuoratis: tam bellum mihi passerem abstulistis
question: Quo passer Lesbiae mortuus per iter tenebricosum ire dicitur?
answer: Ad tenebras Orci, unde negant redire quemquam.
question_en: Where is Lesbia's dead sparrow said to go along the shadowy road?
answer_en: To the darkness of Orcus, whence they say no one returns.
derivation: The folk-underworld: the dead go down a dark road to Orcus and none return — ambient Roman belief about death, evidenced by the sparrow's journey. Anchored to Lesbia's sparrow; answer verbatim in substance.

author: Catullus
source_text: ubi iste post phaselus antea fuit comata silua; nam Cytorio in iugo loquente saepe sibilum edidit coma. Amastri Pontica et Cytore buxifer, tibi haec fuisse et esse cognitissima ait phaselus
question: In quo iugo phaselus ille Catulli, antequam navis fieret, comata silva stetit?
question_en: On what ridge did Catullus' famous yacht stand as a leafy forest before it became a ship?
answer_en: On the ridge of Cytorus, in Pontus.
derivation: The phaselus' Pontic origin: it grew as timber on Mt. Cytorus near Amastris. Anchored to the phaselus of Catullus; place-name answer stated verbatim ('Cytorio in iugo', 'Amastri Pontica').

author: Catullus
source_text: Amastri Pontica et Cytore buxifer, tibi haec fuisse et esse cognitissima ait phaselus
question: Qua arbore mons Cytorus in Ponto abundat, ut Catullus testatur?
question_en: In what tree does Mount Cytorus in Pontus abound, as Catullus attests?
derivation: Cytorus 'buxifer' — box-bearing Cytorus was proverbial for its boxwood, a standing geographic epithet. Anchored to the named mountain; one-word answer supported by the epithet.

author: Catullus
source_text: sed haec prius fuere: nunc recondita senet quiete seque dedicat tibi, gemelle Castor et gemelle Castoris.
question: Quibus dis phaselus Catulli, cum senuisset, se dedicavit?
question_en: To which gods did Catullus' yacht dedicate itself when it had grown old?
answer_en: To the twins Castor and Pollux.
derivation: The retired ship's votive dedication to the Dioscuri, patron gods of sailors ('gemelle Castor et gemelle Castoris' — the twin of Castor is Pollux). Roman votive custom; anchored to the phaselus; short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: soles occidere et redire possunt: nobis cum semel occidit breuis lux, nox est perpetua una dormienda.
question: Quid nobis, secundum Catullum, dormiendum est, cum semel brevis lux occidit?
question_en: According to Catullus, what must we sleep once our brief light has set?
derivation: Proverb-famous lines from 'Vivamus mea Lesbia': suns can set and return, but for us one perpetual night. Anchored to Catullus' dictum; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: da mi basia mille, deinde centum, dein mille altera, dein secunda centum, deinde usque altera mille, deinde centum.
question: Quot basia primum a Lesbia poscit Catullus, cum eam ad vivendum amandumque vocat?
question_en: How many kisses does Catullus first demand of Lesbia when he calls her to live and love?
derivation: The kiss-arithmetic of c.5 — 'da mi basia mille, deinde centum' — among the most quoted lines in Latin. Anchored to Catullus + Lesbia; number answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: dein, cum milia multa fecerimus, conturbabimus illa, ne sciamus, aut ne quis malus inuidere possit, cum tantum sciat esse basiorum.
question: Quam ob causam Catullus milia basiorum conturbare vult, ne numerus sciatur?
question_en: For what reason does Catullus want to confuse the thousands of kisses, so that the number is not known?
answer_en: So that no ill-wisher can cast the evil eye on them.
derivation: The evil-eye (invidia/fascinatio) superstition: a known count invites malign envy, so the tally must be confused. A stated, checkable motive, not opinion — Roman folk belief at its plainest; answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: quam magnus numerus Libyssae harenae lasarpiciferis iacet Cyrenis oraclum Iouis inter aestuosi et Batti ueteris sacrum sepulcrum; aut quam sidera multa, cum tacet nox, furtiuos hominum uident amores: tam te basia multa basiare uesano satis et super Catullo est
question: Quibus duabus rebus innumerabilibus Catullus multitudinem basiationum Lesbiae comparat?
question_en: To what two countless things does Catullus compare the number of Lesbia's kisses?
answer_en: To the Libyan sand and to the stars.
derivation: The two famous comparanda of c.7: the sands of Libya at Cyrene and the stars of the silent night. Anchored to Catullus + Lesbia; brief two-item answer supported verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: quam magnus numerus Libyssae harenae lasarpiciferis iacet Cyrenis oraclum Iouis inter aestuosi et Batti ueteris sacrum sepulcrum
question: Cuius plantae feraces sunt Cyrenae, quas Catullus 'lasarpiciferas' appellat?
question_en: What plant is Cyrene rich in, which Catullus calls 'silphium-bearing'?
derivation: Cyrene's famous export was silphium (laserpicium) — ambient economic-geographic knowledge, fixed in the epithet 'lasarpiciferis Cyrenis'. Anchored to the named city; one-word answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: quam magnus numerus Libyssae harenae lasarpiciferis iacet Cyrenis oraclum Iouis inter aestuosi et Batti ueteris sacrum sepulcrum
question: Cuius veteris regis sacrum sepulcrum apud Cyrenas iacet, ut Catullus scribit?
question_en: Whose ancient sacred tomb lies at Cyrene, as Catullus writes?
derivation: Battus, founder of Cyrene, whose tomb was a landmark of the city — shared Greco-Roman knowledge, named verbatim ('Batti ueteris sacrum sepulcrum'). Anchored to Cyrene; single-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: 'non' inquam 'mihi tam fuit maligne ut, prouincia quod mala incidisset, non possem octo homines parare rectos.'
question: Quot homines rectos ad lecticam ferendam se in Bithynia paravisse Catullus iactat?
question_en: How many straight-backed men to carry a litter does Catullus boast he acquired in Bithynia?
derivation: The standard team for a grand litter was eight bearers (the octophoros) — daily-life custom evidenced by Catullus' boast. Anchored to Catullus + Bithynia; number answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: 'at certe tamen,' inquiunt 'quod illic natum dicitur esse, comparasti ad lecticam homines.'
question: Quid in provincia Bithynia nasci dicebatur, quod inde advecti homines ad lecticam compararent?
question_en: What was Bithynia said to produce, so that men returning from there acquired them for the litter?
derivation: What a province was 'good for': Bithynia's reputed product was litter-bearers ('quod illic natum dicitur esse... ad lecticam homines'). Ambient provincial stereotype; anchored to Bithynia.

author: Catullus
source_text: hic illa, ut decuit cinaediorem, 'quaeso' inquit 'mihi, mi Catulle, paulum istos commoda: nam uolo ad Serapim deferri.'
question: Ad quem deum se lectica deferri cupivit amica Vari apud Catullum?
question_en: To which god's shrine did Varus' girlfriend want to be carried by litter, in Catullus?
derivation: Visiting the shrine of Serapis by litter — evidence of the Egyptian cult's fashionable presence at Rome. Anchored to Varus' amica in Catullus; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: siue quae septemgeminus colorat aequora Nilus
question: Quo numero ostiorum Nilus apud Catullum 'septemgeminus' vocatur?
question_en: For its how many mouths is the Nile called 'sevenfold' in Catullus?
derivation: The seven mouths of the Nile — a standing fact of ancient geography, fixed in the epithet 'septemgeminus'. Anchored to the Nile; number answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: MARRVCINE Asini, manu sinistra non belle uteris: in ioco atque uino tollis lintea neglegentiorum. hoc salsum esse putas? fugit te, inepte: quamuis sordida res et inuenusta est.
question: Quid Asinius Marrucinus inter iocum atque vinum manu sinistra tollere solebat?
question_en: What did Asinius Marrucinus habitually lift with his left hand amid the jokes and wine?
derivation: Napkin-theft at dinner — guests brought their own lintea, and stealing them was 'sordida res', a breach of table manners. Anchored to the named thief; short answer verbatim ('tollis lintea neglegentiorum').

author: Catullus
source_text: nam sudaria Saetaba ex Hiberis miserunt mihi muneri Fabullus et Veranius: haec amem necesse est ut Veraniolum meum et Fabullum.
question: Ex qua terra sudaria Saetaba Catullo muneri missa sunt?
question_en: From what land were the Saetaban napkins sent to Catullus as a gift?
derivation: Saetabis in Spain was famous for its linen — 'sudaria Saetaba ex Hiberis' fixes the celebrated provenance. Anchored to the named product; place answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam sudaria Saetaba ex Hiberis miserunt mihi muneri Fabullus et Veranius
question: Qui duo amici sudaria Saetaba Catullo ex Hiberis muneri miserunt?
question_en: Which two friends sent Catullus the Saetaban napkins from Spain as a gift?
derivation: The senders of the keepsake napkins ('mnemosynum mei sodalis') — a names-and-relations fact every reader of Catullus carries, stated verbatim. Two-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: CENABIS bene, mi Fabulle, apud me paucis, si tibi di fauent, diebus, si tecum attuleris bonam atque magnam cenam, non sine candida puella et uino et sale et omnibus cachinnis.
question: Qua condicione Fabullus apud Catullum bene cenabit?
question_en: On what condition will Fabullus dine well at Catullus' house?
answer_en: If he brings the dinner with him himself.
derivation: The famous joke-invitation: the guest must supply the whole dinner. The condition is stated verbatim and is the checkable point of the best-known dinner invitation in Latin. Anchored to Fabullus + Catullus. [Answer trimmed to the core condition during validation; the girl-wine-wit list is elaboration in the same sentence.]

author: Catullus
source_text: sed contra accipies meros amores seu quid suauius elegantiusue est: nam unguentum dabo, quod meae puellae donarunt Veneres Cupidinesque
question: Quid Catullus Fabullo, cenam suam adferenti, contra se daturum promittit?
answer: Unguentum, quod puellae suae Veneres Cupidinesque donaverunt.
question_en: What does Catullus promise to give Fabullus in return for bringing his own dinner?
answer_en: A perfume, given to his girl by the Venuses and Cupids.
derivation: Catullus' sole contribution to the dinner: the unguentum — perfume at table was a fixture of Roman dining. Anchored to Fabullus + Catullus; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam tui Catulli plenus sacculus est aranearum.
question: Quo plenus est sacculus Catulli, cum Fabullum ad cenam vocat?
question_en: What is Catullus' purse full of when he invites Fabullus to dinner?
derivation: The purse full of cobwebs — the proverbial image of an empty wallet, quoted ever since. Anchored to Catullus + the invitation to Fabullus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: di magni, horribilem et sacrum libellum! quem tu scilicet ad tuum Catullum misti, continuo ut die periret, Saturnalibus, optimo dierum!
question: Quo festo die Calvus poeta Catullo libellum pessimorum poetarum dono misit?
question_en: On what festival day did the poet Calvus send Catullus a booklet of dreadful poets as a present?
derivation: Gift-exchange at the Saturnalia — Calvus' joke-gift of bad poetry arrives 'Saturnalibus'. Festival custom anchored to Calvus + Catullus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: quem tu scilicet ad tuum Catullum misti, continuo ut die periret, Saturnalibus, optimo dierum!
question: Quem diem Catullus 'optimum dierum' appellat?
question_en: Which day does Catullus call 'the best of days'?
derivation: 'Saturnalibus, optimo dierum' — the classic tag for the Saturnalia as the Roman world's favorite holiday. Anchored to Catullus; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: suus cuique attributus est error; sed non uidemus manticae quod in tergo est.
question: Quid, ut est in proverbio apud Catullum, in tergo nostro positum non videmus?
question_en: According to the proverb in Catullus, what do we not see, though it sits on our own back?
derivation: The fable of the two wallets (our own faults carried behind us, unseen) — a proverb Catullus quotes as common wisdom. Checkable point, one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: puto esse ego illi milia aut decem aut plura perscripta, nec sic ut fit in palimpsesto relata: cartae regiae, noui libri, noui umbilici, lora rubra membranae, derecta plumbo et pumice omnia aequata.
question: In quo, ut fieri solet, poetae versus nondum perpolitos referebant, id quod Suffenus dedignabatur?
question_en: On what, as was usual, did poets set down their unpolished verses — the thing Suffenus disdained?
derivation: Roman book culture: drafts went 'ut fit' onto palimpsest (scraped, reused sheets), while Suffenus wasted royal paper, new bosses, red straps, parchment wrappers, lead ruling and pumice on his drivel. The normal practice is stated verbatim ('ut fit in palimpsesto'). Anchored to Suffenus in Catullus.

author: Catullus
source_text: MINISTER uetuli puer Falerni inger mi calices amariores, ut lex Postumiae iubet magistrae ebrioso acino ebriosioris.
question: Cuius vini calices puer minister apud Catullum ingerere iubetur?
question_en: Cups of what wine is the serving-boy in Catullus ordered to pour?
derivation: Falernian, the most celebrated Roman wine, served old and unmixed ('uetuli Falerni') — named-wine food culture. Anchored to Catullus' drinking poem; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: inger mi calices amariores, ut lex Postumiae iubet magistrae ebrioso acino ebriosioris.
question: Quae magistra bibendi apud Catullum lege sua calices amariores iubet?
question_en: Which mistress of the drinking in Catullus orders stronger cups by her rule?
derivation: The Roman symposiac custom of a magister (here magistra) bibendi whose 'lex' set how the party drank — evidenced by 'lex Postumiae magistrae'. Anchored by name; single-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: paterna prima lancinata sunt bona, secunda praeda Pontica, inde tertia Hibera, quam scit amnis aurifer Tagus
question: Qui amnis Hiberus apud Catullum 'aurifer' appellatur?
question_en: Which Spanish river is called 'gold-bearing' in Catullus?
derivation: The gold-bearing Tagus — a standing fact of ancient geography (gold washed from its sands), fixed in the epithet 'amnis aurifer Tagus'. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: eone nomine, imperator unice, fuisti in ultima occidentis insula, ut ista uestra diffututa mentula ducenties comesset aut trecenties?
question: Quae terra apud Catullum 'ultima occidentis insula' dicitur, in qua imperator unicus fuit?
question_en: What land is called in Catullus 'the farthest island of the West,' where the one and only commander campaigned?
derivation: Britain as the world's western edge — the poem names Britannia just above ('nunc Galliae timetur et Britanniae') and the 'imperator unicus' is Caesar on his British expedition; cf. 'ultimosque Britannos' in c.11. Geographic commonplace of the age.

author: Catullus
source_text: eone nomine urbis opulentissime socer generque, perdidistis omnia?
question: Qui duo viri, socer generque coniuncti, apud Catullum omnia perdidisse dicuntur?
question_en: Which two men, joined as father-in-law and son-in-law, are said in Catullus to have ruined everything?
derivation: The famous tag 'socer generque, perdidistis omnia' — Caesar (whose daughter Julia married Pompey) and Pompey, the canonical socer-gener pair of the age; the identification is the shared historical knowledge the line assumes.

author: Catullus
source_text: PAENE insularum, Sirmio, insularumque ocelle, quascumque in liquentibus stagnis marique uasto fert uterque Neptunus
question: Quam paeninsulam Catullus 'ocellum insularum paeninsularumque' salutat?
question_en: Which peninsula does Catullus greet as 'the eye of all islands and peninsulas'?
derivation: Sirmio, the promontory on Lake Benacus (Garda) where Catullus' home stood — the famous homecoming apostrophe. Named place, one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: quam te libenter quamque laetus inuiso, uix mi ipse credens Thuniam atque Bithunos liquisse campos et uidere te in tuto.
question: Quibus campis relictis Catullus Sirmionem suam laetus revisit?
question_en: Having left what plains did Catullus joyfully revisit his Sirmio?
answer_en: The plains of Thynia and Bithynia.
derivation: Catullus' return home from service on the staff in Bithynia — a fixture of his biography, stated verbatim ('Thuniam atque Bithunos liquisse campos'). Anchored to Catullus + Sirmio; short place answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: tu Lucina dolentibus Iuno dicta puerperis, tu potens Triuia et notho es dicta lumine Luna.
question: Quibus tribus nominibus, praeter Latoniae, Diana in hymno Catulli invocatur?
question_en: By what three names, besides Latonia, is Diana invoked in Catullus' hymn?
derivation: The triple identity of Diana in Roman cult — Lucina of childbirth, Trivia of the crossroads, Luna in the sky — all named verbatim in the hymn. Anchored to Diana + Catullus; short list answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: o Latonia, maximi magna progenies Iouis, quam mater prope Deliam deposiuit oliuam
question: Prope quam arborem Latona Dianam peperisse apud Catullum canitur?
question_en: Near what tree is Latona sung in Catullus to have given birth to Diana?
answer_en: Near the olive tree of Delos.
derivation: The birth of Diana (and Apollo) on Delos beside the sacred tree — canonical myth; the hymn fixes the Delian olive verbatim. Anchored to Latona + Diana; short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: tu potens Triuia et notho es dicta lumine Luna.
question: Quali lumine Luna lucere dicitur in hymno Catulli ad Dianam?
question_en: With what kind of light is Luna said to shine in Catullus' hymn to Diana?
derivation: The ancient commonplace that the moon shines with borrowed, not her own, light ('notho lumine') — shared astronomical-religious knowledge. Anchored to Luna in Catullus' Diana hymn; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam quo tempore legit incohatam Dindymi dominam, ex eo misellae ignes interiorem edunt medullam. ignosco tibi, Sapphica puella musa doctior; est enim uenuste Magna Caecilio incohata Mater.
question: Quod carmen Caecilius, poeta tener et Catulli sodalis, incohaverat?
question_en: What poem had Caecilius, the tender poet and Catullus' companion, begun?
answer_en: The Great Mother, the mistress of Dindymus.
derivation: Literary culture: Caecilius' unfinished poem on Cybele, the Magna Mater ('Dindymi dominam... Magna... incohata Mater'). Anchored to the named poet; short titled answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam quo tempore legit incohatam Dindymi dominam, ex eo misellae ignes interiorem edunt medullam.
question: Cuius montis domina Magna Mater apud Catullum appellatur?
question_en: Of what mountain is the Great Mother called mistress in Catullus?
derivation: Cybele as 'Dindymi domina' — mistress of Mt. Dindymus in Phrygia, her canonical seat (so too 'Dindymenae dominae' in c.63). Cult-geography fact not covered by the Fasti 4 pairs; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: POETAE tenero, meo sodali, uelim Caecilio, papyre, dicas Veronam ueniat, Noui relinquens Comi moenia Lariumque litus.
question: Quibus moenibus quoque litore relictis Caecilius poeta Veronam venire iubetur?
question_en: Leaving what city walls and what shore is the poet Caecilius bidden to come to Verona?
answer_en: The walls of Novum Comum and the shore of Larius (Como).
derivation: Transpadane geography: Novum Comum (Caesar's new foundation) on Lake Larius, and Verona as Catullus' town. Anchored to the named poet and places; short place answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam sanctae Veneri Cupidinique uouit, si sibi restitutus essem desissemque truces uibrare iambos, electissima pessimi poetae scripta tardipedi deo daturam infelicibus ustulanda lignis.
question: Quis deus apud Catullum 'tardipes' vocatur, cui scripta pessimi poetae ustulanda dantur?
question_en: Which god is called 'slow-footed' in Catullus, to whom the worst poet's writings are given to burn?
derivation: The lame fire-god: 'tardipedi deo' is the canonical periphrasis for Vulcan, to whose flames the vowed writings go. The lameness of Vulcan is shared myth; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: nunc o caeruleo creata ponto, quae sanctum Idalium Vriosque apertos quaeque Ancona Cnidumque harundinosam colis quaeque Amathunta quaeque Golgos quaeque Durrachium Hadriae tabernam
question: Quae dea, caeruleo ponto creata, Idalium, Amathunta Golgosque colit apud Catullum?
question_en: Which goddess, born of the blue sea, dwells in Idalium, Amathus, and Golgi according to Catullus?
derivation: Venus' sea-birth and her canonical Cypriot cult seats (Idalium, Amathus, Golgi, plus Cnidus and Ancona) — ambient religious geography. Anchored by the named shrines; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: quaeque Durrachium Hadriae tabernam, acceptum face redditumque uotum, si non illepidum neque inuenustum est.
question: Quae urbs apud Catullum 'Hadriae taberna' nominatur?
question_en: Which city is styled 'the tavern of the Adriatic' in Catullus?
derivation: Dyrrachium, the great crossing-port between Italy and Greece, dubbed the Adriatic's roadhouse — a checkable geographic epithet, verbatim. One-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: tu praeter omnes une de capillatis, cuniculosae Celtiberiae fili, Egnati. opaca quem bonum facit barba et dens Hibera defricatus urina.
question: Quo animali abundat Celtiberia, quam Catullus 'cuniculosam' appellat?
question_en: In what animal does Celtiberia abound, which Catullus calls 'rabbity'?
derivation: Spain's proverbial rabbits: 'cuniculosae Celtiberiae' fixes the land's famous fauna (the cuniculus was the Iberian animal par excellence). Anchored to Celtiberia; one-word answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: nunc Celtiber es: Celtiberia in terra, quod quisque minxit, hoc sibi solet mane dentem atque russam defricare gingiuam, ut quo iste uester expolitior dens est, hoc te amplius bibisse praedicet loti.
question: Quo liquore Celtiberi mane dentes gingivasque defricare solent, ut Catullus tradit?
question_en: With what liquid do the Celtiberians customarily scrub their teeth and gums each morning, as Catullus relates?
derivation: A genuine ethnographic datum (also in Strabo and Diodorus): Celtiberians whitened teeth with urine. Stated as the people's custom ('solet'), anchored to Celtiberia; short answer verbatim in substance.

author: Catullus
source_text: SALAX taberna uosque contubernales, a pilleatis nona fratribus pila
question: Qui fratres gemini apud Catullum 'pilleati' dicuntur?
question_en: Which twin brothers are called 'felt-capped' in Catullus?
derivation: The pilleus (the egg-half felt cap) is the canonical attribute of the Dioscuri; Catullus locates the tavern nine pillars from 'the felt-capped brothers' (their temple in the Forum). Shared iconographic knowledge; two-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: si urbanus esses aut Sabinus aut Tiburs aut pinguis Vmber aut obesus Etruscus aut Lanuuinus ater atque dentatus aut Transpadanus, ut meos quoque attingam, aut quilubet, qui puriter lauit dentes, tamen renidere usque quaque te nollem
question: Quibus popularibus se ipsum adnumerat Catullus, cum gentes Italiae recenset?
question_en: Among which countrymen does Catullus count himself when he lists the peoples of Italy?
derivation: Catullus' own origin: 'Transpadanus, ut meos quoque attingam' — the Veronese poet claims the people beyond the Po as his own. A biographic fact every reader carries; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: paulum quid lubet allocutionis, maestius lacrimis Simonideis.
question: Cuius poetae Graeci lacrimae apud Catullum summae maestitiae exemplum sunt?
question_en: Which Greek poet's tears stand in Catullus as the byword for utmost sadness?
derivation: Simonides of Ceos was proverbial for his laments and dirges; Catullus asks for a consolation 'sadder than Simonidean tears'. Shared literary knowledge; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: ANNALES Volusi, cacata carta, uotum soluite pro mea puella.
question: Cuius poetae Annales Catullus 'cacatam cartam' vocat?
question_en: Which poet's Annals does Catullus call 'crapped-on paper'?
derivation: A celebrated literary verdict (repeated in c.95): Volusius' Annales as waste paper. Anchored to the named poet and work; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: O FVNDE noster seu Sabine seu Tiburs (nam te esse Tiburtem autumant, quibus non est cordi Catullum laedere; at quibus cordi est, quouis Sabinum pignore esse contendunt)
question: Quo nomine fundum Catulli appellabant ii, quibus non erat cordi eum laedere?
question_en: By what name did those who had no wish to wound Catullus call his farm?
derivation: The social geography of villa addresses: fashionable Tibur versus rustic Sabine country — flatterers called the farm Tiburtine, mockers Sabine. The point is stated verbatim; anchored to Catullus' fundus.

author: Catullus
source_text: hic me grauedo frigida et frequens tussis quassauit usque, dum in tuum sinum fugi, et me recuraui otioque et urtica.
question: Quibus duobus remediis Catullus gravedinem et tussim in fundo suo recuravit?
question_en: With what two remedies did Catullus cure his cold and cough at his farm?
derivation: Roman folk medicine: the nettle (urtica) taken as a remedy for cough and chill, plus rest. Anchored to Catullus' illness; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: hoc ut dixit, Amor sinistra ut ante dextra sternuit approbationem.
question: Quo signo Amor amoribus Septimii et Acmes favit, ut Catullus narrat?
question_en: By what sign did Love show favor to the love of Septimius and Acme, as Catullus tells?
answer_en: By a sneeze: he sneezed his approval.
derivation: The sneeze as an omen of divine approval — a widespread ancient belief, here performed by Amor himself ('sternuit approbationem'). Anchored to the named lovers; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: linquantur Phrygii, Catulle, campi Nicaeaeque ager uber aestuosae: ad claras Asiae uolemus urbes.
question: Cuius urbis aestuosae agrum uberem Catullus vere ineunte reliquit, ad claras Asiae urbes volaturus?
question_en: The fertile land of what sweltering city did Catullus leave at the coming of spring, to fly to the famous cities of Asia?
derivation: Nicaea, chief city of Bithynia, with its fertile plain — the departure point of Catullus' spring journey home. Named city; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: DISERTISSIME Romuli nepotum, quot sunt quotque fuere, Marce Tulli, quotque post aliis erunt in annis, gratias tibi maximas Catullus agit
question: Quem oratorem Catullus 'disertissimum Romuli nepotum' salutat?
question_en: Which orator does Catullus hail as 'most eloquent of the descendants of Romulus'?
derivation: Catullus' famous (mock-)homage to Cicero, named in the vocative 'Marce Tulli'. Cicero as the age's paragon of eloquence is shared knowledge; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: HESTERNO, Licini, die otiosi multum lusimus in meis tabellis, ut conuenerat esse delicatos: scribens uersiculos uterque nostrum ludebat numero modo hoc modo illoc, reddens mutua per iocum atque uinum.
question: Quocum Catullus die otioso versiculos in tabellis suis per iocum atque vinum ludens scripsit?
question_en: With whom did Catullus, on a day of leisure, playfully write verses on his tablets amid jokes and wine?
derivation: The famous day of improvising versiculi on wax tablets with Licinius (Calvus, the orator-poet) — neoteric literary culture at play. Anchored by name; short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: caue despuas, ocelle, ne poenas Nemesis reposcat a te. est uehemens dea: laedere hanc caueto.
question: Quae dea vehemens poenas a superbis reposcit, ut Catullus Licinium monet?
question_en: Which vehement goddess exacts penalties from the scornful, as Catullus warns Licinius?
derivation: Nemesis as the punisher of pride and scorn — 'est uehemens dea: laedere hanc caueto' — shared religious knowledge. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: otium et reges prius et beatas perdidit urbes.
question: Quid, ut Catullus scribit, et reges prius et beatas urbes perdidit?
question_en: What, as Catullus writes, has destroyed kings and prosperous cities before now?
derivation: The proverbial close of c.51: otium ruins kings and rich cities. A checkable sententia attached to Catullus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: RISI nescio quem modo e corona, qui, cum mirifice Vatiniana meus crimina Caluos explicasset admirans ait haec manusque tollens, 'di magni, salaputium disertum!'
question: Cuius viri crimina Calvus orator, Catulli sodalis, mirifice in foro explicavit?
question_en: Whose crimes did the orator Calvus, Catullus' companion, marvelously set forth in court?
derivation: Calvus' celebrated prosecution of Vatinius — his 'Vatinian' speeches were classics of Roman oratory ('Vatiniana crimina explicasset'). Anchored by both names; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: in Magni simul ambulatione femellas omnes, amice, prendi, quas uultu uidi tamen sereno.
question: Cuius imperatoris ambulatio Romae erat, in qua Catullus Camerium inter femellas quaesivit?
question_en: Whose promenade was it at Rome, in which Catullus hunted for Camerius among the girls?
derivation: 'Magni ambulatio' — the Porticus of Pompey, Rome's fashionable promenade and pickup spot ('Magnus' = Pompeius Magnus is the shared identification). Leisure topography of the city; short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: NON custos si fingar ille Cretum, non Ladas ego pinnipesue Perseus, non si Pegaseo ferar uolatu, non Rhesi niueae citaeque bigae
question: Cuius regis Thracii bigae niveae citaeque inter exempla celeritatis apud Catullum numerantur?
question_en: Which Thracian king's snow-white, swift chariot team is counted among the exemplars of speed in Catullus?
derivation: The white horses of Rhesus, famed from the Iliad's Doloneia — canonical myth of swiftness ('Rhesi niueae citaeque bigae'). One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: NON custos si fingar ille Cretum, non Ladas ego pinnipesue Perseus, non si Pegaseo ferar uolatu
question: Quis heros apud Catullum 'pinnipes' vocatur?
question_en: Which hero is called 'wing-footed' in Catullus?
derivation: Perseus' winged sandals — his canonical attribute, fixed in the epithet 'pinnipes'. Listed with Ladas, Pegasus, and the guardian of Crete (Talos) as bywords for speed; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: BONONIENSIS Rufa Rufulum fellat, uxor Meneni, saepe quam in sepulcretis uidistis ipso rapere de rogo cenam
question: Unde Rufa Bononiensis in sepulcretis cenam rapere solebat, ut Catullus refert?
question_en: From where in the graveyards did Rufa of Bononia habitually snatch her dinner, as Catullus reports?
derivation: Evidence of the funerary custom of burning a food offering (the cena) on the pyre — so destitute scavengers could steal it. Anchored to the named Rufa; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: NVM te leaena montibus Libystinis aut Scylla latrans infima inguinum parte tam mente dura procreauit ac taetra
question: Qua corporis parte Scylla apud Catullum latrare dicitur?
question_en: From what part of her body is Scylla said to bark in Catullus?
answer_en: From the lowest part of her groin.
derivation: Scylla's canonical monstrous form: a girl ringed with barking dogs at her loins. Shared myth-iconography, stated verbatim; anchored to Scylla by name.

author: Catullus
source_text: COLLIS o Heliconii cultor, Vraniae genus, qui rapis teneram ad uirum uirginem, o Hymenaee Hymen, o Hymen Hymenaee
question: Cuius Musae genus Hymenaeus, collis Heliconii cultor, in epithalamio Catulli appellatur?
question_en: Of which Muse is Hymenaeus, dweller on the Heliconian hill, called the offspring in Catullus' wedding song?
derivation: The wedding god's genealogy: Hymen son of the Muse Urania, dwelling on Helicon — stated verbatim ('Vraniae genus'). Anchored to Hymenaeus; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: cinge tempora floribus suaue olentis amaraci, flammeum cape laetus, huc huc ueni, niueo gerens luteum pede soccum
question: Cuius herbae suave olentis floribus Hymenaeus tempora cingere iubetur apud Catullum?
question_en: With the flowers of what sweet-smelling plant is Hymenaeus told to wreathe his temples in Catullus?
derivation: The wedding god's garland of marjoram — with the flammeum in hand and the yellow slipper on his foot, part of the fixed bridal iconography. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: tollite, o pueri, faces: flammeum uideo uenire. ite concinite in modum 'io Hymen Hymenaee io, io Hymen Hymenaee.'
question: Quo velamine conspecto adventus novae nuptae in deductione cognoscitur, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: By the sight of what veil is the arrival of the new bride recognized in the procession, as Catullus sings?
answer_en: By the flammeum (the flame-colored bridal veil).
