derivation: The flammeum, the bride's flame-yellow veil — the visual signal of her coming, at which the boys raise the torches. Central wedding costume of Roman mores; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: excitusque hilari die, nuptialia concinens uoce carmina tinnula, pelle humum pedibus, manu pineam quate taedam.
question: Ex qua arbore taeda nuptialis, quam Hymenaeus manu quatit, facta erat?
question_en: From what tree was the wedding torch made that Hymenaeus shakes in his hand?
derivation: The pine torch ('pineam taedam') of the wedding procession — the taeda was so identified with marriage that it stood for the rite itself. Anchored to Hymenaeus' torch; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: namque Iunia Manlio, qualis Idalium colens uenit ad Phrygium Venus iudicem, bona cum bona nubet alite uirgo
question: Cui viro Iunia Aurunculeia in epithalamio Catulli nubit?
question_en: To what man is Junia Aurunculeia wedded in Catullus' epithalamium?
derivation: The named couple of c.61: Junia (Aurunculeia, as she is addressed later) marries Manlius, whose hoped-for son is 'Torquatus paruulus'. Anchored by both names; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: namque Iunia Manlio, qualis Idalium colens uenit ad Phrygium Venus iudicem, bona cum bona nubet alite uirgo
question: Quis erat 'Phrygius iudex', ad quem Venus Idalium colens venisse dicitur apud Catullum?
question_en: Who was the 'Phrygian judge' to whom Venus of Idalium is said to have come in Catullus?
derivation: The Judgment of Paris — 'Phrygius iudex' is the canonical periphrasis for Paris judging the goddesses; the bride is as fair as Venus before him. Shared myth; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: ut libentius, audiens se citarier ad suum munus, huc aditum ferat dux bonae Veneris, boni coniugator amoris.
question: Quis deus in nuptiis 'boni coniugator amoris' a Catullo vocatur?
question_en: Which god is called at weddings 'the joiner of good love' by Catullus?
derivation: Hymenaeus as the god without whom no honorable union stands ('nil potest sine te Venus') — the presiding deity of the Roman wedding, invoked with the cry 'io Hymen Hymenaee'. One-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: te suis tremulus parens inuocat, tibi uirgines zonula soluunt sinus, te timens cupida nouos captat aure maritus.
question: Quid virgines nupturae Hymenaeo invocato solvunt, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: What do maidens about to wed loosen when Hymenaeus is invoked, as Catullus sings?
derivation: The loosening of the bridal girdle — 'tibi uirgines zonula soluunt sinus' — a fixed rite of the wedding night. Anchored to Hymenaeus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: ne diu taceat procax Fescennina iocatio, nec nuces pueris neget desertum domini audiens concubinus amorem.
question: Quo nomine iocatio procax, quae in nuptiis Romanis cani solet, apud Catullum vocatur?
question_en: By what name is the ribald joking customarily sung at Roman weddings called in Catullus?
derivation: The fescennina iocatio — the licensed ribaldry of the wedding procession, a named Roman custom ('procax Fescennina iocatio'). Translatable as the name of a rite; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: da nuces pueris, iners concubine! satis diu lusisti nucibus: lubet iam seruire Talasio. concubine, nuces da.
question: Quid concubinus pueris in nuptiis dare iubetur apud Catullum?
question_en: What is the concubinus ordered to give to the boys at the wedding in Catullus?
derivation: The scattering of nuts to the boys at a wedding ('da nuces pueris') — the classic Roman nuptial custom, the sign of putting away boyhood things. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: da nuces pueris, iners concubine! satis diu lusisti nucibus: lubet iam seruire Talasio. concubine, nuces da.
question: Quod numen nuptiale Romanum apud Catullum nominatur, cui post lusum nucum serviendum est?
question_en: What Roman wedding divinity is named in Catullus, whom one must now serve once the play with nuts is over?
derivation: Talasius (Talassio), the native Roman marriage-cry and wedding numen invoked at the deductio — 'lubet iam seruire Talasio' marks the passage into married life. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: sordebant tibi uillicae, concubine, hodie atque heri: nunc tuum cinerarius tondet os.
question: Quis servus os concubini iam adulti tondet, ut in epithalamio Catulli canitur?
question_en: Which slave now shaves the face of the grown concubinus, as is sung in Catullus' wedding poem?
derivation: The cinerarius, the slave who dressed hair with irons heated in ash — a fixture of the Roman household; his shaving the concubinus marks the end of the boy's favor. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: transfer omine cum bono limen aureolos pedes, rasilemque subi forem.
question: Quid nova nupta aureolis pedibus omine cum bono transferre iubetur apud Catullum?
question_en: What is the new bride told to cross with her golden feet under a good omen in Catullus?
answer_en: The threshold of her husband's house.
derivation: The threshold rite of the Roman wedding: the bride must pass the limen 'omine cum bono' (touching it was ill-omened, hence she was lifted or stepped over). Anchored to the nova nupta; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: mitte brachiolum teres, praetextate, puellulae: iam cubile adeat uiri.
question: Quis puer brachiolum puellulae nuptae dimittere iubetur, cum illa cubile viri adit?
question_en: Which boy is told to let go of the little bride's arm as she goes to her husband's bed?
answer_en: The boy in the toga praetexta.
derivation: The deductio detail that a freeborn boy in the toga praetexta escorted the bride on his arm to the marriage chamber. Roman wedding protocol; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: uos bonae senibus uiris cognitae bene feminae, collocate puellulam.
question: Quae feminae puellulam nuptam in cubili viri collocant apud Catullum?
answer: Bonae feminae, senibus viris bene cognitae.
question_en: Which women lay the little bride in her husband's bed in Catullus?
answer_en: Good matrons, well known to their aged husbands (women of one husband).
derivation: The pronubae: only matrons of proven single marriage ('senibus uiris cognitae bene') bedded the bride — a fixed requirement of the rite. Short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: talis illius a bona matre laus genus approbet, qualis unica ab optima matre Telemacho manet fama Penelopeo.
question: A qua matre optima Telemacho unica fama manet, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: From what best of mothers does Telemachus' unmatched good name endure, as Catullus sings?
derivation: Penelope as the canonical chaste mother whose virtue guarantees her son's fame ('Telemacho... Penelopeo'). Shared Homeric knowledge; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: VESPER adest, iuuenes, consurgite: Vesper Olympo exspectata diu uix tandem lumina tollit. surgere iam tempus, iam pinguis linquere mensas, iam ueniet uirgo, iam dicetur hymenaeus.
question: Quo sidere oriente virgo nuptum venit atque hymenaeus dicitur, ut apud Catullum canitur?
question_en: At the rising of what star does the bride come to be married and the wedding hymn get sung, as in Catullus?
answer_en: At the rising of Vesper (the evening star).
derivation: The Roman wedding began at dusk: the rise of Vesper is the signal to leave the tables, for the bride's coming and the hymenaeus. Anchored to the named star; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: namque tuo aduentu uigilat custodia semper, nocte latent fures, quos idem saepe reuertens, Hespere, mutato comprendis nomine Eous
question: Quo nomine Hesperus, cum mane revertitur, mutato nomine appellatur apud Catullum?
question_en: By what changed name is Hesperus called when he returns at morning, according to Catullus?
derivation: The evening star and the morning star are one body under two names — ancient astronomical knowledge stated verbatim ('mutato comprendis nomine Eous'). Anchored to Hesperus; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: at si forte eadem est ulmo coniuncta marito, multi illam agricolae, multi coluere iuuenci
question: Cui arbori 'marito' vitis coniungi solet, ut in carmine nuptiali Catulli canitur?
question_en: To what tree as its 'husband' is the vine customarily wedded, as sung in Catullus' wedding poem?
derivation: The vine trained on the elm — the standard Italian husbandry practice, proverbially the 'marriage' of vine and elm, and the poem's simile for the bride. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: uirginitas non tota tua est, ex parte parentum est, tertia pars patrest, pars est data tertia matri, tertia sola tua est: noli pugnare duobus, qui genero suo iura simul cum dote dederunt.
question: Quota pars virginitatis ipsius puellae est, ut iuvenes in carmine nuptiali Catulli canunt?
answer: Tertia sola; ceterae patris matrisque sunt.
question_en: What share of her maidenhood belongs to the girl herself, as the youths sing in Catullus' wedding song?
answer_en: Only a third; the other thirds are her father's and her mother's.
derivation: The famous arithmetic of c.62: a girl's virginity is one-third her father's, one-third her mother's, one-third her own — the ideology of patria potestas over marriage, with the dowry clinching the parents' rights. Number answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: stimulatus ibi furenti rabie, uagus animis, deuolsit ili acuto sibi pondera silice
question: Quo instrumento Attis, furenti rabie stimulatus, se ipse evirauit apud Catullum?
question_en: With what implement did Attis, goaded by raving frenzy, unman himself in Catullus?
derivation: The flint knife of the self-gelding — the archaic ritual instrument ('acuto silice'), a cult detail of the Galli not among the Fasti 4 pairs. Anchored to Attis; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: niueis citata cepit manibus leue typanum, typanum tuum, Cybebe, tua, mater initia, quatiensque terga tauri teneris caua digitis canere haec suis adorta est tremebunda comitibus.
question: Quod instrumentum proprium initiorum Cybeles Attis manibus cepit et quassavit?
question_en: What instrument, proper to Cybele's initiations, did Attis take up in his hands and shake?
answer_en: The tympanum, the hollow bull's-hide drum.
derivation: The tympanum as Cybele's own instrument ('typanum tuum, Cybebe, tua, mater initia'), made of stretched bull's hide ('terga tauri caua') — the signature sound of the Phrygian cult, complementing (not duplicating) the Fasti Megalensia pairs.

author: Catullus
source_text: ubi cymbalum sonat uox, ubi tympana reboant, tibicen ubi canit Phryx curuo graue calamo, ubi capita Maenades ui iaciunt hederigerae
question: Quali calamo tibicen Phryx in sacris Cybeles gravem cantum canit apud Catullum?
question_en: On what kind of reed does the Phrygian piper play his deep strain in Cybele's rites, according to Catullus?
derivation: The curved Phrygian pipe (the aulos with upturned horn bell) — a real feature of the Magna Mater's music, alongside cymbals and drums. Anchored to the Phrygian piper of Cybele; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: ibi iuncta iuga resoluens Cybele leonibus laeuumque pecoris hostem stimulans ita loquitur.
question: Quod animal Cybele iugo solvit et in Attin fugitivum immisit apud Catullum?
question_en: What animal did Cybele loose from the yoke and send against the runaway Attis in Catullus?
answer_en: A lion, the left-hand one of her team.
derivation: The episode of the loosed lion: Cybele unyokes the left beast of her lion-team to drive Attis back to the forests — a story-fact distinct from the Fasti pair on why lions draw her chariot. Short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: facit impetum. illa demens fugit in nemora fera; ibi semper omne uitae spatium famula fuit.
question: Quamdiu Attis in nemoribus Phrygiis famula Cybeles mansit, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: For how long did Attis remain Cybele's handmaid in the Phrygian forests, as Catullus sings?
answer_en: For the whole span of life.
derivation: The end of the Attis poem: lifelong servitude to the goddess ('semper omne uitae spatium famula fuit'). Anchored to Attis + Cybele; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: ibi Somnus excitam Attin fugiens citus abiit; trepidante eum recepit dea Pasithea sinu.
question: Quae dea Somnum, ab Attide excita fugientem, sinu suo recepit?
question_en: Which goddess received Sleep in her bosom as he fled from the awakened Attis?
derivation: Pasithea, the Grace given to Hypnos/Somnus as his consort (Iliad 14) — the canonical pairing of Sleep and Pasithea, stated verbatim. One-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: mihi ianuae frequentes, mihi limina tepida, mihi floridis corollis redimita domus erat, linquendum ubi esset orto mihi Sole cubiculum.
question: Quo ornatu domus adulescentis dilecti, qualis Attis fuerat, ab amatoribus redimiri solebat?
question_en: With what adornment was the house of an admired youth, such as Attis had been, customarily wreathed by admirers?
derivation: The lover's custom of hanging garlands at the beloved's door — Attis recalls his house 'floridis corollis redimita' when he was the flower of the gymnasium. Greek-Roman courtship mores; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: PELIACO quondam prognatae uertice pinus dicuntur liquidas Neptuni nasse per undas Phasidos ad fluctus et fines Aeetaeos
question: In cuius montis vertice natae sunt pinus, ex quibus navis Argonautarum facta est, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: On the peak of what mountain grew the pines from which the Argonauts' ship was built, as Catullus sings?
derivation: The Argo's timber from Mt. Pelion — the canonical opening fact of the Argonaut story ('Peliaco prognatae uertice pinus'). One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: dicuntur liquidas Neptuni nasse per undas Phasidos ad fluctus et fines Aeetaeos
question: Ad cuius fluminis fluctus Argonautae navigaverunt, fines Aeetis regis petentes?
question_en: To the waters of what river did the Argonauts sail, making for the realm of King Aeetes?
derivation: The Phasis, the river of Colchis in Aeetes' kingdom, the goal of the voyage — mythic geography stated verbatim ('Phasidos ad fluctus et fines Aeetaeos'). One-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: cum lecti iuuenes, Argiuae robora pubis, auratam optantes Colchis auertere pellem ausi sunt uada salsa cita decurrere puppi
question: Quam pellem lecti iuvenes Argivi Colchis avertere ausi sunt, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: What fleece did the chosen Argive youths dare to carry off from the Colchians, as Catullus sings?
derivation: The Golden Fleece as the object of the Argonauts' voyage ('auratam... Colchis auertere pellem') — myth as shared story; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: diua quibus retinens in summis urbibus arces ipsa leui fecit uolitantem flamine currum, pinea coniungens inflexae texta carinae.
question: Quae dea navem Argonautis ipsa fecit, ut Catullus refert?
answer: Minerva, quae arces urbium summas tenet.
question_en: Which goddess herself built the ship for the Argonauts, as Catullus relates?
answer_en: Minerva (Athena), who holds the citadels atop cities.
derivation: Athena as builder of the Argo — the 'diua retinens in summis urbibus arces' is the canonical periphrasis for the citadel-goddess Minerva. Shared myth; the identification is the ambient knowledge the line assumes.

author: Catullus
source_text: illa rudem cursu prima imbuit Amphitriten; quae simul ac rostro uentosum proscidit aequor... emersere freti candenti e gurgite uultus aequoreae monstrum Nereides admirantes.
question: Quae navis prima rudem Amphitriten cursu imbuisse a Catullo canitur?
question_en: What ship is sung by Catullus to have been the first to initiate the untried sea with sailing?
derivation: The Argo as the first ship ever to sail ('rudem cursu prima imbuit Amphitriten' — Amphitrite standing for the sea), at which the astonished Nereids surfaced. The poem leaves the ship unnamed; 'Argo' is the universal identification of the Argonauts' vessel.

author: Catullus
source_text: teque adeo eximie taedis felicibus aucte, Thessaliae columen Peleu, cui Iuppiter ipse, ipse suos diuum genitor concessit amores
question: Quis deus suos ipse amores Peleo concessit, cum is Thetidem duceret?
question_en: Which god himself yielded his own beloved to Peleus when he married Thetis?
derivation: Jupiter's renunciation of Thetis in favor of the mortal Peleus ('cui Iuppiter ipse... concessit amores') — the famous premise of the marriage. Anchored to Peleus + Thetis; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: tene suam Tethys concessit ducere neptem, Oceanusque, mari totum qui amplectitur orbem?
question: Quorum numinum neptis erat Thetis, quam Peleus uxorem duxit?
question_en: Of which divinities was Thetis the granddaughter, whom Peleus took to wife?
derivation: Thetis' genealogy: granddaughter of Tethys and of Oceanus 'who embraces the whole world with sea' — stated verbatim. Two-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: deseritur Cieros, linquunt Pthiotica Tempe Crannonisque domos ac moenia Larisaea, Pharsalum coeunt, Pharsalia tecta frequentant.
question: Quo in oppido Thessaliae nuptiae Pelei et Thetidis celebratae sunt apud Catullum?
question_en: In what town of Thessaly was the wedding of Peleus and Thetis celebrated according to Catullus?
derivation: All Thessaly abandons Cieros, Tempe, Crannon and Larisa to gather at Pharsalus for the royal wedding — the poem's own setting of the feast. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: puluinar uero diuae geniale locatur sedibus in mediis, Indo quod dente politum tincta tegit roseo conchyli purpura fuco.
question: Quo ex dente pulvinar geniale Thetidis politum erat, ut Catullus describit?
question_en: With what tusk was the bridal couch of Thetis polished, as Catullus describes?
derivation: Roman luxury realia: ivory as 'Indian tooth' ('Indo dente politum'), the couch draped in shellfish purple. Anchored to the goddess's marriage couch; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: namque fluentisono prospectans litore Diae, Thesea cedentem celeri cum classe tuetur indomitos in corde gerens Ariadna furores
question: In qua insula Ariadna a Theseo deserta est, ut in veste nuptiali apud Catullum picta erat?
question_en: On what island was Ariadne abandoned by Theseus, as was depicted on the wedding coverlet in Catullus?
derivation: Ariadne watching Theseus' fleet recede from the shore of Dia (the island later identified with Naxos) — the central scene of the coverlet ecphrasis. Anchored to Ariadne + Theseus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam perhibent olim crudeli peste coactam Androgeoneae poenas exsoluere caedis electos iuuenes simul et decus innuptarum Cecropiam solitam esse dapem dare Minotauro.
question: Cuius caedis poenas Cecropia urbs Minotauro dapem dando exsolvebat?
question_en: For whose murder did the city of Cecrops pay the penalty by giving a feast to the Minotaur?
derivation: Athens' tribute to Crete as blood-price for the killing of Androgeos, Minos' son ('Androgeoneae poenas... caedis') — canonical backstory of the Minotaur myth. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: electos iuuenes simul et decus innuptarum Cecropiam solitam esse dapem dare Minotauro.
question: Quam dapem Athenae Minotauro dare solitae erant, ut Catullus refert?
question_en: What feast were the Athenians accustomed to give the Minotaur, as Catullus relates?
answer_en: Chosen young men and the flower of their unwed girls.
derivation: The human tribute of youths and maidens fed to the Minotaur — the shared story ('perhibent') stated verbatim. Anchored to Athens (Cecropia) + the Minotaur; short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: inde pedem sospes multa cum laude reflexit errabunda regens tenui uestigia filo, ne labyrintheis e flexibus egredientem tecti frustraretur inobseruabilis error.
question: Quo auxilio Theseus e labyrintheis flexibus sospes egressus est apud Catullum?
question_en: By what aid did Theseus come safely out of the labyrinth's windings in Catullus?
answer_en: By guiding his steps with a slender thread.
derivation: Ariadne's thread — the guiding filum that defeats the 'inobseruabilis error' of the labyrinth. Canonical myth stated verbatim; anchored to Theseus; short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: certe ego te in medio uersantem turbine leti eripui, et potius germanum amittere creui, quam tibi fallaci supremo in tempore dessem.
question: Quem 'germanum' Ariadna amittere statuit, ut Thesea e turbine leti eriperet?
question_en: Which 'brother' did Ariadne resolve to lose in order to snatch Theseus from the whirlwind of death?
derivation: Ariadne's own words: she chose to lose her germanus — the Minotaur, her half-brother by Pasiphae — rather than fail Theseus. The identification is the canonical genealogy the line assumes.

author: Catullus
source_text: quare facta uirum multantes uindice poena Eumenides, quibus anguino redimita capillo frons exspirantis praeportat pectoris iras, huc huc aduentate
question: Quo capillo frons Eumenidum redimita est, ut Catullus describit?
question_en: With what hair is the brow of the Eumenides wreathed, as Catullus describes?
derivation: The canonical iconography of the Furies: snake-wreathed brows ('anguino redimita capillo frons'), avengers of men's deeds. Anchored to the Eumenides; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: quod tibi si sancti concesserit incola Itoni... annuit, ut tauri respergas sanguine dextram, tum uero facito ut memori tibi condita corde haec uigeant mandata... funestam antennae deponant undique uestem, candidaque intorti sustollant uela rudentes
question: Qualia vela Theseus victor tollere debebat, ut patri Aegeo salutem suam significaret?
question_en: What kind of sails was the victorious Theseus to hoist to signal his safety to his father Aegeus?
derivation: Aegeus' charge: put off the mourning canvas and raise white sails if Theseus lives — the sail-signal he then forgot. Canonical myth stated verbatim ('candidaque... sustollant uela'); anchored to Theseus + Aegeus.

author: Catullus
source_text: at pater, ut summa prospectum ex arce petebat... cum primum infecti conspexit lintea ueli, praecipitem sese scopulorum e uertice iecit, amissum credens immiti Thesea fato.
question: Quid fecit Aegeus, cum lintea infecti veli ex summa arce conspexit?
answer: Praecipitem se e vertice scopulorum iecit.
question_en: What did Aegeus do when he caught sight of the darkened sail from the top of the citadel?
answer_en: He threw himself headlong from the cliff top.
derivation: The death of Aegeus: seeing the dark sail, he leapt from the rocks believing Theseus lost — whence the Aegean's name in the shared story. Stated verbatim; anchored by name; short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: at parte ex alia florens uolitabat Iacchus cum thiaso Satyrorum et Nysigenis Silenis, te quaerens, Ariadna, tuoque incensus amore.
question: Quis deus, thiaso Satyrorum et Silenorum comitatus, Ariadnam desertam amore incensus quaesivit?
question_en: Which god, attended by his troop of Satyrs and Sileni, came seeking the abandoned Ariadne, aflame with love?
derivation: Bacchus' rescue of Ariadne on Dia — the sequel scene of the coverlet ('te quaerens, Ariadna, tuoque incensus amore'). Canonical myth; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: pars obscura cauis celebrabant orgia cistis, orgia quae frustra cupiunt audire profani
question: Quibus in vasis Bacchae orgia obscura celebrabant, quae profanis audire non licet?
question_en: In what vessels did the Bacchants carry their secret rites, which the uninitiated long in vain to hear?
derivation: The cista mystica of Bacchic cult: the covered basket hiding the sacred objects from the profani — real mystery-cult realia stated verbatim. Anchored to the Bacchic thiasos; short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: quorum post abitum princeps e uertice Pelei aduenit Chiron portans siluestria dona: nam quoscumque ferunt campi... hos indistinctis plexos tulit ipse corollis
question: Quis primus e vertice Pelii ad nuptias Pelei advenit, silvestria dona portans?
question_en: Who arrived first from the peak of Pelion at Peleus' wedding, bearing woodland gifts?
derivation: Chiron the centaur of Pelion, first of the wedding guests, bringing garlands of wild flowers — the mountain is his canonical home. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: non sine nutanti platano lentaque sorore flammati Phaethontis et aerea cupressu.
question: Quae arbor 'soror flammati Phaethontis' apud Catullum appellatur?
question_en: What tree is called 'the sister of burnt Phaethon' in Catullus?
derivation: The Heliades, Phaethon's sisters, transformed into poplars as they mourned him — the periphrasis 'lenta soror flammati Phaethontis' assumes this shared metamorphosis. One-word answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: inde pater diuum sancta cum coniuge natisque aduenit caelo, te solum, Phoebe, relinquens unigenamque simul cultricem montibus Idri: Pelea nam tecum pariter soror aspernata est, nec Thetidis taedas uoluit celebrare iugales.
question: Qui dei gemini soli nuptias Pelei et Thetidis celebrare noluerunt, ut Catullus canit?
answer: Phoebus et soror eius unigena, Diana.
question_en: Which twin gods alone refused to attend the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, as Catullus sings?
answer_en: Phoebus and his twin sister, Diana.
derivation: A pointed detail of Catullus' version: Apollo and his sister scorned Peleus and stayed away from the wedding. Anchored to the named wedding; short answer verbatim in substance.

author: Catullus
source_text: cum interea infirmo quatientes corpora motu ueridicos Parcae coeperunt edere cantus... currite ducentes subtegmina, currite, fusi.
question: Quae deae in nuptiis Pelei veridicum carmen cecinerunt, fila fusis ducentes?
question_en: Which goddesses sang the truth-telling song at Peleus' wedding while drawing the threads on their spindles?
derivation: The Parcae spinning as they prophesy — distaff, thread and spindle ('currite ducentes subtegmina, currite, fusi') are their canonical apparatus. Anchored to the wedding of Peleus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nascetur uobis expers terroris Achilles, hostibus haud tergo, sed forti pectore notus, qui persaepe uago uictor certamine cursus flammea praeuertet celeris uestigia ceruae.
question: Quis filius Peleo et Thetidi nasciturus a Parcis canitur?
question_en: What son do the Fates sing will be born to Peleus and Thetis?
derivation: The prophecy of Achilles' birth, fearless and swifter than the deer ('flammea praeuertet celeris uestigia ceruae'). The central genealogical fact of the myth; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: non illi quisquam bello se conferet heros, cum Phrygii Teucro manabunt sanguine Troicaque obsidens longinquo moenia bello, periuri Pelopis uastabit tertius heres.
question: Quis 'periuri Pelopis tertius heres' apud Catullum Troiae moenia longinquo bello vastabit?
question_en: Who is the 'third heir of perjured Pelops' who in Catullus will lay waste the walls of Troy in a long war?
derivation: The genealogical riddle assumes the shared line Pelops - Atreus - Agamemnon: the third heir who besieged Troy. Pelops 'periurus' for his betrayal of Myrtilus. Canonical; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: testis erit magnis uirtutibus unda Scamandri, quae passim rapido diffunditur Hellesponto
question: In quod fretum Scamander amnis diffunditur, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: Into what strait does the river Scamander pour, as Catullus sings?
derivation: Trojan geography: the Scamander empties into the Hellespont — stated verbatim, and choked with corpses by Achilles in the prophecy. One-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: denique testis erit morti quoque reddita praeda, cum teres excelso coaceruatum aggere bustum excipiet niueos perculsae uirginis artus... alta Polyxenia madefient caede sepulcra
question: Cuius virginis caede sepulcrum Achillis madefactum est, ut Parcae apud Catullum cecinerunt?
question_en: By the slaughter of what maiden was the tomb of Achilles drenched, as the Fates sang in Catullus?
derivation: Polyxena sacrificed at Achilles' burial mound ('alta Polyxenia madefient caede sepulcra') — the canonical grim close of the Achilles saga. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: praesentes namque ante domos inuisere castas heroum, et sese mortali ostendere coetu, caelicolae nondum spreta pietate solebant.
question: Quid caelicolae facere solebant aetate heroum, nondum spreta pietate, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: What did the gods customarily do in the age of heroes, before piety was scorned, as Catullus sings?
answer_en: They visited the chaste homes of heroes in person.
derivation: The famous epilogue of c.64: in the pious heroic age the gods showed themselves bodily among mortals — the moral hinge of the poem, stated verbatim. Short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: saepe uagus Liber Parnasi uertice summo Thyiadas effusis euantis crinibus egit, cum Delphi tota certatim ex urbe ruentes acciperent laeti diuum fumantibus aris.
question: In cuius montis vertice Liber Thyiadas euantis crinibus effusis egit, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: On the peak of what mountain did Liber drive the crying Thyiads with streaming hair, as Catullus sings?
derivation: The Bacchic revels of the Thyiads on Parnassus above Delphi, the whole city pouring out to receive the god — canonical cult geography. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: namque mei nuper Lethaeo in gurgite fratris pallidulum manans alluit unda pedem, Troia Rhoeteo quem subter litore tellus ereptum nostris obterit ex oculis.
question: Quo in litore frater Catulli mortuus sepultus iacet?
question_en: On what shore does Catullus' dead brother lie buried?
answer_en: Under the Rhoetean shore, in the Troad.
derivation: The burial place of Catullus' brother — Trojan earth by the Rhoetean promontory — the biographic fact behind cc.65, 68 and 101. Anchored to Catullus' frater; short place answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: qualia sub densis ramorum concinit umbris Daulias, absumpti fata gemens Ityli
question: Cuius absumpti fata Daulias ales sub umbris ramorum gemit apud Catullum?
question_en: Whose destruction does the Daulian bird lament beneath the shady branches in Catullus?
derivation: The nightingale ('Daulias', from Daulis) eternally mourning her slain son Itylus — the shared Greek myth of the mother turned songbird. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: sed tamen in tantis maeroribus, Ortale, mitto haec expressa tibi carmina Battiadae
question: Quis poeta Graecus 'Battiades' apud Catullum vocatur, cuius carmina expressa Ortalo mittuntur?
question_en: Which Greek poet is called 'the Battiad' in Catullus, whose translated verses are sent to Hortalus?
derivation: 'Battiades' — son/descendant of Battus of Cyrene — is the standing name for Callimachus, whose Lock of Berenice Catullus translates as c.66. Shared literary knowledge; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: idem me ille Conon caelesti in limine uidit e Beroniceo uertice caesariem fulgentem clare
question: Quis astronomus comam de vertice Berenices sectam inter sidera vidit, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: Which astronomer saw the lock cut from Berenice's head shining among the stars, as Catullus sings?
derivation: Conon of Samos, the court astronomer who identified the Coma Berenices constellation — the historical fact behind Callimachus' and Catullus' poem. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: atque ibi me cunctis pro dulci coniuge diuis non sine taurino sanguine pollicita es, si reditum tetulisset.
question: Qua condicione Berenice regina comam suam cunctis divis pollicita est?
answer: Si coniunx rex ex bello reditum tulisset.
question_en: On what condition did Queen Berenice promise her lock of hair to all the gods?
answer_en: If her husband the king returned safe from the war.
derivation: Berenice's vow: the lock promised, with bull's blood, for her royal husband's safe return from the Assyrian campaign — the aition of the Coma Berenices. Anchored to Berenice; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: ille quoque euersus mons est, quem maximum in oris progenies Thiae clara superuehitur, cum Medi peperere nouum mare, cumque iuuentus per medium classi barbara nauit Athon.
question: Quem montem Medi perfoderunt, ut classis barbara per medium navigaret, ut apud Catullum legitur?
question_en: What mountain did the Medes cut through so that their barbarian fleet sailed through its middle, as we read in Catullus?
derivation: Xerxes' canal through Mount Athos — 'the Medes made a new sea' — celebrated Persian-War history used as proof that iron conquers even mountains. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: Iuppiter, ut Chalybon omne genus pereat, et qui principio sub terra quaerere uenas institit ac ferri stringere duritiem!
question: Quis populus primus venas sub terra quaerere ferrique duritiem stringere institit, ut Catullus tradit?
question_en: What people first set about seeking veins of metal underground and forging the hardness of iron, as Catullus relates?
derivation: The Chalybes of Pontus as the proverbial inventors of iron-working — shared ancient ethnography, cursed by the lock for the shears that cut it. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: ut Triuiam furtim sub Latmia saxa relegans dulcis amor gyro deuocet aereo
question: Sub quae saxa Trivia, dulci amore devocata, furtim descendere solet apud Catullum?
question_en: Beneath what rocks does Trivia, called down by sweet love, steal away in Catullus?
derivation: The Moon (Trivia/Selene) drawn from her course to Mt. Latmus by love — the Endymion myth, whose sleeping shepherd is the canonical beloved the line assumes. Short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: ne solum in lumine caeli ex Ariadnaeis aurea temporibus fixa corona foret, sed nos quoque fulgeremus deuotae flaui uerticis exuuiae
question: Cuius heroinae corona aurea in lumine caeli fixa fulget, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: Whose golden crown shines fixed in the light of heaven, as Catullus sings?
derivation: The catasterism of Ariadne's crown (the Corona Borealis) — 'ex Ariadnaeis aurea temporibus fixa corona' — the precedent the deified lock cites. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: Virginis et saeui contingens namque Leonis lumina, Callisto iuncta Lycaoniae, uertor in occasum, tardum dux ante Booten, qui uix sero alto mergitur Oceano.
question: Quae sidera coma Berenices in caelo posita contingit, ut ipsa apud Catullum narrat?
answer: Virginis et Leonis lumina, iuncta Callisto, ante Booten.
question_en: What constellations does the Lock of Berenice touch in its place in the sky, as it tells in Catullus?
answer_en: The lights of Virgo and Leo, next to Callisto (the Great Bear), ahead of Bootes.
derivation: The actual celestial position of the Coma Berenices — between Virgo and Leo, by the Bear (Callisto of Lycaon's line), preceding slow-setting Bootes — real astronomy stated verbatim. Short list answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: nunc uos, optato quas iunxit lumine taeda, non prius unanimis corpora coniugibus tradite nudantes reiecta ueste papillas, quam iucunda mihi munera libet onyx, uester onyx, casto colitis quae iura cubili.
question: Quid nuptae castae comae Berenices, sideri novo, ante concubium libare iubentur?
question_en: What are chaste brides bidden to pour in offering to the Lock of Berenice, the new star, before the wedding night?
derivation: The cult the deified lock claims for itself: brides of chaste unions must first offer unguent from the onyx flask — Ptolemaic-Roman bridal rite stated verbatim. Short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: pace tua fari hic liceat, Ramnusia uirgo, namque ego non ullo uera timore tegam
question: Quae dea 'Ramnusia virgo' apud Catullum appellatur?
question_en: Which goddess is called 'the Rhamnusian maiden' in Catullus?
derivation: Nemesis of Rhamnus in Attica, site of her famous cult statue — 'Ramnusia uirgo' (so too in c.68) is her standing periphrasis, invoked before bold speech. One-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: Brixia Cycneae supposita speculae, flauus quam molli praecurrit flumine Mella, Brixia Veronae mater amata meae
question: Quod flumen flavum Brixiam molli cursu praeterfluit apud Catullum?
question_en: What yellow river flows gently past Brixia in Catullus?
derivation: Transpadane geography: the river Mella at Brixia (Brescia), below the 'Cycnean height'. Named city and river; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: Brixia Veronae mater amata meae
question: Quae urbs 'Veronae mater amata' a Catullo appellatur?
question_en: Which city is called by Catullus 'the beloved mother of Verona'?
derivation: Brixia as mother-city of Catullus' Verona — a civic-genealogy fact of the Transpadane towns, stated verbatim. One-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: tempore quo primum uestis mihi tradita pura est, iucundum cum aetas florida uer ageret, multa satis lusi
question: Quae vestis adulescenti Romano, ut Catullo, primum tradebatur, cum aetas florida ver ageret?
question_en: What garment was first handed to a Roman youth, as to Catullus, when his blossoming years kept their spring?
answer_en: The plain white toga — the toga of manhood.
derivation: The coming-of-age rite: receiving the uestis pura (toga uirilis) marked the start of a young man's freedom — Catullus dates his first loves by it. Roman custom; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: Troia (nefas!) commune sepulcrum Asiae Europaeque, Troia uirum et uirtutum omnium acerba cinis
question: Quid Catullus Troiam appellat, quarum terrarum sepulcrum?
question_en: What does Catullus call Troy — the grave of which lands?
answer_en: The common grave of Asia and Europe.
derivation: The famous apostrophe: Troy as 'commune sepulcrum Asiae Europaeque', the bitter ash of all men and virtues — a quotable, checkable dictum. Short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: coniugis ut quondam flagrans aduenit amore Protesilaeam Laodamia domum inceptam frustra, nondum cum sanguine sacro hostia caelestis pacificasset eros.
question: Cuius herois domum Laodamia, flagrans amore, coniunx advenit apud Catullum?
question_en: To which hero's house did Laodamia come as a bride, aflame with love, in Catullus?
derivation: The canonical pair Laodamia and Protesilaus — the bridegroom fated to fall first at Troy, as the Parcae knew. Anchored by both names; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: Protesilaeam Laodamia domum inceptam frustra, nondum cum sanguine sacro hostia caelestis pacificasset eros. nil mihi tam ualde placeat, Ramnusia uirgo, quod temere inuitis suscipiatur eris.
question: Quo omisso domus Protesilai 'incepta frustra' apud Catullum dicitur?
answer: Sanguine sacro hostiae, nondum caelestibus dato.
question_en: For the omission of what is the house of Protesilaus called 'begun in vain' in Catullus?
answer_en: The sacred blood of a victim, not yet offered to the gods.
derivation: The religious rule the story teaches: nothing begun without sacrifice and the gods' consent prospers ('quam ieiuna pium desiderat ara cruorem'). A stated, checkable rite-fact; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam tum Helenae raptu primores Argiuorum coeperat ad sese Troia ciere uiros
question: Cuius feminae raptu Troia primores Argivorum ad sese civit, ut Catullus scribit?
question_en: By the abduction of what woman did Troy begin to summon the chiefs of the Argives against herself, as Catullus writes?
derivation: The rape of Helen as the cause of the Trojan War — the most shared of Greek myth-facts, stated verbatim ('Helenae raptu'). One-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: quale ferunt Grai Pheneum prope Cylleneum siccare emulsa pingue palude solum, quod quondam caesis montis fodisse medullis audit falsiparens Amphitryoniades
question: Quis barathrum, quo palus prope Pheneum Cylleneum siccatur, fodisse dicitur apud Catullum?
question_en: Who is said in Catullus to have dug the chasm that drains the marsh near Pheneus by Mount Cyllene?
answer_en: Hercules, the falsely-fathered son of Amphitryon.
derivation: The Greek local legend ('ferunt Grai') that Heracles cut the katavothra draining the Pheneus plain in Arcadia — 'falsiparens Amphitryoniades' names him by his putative father. Short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: tempore quo certa Stymphalia monstra sagitta perculit imperio deterioris eri, pluribus ut caeli tereretur ianua diuis, Hebe nec longa uirginitate foret.
question: Quae monstra Hercules certa sagitta perculit, imperio deterioris eri, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: What monsters did Hercules strike down with his sure arrow, at the command of a lesser master, as Catullus sings?
answer_en: The Stymphalian ones (the birds of Stymphalus).
derivation: The labor of the Stymphalian birds, shot with arrows at Eurystheus' bidding ('deterioris eri' — the canonical lesser master). Shared myth; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: pluribus ut caeli tereretur ianua diuis, Hebe nec longa uirginitate foret.
question: Quam deam Hercules, in caelum receptus, virginitate solvit atque uxorem duxit?
question_en: Which goddess did Hercules, received into heaven, release from maidenhood and take to wife?
derivation: Hercules' apotheosis and marriage to Hebe — the reward of the labors ('Hebe nec longa uirginitate foret'). Canonical myth; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: quare illud satis est, si nobis is datur unis quem lapide illa dies candidiore notat.
question: Quo lapide dies felicior notari solet, ut apud Catullum legitur?
question_en: With what kind of stone is a luckier day customarily marked, as we read in Catullus?
derivation: The Roman custom of marking lucky days with a white pebble ('lapide... candidiore notat') — a proverbial practice attested across Latin literature. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: hic, uelut in nigro iactatis turbine nautis lenius aspirans aura secunda uenit iam prece Pollucis, iam Castoris implorata
question: Quibus deis precibus imploratis nautis turbine iactatis aura secunda venit, ut Catullus scribit?
question_en: To which gods do sailors tossed in the storm address the prayers that bring the favoring breeze, as Catullus writes?
derivation: The Dioscuri as rescuers of storm-tossed sailors, invoked by name at sea — the practice itself (distinct from the votive dedication in c.4). Two-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: dicit: sed mulier cupido quod dicit amanti, in uento et rapida scribere oportet aqua.
question: Ubi scribi oportet quod mulier cupido amanti dicit, ut est in illo Catulli dicto?
question_en: Where ought one to write what a woman says to her eager lover, according to Catullus' famous saying?
answer_en: On the wind and on running water.
derivation: The proverb of c.70: lovers' promises written on wind and water — quoted ever since as the emblem of unreliable vows. Short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: hoc ne ipsi accideret, patrui perdepsuit ipsam uxorem, et patruum reddidit Arpocratem.
question: Cuius dei nomine Catullus hominem ad silentium redactum significat, cum 'reddidit Arpocratem' dicit?
question_en: By the name of what god does Catullus signify a man reduced to silence when he says he 'made him a Harpocrates'?
derivation: Harpocrates, the Egyptian child-god shown with finger to lips, proverbial for enforced silence — evidence of the cult's currency at Rome (so too in c.102). The point is checkable and translatable.

author: Catullus
source_text: CHOMMODA dicebat, si quando commoda uellet dicere, et insidias Arrius hinsidias... Ionios fluctus, postquam illuc Arrius isset, iam non Ionios esse sed Hionios.
question: Quid Arrius verbis perperam addebat, cum 'chommoda' pro 'commoda' et 'hinsidias' pro 'insidias' diceret?
question_en: What did Arrius wrongly add to his words when he said 'chommoda' for 'commoda' and 'hinsidias' for 'insidias'?
derivation: Misplaced aspiration as a social marker of speech: Arrius' hypercorrect h's turned even the Ionian sea 'Hionian'. The fact — that aspiration betrayed one's class and schooling — is cultural and survives translation; the quoted examples carry the point.

author: Catullus
source_text: ODI et amo. quare id faciam, fortasse requiris. nescio, sed fieri sentio et excrucior.
question: Quid Catullus simul se facere sentit, nescius quare, in celeberrimo suo disticho?
question_en: What does Catullus feel himself doing at once, not knowing why, in his most famous couplet?
derivation: 'Odi et amo' — the most famous distich in Latin, proverbial for the torment of contradictory passion. Anchored to Catullus; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam magus ex matre et gnato gignatur oportet, si uera est Persarum impia religio
question: Ex quo coniugio magus apud Persas gigni oportet, si vera est eorum religio, ut Catullus refert?
question_en: From what union must a magus be born among the Persians, if their religion is true, as Catullus reports?
answer_en: From a mother and her son.
derivation: The Greco-Roman ethnographic claim (also in Xanthus and Strabo) that Persian magi sprang from mother-son unions — 'Persarum impia religio'. Anchored to the Persians and their magi; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: gratus ut accepto ueneretur carmine diuos omentum in flamma pingue liquefaciens.
question: Quid magus Persarum in flamma liquefacit, dum divos carmine veneratur, ut Catullus scribit?
question_en: What does the Persian magus melt in the flame while venerating the gods with chant, as Catullus writes?
derivation: Magian ritual as Romans understood it: the fatty omentum melted in the sacrificial flame while hymns are chanted. Ethnographic rite-fact stated verbatim; short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: NIL nimium studeo, Caesar, tibi uelle placere, nec scire utrum sis albus an ater homo.
question: Quid Catullus de Caesare scire se non curare profitetur?
answer: Utrum albus an ater homo sit.
question_en: What does Catullus profess not to care to know about Caesar?
answer_en: Whether he is a white man or a black one.
derivation: The proverbial idiom 'albus an ater' — not to know whether a man is white or black = to care nothing for him — hurled at Caesar himself. Anchored to Caesar + Catullus; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: ZMYRNA mei Cinnae nonam post denique messem quam coepta est nonamque edita post hiemem, milia cum interea quingenta Hortensius uno
question: Post quot messes et hiemes Zmyrna Cinnae poetae denique edita est?
question_en: After how many harvests and winters was the Zmyrna of the poet Cinna finally published?
answer_en: After the ninth harvest and the ninth winter (nine years).
derivation: The nine-year gestation of Cinna's Zmyrna — the neoteric ideal of slow perfection, set against Hortensius' five hundred thousand verses in one span. Number answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: at Volusi annales Paduam morientur ad ipsam et laxas scombris saepe dabunt tunicas.
question: Quibus piscibus annales Volusi laxas tunicas dabunt, ut Catullus praedicit?
question_en: To what fish will the Annals of Volusius furnish loose wrappers, as Catullus predicts?
derivation: The fate of bad books: waste paper for wrapping fish ('laxas scombris... tunicas') — a judgment that became proverbial (cf. Martial). Anchored to Volusius' Annales; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: Zmyrna cauas Satrachi penitus mittetur ad undas, Zmyrnam cana diu saecula peruoluent.
question: Ad cuius fluminis cavas undas Zmyrna Cinnae penitus mittetur, ut Catullus vaticinatur?
question_en: To the deep waters of what river will Cinna's Zmyrna travel, as Catullus prophesies?
derivation: The Satrachus in Cyprus — the river of the Zmyrna/Adonis story, where the learned poem will be read for grey centuries. Anchored to the named poem; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: PARVA mei mihi sint cordi monimenta ..., at populus tumido gaudeat Antimacho.
question: Quo epitheto Antimachus poeta apud Catullum notatur, quo populus gaudeat?
question_en: With what epithet is the poet Antimachus branded in Catullus, in whom the crowd may take its pleasure?
derivation: The Callimachean verdict on Antimachus of Colophon — 'tumidus', the byword for bloated epic against the small polished poem. Literary-culture judgment; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: certe non tanto mors immatura dolori est Quintiliae, quantum gaudet amore tuo.
question: Cuius feminae mortem immaturam Calvus, Catulli sodalis, luxit?
question_en: The untimely death of what woman did Calvus, Catullus' companion, mourn?
derivation: Quintilia, Calvus' beloved (his elegies on her were famous), consoled by Catullus in c.96. Anchored to Calvus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: MVLTAS per gentes et multa per aequora uectus aduenio has miseras, frater, ad inferias, ut te postremo donarem munere mortis et mutam nequiquam alloquerer cinerem.
question: Quo modo vectus Catullus ad inferias fratris sui pervenit?
answer: Multas per gentes et multa per aequora.
question_en: By what journey did Catullus come to his brother's funeral rites?
answer_en: Borne through many peoples and over many seas.
derivation: The famous opening of c.101: the long journey over lands and seas to the brother's grave in the Troad — the most quoted funerary lines in Latin. Anchored to Catullus + frater; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nunc tamen interea haec, prisco quae more parentum tradita sunt tristi munere ad inferias, accipe fraterno multum manantia fletu
question: Quo more inferiae ad sepulcrum fratris Catulli traditae sunt?
question_en: By what custom were the funeral offerings presented at the grave of Catullus' brother?
answer_en: By the ancient custom of the ancestors.
derivation: The inferiae — the offerings owed to the dead — handed down 'prisco more parentum': Roman funerary religion at its most explicit. Anchored to the rite by name; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: atque in perpetuum, frater, aue atque uale.
question: Quibus verbis Catullus fratrem mortuum in perpetuum salutat?
question_en: With what words does Catullus salute his dead brother forever?
derivation: 'Ave atque vale' — the canonical Roman farewell to the dead, closing c.101 'in perpetuum'; the phrase became the epitome of Latin funerary address. Short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: aduenio has miseras, frater, ad inferias, ut te postremo donarem munere mortis et mutam nequiquam alloquerer cinerem.
question: Quid Catullus ad sepulcrum fratris nequiquam alloquitur?
question_en: What does Catullus address in vain at his brother's tomb?
derivation: The dead as 'muta cinis' — the cremated remains that cannot answer — evidencing Roman cremation and the pathos of address to the ash. Anchored to the brother's grave; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: MENTVLA conatur Pipleium scandere montem: Musae furcillis praecipitem eiciunt.
question: Quibus numinibus sacer est mons Pipleius, quem poetaster apud Catullum scandere frustra conatur?
question_en: To what divinities is the Piplean mount sacred, which the would-be poet in Catullus tries in vain to climb?
derivation: Pipla/Pimpleia in Pieria as the Muses' own mountain — climbing it stands for writing poetry, and the Muses pitchfork the intruder off. Shared literary geography; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: AVFILENA, uiro contentam uiuere solo, nuptarum laus ex laudibus eximiis
question: Quae laus nuptarum ex laudibus eximia est, ut Catullus scribit?
question_en: What is the choicest praise of married women, as Catullus writes?
answer_en: To live content with one husband alone.
derivation: The univira ideal — the one-husband woman as the crown of wifely praise — a central Roman value (cf. epitaphs' 'uni nupta'). Stated verbatim; short answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: CONSVLE Pompeio primum duo, Cinna, solebant Maeciliam: facto consule nunc iterum manserunt duo, sed creuerunt milia in unum singula.
question: Quotiens Pompeius consul factus erat, cum Catullus carmen de Maecilia ad Cinnam scripsit?
question_en: How many times had Pompey been made consul when Catullus wrote his poem about Maecilia to Cinna?
derivation: Dating by consulship: the epigram spans from Pompey's first consulship to 'facto consule nunc iterum' (his second, 55 BC). Pompey's two consulships are the checkable fact; anchored by name.

author: Catullus
source_text: cur non diuitiis Croesum superare potis sit, uno qui in saltu tot bona possideat
question: Quis rex apud Catullum, ut in proverbio, divitiarum summarum exemplum est?
question_en: Which king stands in Catullus, proverbially, as the exemplar of supreme wealth?
derivation: Croesus of Lydia as the byword for riches ('diuitiis Croesum superare') — the shared proverb of wealth. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: Hunc lucum tibi dedico consecroque, Priape, qua domus tua Lampsaci est quaque ... Priape. nam te praecipue in suis urbibus colit ora Hellespontia, ceteris ostriosior oris.
question: In qua urbe Hellespontia domus Priapi esse dicitur apud Catullum?
question_en: In what city on the Hellespont is the home of Priapus said to be, according to Catullus?
derivation: Lampsacus as the canonical cult-home of Priapus, whom the Hellespontine coast worships above all — shared religious geography. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam te praecipue in suis urbibus colit ora Hellespontia, ceteris ostriosior oris.
question: Quae ora, Priapum praecipue colens, ceteris oris ostriosior est, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: What coast, the chief worshipper of Priapus, is richer in oysters than all other shores, as Catullus sings?
derivation: The oyster-beds of the Hellespont ('ostriosior') — a food-geography fact of the ancient table, fixed in the epithet. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Hospes, quod deico paullum est, asta ac pellege.
question: Quo vocabulo celeberrimum Claudiae elogium sepulcrale eum qui praeterit statim compellat?
question_en: With what word of address does the most famous epitaph of Claudia immediately hail the passer-by?
derivation: Opening word of the most famous Roman epitaph, the elogium of Claudia (CLE 52 = CIL 1.1211), anthologized in every Latin reader. 'Hospes' is the classic epigraphic address to the passer-by (so too B 53, 838, 1532). Anchored to the named celebrated text; single verifiable answer (the poem's first word). Criterion 8 holds because the famous poem's content, not an obscure person, carries the fact.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Suom mareitum corde deilexit souo.
question: Quem Claudia, ut eius elogium celeberrimum testatur, corde suo dilexit?
question_en: Whom, as her most famous epitaph attests, did Claudia love with her whole heart?
derivation: Content fact of the celebrated Claudia elogium: she loved her husband with her heart. Anchored to Claudia's famous epitaph; single answer supported verbatim by 'Suom mareitum corde deilexit souo' (archaic spelling of suum maritum ... suo). Ambient knowledge for Latin readers because the poem is a stock anthology piece.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Gnatos duos creauit.
question: Quot filios Claudia, cuius elogium sepulcrale celeberrimum est, peperit?
question_en: How many sons did Claudia, whose funeral elogium is most famous, bear?
derivation: Number fact of the celebrated Claudia elogium: 'Gnatos duos creauit' (gnatos = natos). Anchored to the famous named text; single number answer, supported verbatim. Closed-book for anyone who knows the anthologized poem.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Gnatos duos creauit. Horum alterum in terra linquit, alium sub terra locat.
question: Quot ex duobus filiis suis Claudia moriens in terra superstites reliquit?
question_en: How many of her two sons did the dying Claudia leave surviving on earth?
derivation: The famous antithesis of the Claudia elogium: of her two sons she leaves one on the earth and places the other beneath it, i.e. one son survived her and one predeceased her. Anchored to Claudia's celebrated epitaph; single number answer supported verbatim ('Horum alterum in terra linquit, alium sub terra locat').

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Domum servavit. Lanam fecit.
question: Quae duo officia domestica in celeberrimo Claudiae elogio laudantur?
question_en: Which two domestic duties are praised in the most famous elogium of Claudia?
answer_en: She kept the house and worked wool.
derivation: The most quoted line of Roman funerary epigraphy: 'Domum servavit. Lanam fecit.' — the two canonical virtues of the Roman matrona (housekeeping and wool-working, cf. the lanifica ideal). Anchored to the famous Claudia elogium; the paired answer is stated verbatim. Quintessential criterion-8 material: the matron ideal is shared Roman culture, and this poem is its textbook attestation.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Dixi. Abei.
question: Quo verbo extremo Claudiae elogium hospitem dimittit?
question_en: With what final word does the elogium of Claudia dismiss the passer-by?
answer_en: 'Go' (abi; on the stone in archaic spelling 'abei').
derivation: The famously abrupt close of the Claudia elogium: 'Dixi. Abei.' — 'I have spoken. Go.' The final word is abi in its archaic spelling abei; the answer normalizes the spelling of the same word. Anchored to the celebrated named text; single verifiable answer; the brusque dismissal is one of the poem's most remembered features and survives translation.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: tantum est. hoc voluit nescius ne esses. vale.
question: Qua brevi formula tituli sepulcrales Romani significant nihil iam restare quod legatur?
question_en: With what brief formula do Roman epitaphs signal that nothing more remains to be read?
derivation: The laconic closing formula of Roman epitaphs, attested here on the stone of the praeco Olus Granius: 'tantum est' — that is all — followed by the farewell 'vale'. Convention-level fact of the epigraphic genre (the individual named on the stone is deliberately not asked about); the formula itself is what a reader of Roman inscriptions carries. Supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Mi fili, mater rogat ut me ad te recipias.
question: Quid mater orba in titulis sepulcralibus Romanis filium mortuum rogare solet?
question_en: What does a bereaved mother, in Roman epitaphs, customarily ask of her dead son?
answer_en: That he receive her (to himself, among the dead).
derivation: The touching formula of bereaved parents asking the dead child to 'receive' them when they die: 'mater rogat ut me ad te recipias', attested twice in this collection (B 151 and B 1892 'mater tua rogat te ut se ad te recipias'). A recognized, much-anthologized convention of Roman funerary culture, not the detail of one household; short indirect-command answer with indirect reflexive se referring to the mother.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: vive dum vivis, nec quidquam denegaveris animo indulgere, quem commodavit deus.
question: Qua brevi sententia carmina sepulcralia Romana convivalia monent praesenti vita fruendum esse?
question_en: With what brief maxim do Roman convivial epitaphs advise that one must enjoy life while one has it?
derivation: The proverbial carpe-diem motto of the convivial epitaph, stated verbatim in this banquet poem ('Adeste amici...'). A famous saying whose wording is itself the checkable fact; convention-level, so criterion 8 holds via the shared formula rather than any individual. Translatable as a maxim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Dum vixi, bibi libenter. bibite vos, qui vivitis!
question: Quid tituli sepulcrales convivales Romani eos qui vivunt facere iubent?
question_en: What do the convivial Roman epitaphs bid those who are alive to do?
derivation: The drinking exhortation of the convivial epitaph type: the dead man drank gladly while he lived and bids the living drink ('bibite vos, qui vivitis'), corroborated in this collection by B 190 ('Baccho madentes') and B 1500 ('Es, bibe, lude, veni'). A celebrated genre convention of Roman funerary culture; single short answer supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Quod edi bibi, mecum habeo, quod reliqui, perdidi.
question: Secundum notissimam sententiam sepulcralem 'Quod edi bibi, mecum habeo', quid mortuus perdidit?
question_en: According to the famous epitaph maxim 'What I ate and drank I have with me', what has the dead man lost?
derivation: The celebrated Epicurean tomb maxim (the 'Sardanapalus' sentiment known already to Cicero, Tusc. 5.101): only what one has eaten and drunk remains one's own; what one left behind is lost. The completion of the famous saying is the checkable fact; anchored by quoting its well-known opening; supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Qui legis hunc titulum, mortalem te esse memento.
question: Quid tituli sepulcrales Romani eum qui legit meminisse iubent?
question_en: What do Roman epitaphs bid their reader remember?
derivation: The memento-mori formula of Roman epitaphs, stated verbatim: 'mortalem te esse memento', echoed in this collection by B 83 ('hoc est veniundum tibi') and B 799. One of the most famous conventions of Roman funerary (and triumphal) culture; convention-level anchoring to the genre of tituli sepulcrales; short indirect-statement answer.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Debita libertas iuveni mihi lege negata morte immatura reddita perpetua est.
question: Quid mors, ut in titulis sepulcralibus servorum Romanorum legitur, servis tandem perpetuum dedit?
question_en: What, as one reads in the epitaphs of Roman slaves, did death at last give slaves in perpetuity?
derivation: The distinctively Roman slave-epitaph topos: death confers the freedom life (and law) denied — 'debita libertas ... morte ... reddita perpetua est', corroborated by B 1331 ('nunc mors perpetua libertatem dedit'). Rooted in the Roman institutions of slavery and manumission, so culturally salient at the level of shared custom, not of the anonymous individual; single short answer supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: quisque huic tumulo possuit ardente lucernam, illius cineres aurea terra tegat.
question: Quod munus ardens ad tumulos mortuorum ponere Romani pii solebant?
question_en: What burning offering did dutiful Romans customarily place at the tombs of the dead?
derivation: The custom of placing a lit lamp (lucerna) at the tomb, attested by this epitaph's reciprocal blessing on whoever sets one there ('quisque huic tumulo possuit ardente lucernam'). Grave lamps are a staple of Roman funerary cult and archaeology — ambient cultural knowledge; the stone's obscure Septima is not the subject. Single-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Tu qui carpis iter gressu properante, viator, siste gradum, quaeso. quod peto, parva mora est.
question: Quid tituli sepulcrales Romani a viatore gressu properante primum petere solent?
question_en: What do Roman epitaphs customarily first ask of the hurrying traveler?
derivation: The proverbial 'siste, viator' convention: the tomb by the roadside asks the passer-by to stop (and then read), promising only a small delay. Attested verbatim here ('siste gradum, quaeso') and throughout the collection (B 52 'asta ac pellege', B 53 'rogat ut resistas', B 848). A defining, famous convention of the genre; convention-level anchoring; short answer.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Dic rogo qui transis: sit tibi terra levis.
question: Quae verba fausta viator praeteriens mortuo dicere rogatur in titulis sepulcralibus Romanis?
question_en: What words of good omen is the passing traveler asked to say to the dead in Roman epitaphs?
answer_en: 'Sit tibi terra levis' ('may the earth lie light upon you').
derivation: The most famous of all Roman epitaph formulas, abbreviated S.T.T.L. on countless stones: the passer-by is asked to speak the wish that the earth lie light on the dead. Attested verbatim here and repeatedly in the collection (B 1194, 1269, 1308, 1497). Convention-level cultural knowledge par excellence; single fixed-formula answer.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Evasi effugi. Spes et Fortuna valete, nil mihi vobiscum est, ludificate alios.
question: Quibus deabus notissima formula sepulcralis 'Evasi, effugi' valedicit?
question_en: To which goddesses does the famous epitaph formula 'I have escaped, I have got away' bid farewell?
derivation: The celebrated 'Evasi, effugi' epigram (a Latin rendering of a famous Greek sepulchral couplet): the dead man bids farewell to Hope and Fortune and tells them to make sport of others. Anchored to the named famous formula and to the two named goddesses; two-name answer supported verbatim ('Spes et Fortuna valete').

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: vixit an. XV mensib. III dieb. XI hor. VII.
question: Praeter annos mensesque et dies, quas etiam partes temporis minores tituli sepulcrales Romani in aetate defunctorum nonnumquam enumerant?
question_en: Besides years, months, and days, what still smaller units of time do Roman epitaphs sometimes count in stating the age of the dead?
derivation: The 'vixit annos' age formula and its famous precision: Roman epitaphs count a life down to years, months, days, and even hours, as here ('vixit an. XV mensib. III dieb. XI hor. VII' — 15 years, 3 months, 11 days, 7 hours). A hallmark convention of Roman epigraphy noted in every handbook; convention-level anchoring (the girl Salvidiena herself is not asked about); single short answer supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Dis Manibus sacrum. memoriae aeternae C. Valeri Saturnini, qui vixit annis noviens denis, prope convenientibus annis.
question: Quibus numinibus tituli sepulcrales Romani, litteris D M notati, dedicari solent?
question_en: To which divinities are Roman tombstones, marked with the letters D M, customarily dedicated?
answer_en: To the Di Manes, the spirits of the dead.
derivation: The universal Roman dedication formula D(is) M(anibus): tombs are consecrated to the deified spirits of the dead, the Di Manes. Attested verbatim here ('Dis Manibus sacrum') and in B 439; cf. B 1269 'sacri sunt Manes'. The single most recognizable convention of Roman epigraphy — flagship criterion-8 material; fixed two-word answer.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Lecto merum profunde.
question: Quem liquorem viator ad sepulcrum mortui profundere in titulis Romanis iubetur?
question_en: What drink is the traveler bidden, in Roman epitaphs, to pour out at the tomb of the dead?
derivation: The rite of the wine libation to the dead: this epitaph closes by ordering the reader to pour unmixed wine on the burial couch ('Lecto merum profunde'), and B 838 likewise has the dead ask for a share of the drink ('misce bibe da mi'). Wine offerings at the tomb (as at the Parentalia) are ambient Roman religious custom; single-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Moneo te lectis litteris, ne contemnas et velis titulum movere, et corpori iniuriam facere. Si quis autem sibi admiserit, non bono suo fecerit, et superos et inferos iratos habeat.
question: Quos deos iratos habiturum esse tituli sepulcrales Romani eum minantur qui sepulcrum violaverit?
question_en: Which gods do Roman epitaphs threaten will be angry at anyone who violates the tomb?
answer_en: The gods above and the gods below.
derivation: The tomb-violation curse, a famous fixture of ancient epitaphs: whoever moves the stone or harms the body 'et superos et inferos iratos habeat' — will have both the gods above and the gods below against him; cf. B 838 and B 1532 ('noli ossa mea violare'). Convention-level religious fact of Roman funerary culture; paired answer supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Balnea vina Venus corrumpunt corpora nostra, set vitam faciunt balnea vina Venus.
question: Quae tria, ut celeberrimus titulus sepulcralis Romanus ait, corpora nostra corrumpunt sed vitam faciunt?
question_en: What three things, as a most famous Roman epitaph says, ruin our bodies but make life worth living?
derivation: The proverbial 'balnea vina Venus' epitaph, one of the most quoted of all Roman inscriptions: the three great pleasures of Roman life corrupt the body yet make life itself. Anchored to the celebrated saying; fixed three-item answer supported verbatim; the trio (baths, wine, love) is quintessential shared Roman culture and fully translatable.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Viator, viator! Quod tu es, ego fui; quod nunc sum, et tu eris
question: Quibus verbis pergit notissima formula sepulcralis quae incipit 'Quod tu es, ego fui'?
answer: Quod nunc sum, et tu eris.
question_en: With what words does the famous epitaph formula that begins 'What you are, I was' continue?
answer_en: 'What I am now, you too will be.'
derivation: The most famous memento-mori formula of the sepulchral tradition — 'quod tu es, ego fui; quod nunc sum, et tu eris' — addressed to the viator, with variants in this very collection (B 799 'fuimus quandoque quod estis'; CIL 8.9913 'Quod tu, et ego; quod ego, et omnes'). The completion of the celebrated saying is the checkable fact; supported verbatim; the maxim survives in many languages.

author: Gaius
source_text: Nam quod quisque populus ipse sibi ius constituit, id ipsius proprium est vocaturque ius civile, quasi ius proprium civitatis.
question: Quo nomine Gaius id ius appellat, quod quisque populus ipse sibi constituit?
question_en: By what name does Gaius call the law that each people establishes for itself?
derivation: The famous opening definition of ius civile in Gaius's Institutes: the law a people makes for itself is its own and is called ius civile. Closed-book foundational maxim, anchored to Gaius, single named-term answer present verbatim ('vocaturque ius civile').

author: Gaius
source_text: Quod vero naturalis ratio inter omnes homines constituit, id apud omnes populos peraeque custoditur vocaturque ius gentium, quasi quo iure omnes gentes utuntur.
question: Quo nomine Gaius id ius appellat, quod naturalis ratio inter omnes homines constituit?
question_en: By what name does Gaius call the law that natural reason has established among all men?
derivation: Gaius's paired definition: what natural reason establishes among all men is called ius gentium. Closed-book foundational maxim, anchored to Gaius, single named-term answer verbatim ('vocaturque ius gentium').

author: Gaius
source_text: Constant autem iura populi Romani ex legibus, plebiscitis, senatus consultis, constitutionibus principum, edictis eorum, qui ius edicendi habent, responsis prudentium.
question: Ex quibus rebus iura populi Romani constare Gaius scribit?
answer: Ex legibus, plebiscitis, senatus consultis, constitutionibus principum, edictis eorum qui ius edicendi habent, et responsis prudentium.
question_en: Of what does Gaius say the law of the Roman people consists?
answer_en: Of statutes, plebiscites, decrees of the senate, enactments of the emperors, edicts of those who have the right to issue edicts, and the responses of the jurists.
derivation: Gaius's canonical enumeration of the sources (fontes) of Roman law. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, a closed list of named institutions present verbatim; indirect statement (constare) governed by scribit.

author: Gaius
source_text: unde olim patricii dicebant plebiscitis se non teneri, quia sine auctoritate eorum facta essent; sed postea lex Hortensia lata est, qua cautum est, ut plebiscita universum populum tenerent.
question: Qua lege cautum est ut plebiscita universum populum tenerent, ut Gaius tradit?
question_en: By what law was it provided that plebiscites should bind the whole people, as Gaius reports?
derivation: Gaius records the lex Hortensia, which made plebiscites binding on the entire people (patricians included). Closed-book famous legal-history fact, anchored to the named law, single named-entity answer verbatim ('lex Hortensia lata est, qua cautum est...').

author: Gaius
source_text: Omne autem ius, quo utimur, vel ad personas pertinet vel ad res vel ad actiones.
question: Ad quae tria omne ius quo utimur pertinet, ut Gaius initio Institutionum docet?
answer: Ad personas, ad res, ad actiones.
question_en: To which three things does all the law we use pertain, as Gaius teaches at the opening of the Institutes?
answer_en: To persons, to things, and to actions.
derivation: Gaius's tripartite division of all law into personae, res, actiones, the organizing scheme of the Institutes (and quoted later at Dig. 1.5.1). Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, three-part answer verbatim; indirect statement (pertinere) governed by scribit.

author: Gaius
source_text: Et quidem summa divisio de iure personarum haec est, quod omnes homines aut liberi sunt aut servi.
question: Quae est summa divisio de iure personarum secundum Gaium?
answer: Omnes homines aut liberi sunt aut servi.
question_en: What is the chief division in the law of persons according to Gaius?
answer_en: All men are either free or slaves.
derivation: The most famous single sentence of the law of persons: the summa divisio that all men are either free or slaves. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Gaius + ius personarum, short verifiable answer verbatim.

author: Gaius
source_text: Rursus liberorum hominum alii ingenui sunt, alii libertini. Ingenui sunt, qui liberi nati sunt; libertini, qui ex iusta servitute manumissi sunt.
question: In quae duo genera liberos homines Gaius dividit?
question_en: Into which two classes does Gaius divide free men?
derivation: Gaius's subdivision of free men into ingenui (born free) and libertini (manumitted from lawful slavery). Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, two named-term answer verbatim ('alii ingenui sunt, alii libertini').

author: Gaius
source_text: Rursus libertinorum tria sunt genera: Nam aut cives Romani aut Latini aut dediticiorum numero sunt.
question: Quae tria genera libertinorum Gaius distinguit?
question_en: Which three classes of freedmen does Gaius distinguish?
derivation: Gaius's threefold classification of freedmen: cives Romani, Latini (Iuniani), dediticii. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius + libertini, three named-entity answer verbatim ('aut cives Romani aut Latini aut dediticiorum numero sunt').

author: Gaius
source_text: Nam in cuius persona tria haec concurrunt, ut maior sit annorum triginta, et ex iure Quiritium domini, et iusta ac legitima manumissione liberetur, id est vindicta aut censu aut testamento, is civis Romanus fit.
question: Quibus tribus modis iusta ac legitima manumissio fieri potest secundum Gaium?
question_en: By which three modes can a lawful and formal manumission be effected according to Gaius?
answer_en: By the rod (vindicta), by the census, and by will.
derivation: The classic triad of formal manumission: vindicta, censu, testamento. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius + manumissio, three named-mode answer verbatim ('id est vindicta aut censu aut testamento').

author: Gaius
source_text: Quod autem de aetate servi requiritur, lege Aelia Sentia introductum est. Nam ea lex minores XXX annorum servos non aliter voluit manumissos cives Romanos fieri, quam si vindicta, apud consilium iusta causa manumissionis adprobata, liberati fuerint.
question: Servos cuius aetatis lex Aelia Sentia non aliter manumissos cives Romanos fieri voluit quam vindicta, iusta causa probata, ut Gaius scribit?
question_en: Slaves of what age did the lex Aelia Sentia allow to become Roman citizens on manumission only by vindicta, after a just cause had been approved, as Gaius writes?
derivation: Gaius: under the lex Aelia Sentia slaves under 30 could become cives Romani on manumission only by vindicta with a just cause approved before the council. Closed-book numeric/legal fact, anchored to the named law, number answer verbatim ('minores XXX annorum servos').

author: Gaius
source_text: Item in potestate nostra sunt liberi nostri, quos iustis nuptiis procreavimus. Quod ius proprium civium Romanorum est.
question: Quorum hominum proprium esse patriam in liberos potestatem Gaius adfirmat?
question_en: To which men does Gaius affirm that paternal power over children belongs as their own peculiar right?
derivation: Gaius's hallmark claim that patria potestas over legitimate children is a right peculiar to Roman citizens. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius + patria potestas, single named-entity answer verbatim ('Quod ius proprium civium Romanorum est'); indirect statement (proprium esse) governed by adfirmat.

author: Gaius
source_text: Fratris filiam uxorem ducere licet: Idque primum in usum uenit, cum divus Claudius Agrippinam, fratris sui filiam, uxorem duxisset.
question: Quis primus fratris filiam, scilicet Agrippinam, uxorem duxit, unde id in usum venit, ut Gaius refert?
question_en: Who first married his brother's daughter, namely Agrippina, whence the practice came into use, as Gaius reports?
derivation: Gaius records that marrying a brother's daughter first came into use when the emperor Claudius married Agrippina, his brother's daughter. Closed-book historical fact, anchored to Claudius + Agrippina, single named-entity answer verbatim ('cum divus Claudius Agrippinam, fratris sui filiam, uxorem duxisset').

author: Gaius
source_text: Olim itaque tribus modis in manum conveniebant: usu, farreo, coemptione.
question: Quibus tribus modis mulieres olim in manum conveniebant secundum Gaium?
question_en: By which three modes did women formerly pass into marital subordination (manus) according to Gaius?
answer_en: By usage (usu), by the spelt-cake rite (farreo), and by coemptio.
derivation: Gaius's classic triad of the modes of entering manus: usu, farreo, coemptione. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius + manus, three named-mode answer verbatim ('tribus modis in manum conveniebant: usu, farreo, coemptione').

author: Gaius
source_text: Est autem kapitis diminutio prioris status permutatio: Eaque tribus modis accidit: Nam aut maxima est kapitis diminutio aut minor, quam quidam mediam vocant, aut minima.
question: In quot species capitis diminutionem dividi Gaius tradit?
answer: In tres: maximam, minorem sive mediam, et minimam.
question_en: Into how many kinds does Gaius report that capitis diminutio (loss of legal status) is divided?
answer_en: Into three: the greatest (maxima), the lesser or middle (media), and the least (minima).
derivation: Gaius's threefold division of capitis diminutio into maxima, minor (media), and minima. Closed-book legal-doctrine fact with a determinate count, anchored to Gaius + capitis diminutio, three-part answer verbatim ('tribus modis accidit: ... maxima ... minor, quam quidam mediam vocant ... minima').
