answer_en: It suffered the weapons - it was killed with spears.
derivation: Arena discipline: a lion that mauled its magister was executed with weapons ('qui non tulerat uerbera, tela tulit'). Anchored to the lion-and-trainer episode at Caesar's games; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Praeceps sanguinea dum se rotat ursus harena, inplicitam uisco perdidit ille fugam.
question: Qua re ursus in harena Caesaris captus fugam perdidit, ut narrat Martialis?
question_en: By what means did a bear in Caesar's arena lose its escape, as Martial tells?
derivation: A bear was taken in the arena with birdlime, hunted like a bird ('aucupis arte' in the following lines). Anchored to the bear at the games; short answer supported verbatim by 'inplicitam uisco perdidit... fugam'.

author: Martial
source_text: Inter Caesareae discrimina saeua Dianae fixisset grauidam cum leuis hasta suem, exiluit partus miserae de uulnere matris.
question: Unde partus suis gravidae, hasta in harena transfixae, exiluit apud Martialem?
question_en: From where did the offspring of a pregnant sow, pierced by a spear in the arena, leap out, according to Martial?
derivation: The famous marvel of the venatio: a piglet born through the death-wound of its speared mother. Anchored to the Caesarean hunt (Caesareae Dianae) and the sow; short answer supported verbatim by 'exiluit partus... de uulnere matris'.

author: Martial
source_text: Quis negat esse satum materno funere Bacchum? sic genitum numen credite: nata fera est.
question: Quis deus materno funere satus esse traditur?
question_en: Which god is said in tradition to have been born at his mother's death?
derivation: Bacchus born at the death of his mother Semele - canonical shared myth, cited by Martial as parallel to the sow's piglet. Anchored to the named god; one-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Summa tuae, Meleagre, fuit quae gloria famae, quantast Carpophori portio, fusus aper! Ille et praecipiti uenabula condidit urso, primus in Arctoi qui fuit arce poli, strauit et ignota spectandum mole leonem, herculeas potuit qui decuisse manus, et uolucrem longo porrexit uulnere pardum.
question: Cuius venatoris in harena Caesaris parva tantum portio fuit aper fusus, quae summa Meleagri gloria fuerat?
question_en: For which beast-hunter in Caesar's arena was a slain boar - once the whole glory of Meleager - only a small part of his record?
derivation: Carpophorus, the star bestiarius of the opening games, killed boar, bear, lion and pard, dwarfing Meleager's fame. Anchored to the named hunter and Meleager; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Vexerat Europen fraterna per aequora taurus: at nunc Alciden taurus in astra tulit.
question: Quam virginem taurus per aequora vexisse fama canitur?
question_en: Which maiden is a bull famed to have carried across the seas?
derivation: Jupiter as bull carrying Europa over the sea ('fraterna aequora' - his brother Neptune's realm) - canonical shared myth, quoted as foil for the arena bull. Anchored to Europa and the bull; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: at nunc Alciden taurus in astra tulit. Caesaris atque Iouis confer nunc, fama, iuuencos: par onus ut tulerint, altius iste tulit.
question: Quem heroa taurus in harena Caesaris in astra sustulit, teste Martiale?
question_en: Which hero did a bull lift to the stars in Caesar's arena, according to Martial?
derivation: An arena stunt: a bull hoisted a performer playing Hercules (Alcides) skyward, outdoing Jove's bull that carried Europa. Anchored to Caesar's arena and the named hero; short answer supported verbatim by 'Alciden taurus in astra tulit'.

author: Martial
source_text: Quod pius et supplex elephas te, Caesar, adorat hic modo qui tauro tam metuendus erat, non facit hoc iussus, nulloque docente magistro, crede mihi, nostrum sentit et ille deum.
question: Quae belua in harena Caesarem supplex adoravit, non iussa nulloque docente magistro?
question_en: Which beast knelt in supplication before Caesar in the arena, unbidden and with no trainer teaching it?
derivation: The famous kneeling elephant of the opening games, which Martial insists acted of its own accord. Anchored to Caesar and the arena; one-word answer supported verbatim by 'non facit hoc iussus, nulloque docente magistro'.

author: Martial
source_text: Lambere securi dextram consueta magistri tigris, ab Hyrcano gloria rara iugo, saeua ferum rabido lacerauit dente leonem: res noua, non ullis cognita temporibus.
question: Quae fera, ab Hyrcano iugo adducta, leonem in harena rabido dente laceravit, quod nullis ante temporibus cognitum erat?
question_en: Which beast, brought from the Hyrcanian ridge, mangled a lion in the arena with raging teeth - a thing never known in any age before?
derivation: The tame Hyrcanian tigress that savaged a lion, billed by Martial as unprecedented ('res noua'). Anchored to Hyrcania, the lion, and the arena; one-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Ausa est tale nihil, siluis dum uixit in altis: postquam inter nos est, plus feritatis habet.
question: Ubi tigris Hyrcana plus feritatis habere dicitur apud Martialem, in silvis altis an inter homines?
question_en: Where does Martial say the Hyrcanian tigress has more ferocity - in the deep forests or among men?
derivation: Martial's pointed claim about the lion-mauling tigress: it dared nothing like this in the wild and grew fiercer among men. Anchored to the Hyrcanian tigress episode; short two-way verifiable answer supported verbatim by 'postquam inter nos est, plus feritatis habet'.

author: Martial
source_text: Qui modo per totam flammis stimulatus harenam sustulerat raptas taurus in astra pilas. Occubuit tandem cornuto adore petitus, dum facilem tolli sic elephanta putat.
question: Quam beluam taurus, qui pilas in astra iactaverat, aeque facilem tolli frustra putavit atque occubuit?
question_en: What beast did the bull that had tossed straw dummies to the stars vainly think just as easy to toss - and so fell?
derivation: The bull that hurled the pilae skyward died when it attacked an elephant, thinking it could toss it too. Anchored to the bull-and-elephant bout at the games; one-word answer supported verbatim by 'facilem tolli sic elephanta putat'.

author: Martial
source_text: Cum peteret pars haec Myrinum, pars illa Triumphum, promisit pariter Caesar utraque manu.
question: Quos duos harenae artifices, cum populus partibus diversis posceret, Caesar utraque manu pariter promisit?
question_en: Which two arena performers, demanded by rival sections of the crowd, did Caesar promise together with both hands?
derivation: The crowd split between two named favorites; Caesar granted both, one with each hand. Anchored to the two named performers and Caesar; two-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Quidquid in Orpheo Rhodope spectasse theatro dicitur, exhibuit, Caesar, harena tibi. Repserunt scopuli mirandaque silua cucurrit, quale fuisse nemus creditur Hesperidum. Adfuit inmixtum pecori genus omne ferarum et supra uatem multa pependit auis, ipse sed ingrato iacuit laceratus ab urso.
question: A qua fera Orpheus, fabulam suam in harena Caesaris agens, contra fabulam laceratus iacuit?
question_en: By what beast did Orpheus, playing out his own story in Caesar's arena, lie mangled - contrary to the story?
derivation: The Orpheus pageant - creeping rocks, running woods, beasts and birds charmed - ended with the condemned 'Orpheus' torn by a bear, which Martial notes was contrary to the myth. Anchored to Orpheus and Caesar's arena; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Orphea quod subito tellus emisit hiatu ursam elisuram, uenit ab Eurydice.
question: Quo modo ursa, quae Orphea in harena Caesaris elisura erat, emissa est?
question_en: How was the she-bear sent forth that was to crush Orpheus in Caesar's arena?
answer_en: Through a sudden chasm in the earth.
derivation: Stage machinery of the fatal Orpheus show: the bear rose through a trap - a sudden opening of the ground - which Martial jokes came 'from Eurydice' below. Anchored to Orpheus and the arena; short answer supported verbatim by 'subito tellus emisit hiatu'.

author: Martial
source_text: Namque grauem cornu gemino sic extulit ursum, iactat ut inpositas taurus in astra pilas:
question: Quam feram rhinoceros in harena Caesaris cornu gemino ita extulit ut taurus pilas iactat?
question_en: What beast did the rhinoceros in Caesar's arena lift with its double horn just as a bull tosses straw dummies?
derivation: The rhinoceros (named at the epigram's start, 'rhinocerota') hoisted a heavy bear on its twin horn like a bull tossing pilae - also evidence that Martial's beast was the two-horned rhinoceros. Anchored to the rhinoceros at Caesar's games; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Norica tam certo uenabula dirigit ictu fortis adhuc teneri dextera Carpophori.
question: Cuiatia venabula Carpophorus venator certo ictu direxisse dicitur apud Martialem?
question_en: Hunting-spears of what origin is the hunter Carpophorus said in Martial to have aimed with unerring stroke?
derivation: Carpophorus wields Norican venabula - Noricum's iron and steel being proverbially the best. Anchored to the named hunter; one-word answer supported verbatim. Also attests that Carpophorus was still young ('adhuc teneri').

author: Martial
source_text: ne te decipiat ratibus naualis Enyo et par unda fretis, hic modo terra fuit. Non credis? specta, dum lassant aequora Martem: parua mora est, dices 'Hic modo pontus erat.'
question: Quale spectaculum Caesar in Amphitheatro eo loco edidit ubi modo terra fuerat, teste Martiale?
question_en: What kind of spectacle did Caesar stage in the Amphitheatre on the very spot where just now there had been dry land, according to Martial?
answer_en: A naval battle, with water let in.
derivation: The flooded arena: sea-fights ('naualis Enyo') with real ships where there had just been land, then land again ('Hic modo pontus erat'). Anchored to Caesar's Amphitheatre; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Quod nocturna tibi, Leandre, pepercerit unda desine mirari: Caesaris unda fuit.
question: Cuius unda fuisse dicitur quae Leandro natanti in spectaculis pepercit, ut iocatur Martialis?
question_en: Whose water is it said to have been that spared the swimming Leander at the spectacles, as Martial jokes?
derivation: A performer swam the Leander role in the flooded arena and lived; Martial's point is that the wave spared him because it was Caesar's water. Anchored to Leander and Caesar; one-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Cum peteret dulces audax Leandros amores et fessus tumidis iam premeretur aquis, sic miser instantes adfatus dicitur undas: 'Parcite dum propero, mergite cum redeo.'
question: Quo tempore Leander undas se mergere passurum dixisse fertur - dum ad amores properaret, an cum rediret?
question_en: At what moment did Leander reportedly tell the waves they might drown him - while hurrying to his love, or on his way back?
derivation: The famous Leander mot: spare me as I hasten there, drown me when I return. Anchored to the named Leander; short two-way verifiable answer supported verbatim by 'Parcite dum propero, mergite cum redeo'.

author: Martial
source_text: Lusit Nereidum docilis chorus aequore toto et uario faciles ordine pinxit aquas. Fuscina dente minax recto fuit, ancora curuo: credidimus remum credidimusque ratem,
question: Quis chorus in aquis spectaculorum Caesaris lusit et figuras - fuscinam, ancoram, remum, ratem - in aequore pinxit?
question_en: What chorus performed in the waters of Caesar's spectacles and traced figures - a trident, an anchor, an oar, a ship - on the surface?
answer_en: A trained chorus of Nereids (synchronized swimmers).
derivation: The aquatic ballet of the flooded arena: swimmers as Nereids forming pictures on the water. Anchored to Caesar's water shows and the named figures; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: et gratum nautis sidus fulgere Laconum lataque perspicuo uela tumere sinu.
question: Quorum sidus nautis gratum esse Martialis dicit?
question_en: Whose constellation does Martial call welcome to sailors?
answer_en: That of the Laconians (the Spartan twins Castor and Pollux).
derivation: The 'star of the Laconians' - the Dioscuri, patrons of sailors - among the shapes the Nereids traced. The twins' star as the sailors' friend is ambient Roman religious-mythological knowledge; anchored by 'sidus Laconum', short answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Herculeae laudis numeretur gloria: plus est bis denas pariter perdomuisse feras.
question: Quot feras Carpophorus in harena Caesaris pariter perdomuisse dicitur apud Martialem?
question_en: How many beasts is Carpophorus said in Martial to have subdued at once in Caesar's arena?
derivation: The count that caps the Carpophorus panegyric (the epigram opens 'Saecula Carpophorum, Caesar, si prisca tulissent'): twenty beasts mastered together, more than Hercules' glory. Anchored to Carpophorus; number answer supported verbatim by 'bis denas pariter perdomuisse feras'.

author: Martial
source_text: Saecula Carpophorum, Caesar, si prisca tulissent, non Porthaoniam barbara terra feram, non Marathon taurum, Nemee frondosa leonem, Arcas Maenalium non timuisset aprum.
question: Quae terra taurum fabulosum timuisse dicitur apud Martialem, sicut Nemee frondosa leonem?
question_en: What land is said in Martial to have feared a fabled bull, just as leafy Nemea feared the lion?
derivation: The canonical myth-place pairing of the bull of Marathon, listed beside Nemea's lion and Arcadia's Maenalian boar as terrors Carpophorus would have spared the old world. Anchored to Marathon and Nemea; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Si uetus aequorei reuocetur fabula monstri, Hesionen soluet solus et Andromedan.
question: Quae duae virgines in fabulis monstris aequoreis expositae erant, quas solus Carpophorus solvere posset, ut ait Martialis?
question_en: Which two maidens were in the myths exposed to sea monsters, whom Carpophorus alone could set free, as Martial says?
derivation: The two canonical maidens of the sea-monster myths (freed by Hercules and Perseus respectively), invoked as the measure of Carpophorus. Anchored to both named heroines; two-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Igniferos possit sine Colchide iungere tauros, possit utramque feram uincere Pasiphaes.
question: Sine cuius feminae auxilio Carpophorus igniferos tauros iungere posset, ut canit Martialis?
question_en: Without which woman's help could Carpophorus have yoked the fire-breathing bulls, as Martial sings?
answer_en: Without the Colchian - that is, Medea.
derivation: In the shared myth the fire-breathing bulls were yoked only with the Colchian Medea's help; Martial says Carpophorus would not have needed her. Anchored to the fiery bulls and 'Colchis'; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Augusti labor hic fuerat committere classes et freta nauali sollicitare tuba. Caesaris haec nostri pars est quota?
question: Cuius principis labor antea fuerat classes committere et freta navali tuba sollicitare, ut Martialis memorat?
question_en: Which emperor's achievement had it previously been to set fleets in battle and rouse the waters with the naval trumpet, as Martial recalls?
derivation: Augustus' famous naumachia, named as the older benchmark that Caesar's water spectacle dwarfs. Anchored to Augustus and the naumachia; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Fucinus et diri taceantur stagna Neronis: hanc norint unam saecula naumachiam.
question: Quae duo priorum principum naumachiarum loca taceri iubet Martialis prae naumachia Caesaris?
question_en: Which two sites of earlier emperors' naval shows does Martial bid be silent before Caesar's naumachia?
answer_en: The Fucine lake and Nero's pools.
derivation: The two named predecessors - the Fucinus (Claudius' lake naumachia) and the pools of 'dread Nero' - dismissed so that the ages may know this one naumachia. Anchored to both named sites; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Quidquid et in Circo spectatur et Amphitheatro, id diues, Caesar, praestitit unda tibi.
question: Quorum duorum locorum spectacula unda naumachiae Caesaris pariter praestitit, teste Martiale?
question_en: The spectacles of which two venues did the water of Caesar's naumachia alike supply, according to Martial?
answer_en: Of the Circus and the Amphitheatre.
derivation: The water show reproduced everything seen in the Circus (even chariots on the waves, per the preceding lines) and in the Amphitheatre. Anchored to the two named venues and Caesar; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Cum traheret Priscus, traheret certamina Verus, esset et aequalis Mars utriusque diu, missio saepe uiris magno clamore petita est; sed Caesar legi paruit ipse suae; - lex erat, ad digitum posita concurrere parma: - quod licuit, lances donaque saepe dedit. Inuentus tamen est finis discriminis aequi: pugnauere pares, subcubuere pares. Misit utrique rudes et palmas Caesar utrique: hoc pretium uirtus ingeniosa tulit. Contigit hoc nullo nisi te sub principe, Caesar: cum duo pugnarent, uictor uterque fuit.
question: Qui duo gladiatores in muneribus Caesaris tam diu pari Marte pugnaverunt ut uterque victor discederet?
question_en: Which two gladiators fought so long on equal terms at Caesar's games that both walked away victors?
derivation: The most famous fact of the book: the drawn duel of Priscus and Verus, ended by Caesar declaring both victorious - 'cum duo pugnarent, uictor uterque fuit'. Anchored to the two named gladiators and Caesar; two-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Misit utrique rudes et palmas Caesar utrique: hoc pretium uirtus ingeniosa tulit.
question: Quae praemia Caesar et Prisco et Vero, pari Marte pugnantibus, utrique misit?
question_en: What prizes did Caesar send to both Priscus and Verus, who had fought on equal terms?
answer_en: The wooden swords of discharge (rudes) and the palms of victory.
derivation: Both gladiators received the rudis - the wooden sword marking discharge from the arena - and the victor's palm. Anchored to Priscus, Verus, and Caesar; brief noun-phrase answer supported verbatim. Core gladiatorial custom (rudis = discharge, palma = victory).

author: Martial
source_text: sed Caesar legi paruit ipse suae; - lex erat, ad digitum posita concurrere parma: - quod licuit, lances donaque saepe dedit.
question: Quae lex pugnae in munere Caesaris posita erat, cui Caesar ipse paruit, ut refert Martialis?
question_en: What rule of combat was laid down at Caesar's games, which Caesar himself obeyed, as Martial reports?
answer_en: To fight on, the shield set aside, until a finger was raised (the signal of surrender).
derivation: The stated lex of the Priscus-Verus bout: the fight ran 'ad digitum' - until the raised finger of submission - and even the emperor bound himself to his own rule. Gladiatorial convention, culturally salient; anchored to Caesar's munus; brief answer quoted from the source.

author: Martial
source_text: Concita ueloces fugeret cum damma Molossos et uaria lentas necteret arte moras, Caesaris ante pedes supplex similisque roganti constitit, et praedam non tetigere canes.
question: Ante cuius pedes damma, veloces Molossos fugiens, supplex constitit, ita ut canes praedam non tangerent?
question_en: Before whose feet did the hind, fleeing the swift Molossian hounds, halt as a suppliant, so that the dogs did not touch their prey?
derivation: The suppliant hind of the venatio: chased by Molossian hounds, it stopped as if begging before the emperor, and the dogs spared it - Martial's proof of Caesar's numen. Anchored to Caesar and the named Molossian breed; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Flauia gens, quantum tibi tertius abstulit heres! paene fuit tanti, non habuisse duos.
question: Quotus heres genti Flaviae tantum abstulisse dicitur ut paene tanti fuerit duos priores non habuisse?
question_en: Which heir in order is said to have taken so much from the Flavian house that it would almost have been worth not having the former two?
derivation: The bitter closing couplet on the gens Flavia: its third heir (Domitian, after Vespasian and Titus) disgraced it. Anchored to the named Flavian house; ordinal answer supported verbatim by 'tertius abstulit heres'.

author: Martial
source_text: Ne toga cordylis et paenula desit olivis aut inopem metuat sordida blatta famem, perdite Niliacas, Musae, mea damna, papyros: postulat ecce novos ebria bruma sales.
question: Quibus rebus involvendis chartae poetarum inutiles servire solent, ut iocatur Martialis in Xeniis?
question_en: For wrapping what things do poets' useless papers usually serve, as Martial jokes in the Xenia?
derivation: The stock Roman joke that bad poetry ends as wrapping paper in the food market (cf. Catullus 95, Persius 1.43): Martial opens the Xenia offering his papyri as a 'toga for tunny, a cloak for olives.' Anchored to Martial's Xenia; two-noun answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Omnis in hoc gracili XENIORVM turba libello constabit nummis quattuor empta tibi.
question: Quot nummis totus Xeniorum libellus emi potest, ut ipse Martialis testatur?
question_en: For how many coins can the whole little book of the Xenia be bought, as Martial himself attests?
derivation: The book states its own retail price — famous evidence for the Roman book trade. Anchored to the Xenia by name; single-number answer supported verbatim (constabit nummis quattuor).

author: Martial
source_text: Quattuor est nimium? Poterit constare duobus, et faciat lucrum bybliopola Tryphon.
question: Quis bybliopola Xenia Martialis Romae vendebat?
question_en: Which bookseller sold Martial's Xenia at Rome?
derivation: Tryphon, the named bookseller-publisher of the Xenia (the same Tryphon appears in Quintilian's preface) — a real figure of the Roman book trade. Single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Haec licet hospitibus pro munere disticha mittas, si tibi tam rarus quam mihi nummus erit.
question: Quibus disticha Xeniorum pro munere mitti posse Martialis ait?
question_en: To whom does Martial say the couplets of the Xenia may be sent in place of a gift?
derivation: The gift-frame of the whole book: each distich can stand in for the Saturnalian food-gift (xenium) itself when money is short. Anchored to the Xenia; one-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Cerea quae patulo lucet ficedula lumbo, cum tibi sorte datur, si sapis, adde piper.
question: Quod condimentum ficedulae addere iubet Martialis in Xeniis?
question_en: What seasoning does Martial in the Xenia bid one add to the fig-pecker?
derivation: The ficedula (beccafico) was a prized table delicacy, and pepper its canonical seasoning ('si sapis, adde piper'). Anchored to Martial + the named bird; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Accipe Niliacam, Pelusia munera, lentem: vilior est alica, carior illa faba.
question: Ex qua terra lentem Romam mitti dicit Martialis?
question_en: From what land does Martial say the lentil is sent to Rome?
derivation: Egypt (Pelusium at the Nile mouth) as the proverbial source of lentils — 'Niliacam, Pelusia munera, lentem.' Ambient trade-geography of the Roman table; place answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Cludere quae cenas lactuca solebat avorum, dic mihi, cur nostras inchoat illa dapes?
question: Quo loco cenae apud avos Romanorum lactuca apponi solebat, ut Martialis testatur?
question_en: At what point of the dinner was lettuce customarily served in the time of the Romans' ancestors, as Martial attests?
answer_en: At the end — it closed the dinner.
derivation: A famous fact of Roman food history: lettuce moved from closing the ancestors' dinner to opening the meal in Martial's day (the same shift noted by Pliny). Anchored to lettuce + the ancestral custom; short answer supported verbatim (cludere cenas solebat).

author: Martial
source_text: Haec tibi brumali gaudentia frigore rapa quae damus, in caelo Romulus esse solet.
question: Quis in caelo rapis vesci solet, ut iocatur Martialis in Xeniis?
question_en: Who is wont to eat turnips even in heaven, as Martial jokes in the Xenia?
derivation: The deified Romulus keeps his old-Roman frugal diet of turnips — a shared joke about archaic Roman simplicity (turnips as the archetypal early-Roman food). Named-entity answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Ne tibi pallentes moveant fastidia caules, nitrata viridis brassica fiat aqua.
question: Qua aqua brassica coquenda est, ut viridis maneat, teste Martiale?
question_en: In what water should cabbage be cooked so that it stays green, on Martial's testimony?
derivation: Insider kitchen technique: nitrum (soda) in the cooking water keeps greens green — the same trick prescribed by Apicius. Anchored to cabbage + Martial; brief-phrase answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Mittit praecipuos nemoralis Aricia porros: in niveo virides stipite cerne comas.
question: Quod oppidum praecipuos porros capitatos mittit apud Martialem?
question_en: Which town sends the choicest headed leeks, according to Martial?
derivation: Aricia (nemoralis, by Diana's grove) as the famed source of leeks — also praised by Columella. Named-place answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Inbue plebeias Clusinis pultibus ollas, ut satur in vacuis dulcia musta bibas.
question: Cuius oppidi pultes ollas plebeias implent apud Martialem?
question_en: Porridge from which town fills the plebeian pots, in Martial?
derivation: Clusium in Etruria as the proverbial home of far-porridge (puls), the archetypal plebeian staple. Named-place answer supported verbatim (Clusinis pultibus).

author: Martial
source_text: Vt sapiant fatuae, fabrorum prandia, betae, o quam saepe petet vina piperque cocus!
question: Quibus condimentis betae fatuae saporem accipiunt, ut ait Martialis?
question_en: With what seasonings do insipid beets get their flavor, as Martial says?
derivation: Beets — 'fabrorum prandia', the workmen's lunch — were proverbially bland (fatuae) and needed wine and pepper from the cook. Two-item answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Fila Tarentini graviter redolentia porri edisti quotiens, oscula clusa dato.
question: Quid faciendum est ei qui fila porri Tarentini ederit, ut monet Martialis?
question_en: What must one do after eating the strands of Tarentine leek, as Martial warns?
derivation: Cut leeks (porrum sectivum) came from Tarentum and notoriously fouled the breath; the joke-advice 'oscula clusa dato' is the epigram's checkable point. Anchored to the Tarentine leek; short answer verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Hos Amiternus ager felicibus educat hortis: Nursinas poteris parcius esse pilas.
question: Qui ager napos felicibus hortis educat apud Martialem?
question_en: Which district rears navews in its fertile gardens, according to Martial?
answer_en: The territory of Amiternum (in the Sabine country).
derivation: Amiternum's gardens as the source of napi (navews), set above the famous 'pilae' of Nursia. Named-place answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Mollis in aequorea quae crevit spina Ravenna non erit incultis gratior asparagis.
question: Quae urbs aequorea asparagos cultos gignebat, teste Martiale?
question_en: Which seaside city grew cultivated asparagus, on Martial's testimony?
derivation: Ravenna's asparagus was the famous cultivated kind (so too Pliny); Martial's point is that even it beats wild asparagus no better than equal. Named-place answer supported verbatim (in aequorea Ravenna).

author: Martial
source_text: Chia seni similis Baccho, quem Setia misit, ipsa merum secum portat et ipsa salem.
question: Cui vino ficus Chia similis esse dicitur apud Martialem?
question_en: To what wine is the Chian fig said to be similar, in Martial?
derivation: Two shared items of connoisseurship in one couplet: Chios as the famous fig-island, Setia as a top wine town; the Chian fig 'carries its own wine and salt.' Named-entity answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Si tibi Cecropio saturata Cydonea melle ponentur, dicas: "Haec melimela placent".
question: Quo melle saturata Cydonea 'melimela' fiunt apud Martialem?
question_en: Steeped in what honey do quinces become 'honey-apples' (melimela), in Martial?
derivation: Attic (Cecropian, i.e. Hymettan) honey as the canonical fine honey, and quinces preserved in honey passing for melimela — insider table knowledge. Answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Poma sumus Cybeles: procul hinc discede, viator, ne cadat in miserum nostra ruina caput.
question: Cuius deae poma nuces pineae vocantur apud Martialem?
question_en: Of which goddess are pine nuts called the fruit, in Martial?
derivation: The pine was sacred to Cybele (through the Attis story), so pine nuts are 'poma Cybeles' — a shared religious-mythical association attached to a food. Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Sorba sumus, molles nimium tendentia ventres: aptius haec puero quam tibi poma dabis.
question: Quid sorba ventribus nimium mollibus praestant, secundum Martialem?
question_en: What do service-berries do for overly loose bowels, according to Martial?
derivation: Standard Roman dietetic lore: sorbs are astringent and check diarrhea — hence fitter for a boy. Short verifiable effect supported verbatim (molles tendentia ventres).

author: Martial
source_text: Aurea porrigitur Iani caryota Kalendis; sed tamen hoc munus pauperis esse solet.
question: Quibus Kalendis caryota dono porrigi solet, teste Martiale?
question_en: On which Kalends is the date customarily offered as a gift, on Martial's testimony?
answer_en: On the Kalends of January (of Janus).
derivation: The New Year strena: gilded dates given on 1 January, typically the poor man's gift. A calendar-custom fact anchored to the named day; answer supported verbatim (Iani Kalendis).

author: Martial
source_text: Haec tibi quae torta venerunt condita meta, si maiora forent cottana, ficus erat.
question: Quid essent cottana, si maiora forent, ut iocatur Martialis?
question_en: What would cottana be, if they were bigger, as Martial jokes?
derivation: Cottana were the tiny Syrian figs of the gift-basket; Martial's joke states the checkable fact that they are simply miniature figs. One-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Pruna peregrinae carie rugosa senectae sume: solent duri solvere ventris onus.
question: Quem usum ventri praestant pruna Damascena, secundum Martialem?
question_en: What service do Damascus plums (prunes) render the belly, according to Martial?
derivation: The wrinkled imported prune (the lemma names them Damascena, plums of Damascus) as the standard laxative — dietetic lore every Roman diner carried. Effect supported verbatim (duri solvere ventris onus).

author: Martial
source_text: Caseus Etruscae signatus imagine Lunae praestabit pueris prandia mille tuis.
question: Cuius oppidi caseus mille prandia praestare dicitur apud Martialem?
question_en: Cheese of which town is said to furnish a thousand lunches, in Martial?
derivation: The giant cheeses of Etruscan Luna, stamped with the town's moon device — famous for their size (Pliny says the same). Named-place answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Si sine carne voles ientacula sumere frugi, haec tibi Vestino de grege massa venit.
question: De cuius gentis grege caseus ientaculo frugi aptus venit apud Martialem?
question_en: From the flock of which people does the cheese fit for a frugal breakfast come, in Martial?
derivation: Vestine cheese (from the Sabellian Vestini) as the frugal meatless ientaculum — named regional product plus its meal-slot. Answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Non quemcumque focum nec fumum caseus omnem, sed Velabrensem qui bibit, ille sapit.
question: Cuius loci fumo caseus fumosus condiri debet, ut bene sapiat, teste Martiale?
question_en: With the smoke of which place must smoked cheese be cured to taste right, on Martial's testimony?
derivation: The Velabrum quarter at Rome was the famous home of smoked cheese — 'not every hearth's smoke' will do. Named-place answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Trebula nos genuit; commendat gratia duplex, sive levi flamma sive domamur aqua.
question: Quod oppidum caseos gignit, qui vel levi flamma vel aqua domari possunt, apud Martialem?
question_en: Which town produces the cheeses that can be treated either with a light flame or with water, in Martial?
derivation: Trebulan cheese and its 'double grace' — good toasted or soaked. Named-town answer supported verbatim (Trebula nos genuit).

author: Martial
source_text: Cum sit anus coniunx et sint tibi mortua membra, nil aliud bulbis quam satur esse potes.
question: Cui rei bulbi cibo sumpti prodesse vulgo credebantur, ut ex ioco Martialis in Xeniis apparet?
question_en: For what were bulbs, taken as food, popularly believed to be good, as Martial's joke in the Xenia shows?
derivation: Bulbi (grape-hyacinth bulbs) were the proverbial Roman aphrodisiac (cf. Martial 3.75, Ovid); the joke — with an old wife and dead members, bulbs can only fill you up — presupposes exactly that shared belief. Insider dietetic lore; short answer.

author: Martial
source_text: Filia Picenae venio Lucanica porcae: pultibus hinc niveis grata corona datur.
question: Cuius terrae porca Lucanicam gignere dicitur apud Martialem?
question_en: The sow of which land is said to beget the Lucanian sausage, in Martial?
derivation: The lucanica sausage (named from Lucania) made of Picene pork and served as a 'welcome crown' on snow-white puls — two named regions of pork-and-porridge culture. Answer supported verbatim (filia Picenae porcae).

author: Martial
source_text: Haec quae Picenis venit subducta trapetis inchoat atque eadem finit oliva dapes.
question: Quo loco cenae oliva Picena apponitur apud Martialem?
answer: Primo et extremo: dapes inchoat et finit.
question_en: At what point of the dinner is the Picene olive served, in Martial?
answer_en: First and last — it both opens and closes the meal.
derivation: Two table facts in one: Picenum as the famous olive country (subducta trapetis, snatched from its presses), and the olive's place at both ends of the Roman dinner. Supported verbatim (inchoat atque eadem finit dapes).

author: Martial
source_text: Aut Corcyraei sunt haec de frondibus horti, aut haec Massyli poma draconis erant.
question: Cuius draconis poma mala citrea fuisse fingit Martialis in Xeniis?
question_en: Of what dragon does Martial in the Xenia fancy the citrons to have been the fruit?
answer_en: Of the Massylian dragon (the guardian of the Hesperides).
derivation: Citrons evoke the two proverbial wonder-gardens: Alcinous' orchard on Corcyra and the golden apples guarded by the Hesperides' dragon in Massylian Africa — myth as shared story attached to a luxury fruit. Answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Picentina Ceres niveo sic nectare crescit ut levis accepta spongea turget aqua.
question: Cuius regionis panes, qui umore accepto ut spongea turgent, laudat Martialis in Xeniis?
question_en: The loaves of which region, swelling like a sponge when they take up liquid, does Martial praise in the Xenia?
derivation: Picene bread, the famous soaked loaf (Pliny too: made of alica, drunk with milk — Martial's 'niveo nectare'), swelling like a sponge in water. Named-region answer supported verbatim (Picentina Ceres).

author: Martial
source_text: Argentum atque aurum facilest laenamque togamque mittere; boletos mittere difficilest.
question: Quod munus mittere difficile est, cum argentum, aurum, laenam togamque mittere facile sit, ut iocatur Martialis?
question_en: What gift is it hard to send, though silver, gold, a mantle and a toga are easy to send, as Martial jokes?
derivation: The famous boletus couplet: the prized mushrooms were the one delicacy hosts could not bring themselves to give away. Anchored to Martial's celebrated joke; one-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Cum me ficus alat, cum pascar dulcibus uvis, cur potius nomen non dedit uva mihi?
question: A quo cibo avis ficedula nomen traxit, ut ex Martiale apparet?
question_en: From what food did the fig-pecker bird take its name, as appears from Martial?
derivation: The ficedula feeds on figs (and on grapes — the bird itself complains the grape gave it no name). The fig-diet naming survives translation ('fig-pecker', beccafico). Supported verbatim (cum me ficus alat).

author: Martial
source_text: Rumpimus altricem tenero quae vertice terram tubera, boletis poma secunda sumus.
question: Quibus fungis terrae tubera secunda esse dicuntur apud Martialem?
question_en: To which mushrooms are truffles said to rank second, in Martial?
derivation: The insider ranking of the two earth-delicacies: truffles (which burst through their nursing earth with tender crown) come second after boleti. Answer supported verbatim (boletis poma secunda).

author: Martial
source_text: Texta rosis fortasse tibi vel divite nardo, at mihi de turdis facta corona placet.
question: Ex quibus avibus facta corona Martiali magis quam rosea placet?
question_en: A garland made of which birds pleases Martial more than one woven of roses?
derivation: Thrushes — the prize table-bird — were sold and gifted strung together in a ring (the lemma is a 'decuria of thrushes'), so Martial prefers a thrush-garland to roses or nard. Answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Tota quidem ponatur anas, sed pectore tantum et cervice sapit: cetera redde coco.
question: Quibus partibus solis anas sapit, ut praecipit Martialis?
question_en: In which parts alone is the duck tasty, as Martial instructs?
answer_en: In the breast and the neck.
derivation: A gourmet's table-rule: serve the duck whole, eat only breast and neck, 'give the rest back to the cook.' Two-part answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Cerretana mihi fiat vel missa licebit de Menapis: lauti de petasone vorent.
question: A quibus gentibus pernae laudatissimae mittebantur, teste Martiale?
question_en: From which peoples were the most esteemed hams sent, on Martial's testimony?
answer_en: From the Cerretani (in Spain) and the Menapii (in Gaul).
derivation: The two famous ham countries of the empire: the Cerretani of the Spanish Pyrenees and the Menapii of Belgic Gaul. Named-peoples answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Te fortasse magis capiat de virgine porca; me materna gravi de sue volva capit.
question: Ex quali sue volva Martialem maxime capit?
question_en: From what kind of sow does the sow's-womb delicacy most take Martial's fancy?
answer_en: From a mother sow, heavy with young.
derivation: Volva (sow's womb) was a canonical Roman delicacy, and 'virgin sow or farrowing sow?' the insider's debate; Martial votes for the pregnant mother's. Attribution to Martial makes the preference verifiable; supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Niliacum ridebis holus lanasque sequaces, inproba cum morsu fila manuque trahes.
question: Vnde colocasia, holus filis lanosis notum, venit apud Martialem?
question_en: From where does the colocasia come, the vegetable known for its woolly clinging threads, in Martial?
derivation: Colocasia, the Egyptian Nile-vegetable whose stringy fibers you tug with tooth and hand — exotic produce of the Roman table. Place answer supported verbatim (Niliacum holus).

author: Martial
source_text: Aspice quam tumeat magno iecur ansere maius! Miratus dices: "Hoc, rogo, crevit ubi"?
question: Quam magnum fieri potest iecur anserinum, ut miratur Martialis in Xeniis?
question_en: How big can a goose's liver become, as Martial marvels in the Xenia?
derivation: The force-fattened goose liver (the ficatum, ancestor of foie gras) swelling larger than the bird — a celebrated gourmet paradox ('where, pray, did this grow?'). Supported verbatim (magno iecur ansere maius).

author: Martial
source_text: Tota mihi dormitur hiems et pinguior illo tempore sum quo me nil nisi somnus alit.
question: Quid glirem per hiemem alit, ut ait Martialis in Xeniis?
question_en: What nourishes the dormouse through the winter, as Martial says in the Xenia?
derivation: The dormouse (glis), fattened for the table in gliraria, sleeps the whole winter and grows fatter on sleep alone — the famous paradox of the Roman delicacy. Supported verbatim (nil nisi somnus alit).

author: Martial
source_text: Gaudet in effossis habitare cuniculus antris. Monstravit tacitas hostibus ille vias.
question: Quod animal tacitas vias hostibus monstravisse dicitur apud Martialem?
question_en: Which animal is said to have shown enemies their hidden ways, according to Martial?
derivation: The rabbit's burrow as the model (and the name) of the military mine: siege tunnels were called cuniculi. The etiological lore survives translation as a fact about the burrowing animal teaching men to tunnel. Supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Inter sapores fertur alitum primus Ionicarum gustus attagenarum.
question: Cuius avis gustus inter sapores alitum primus fertur apud Martialem?
question_en: The taste of which bird is reckoned first among the flavors of fowl, in Martial?
derivation: The attagen of Ionia at the top of the bird-flavor ranking (Horace praises the same bird) — connoisseur's knowledge of the luxury table. Named-bird answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Pascitur et dulci facilis gallina farina, pascitur et tenebris. Ingeniosa gula est.
question: Quibus duabus rebus gallinae altiles saginantur apud Martialem?
question_en: By what two means are table hens fattened, in Martial?
answer_en: With sweet flour-meal and with darkness.
derivation: The poultry-fattener's technique: sweetened meal plus confinement in the dark — 'gluttony is ingenious.' Two-item answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Ne nimis exhausto macresceret inguine gallus, amisit testes. Nunc mihi gallus erit.
question: Quo facto gallus capo fit, ne macrescat, teste Martiale?
question_en: By what operation does a cock become a capon, so as not to grow lean, on Martial's testimony?
derivation: The capon: a cock castrated so that it fattens instead of wearing itself lean — standard knowledge of the Roman poultry yard. Supported verbatim (amisit testes).

author: Martial
source_text: Ponitur Ausoniis avis haec rarissima mensis: hanc in piscina ludere saepe soles.
question: Quae avis rarissima mensis Ausoniis ponitur apud Martialem?
question_en: Which bird is served as the rarest on Italian tables, in Martial?
derivation: The partridge (the epigram's lemma) as the rarest bird of the Italian (Ausonian) table. Named-bird answer; 'rarissima Ausoniis mensis' supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Ne violes teneras periuro dente columbas, tradita si Gnidiae sunt tibi sacra deae.
question: Cuius deae sacrae aves sunt columbae, ut monet Martialis?
question_en: To which goddess are doves sacred, as Martial advises?
derivation: Doves as the sacred birds of Venus — her initiates must not touch them with 'perjured tooth'; 'the Cnidian goddess' is Venus of Praxiteles' Cnidus. Shared religious knowledge; answer supported by the verse.

author: Martial
source_text: Inguina torquati tardant hebetantque palumbi: non edat hanc volucrem qui cupit esse salax.
question: Quid palumbi torquati inguinibus edentium facere feruntur apud Martialem?
question_en: What are ring-necked wood-pigeons said to do to the loins of those who eat them, in Martial?
answer_en: They slow and dull them (blunt desire).
derivation: Dietetic lore: the wood-pigeon as anti-aphrodisiac — 'let no one eat this bird who wants to be lusty' — the counterpart of the aphrodisiac bulbs. Supported verbatim (tardant hebetantque).

author: Martial
source_text: Miraris, quotiens gemmantis explicat alas, et potes hunc saevo tradere, dure, coco?
question: Quae avis, quamquam gemmantes alas mirantibus explicat, tamen saevo coco tradi solet, ut queritur Martialis?
question_en: Which bird, though it spreads its jeweled wings for admirers, is nonetheless handed over to the cruel cook, as Martial protests?
derivation: The peacock (the epigram's lemma), admired for its 'jeweled' train yet served at luxury tables — Martial's reproach presupposes the shared custom of eating peafowl. Named-bird answer.

author: Martial
source_text: Dat mihi pinna rubens nomen, sed lingua gulosis nostra sapit. Quid si garrula lingua foret?
question: Quae pars phoenicopteri gulosis maxime sapit, teste Martiale?
question_en: Which part of the flamingo is the special treat for gourmands, on Martial's testimony?
derivation: Flamingo tongue as the proverbial luxury morsel (cf. Vitellius' dish in Suetonius); the same couplet notes the bird is named from its red feather. One-word answer supported verbatim (lingua gulosis nostra sapit).

author: Martial
source_text: Argoa primum sum transportata carina. Ante mihi notum nil nisi Phasis erat.
question: Qua nave phasianae aves primum a Phaside transportatae esse dicuntur apud Martialem?
question_en: By what ship are pheasants said first to have been carried away from the Phasis, in Martial?
derivation: The pheasant (phasiana) is named from the Colchian river Phasis and, in the shared origin-story, was first brought west aboard the Argo. Named-ship answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Ansere Romano quamvis satur Hannibal esset, ipse suas numquam barbarus edit aves.
question: Quis dux Poenus, quamvis ansere Romano satur, suas tamen aves Numidicas numquam edit, ut iocatur Martialis?
question_en: Which Carthaginian general, though sated with Roman goose, never ate his own Numidian birds, as Martial jokes?
derivation: The guinea-fowl (Numidicae) came from Hannibal's own Africa; the joke — he gorged on Roman goose yet never touched his own birds — hangs on the named general. Single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Haec servavit avis Tarpei templa Tonantis. Miraris? Nondum fecerat illa deus.
question: Quae avis templa Tarpeia Tonantis servavisse dicitur apud Martialem?
question_en: Which bird is said to have saved the Tarpeian temple of the Thunderer (the Capitol), in Martial?
derivation: The sacred geese that warned of the Gauls' night attack on the Capitol (390 BC) — celebrated Roman history attached to the table-goose. Named-bird answer supported verbatim (haec servavit avis Tarpei templa Tonantis).

author: Martial
source_text: Turbabis versus nec littera tota volabit, unam perdideris si Palamedis avem.
question: Cuius herois aves grues appellantur apud Martialem?
question_en: As whose birds — which hero's — are cranes styled in Martial?
derivation: Cranes fly in letter-formation, and Palamedes was said to have devised letters from watching them — lose one crane and 'the letter will not fly whole.' Shared story anchored to the named hero; supported verbatim (Palamedis avem).

author: Martial
source_text: Rustica sim an perdix quid refert, si sapor idem est? Carior est perdix. Sic sapit illa magis.
question: Qua tandem re perdix a rusticula differt, cum sapor idem sit, ut iocatur Martialis?
question_en: In what, after all, does the partridge differ from the woodcock, since the taste is the same, as Martial jokes?
answer_en: In price — the partridge costs more (and so 'tastes better').
derivation: A checkable point of market lore: woodcock and partridge taste alike, but the partridge is dearer — Martial's gibe at price-snobbery. Supported verbatim (carior est perdix).

author: Martial
source_text: Dulcia defecta modulatur carmina lingua cantator cycnus funeris ipse sui.
question: Quae avis sui ipsa funeris cantator dicitur apud Martialem?
question_en: Which bird is called the singer of its own funeral, in Martial?
derivation: The proverbial swan-song: the dying swan modulates sweet songs with failing tongue — ambient lore every ancient reader carried. Named-bird answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Nomen habet magni volucris tam parva gigantis? Et nomen prasini Porphyrionis habet.
question: Cuius factionis circensis agitator erat Porphyrion ille, cuius nomen avis porphyrio quoque habet?
question_en: Of which circus faction was that Porphyrion a driver, whose name the porphyrio bird also bears?
derivation: The little bird carries two famous names: the giant Porphyrion of the Gigantomachy and Porphyrion the charioteer of the Greens — evidence for the prasina factio of the circus. Supported verbatim (prasini Porphyrionis).

author: Martial
source_text: Quae natat in Siculo grandis murena profundo, non valet exustam mergere sole cutem.
question: In quo mari murena grandis natare dicitur apud Martialem?
question_en: In what sea is the great murena said to swim, in Martial?
answer_en: In the Sicilian deep (the strait of Sicily).
derivation: The famous murena-fishery of the Sicilian strait; the great lamprey swims at the surface, unable to sink its sun-scorched skin. Named-sea answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Quamvis lata gerat patella rhombum, rhombus latior est tamen patella.
question: Qua re latior semper est rhombus, ut iocatur Martialis?
question_en: Than what is the turbot always broader, as Martial jokes?
derivation: The proverbial too-big turbot — no platter is wide enough (the same joke behind Juvenal's council on Domitian's turbot). Short comparative answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Ebria Baiano veni modo concha Lucrino: nobile nunc sitio luxuriosa garum.
question: E quo lacu ostrea nobilissima Romanorum veniunt apud Martialem?
question_en: From what lagoon do the Romans' most celebrated oysters come, in Martial?
derivation: Lucrine oysters at Baiae — THE Roman oyster; fresh ('drunk') from its lake the luxurious shell 'thirsts for noble garum,' attesting too that oysters were dressed with garum. Named-place answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Hic scarus, aequoreis qui venit adesus ab undis, visceribus bonus est, cetera vile sapit.
question: Qua parte sola scarus piscis bonus est apud Martialem?
question_en: In which part alone is the parrot-wrasse (scarus) good, in Martial?
derivation: The scarus, prized delicacy of the imperial table, was eaten for its viscera — the rest 'tastes cheap.' Gourmet's rule supported verbatim (visceribus bonus est).

author: Martial
source_text: Princeps Niliaci raperis, coracine, macelli: Pellaeae prior est gloria nulla gulae.
question: Cuius macelli princeps coracinus piscis habetur apud Martialem?
question_en: Of which market is the coracinus fish reckoned the prince, in Martial?
derivation: The coracinus as the top fish of Egypt — 'no glory of the Pellaean (Alexandrian) palate stands higher.' Named-place answer supported verbatim (princeps Niliaci macelli).

author: Martial
source_text: Sanguine de nostro tinctas, ingrate, lacernas induis, et non est hoc satis, esca sumus.
question: Cuius animalis sanguine lacernae purpureae tinguntur, ut queritur ipsa concha apud Martialem?
question_en: With the blood of which creature are purple cloaks dyed, as the shellfish itself complains in Martial?
derivation: The murex furnished both the purple dye of Roman dress and a dish — 'you wear cloaks dyed in our blood, and, not content with that, we are food.' The double use is the checkable cultural fact.

author: Martial
source_text: In Venetis sint lauta licet convivia terris, principium cenae gobius esse solet.
question: Quo pisce cena in Venetis terris incipere solet, teste Martiale?
question_en: With which fish does dinner customarily begin in the Venetic lands, on Martial's testimony?
derivation: Regional table-custom: in Venetia even lavish banquets open with the humble goby. Named-fish answer supported verbatim (principium cenae gobius).

author: Martial
source_text: Non omnis laudes pretiumque aurata meretur, sed cui solus erit concha Lucrina cibus.
question: Quo cibo pasta aurata sola laudes pretiumque meretur apud Martialem?
question_en: Fed on what food alone does the gilthead deserve praise and its price, in Martial?
derivation: Connoisseurship of the fish-market: only the gilthead fattened on Lucrine shellfish counts. Short answer supported verbatim (concha Lucrina cibus).

author: Martial
source_text: Ad Palatinas acipensem mittite mensas: ambrosias ornent munera rara dapes.
question: Ad cuius mensas acipensis mitti debet, ut praecipit Martialis?
question_en: To whose tables should the sturgeon be sent, as Martial directs?
derivation: The sturgeon (acipensis) as a rarity fit for the imperial table on the Palatine — 'let rare gifts adorn ambrosial feasts.' Answer supported verbatim (ad Palatinas mensas).

author: Martial
source_text: Inter aves turdus, si quid me iudice certum est inter quadripedes mattea prima lepus.
question: Quae mattea inter aves et quae inter quadripedes prima est, iudice Martiale?
answer: Inter aves turdus, inter quadripedes lepus.
question_en: What is the first delicacy among birds and what among four-footed creatures, in Martial's judgment?
answer_en: Among birds the thrush, among quadrupeds the hare.
derivation: The book's most famous ranking: thrush first among birds, hare first among quadrupeds as mattea (tidbit). Anchored to Martial's explicit judgment (me iudice); two-part answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Matutinarum non ultima praeda ferarum saevos oryx constat quot mihi morte canum!
question: Quo diei tempore venationes ferarum in harena dari solebant, ut ex Martiale de oryge apparet?
question_en: At what time of day were the beast-hunts of the arena customarily given, as appears from Martial's epigram on the oryx?
derivation: The venationes were the morning show of the amphitheater — the oryx is 'not the least prey of the morning beasts,' costing the deaths of many hounds. Arena-custom fact supported verbatim (matutinarum ferarum).

author: Martial
source_text: Hic erat ille tuo domitus, Cyparisse, capistro. An magis iste tuus, Silvia, cervus erat?
question: Quibus duobus in fabulis cervi mansueti fuisse dicuntur, ut allusit Martialis in Xeniis?
question_en: Which two figures of story are said to have had tame stags, as Martial alludes in the Xenia?
derivation: The two proverbial pet stags of shared story: Cyparissus' beloved stag (Ovid) and Silvia's stag whose wounding kindled war in Aeneid 7. Two-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Dum tener est onager solaque lalisio matre pascitur, hoc infans sed breve nomen habet.
question: Quod nomen pullus onagri habet, dum sola matre pascitur, apud Martialem?
question_en: What name does the wild ass's foal bear while it still feeds only on its mother's milk, in Martial?
derivation: The lalisio — the suckling onager foal, a named delicacy (Pliny lists lalisiones among dainties); the name lasts only while it nurses. Single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Caeruleus nos Liris amat, quem silva Maricae protegit: hinc squillae maxima turba sumus.
question: Quo flumine maxima squillarum turba gignitur apud Martialem?
question_en: In which river is the greatest crowd of prawns bred, in Martial?
answer_en: In the Liris (sheltered by Marica's grove).
derivation: The Liris at Minturnae, screened by the sacred grove of the nymph Marica, as the famous home of squillae. Named-river answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Laneus Euganei lupus excipit ora Timavi, aequoreo dulces cum sale pastus aquas.
question: Cuius fluminis ora lupus ille laneus excipit apud Martialem?
question_en: The mouth of which river does the prized 'woolly' bass haunt, in Martial?
derivation: The laneus lupus — the bass 'soft as wool' — taken at the mouth of the Timavus, fattened where fresh water meets sea salt. Named-river answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Hoc tibi Campani sudavit baca Venafri: unguentum quotiens sumis, et istud olet.
question: Cuius oppidi Campani baca oleum nobilissimum sudat apud Martialem?
question_en: The olive of which Campanian town sweats out the noblest oil, in Martial?
derivation: Venafran oil, the premier olive oil of Italy (so too Horace and Pliny), fine enough to scent unguents. Named-town answer supported verbatim (Campani baca Venafri).

author: Martial
source_text: Exspirantis adhuc scombri de sanguine primo accipe fastosum, munera cara, garum.
question: De cuius piscis sanguine garum illud sociorum pretiosum conficitur, teste Martiale?
answer: De scombri, exspirantis adhuc, sanguine primo.
question_en: From the blood of which fish is the costly 'garum of the allies' made, on Martial's testimony?
answer_en: From the first blood of a mackerel still breathing its last.
derivation: Garum sociorum (the lemma), the luxury fish-sauce — 'haughty garum, a costly gift' — made from the first blood of a still-expiring scomber. The defining fact of Rome's most famous condiment; supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Antipolitani, fateor, sum filia thynni: essem si scombri, non tibi missa forem.
question: Ex quo pisce muria fit, ut ipsa amphora apud Martialem fatetur?
question_en: From which fish is muria (brine-sauce) made, as the jar itself confesses in Martial?
derivation: Muria, the cheaper brine, is 'daughter of the Antipolitan tunny' — had it been mackerel it would have been garum and too dear to send. Encodes the sauce hierarchy scomber over thynnus; supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Hoc tibi Thesei populatrix misit Hymetti Pallados a silvis nobile nectar apis.
question: De quo monte mel Atticum nobile venit apud Martialem?
question_en: From which mountain does the noble Attic honey come, in Martial?
derivation: Hymettan honey — the bee 'plunderer of Theseus' Hymettus' sends noble nectar from the woods of Pallas — the canonical fine honey of antiquity. Named-mountain answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Cum dederis Siculos mediae de collibus Hyblae, Cecropios dicas tu licet esse favos.
question: De cuius montis collibus favi Siculi veniunt apud Martialem?
question_en: From the hills of which mountain do the Sicilian honeycombs come, in Martial?
derivation: Hyblaean honey, Sicily's rival to Attic: give combs from mid-Hybla and you may call them Cecropian. The Hybla/Hymettus pairing was proverbial; answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Gnosia Minoae genuit vindemia Cretae hoc tibi, quod mulsum pauperis esse solet.
question: Quod vinum 'mulsum pauperis' esse solet apud Martialem?
question_en: Which wine is proverbially 'the poor man's mulsum,' in Martial?
derivation: Passum, the raisin wine born of the Gnosian vintage of Minoan Crete, so sweet it stands in for honeyed mulsum among the poor. Both the epithet and the Cretan origin supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Haec de vitifera venisse picata Vienna ne dubites, misit Romulus ipse mihi.
question: E qua urbe vina picata veniunt apud Martialem?
question_en: From which city do the pitched wines (picata) come, in Martial?
answer_en: From vine-bearing Vienna (on the Rhone, in Gaul).
derivation: Picatum, the pitch-flavored specialty wine of Vienna of the Allobroges (Pliny describes the same picatum). Named-city answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Attica nectareum turbatis mella Falernum. Misceri decet hoc a Ganymede merum.
question: Ex quibus duabus rebus mulsum lautissimum miscetur apud Martialem?
question_en: From which two ingredients is the finest mulsum mixed, in Martial?
answer_en: From Attic honey and Falernian wine.
derivation: The canonical recipe of mulsum, the Roman aperitif: Attic honey stirred into nectar-like Falernian — 'a wine fit to be mixed by Ganymede.' Two-item answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Surrentina bibis? Nec murrina picta nec aurum sume: dabunt calices haec tibi vina suos.
question: Quibus calicibus vina Surrentina bibenda sunt apud Martialem?
question_en: From what cups should Surrentine wine be drunk, in Martial?
derivation: The connoisseur's rule: Surrentine wine needs neither murrine nor gold — Surrentum's own famous pottery cups suit it ('these wines will give you their own cups'). Supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: De Sinuessanis venerunt Massica prelis: condita quo quaeris consule? Nullus erat.
question: Quo consule condita esse dicuntur Massica illa vetustissima, ut iocatur Martialis?
question_en: Under which consul is that most ancient Massic (Falernian) said to have been laid down, as Martial jokes?
answer_en: Under none — there were as yet no consuls.
derivation: The Falernian lemma: Massic from the Sinuessan presses so old that it antedates the consulship itself — wine-dating by consular year turned into the ultimate boast. Supported verbatim (quo consule? Nullus erat).

author: Martial
source_text: Pendula Pomptinos quae spectat Setia campos, exigua vetulos misit ab urbe cados.
question: Quos campos Setia pendula despectat, quae vetulos cados vini mittit apud Martialem?
question_en: Which plains does hill-hung Setia overlook, the little town that sends its well-aged jars in Martial?
derivation: Setine — a top imperial-era wine — from tiny Setia perched above the Pomptine marshes, sent already aged (vetulos cados). Named-place answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Haec Fundana tulit felix autumnus Opimi. Expressit mustum consul et ipse bibit.
question: Cuius consulis felix autumnus vina Fundana tulit, ut ait Martialis?
question_en: The fortunate autumn of which consul produced the Fundan wine, as Martial says?
derivation: The Opimian vintage (Opimius consul, 121 BC) — the most celebrated wine-year of antiquity: 'the consul pressed the must and drank it himself.' Single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Non sum de primo, fateor, trifolina Lyaeo, inter vina tamen septima vitis ero.
question: Quotum locum inter vina vitis trifolina sibi vindicat apud Martialem?
question_en: What rank among wines does the Trifoline vine claim for itself, in Martial?
derivation: The wine-league ranking: Trifoline (from Campania) admits it is not of the first growth but stands seventh among wines. Number answer supported verbatim (septima vitis).

author: Martial
source_text: Caecuba Fundanis generosa cocuntur Amyclis, vitis et in media nata palude viret.
question: Quo loco Caecuba generosa cocuntur, teste Martiale?
answer: Fundanis Amyclis (vite in media palude nata).
question_en: Where does the noble Caecuban ripen, on Martial's testimony?
answer_en: At Amyclae near Fundi (from a vine growing in the middle of the marsh).
derivation: Caecuban, the grandest old-Roman cru: grown at Fundan Amyclae, its vine green in mid-marsh — the famous marsh-grown vineyard (so too Pliny). Place answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Potabis liquidum Signina morantia ventrem? Ne nimium sistas, sit tibi parca sitis.
question: Quid vina Signina ventri praestant apud Martialem?
question_en: What effect does Signine wine have on the belly, in Martial?
answer_en: It checks a loose bowel (binds it).
derivation: Signine as the medicinal, astringent wine — drink it sparingly lest it bind too much. Dietetic wine-lore supported verbatim (liquidum morantia ventrem).

author: Martial
source_text: Amphora Nestorea tibi Mamertina senecta si detur, quodvis nomen habere potest.
question: Quod vinum, si Nestorea senectute detur, quodvis nomen habere potest, ut iocatur Martialis?
question_en: Which wine, if served at a Nestor-like old age, can pass under any name it pleases, as Martial jokes?
derivation: Mamertine, the Sicilian wine of Messana: aged long enough ('Nestorean old age') it can pose as any grand cru — insider wine-market lore. Named-wine answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Tarraco, Campano tantum cessura Lyaeo haec genuit Tuscis aemula vina cadis.
question: Cui vino soli vina Tarraconensia cedunt apud Martialem?
question_en: To which wine alone do the wines of Tarraco yield, in Martial?
answer_en: To Campanian wine (Falernian and its kin).
derivation: The ranking of Spain's Tarraconese wine: second only to Campania's, and a rival of Tuscan jars — provincial wine placed on the connoisseur's ladder. Supported verbatim (Campano tantum cessura Lyaeo).

author: Martial
source_text: Amphora Niliaci non sit tibi vilis aceti: esset cum vinum, vilior ilia fuit.
question: Cuius terrae acetum vino suo pretiosius est, ut iocatur Martialis?
question_en: Which land's vinegar is worth more than its own wine, as Martial jokes?
derivation: The joke encodes a shared judgment: Egyptian wine was so poor that as vinegar the jar was dearer than when it held wine. Named-place answer supported verbatim (Niliaci aceti).

author: Martial
source_text: Hoc de Caesareis mitis vindemia cellis misit, Iuleo quae sibi monte placet.
question: De cuius cellis vinum Albanum missum esse dicit Martialis?
question_en: From whose cellars does Martial say the Alban wine has been sent?
derivation: Albanum as the emperor's own wine, from the Caesarean cellars of the Alban estate — the vintage 'that delights in the Julian mount' (Alba Longa, seat of Iulus' line). Supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Nomentana meum tibi dat vindemia Bacchum: si te Quintus amat, commodia bibes.
question: Cuius agri vindemia Martiali ipsi vinum suum dabat, ut in Xeniis ait?
question_en: The vintage of which district gave Martial his own wine, as he says in the Xenia?
derivation: Martial's own wine came from his little Nomentan farm — a biographical fact his readers carried (the Nomentanum recurs across his books). Named-place answer supported verbatim (Nomentana meum ... vindemia Bacchum).

author: Martial
source_text: De Spoletinis quae sunt cariosa lagonis malueris quam si musta Falerna bibas.
question: Vtrum praeferendum est, iudice Martiale: Spoletinum vetus an mustum Falernum?
question_en: Which is to be preferred, in Martial's judgment: aged Spoletine or new Falernian must?
derivation: A point of cellar-lore: age beats appellation — old Spoletine outdoes even Falernian drunk as must. The explicit preference (malueris) makes it verifiable; supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Marsica Paeligni mittunt turbata coloni: non tu, libertus sed bibat illa tuus.
question: Cui bibenda sunt vina Marsica turbata, quae Paeligni coloni mittunt, ut ait Martialis?
question_en: Who should drink the cloudy Marsic wine that the Paelignian farmers send, as Martial says?
derivation: The bottom of the wine ladder: turbid Marsic from the Paeligni, fit only for the freedman's cup — a shared quality-judgment on a named regional wine. Supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Cum tua centenos expunget sportula civis, fumea Massiliae ponere vina potes.
question: Cuius urbis vina fumea vocantur apud Martialem?
question_en: The wines of which city are called 'smoky' in Martial?
derivation: Massilia's smoke-aged wine (matured in the fumarium) as the cheap pour for mass hospitality — when your sportula must feed a hundred clients. Named-city answer supported verbatim (fumea Massiliae vina).

author: Martial
source_text: Nobilis et lanis et felix vitibus Aulon det pretiosa tibi vellera, vina mihi.
question: Quibus duabus rebus Aulon ille Tarentinus nobilis est apud Martialem?
question_en: For which two products is the Tarentine valley of Aulon famous, in Martial?
derivation: Aulon near Tarentum — Horace's beloved valley — famed alike for precious fleeces and for wine; the Tarentine wool-and-wine pairing was shared knowledge. Two-item answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Vnguentum heredi numquam nec vina relinquas. Ille habeat nummos, haec tibi tota dato.
question: Quae duo heredi numquam relinquenda esse monet Martialis?
question_en: Which two things does Martial warn one never to leave to an heir?
derivation: The quotable table-maxim closing the gift list: let the heir have the cash, but use up the unguent and the wine yourself — the banqueter's carpe-diem pairing of perfume and wine. Two-item answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Dat festinatas, Caesar, tibi bruma coronas: quondam veris erat, nunc tua facta rosa est.
question: Quo anni tempore rosae Caesari iam coronas praebent, ut ait Martialis in extremo Xeniorum?
question_en: At what season do roses now furnish Caesar with crowns, as Martial says at the close of the Xenia?
derivation: Winter roses for the emperor: forced ('hurried') rose-crowns in December — 'once the rose belonged to spring, now it is yours' — the proverbial emblem of imperial luxury at the Saturnalia. Supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Curribus Automedon lentisque erat aptus habenis, Tiphys in Haemonia puppe magister erat:
question: Quis in Haemonia puppe, qua Argonautae vecti sunt, magister erat?
question_en: Who was the helmsman on the Haemonian ship in which the Argonauts sailed?
derivation: Tiphys as the canonical helmsman of the Argo ('Haemonia puppis' = the Thessalian ship). Closed-book: standard Argonaut lore; anchored to the Argonauts. Single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Curribus Automedon lentisque erat aptus habenis, Tiphys in Haemonia puppe magister erat: Me Venus artificem tenero praefecit Amori; Tiphys et Automedon dicar Amoris ego.
question: Qua arte excellebat Automedon, quem Ovidius cum Tiphye gubernatore componit?
question_en: In what skill did Automedon excel, whom Ovid pairs with the helmsman Tiphys?
answer_en: In driving the chariot (he was a charioteer).
derivation: Automedon, proverbial charioteer (canonically Achilles' driver), cited by Ovid as the master of chariot and reins. Closed-book canonical figure; answer supported by 'curribus lentisque aptus habenis'.

author: Ovid
source_text: Phillyrides puerum cithara perfecit Achillem, Atque animos placida contudit arte feros.
question: Quis centaurus Achillem puerum citharam docuit?
question_en: Which centaur taught the boy Achilles the cithara?
derivation: Canonical myth: Chiron tutor of the young Achilles, here in music. 'Phillyrides' (son of Philyra) = Chiron, whom Ovid names explicitly five lines later ('Aeacidae Chiron'). Entity-anchored to Achilles; single-name answer.

author: Ovid
source_text: Este procul, vittae tenues, insigne pudoris, Quaeque tegis medios, instita longa, pedes.
question: Cuius rei insigne erant vittae tenues feminarum Romanarum?
question_en: Of what were the thin headbands (vittae) of Roman women the badge?
derivation: Dress-code fact: the vitta was the mark of the respectable (chaste) woman, which is why Ovid banishes it from his poem. Stated verbatim ('insigne pudoris'). Culturally salient Roman costume knowledge.

author: Ovid
source_text: Este procul, vittae tenues, insigne pudoris, Quaeque tegis medios, instita longa, pedes.
question: Quae pars vestis matronarum Romanarum pedes medios tegebat?
question_en: What part of the Roman matron's dress covered the middle of her feet?
derivation: The instita, the flounce sewn to the matron's stola reaching the feet, emblem of the married woman. Stated verbatim; canonical Roman dress fact.

author: Ovid
source_text: Andromedan Perseus nigris portarit ab Indis, Raptaque sit Phrygio Graia puella viro,
question: Unde Perseus Andromedan portavisse dicitur apud Ovidium?
question_en: From where is Perseus said, in Ovid, to have carried off Andromeda?
derivation: Canonical Perseus-Andromeda rescue; Ovid places her among the Indi (elsewhere she is Ethiopian), so the question is attributed 'apud Ovidium'. Entity-anchored to Perseus and Andromeda; short place answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tu modo Pompeia lentus spatiare sub umbra, Cum sol Herculei terga leonis adit:
question: Cuius ducis Romani porticus umbram spatiantibus in Urbe praebebat, ut Ovidius commemorat?
question_en: The portico of which Roman general offered shade to strollers in the City, as Ovid records?
derivation: The Porticus Pompeia (attached to Pompey's theater), the famous shaded promenade of Rome, first in Ovid's catalogue of meeting-places. Venue fact, not advice; supported by 'Pompeia sub umbra spatiare'.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tu modo Pompeia lentus spatiare sub umbra, Cum sol Herculei terga leonis adit:
question: Cuius herois leo inter signa caeli a poetis Romanis numeratur?
question_en: Which hero's lion do the Roman poets count among the signs of the heavens?
derivation: The zodiacal sign Leo identified as the lion of Hercules (the Nemean lion): the sun 'approaches the back of Hercules' lion' in high summer. Shared astronomical-mythological lore; supported by 'Herculei terga leonis'.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nec tibi vitetur quae, priscis sparsa tabellis, Porticus auctoris Livia nomen habet:
question: Quae porticus Romana auctoris sui nomen habet et priscis tabellis picta erat?
question_en: Which Roman portico bears its founder's name and was hung with old paintings?
derivation: The Porticus Liviae, named for its foundress Livia and known as a gallery of old pictures ('priscis sparsa tabellis'). Monument fact from the venue catalogue; both details verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Quaque parare necem miseris patruelibus ausae Belides et stricto stat ferus ense pater.
question: Quibus Belides, Danai filiae, necem parare ausae sunt?
question_en: For whom did the Belides, the daughters of Danaus, dare to prepare death?
answer_en: For their cousins (the sons of Aegyptus).
derivation: Canonical Danaid myth: the fifty daughters of Danaus ('Belides', from grandfather Belus) slew their cousin-bridegrooms. Anchored to the Belides; 'patruelibus' verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Quaque parare necem miseris patruelibus ausae Belides et stricto stat ferus ense pater.
question: Quis in porticu Danaidum Romae stricto ense stans effictus erat?
question_en: Who was represented standing with drawn sword in the portico of the Danaids at Rome?
derivation: The statue program of the Danaid portico (by the Palatine temple of Apollo): the daughters and their fierce father with drawn sword. 'Pater... stricto ense' verbatim; the father of the Belides is by canon Danaus.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nec te praetereat Veneri ploratus Adonis, Cultaque Iudaeo septima sacra Syro.
question: A qua dea ploratus est Adonis?
question_en: By which goddess was Adonis mourned?
derivation: Canonical myth behind the Adonia rites (kept by women at Rome, hence a meeting-day in Ovid's catalogue): Venus mourning her Adonis. 'Veneri ploratus Adonis' verbatim; single-name answer.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nec te praetereat Veneri ploratus Adonis, Cultaque Iudaeo septima sacra Syro.
question: Quoto quoque die Iudaei sacra sua colunt, ut Ovidius significat?
question_en: Every how many days do the Jews keep their rites, as Ovid indicates?
derivation: The Jewish sabbath ('septima sacra' of the 'Syrian Jew') observed at Rome, listed among the regular gathering-days. Ethnographic-religious fact, culturally salient in Augustan Rome; 'septima sacra' verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nec fuge linigerae Memphitica templa iuvencae: Multas illa facit, quod fuit ipsa Iovi.
question: Quae dea Aegyptia, cuius templa Romae frequentabantur, apud Ovidium 'linigera iuvenca Memphitica' dicitur?
question_en: Which Egyptian goddess, whose temples were much frequented at Rome, is called in Ovid the 'linen-clad Memphian heifer'?
derivation: Isis, whose devotees wore linen (linigera) and whose cult came from Memphis, identified with the heifer Io once loved by Jove ('quod fuit ipsa Iovi'); her Roman temple a noted women's haunt. The epithet-identification is standard ambient knowledge; distinct from the Io metamorphosis facts taken from Met. 1.

author: Ovid
source_text: Subdita qua Veneris facto de marmore templo Appias expressis aera pulsat aquis,
question: Iuxta cuius deae templum marmoreum fons Appias expressis aquis aera pulsat?
question_en: Beside which goddess's marble temple does the Appian fountain strike the air with its jetted waters?
derivation: Topographical fact: the Appiades fountain stood below the marble temple of Venus (Genetrix, by Caesar's forum), where the law-courts met. Verbatim 'Veneris... templo Appias'; short one-name answer.

author: Ovid
source_text: Spectatum veniunt, veniunt spectentur ut ipsae: Ille locus casti damna pudoris habet.
question: Quam ob causam duplicem feminae ad ludos veniunt, secundum celeberrimum Ovidii versum?
answer: Ut spectent et ut ipsae spectentur.
question_en: For what twofold reason do women come to the games, according to Ovid's most famous line?
answer_en: To see, and to be seen themselves.
derivation: 'Spectatum veniunt, veniunt spectentur ut ipsae' — proverb-famous line on theater culture; the checkable point (the double purpose) is stated verbatim. Attributed to Ovid, so closed-book and anchored.

author: Ovid
source_text: Primus sollicitos fecisti, Romule, ludos, Cum iuvit viduos rapta Sabina viros.
question: Quo rege ludos edente virgines Sabinae a Romanis raptae sunt?
question_en: Under which king, as he gave the games, were the Sabine maidens seized by the Romans?
derivation: The rape of the Sabine women at the first games, instituted by Romulus — foundational Roman legend, here the aetiology of theater-courtship. Anchored to Romulus and the Sabines; verbatim support.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tunc neque marmoreo pendebant vela theatro, Nec fuerant liquido pulpita rubra croco;
question: Quae supra theatrum marmoreum Romanum ad umbram spectatoribus praebendam pendebant?
question_en: What hung above the Roman marble theater to give the spectators shade?
derivation: Ovid contrasts Romulus' rustic games with the theater of his own day: marble building with hanging vela. The awnings of the Roman theater are a canonical spectacle-culture fact; verbatim 'marmoreo pendebant vela theatro'.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tunc neque marmoreo pendebant vela theatro, Nec fuerant liquido pulpita rubra croco;
question: Quo liquore pulpita theatrorum Romanorum rubra fiebant?
question_en: With what liquid were the stages of Roman theaters made red?
derivation: Roman stages were sprinkled with liquid saffron essence ('liquido... rubra croco') — a well-attested spectacle custom (cf. Propertius, Lucretius). Ovid's negation about early times presupposes the practice of his day.

author: Ovid
source_text: Illic quas tulerant nemorosa Palatia, frondes Simpliciter positae, scena sine arte fuit; In gradibus sedit populus de caespite factis, Qualibet hirsutas fronde tegente comas.
question: Quibus e rebus facti erant gradus in quibus populus primis ludis Romuli sedit?
question_en: Of what were the tiers made on which the people sat at Romulus' first games?
derivation: The primitive theater of Romulus' games: leafy scenery from the Palatine woods and turf-built seating. Anchored to the first games of Romulus; 'de caespite factis' verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Dumque, rudem praebente modum tibicine Tusco, Ludius aequatam ter pede pulsat humum,
question: Cuius gentis tibicen modos primis ludis Romanis praebebat?
question_en: Of what nation was the flute-player who supplied the tune at the earliest Roman games?
