question_en: By what wild beast was Hyas, the brother of the Hyades, killed?
derivation: Hyas, hunting the lair of a whelped lioness, became the bloody prey of the Libyan beast; his mourning sisters were named Hyades after him (nomina fecit Hyas). Named hero, single-beast answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Chloris eram quae Flora vocor: corrupta Latino nominis est nostri littera Graeca sono.
question: Quo nomine Graeco dea Flora antea vocabatur, ut ipsa apud Ovidium narrat?
question_en: By what Greek name was the goddess Flora formerly called, as she herself tells in Ovid?
derivation: Flora's self-identification: 'Chloris eram quae Flora vocor.' The Greek identity of the Latin flower-goddess is a shared mythological fact; the name (not the letter-change mechanics) is what is asked, so it translates.

author: Ovid
source_text: ver erat, errabam; Zephyrus conspexit, abibam; insequitur, fugio: fortior ille fuit. et dederat fratri Boreas ius omne rapinae, ausus Erecthea praemia ferre domo. vim tamen emendat dando mihi nomina nuptae, inque meo non est ulla querella toro.
question: Cuius venti coniunx facta est Chloris, quae Flora vocatur?
question_en: Of which wind did Chloris, who is called Flora, become the wife?
derivation: Zephyrus seized Chloris and made amends by making her his bride. Canonical pairing (Zephyrus and Flora); single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: est mihi fecundus dotalibus hortus in agris; aura fovet, liquidae fonte rigatur aquae: hunc meus implevit generoso flore maritus, atque ait "arbitrium tu, dea, floris habe."
question: Cuius rei arbitrium Zephyrus maritus Florae dedit?
question_en: Dominion over what did her husband Zephyrus give to Flora?
derivation: Zephyrus filled Flora's dowry-garden with noble flowers and granted her 'arbitrium floris' - her divine province. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: sancta Iovem Iuno nata sine matre Minerva officio doluit non eguisse suo.
question: Quae dea sine matre ex Iove nata est, ut Ovidius in Fastis commemorat?
question_en: Which goddess was born of Jupiter without a mother, as Ovid recalls in the Fasti?
derivation: Minerva 'nata sine matre' - the motherless birth from Jupiter that grieved Juno. Canonical shared myth; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: protinus haerentem decerpsi pollice florem; tangitur, et tacto concipit illa sinu. iamque gravis Thracen et laeva Propontidos intrat, fitque potens voti, Marsque creatus erat.
question: Quo modo Iuno, ut Flora apud Ovidium narrat, Martem sine coniuge concepit?
question_en: How, as Flora tells it in Ovid, did Juno conceive Mars without a husband?
answer_en: By the touch of a flower given by Flora.
derivation: Flora's flower made Juno conceive Mars fatherless (tangitur, et tacto concipit illa sinu... Marsque creatus erat) - the counterpart to Minerva's motherless birth. Brief-phrase answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: qui memor accepti per me natalis "habeto tu quoque Romulea" dixit "in urbe locum."
question: Quis deus Florae locum in urbe Romulea dedit, natalis per eam accepti memor?
question_en: Which god gave Flora a place in the city of Romulus, mindful of the birth he owed to her?
derivation: Mars, remembering that Flora's flower gave him birth, granted her cult a place in Rome. Anchors Flora's Roman cult to a named god; the speaker of the quote is Mars ('qui' = Mars, subject of the preceding couplet, Marsque creatus erat).

author: Ovid
source_text: mella meum munus: volucres ego mella daturas ad violam et cytisos et thyma cana voco.
question: Quid Flora suum munus esse apud Ovidium profitetur, volucres ad thyma vocans?
question_en: What does Flora declare to be her own gift in Ovid, as she calls the honey-making winged creatures to the thyme?
derivation: Flora claims honey as her gift, since she summons the bees to violet, clover, and white thyme. One-word answer verbatim (mella meum munus).

author: Ovid
source_text: plebis ad aediles perducta licentia talis Publicios; animus defuit ante viris. rem populus recipit, multam subiere nocentes: vindicibus laudi publica cura fuit. multa data est ex parte mihi, magnoque favore victores ludos instituere novos;
question: Qui aediles plebis, multa nocentibus imposita, ludos novos Florae instituerunt?
question_en: Which plebeian aediles, after fining the offenders, instituted the new games of Flora?
derivation: The ludi Florales were founded by the plebeian aediles Publicii from fines on encroachers of public land. Named founders; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: parte locant clivum, qui tunc erat ardua rupes, utile nunc iter est, Publiciumque vocant.
question: Qui clivus Romae ex parte multae ab aedilibus stratus est et de eorum nomine vocatur?
question_en: Which slope at Rome was built from part of the fine-money by the aediles and is called after their name?
derivation: From part of the same fines the aediles contracted the road up the once-steep rock, the Clivus Publicius (up the Aventine). Named Roman landmark; answer verbatim (Publiciumque vocant).

author: Ovid
source_text: convenere patres, et, si bene floreat annus, numinibus nostris annua festa vovent. adnuimus voto: consul cum consule ludos Postumio Laenas persoluere mihi.
question: Quibus consulibus ludi annui Florae primum persoluti sunt?
question_en: Under which consuls were the annual games of Flora first paid in full?
answer_en: Under the consuls Laenas and Postumius.
derivation: After the senate vowed annual festivals to Flora if the year flowered well, the consuls Laenas and Postumius discharged the vow (173 BC). Two-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: scaena levis decet hanc: non est, mihi credite, non est illa cothurnatas inter habenda deas.
question: Qualis scaena Floram decet, quae inter deas cothurnatas non habenda est?
question_en: What kind of stage befits Flora, who is not to be counted among the buskined (tragic) goddesses?
derivation: The mimes of the Floralia: the light stage suits Flora, not the tragic buskin. Famous theatrical character of her games; answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: turba quidem cur hos celebret meretricia ludos non ex difficili causa petita subest. non est de tetricis, non est de magna professis: volt sua plebeio sacra patere choro,
question: Quae turba ludos Florales praecipue celebrat, ut Ovidius refert?
question_en: What crowd especially celebrates the games of Flora, as Ovid reports?
derivation: The turba meretricia celebrates the Floralia - the festival's famous license. Anchored to the named games; short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Cur tamen, ut dantur vestes Cerialibus albae, sic haec est cultu versicolore decens?
question: Quali cultu dies Florae decens est, cum Cerialibus vestes albae dentur?
question_en: In what kind of dress is Flora's festival becomingly kept, whereas white clothes are given at the Cerialia?
derivation: The bright multicolored dress of the Floralia, contrasted with the white of the Cerialia (the white-at-Cerialia fact was taken in the liber IV file; the versicolor dress is the new fact). Answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: lumina restabant, quorum me causa latebat, cum sic errores abstulit illa meos: 'vel quia purpureis conlucent floribus agri, lumina sunt nostros visa decere dies; vel quia nec flos est hebeti nec flamma colore, atque oculos in se splendor uterque trahit; vel quia deliciis nocturna licentia nostris convenit: a vero tertia causa venit.'
question: Quae licentia deliciis Florae convenit, quam dea veram luminum suorum causam esse dicit?
question_en: What license suits Flora's delights - the cause the goddess calls the true reason for the lights at her festival?
derivation: Lights (lumina) mark Flora's days; of the three causes the goddess gives, she names the true one: nocturnal license suits her delights. The question targets that single flagged answer (a vero tertia causa venit), so it is verifiable.

author: Ovid
source_text: 'cur tibi pro Libycis clauduntur rete leaenis inbelles capreae sollicitusque lepus?' non sibi respondit silvas cessisse, sed hortos arvaque pugnaci non adeunda ferae.
question: Quae animalia ludis Florae pro Libycis leaenis rete clauduntur?
question_en: What animals are enclosed with nets at Flora's games instead of Libyan lionesses?
derivation: In Flora's circus hunts, harmless roe-deer and the timid hare replace wild beasts, because her domain is gardens and fields, not forests. Famous mild venatio of the Floralia; answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Pelion Haemoniae mons est obversus in Austros: summa virent pinu, cetera quercus habet. Phillyrides tenuit;
question: Quem montem Haemoniae Chiron Phillyrides tenuit?
question_en: Which mountain of Thessaly did Chiron, Philyra's son, inhabit?
derivation: Chiron's home on Mount Pelion in Thessaly (Haemonia) - canonical myth geography. Place-name answer verbatim; Chiron anchored by the patronymic Phillyrides.

author: Ovid
source_text: dumque senex tractat squalentia tela venenis, excidit et laevo fixa sagitta pede est. ingemuit Chiron, traxitque e corpore ferrum: adgemit Alcides Haemoniusque puer.
question: Quo telo Chiron centaurus volnus letale accepit?
answer: Sagitta Herculis, in pedem laevum lapsa.
question_en: By what weapon did the centaur Chiron receive his fatal wound?
answer_en: By Hercules' arrow, which fell on his left foot.
derivation: While handling Hercules' poison-crusted shafts, Chiron let one fall and it fixed in his left foot; the hydra's venom proved past cure. Canonical death of Chiron; supported verbatim (tela venenis... laevo fixa sagitta pede).

author: Ovid
source_text: stabat, ut ante patrem, lacrimis perfusus Achilles: sic flendus Peleus, si moreretur, erat. saepe manus aegras manibus fingebat amicis: morum, quos fecit, praemia doctor habet. oscula saepe dedit, dixit quoque saepe iacenti 'vive, precor, nec me, care, relinque, pater.'
question: Quis puer Chironem morientem tamquam patrem flevit, ab eo doctus?
question_en: Which boy wept for the dying Chiron as for a father, having been taught by him?
derivation: Achilles at Chiron's deathbed, calling his teacher 'father' - Chiron as the tutor of Achilles is shared myth (morum... doctor). Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: nona dies aderat, cum tu, iustissime Chiron, bis septem stellis corpora cinctus eras.
question: Quot stellis Chiron, inter sidera receptus, corpora cinctus est?
question_en: With how many stars was Chiron girt when he was received among the constellations?
derivation: On the ninth day Chiron became a constellation girt with twice seven stars. Number answer verbatim; parallel to the liber III pair on Ariadne's nine-star crown.

author: Ovid
source_text: ritus erit veteris, nocturna Lemuria, sacri: inferias tacitis manibus illa dabunt.
question: Quibus inferiae nocturnis Lemuribus dantur, ut Ovidius canit?
question_en: To whom are offerings made at the nocturnal Lemuria, as Ovid sings?
answer_en: To the silent shades of the dead (the Manes).
derivation: The Lemuria are night rites of the old order giving inferiae to the silent Manes. Festival-purpose fact, named rite; answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: nox ubi iam media est somnoque silentia praebet, et canis et variae conticuistis aves, ille memor veteris ritus timidusque deorum surgit (habent gemini vincula nulla pedes),
question: Quo pedum habitu et qua noctis hora surgit qui Lemuria rite facit?
question_en: In what state of foot and at what hour of the night does the performer of the Lemuria rise?
derivation: The householder rises at midnight with no bindings on his feet (habent gemini vincula nulla pedes) to perform the Lemuria. Rite detail carried by every reader of the famous passage; supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: signaque dat digitis medio cum pollice iunctis, occurrat tacito ne levis umbra sibi.
question: Quod signum digitis dat, ne umbra sibi occurrat, qui Lemuria nocte facit?
question_en: What sign does the celebrant of the Lemuria make with his fingers, lest a shade meet him?
answer_en: He joins his fingers with the thumb in their midst (the 'fig' sign).
derivation: The apotropaic finger-sign of the Lemuria: thumb thrust between the closed fingers. Gesture-fact verbatim; the gesture, not any Latin wordplay, is the content, so it translates.

author: Ovid
source_text: cumque manus puras fontana perluit unda, vertitur et nigras accipit ante fabas, aversusque iacit; sed dum iacit, 'haec ego mitto, his' inquit 'redimo meque meosque fabis.'
question: Cuius coloris fabas aversus iacit qui Lemuria facit?
question_en: Beans of what color does the performer of the Lemuria throw with face averted?
derivation: The black beans of the Lemuria, thrown behind the back after washing in spring water. The bean-and-ghost complex is criterion 8's home turf; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: aversusque iacit; sed dum iacit, 'haec ego mitto, his' inquit 'redimo meque meosque fabis.' hoc novies dicit nec respicit: umbra putatur colligere et nullo terga vidente sequi.
question: Quotiens inter Lemuria dicuntur verba 'haec ego mitto, his redimo meque meosque fabis'?
question_en: How many times during the Lemuria are the words 'these I send; with these beans I redeem me and mine' spoken?
derivation: The redemption formula spoken nine times without looking back, while the shade is thought to gather the beans unseen. Number answer verbatim (hoc novies dicit nec respicit).

author: Ovid
source_text: rursus aquam tangit, Temesaeaque concrepat aera, et rogat ut tectis exeat umbra suis.
question: Quid concrepat qui, Lemuribus sacra faciens, umbram tectis suis exire rogat?
question_en: What does the celebrant clash when, performing the Lemuria, he asks the shade to leave his house?
derivation: The clashing of bronze (from Temesa, famed for copper) to drive the ghost out. Rite-implement fact; answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: cum dixit novies 'manes exite paterni' respicit, et pure sacra peracta putat.
question: Quibus verbis novies dictis sacra Lemurum pure peracta putantur?
question_en: With what words, spoken nine times, are the rites of the Lemuria thought to be purely completed?
derivation: The ghost-banishing formula of the Lemuria, said nine times before the celebrant looks back. The formula itself is the famous fact; quoted verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Romulus ut tumulo fraternas condidit umbras, et male veloci iusta soluta Remo, Faustulus infelix et passis Acca capillis spargebant lacrimis ossa perusta suis; inde domum redeunt sub prima crepuscula maesti, utque erat, in duro procubuere toro. umbra cruenta Remi visa est adsistere lecto, atque haec exiguo murmure verba loqui:
question: Quibus umbra cruenta Remi noctu adstitisse dicitur?
question_en: To whom is the bloody ghost of Remus said to have appeared by night?
derivation: The aetiology of the Lemuria: Remus' bloody shade stood by the bed of Faustulus and Acca and asked for a day of honor. Two-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Romulus obsequitur, lucemque Remuria dicit illam, qua positis iusta feruntur avis. aspera mutata est in lenem tempore longo littera, quae toto nomine prima fuit; mox etiam lemures animas dixere silentum: hic sensus verbi, vis ea vocis erat.
question: Quo nomine Romulus diem manibus Remi sacrum appellavit, unde postea Lemuria dicta sunt?
question_en: What name did Romulus give the day sacred to Remus' shade, from which the Lemuria were later so called?
derivation: Ovid's aetiology: Romulus named the day Remuria for Remus, and in time the name became Lemuria. The fact asked is the original name, a translatable name-fact; the letter-change is background, not the answer.

author: Ovid
source_text: fana tamen veteres illis clausere diebus, ut nunc ferali tempore operta vides;
question: Quo statu fana deorum per dies Lemurum apud veteres erant?
question_en: In what state were the temples of the gods during the days of the Lemuria among the ancients?
derivation: The ancients closed the temples on the days of the Lemuria, as they are shut in the season of the dead. Distinct festival from the Parentalia closure taken in the liber II file; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: nec viduae taedis eadem nec virginis apta tempora: quae nupsit, non diuturna fuit. hac quoque de causa, si te proverbia tangunt, mense malas Maio nubere volgus ait.
question: Quo mense malas nubere volgus ait, ut proverbium apud Ovidium fert?
question_en: In what month does the common saying, as Ovid reports the proverb, declare that bad women marry?
derivation: The famous proverb against May weddings - 'mense malas Maio nubere volgus ait' - grounded in the Lemuria's ill-omened days. Proverb with a checkable point; month answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: sed tamen haec tria sunt sub eodem tempore festa inter se nulla continuata die.
question: Quot diebus, nullo inter se continuato, Lemuria aguntur?
question_en: On how many days, none of them consecutive, are the Lemuria held?
derivation: The Lemuria fall on three days at the same season, none adjoining another (May 9, 11, 13). Number answer verbatim (haec tria... festa inter se nulla continuata die).

author: Ovid
source_text: Iuppiter et lato qui regnat in aequore frater carpebant socias Mercuriusque vias; tempus erat quo versa iugo referuntur aratra, et pronus saturae lac bibit agnus ovis. forte senex Hyrieus, angusti cultor agelli, hos videt, exiguam stabat ut ante casam, atque ita 'longa via est, nec tempora longa supersunt', dixit 'et hospitibus ianua nostra patet.'
question: Quos tres deos senex Hyrieus hospitio accepit, antequam Orion ei nasceretur?
question_en: Which three gods did old Hyrieus receive as guests before Orion was born to him?
derivation: The birth-tale of Orion: Hyrieus hosted Jupiter, his brother who rules the wide sea (Neptune), and Mercury. Three-name answer; Neptune identified by the standard periphrasis in the quote.

author: Ovid
source_text: adnuerant omnes. omnes ad terga iuvenci constiterant—pudor est ulteriora loqui. tum superiniecta texere madentia terra: iamque decem menses, et puer ortus erat. hunc Hyrieus, quia sic genitus, vocat Uriona:
question: Quot post menses, corio iuvenci terra obruto, puer Orion ortus est?
question_en: After how many months, once the ox-hide had been buried in the earth, was the boy Orion born?
derivation: Orion born from the ox-hide the gods had used, buried and covered with earth, after ten months - granting Hyrieus a son without a wife. Number answer verbatim; the name-pun (Urion) is left aside as untranslatable.

author: Ovid
source_text: scorpion immisit Tellus: fuit impetus illi curva gemelliparae spicula ferre deae; obstitit Orion. Latona nitentibus astris addidit et 'meriti praemia' dixit 'habe.'
question: Cui bestiae, a Tellure immissae, Orion pro Latona obstitit?
question_en: What creature, sent by Tellus, did Orion block to protect Latona?
derivation: Orion's catasterism: he blocked the scorpion Tellus sent against Latona, and she set him among the stars as his reward. Single-beast answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Ultor ad ipse suos caelo descendit honores templaque in Augusto conspicienda foro.
question: Quo in foro templum Martis Ultoris conspicitur?
question_en: In which forum is the temple of Mars Ultor to be seen?
derivation: Mars Ultor's temple stands conspicuous in the Forum Augustum - the centerpiece of Augustan Rome. Named god with cult title, named place; verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: 'si mihi bellandi pater est Vestaeque sacerdos auctor, et ulcisci numen utrumque paro, Mars, ades et satia scelerato sanguine ferrum, stetque favor causa pro meliore tuus. templa feres et, me victore, vocaberis Ultor.' voverat, et fuso laetus ab hoste redit.
question: Quod cognomen Marti iuvenis Caesar vovit, cum patrem Vestaeque sacerdotem ulcisci pararet?
question_en: What cult title did the young Caesar vow to Mars when he prepared to avenge his father, the priest of Vesta?
derivation: The vow at Philippi: young Augustus promised Mars a temple and the name Ultor if victorious over his father's murderers. Single-title answer verbatim (vocaberis Ultor).

author: Ovid
source_text: signa, decus belli, Parthus Romana tenebat, Romanaeque aquilae signifer hostis erat; isque pudor mansisset adhuc, nisi fortibus armis Caesaris Ausoniae protegerentur opes. ille notas veteres et longi dedecus aevi sustulit: agnorunt signa recepta suos.
question: A quo populo Caesar Augustus signa Romana cum Crassis amissa recepit?
question_en: From what people did Caesar Augustus recover the Roman standards lost with the Crassi?
derivation: The Parthian who held the Roman standards and eagles was made to give them back by Caesar (20 BC) - Mars earned the name Ultor a second time. People-name answer verbatim (Parthus... signa recepta).

author: Ovid
source_text: sollemnes ludos Circo celebrate, Quirites: non visa est fortem scaena decere deum.
question: Quo loco ludi sollemnes Marti Ultori celebrantur, cum scaena fortem deum non deceat?
question_en: Where are the solemn games for Mars Ultor celebrated, since the stage was not thought to befit the strong god?
derivation: The games of Mars Ultor are circus games, not stage plays - the stage does not suit the warrior god. Venue answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Pliadas aspicies omnes totumque sororum agmen, ubi ante Idus nox erit una super: tum mihi non dubiis auctoribus incipit aestas, et tepidi finem tempora veris habent.
question: Quibus stellis omnibus conspectis incipit aestas, ut Ovidius non dubiis auctoribus tradit?
question_en: With the full appearance of which stars does summer begin, as Ovid records on sure authorities?
derivation: The famous calendar rule: when the whole troop of the Pleiades is seen, summer begins and warm spring ends. Shared Greco-Roman seasonal lore (the one star-rising that is proverbial); answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: taurus init caelum: te, Sidoni, Iuppiter implet, parsque tuum terrae tertia nomen habet.
question: Quae puella Sidonia, a Iove in tauri forma per mare vecta, nomen parti terrae tertiae dedit?
question_en: Which Sidonian girl, carried over the sea by Jupiter in the form of a bull, gave her name to a third part of the earth?
derivation: The catasterism of Taurus: Jupiter as bull bore the Sidonian girl whose name a third of the earth bears - Europa, identified beyond doubt by the continent-fact in the verse itself (parsque tuum terrae tertia nomen habet). Canonical name-answer, like the 'Trojan judge = Paris' precedent.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tum quoque priscorum Virgo simulacra virorum mittere roboreo scirpea ponte solet.
question: Qualia simulacra Virgo Vestalis de ponte roboreo in Tiberim mittere solet?
question_en: What kind of effigies does the Vestal Virgin customarily throw from the oaken bridge into the Tiber?
answer_en: Rush effigies of men of old (the Argei).
derivation: The rite of the Argei: the Vestal casts rush-woven images of ancient men from the wooden (Sublician) bridge in mid-May. Famous rite; answer verbatim (priscorum simulacra virorum... scirpea).

author: Ovid
source_text: templa tibi posuere patres spectantia Circum Idibus; ex illo est haec tibi festa dies.
question: Quo die mensis Maii patres Mercurio templum, Circum spectans, posuerunt?
question_en: On what day of May did the fathers found the temple of Mercury that looks toward the Circus?
derivation: Mercury's temple facing the Circus (Maximus) was dedicated on the Ides of May, whence that is his festival day. Date fact anchored to the named god and landmark; verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: est aqua Mercurii portae vicina Capenae; si iuvat expertis credere, numen habet.
question: Cui portae vicina est aqua Mercurii, quam mercatores petunt?
question_en: Near which gate is the water of Mercury, which the merchants seek out?
derivation: The spring called aqua Mercurii lies near the Porta Capena and is held to have divine power. Named landmark, place answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: huc venit incinctus tunica mercator et urna purus suffita, quam ferat, haurit aquam. uda fit hinc laurus, lauro sparguntur ab uda omnia quae dominos sunt habitura novos.
question: Qua re mercator merces suas, dominos novos habituras, aqua Mercurii spargit?
question_en: With what does the merchant sprinkle his wares, destined for new owners, using Mercury's water?
derivation: The merchant's purification on Mercury's day: laurel dipped in the aqua Mercurii is sprinkled over all goods that will change owners. Rite-implement answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: 'ablue praeteriti periuria temporis', inquit 'ablue praeteritae perfida verba die.
question: Quid mercator aqua Mercurii ablui sibi precatur?
question_en: What does the merchant pray to have washed away by Mercury's water?
derivation: The merchant's notorious prayer: wash away my past perjuries and treacherous words. Short-phrase answer verbatim; culturally salient satire of trade morals.

author: Ovid
source_text: da modo lucra mihi, da facto gaudia lucro, et fac ut emptori verba dedisse iuvet.'
question: Quid mercator, periuriis ablutis, sibi dari a Mercurio poscit?
question_en: What does the merchant, his perjuries washed away, demand that Mercury give him?
answer_en: Profits (and joy in cheating the buyer).
derivation: The climax of the prayer: 'da modo lucra mihi' - and let it be a pleasure to have duped the buyer. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: talia Mercurius poscenti ridet ab alto, se memor Ortygias subripuisse boves.
question: Quas boves Mercurius se subripuisse meminit, cum precanti mercatori ridet?
question_en: What cattle does Mercury remember having stolen, as he laughs at the praying merchant?
derivation: Mercury laughs at perjured merchants because he himself stole the Ortygian (Delian, i.e. Apollo's) cattle - the canonical cattle-theft of the infant god. Answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: abstulerant raptas Phoeben Phoebesque sororem Tyndaridae fratres, hic eques, ille pugil. bella parant repetuntque suas et frater et Idas, Leucippo fieri pactus uterque gener.
question: Quas puellas Tyndaridae fratres rapuerunt, Idae fratrique eius pactas?
question_en: Which girls did the Tyndarid brothers carry off, though pledged to Idas and his brother?
answer_en: Phoebe and her sister, the daughters of Leucippus.
derivation: The rape of the Leucippides by Castor and Pollux, which brought on the fight with Idas and Lynceus. Named parties on all sides; answer supported verbatim (Phoeben Phoebesque sororem... Leucippo... gener).

author: Ovid
source_text: pectora traiectus Lynceo Castor ab ense non exspectato volnere pressit humum;
question: Cuius ense Castor, pectora traiectus, occubuit?
question_en: By whose sword did Castor fall, pierced through the breast?
derivation: Castor slain by Lynceus' sword in the battle at Aphidna. Single-name answer verbatim (Lynceo... ab ense).

author: Ovid
source_text: iamque tibi, Pollux, caelum sublime patebat, cum "mea" dixisti "percipe verba, pater: quod mihi das uni caelum, partire duobus; dimidium toto munere maius erit." dixit et alterna fratrem statione redemit:
question: Quo pacto Pollux fratrem Castorem a morte redemit?
question_en: By what arrangement did Pollux redeem his brother Castor from death?
answer_en: By dividing his own heaven with him, in alternating turns.
derivation: Pollux asked Jupiter to split his sole immortality between the two, and redeemed his brother 'alterna statione' - the shared alternating divinity of the Dioscuri. Brief-phrase answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Proxima Volcani lux est, Tubilustria dicunt: lustrantur purae, quas facit ille, tubae.
question: Cuius dei est lux Tubilustriorum mense Maio, qua tubae lustrantur?
question_en: To which god belongs the day of the Tubilustria in May, on which the trumpets are purified?
derivation: The May Tubilustrium is Vulcan's day: the pure trumpets, which he makes, are purified. Distinct from the March Tubilustrium taken in the liber III file (there tied to Minerva's Quinquatrus); god-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: ne tamen ignores volgique errore traharis, Iunius a nostro nomine nomen habet.
question: Quae dea Iunium mensem a suo nomine nomen habere apud Ovidium adfirmat?
question_en: Which goddess asserts in Ovid that the month of June takes its name from her own?
derivation: The month-name debate of the proem: the question asks only the checkable fact - that Juno is the goddess who lays claim to June - not which etymology is correct (Ovid leaves the crux unresolved). The speaker of the quoted line is Juno.

author: Ovid
source_text: si genus aspicitur, Saturnum prima parentem feci, Saturni sors ego prima fui.
question: Cuius dei filia Iuno est, cuius se primam sortem fuisse gloriatur?
question_en: Of which god is Juno the daughter, boasting that she was his first-born lot?
derivation: Juno as Saturn's first child - the ground of her epithet Saturnia. Canonical genealogy; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: a patre dicta meo quondam Saturnia Roma est: haec illi a caelo proxima terra fuit.
question: Quo nomine Roma quondam a Saturno dicta est, ut Iuno apud Ovidium refert?
question_en: By what name was Rome once called after Saturn, as Juno relates in Ovid?
derivation: The old name Saturnia for the site of Rome, the first land Saturn reached after heaven. Complements (without repeating) the liber I pair on Latium named from Saturn's hiding; name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: causa duplex irae: rapto Ganymede dolebam, forma quoque Idaeo iudice victa mea est.
question: Quae duplex causa irae Iunonis in Dardaniam domum fuit?
answer: Ganymedes raptus et forma iudice Idaeo victa.
question_en: What was the twofold cause of Juno's anger against the Dardanian house?
answer_en: The rape of Ganymede and her beauty's defeat before the Idaean judge (Paris).
derivation: Juno's own statement of her two grievances against Troy: Ganymede carried off, and losing the beauty-judgment of Paris. Canonical shared myth; two-part answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: inspice quos habeat nemoralis Aricia fastos et populus Laurens Lanuviumque meum: est illic mensis Iunonius.
question: Quo nomine mensis in fastis Ariciae, populi Laurentis Lanuviique appellatur, ut Iuno testatur?
question_en: What is a month called in the calendars of Aricia, the Laurentine people, and Lanuvium, as Juno attests?
derivation: The neighboring Latin towns' calendars have a month Junonius - Juno's evidence in the name-debate. A checkable calendar fact of Latium; name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: populum digessit ab annis Romulus, in partes distribuitque duas; haec dare consilium, pugnare paratior illa est, haec aetas bellum suadet, at illa gerit. sic statuit, mensesque nota secrevit eadem: Iunius est iuvenum; qui fuit ante, senum.
question: In quot partes Romulus populum ab annis digessit?
question_en: Into how many parts did Romulus divide the people by age?
answer_en: Into two: the elders and the young.
derivation: Romulus' division of the people into two age-classes - the elders to counsel, the young to fight. Institutional fact anchored to Romulus; number answer verbatim (in partes... duas; iuvenum... senum).

author: Ovid
source_text: Prima dies tibi, Carna, datur. dea cardinis haec est: numine clausa aperit, claudit aperta suo.
question: Cui deae prima dies mensis Iunii data est?
question_en: To which goddess is the first day of June given?
derivation: The Kalends of June belong to Carna. Calendar fact, named goddess; verbatim (prima dies tibi, Carna, datur).

author: Ovid
source_text: Prima dies tibi, Carna, datur. dea cardinis haec est: numine clausa aperit, claudit aperta suo.
question: Cuius rei dea est Carna, quae clausa aperit et aperta claudit?
question_en: Of what is Carna the goddess, she who opens what is closed and closes what is open?
derivation: Carna as dea cardinis, the hinge-goddess of doorways. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: adiacet antiquus Tiberino lucus Alerni: pontifices illuc nunc quoque sacra ferunt.
question: In quem lucum, Tiberi adiacentem, pontifices nunc quoque sacra ferunt, ut Ovidius refert?
question_en: To what grove beside the Tiber do the pontiffs still bring sacred rites, as Ovid reports?
derivation: The ancient grove of Alernus by the Tiber, still served by the pontiffs in Ovid's day - a public state cult, less celebrated but citywide, exactly the merely-verifiable shared fact the bar admits. Named place answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: inde sata est nymphe (Cranaen dixere priores) nequiquam multis saepe petita procis.
question: Quo nomine priores nympham dixerunt quae postea dea Carna facta est?
question_en: By what name did earlier generations call the nymph who afterwards became the goddess Carna?
derivation: Carna's earlier identity as the nymph Cranae, born by the grove of Alernus. Name answer verbatim (Cranaen dixere priores).

author: Ovid
source_text: stulta! videt Ianus quae post sua terga gerantur: nil agis, et latebras respicit ille tuas. nil agis, en! dixi: nam te sub rupe latentem occupat amplexu, speque potitus ait 'ius pro concubitu nostro tibi cardinis esto: hoc pretium positae virginitatis habe.'
question: Quod ius Ianus nymphae Cranae pro concubitu dedit?
question_en: What right did Janus give the nymph Cranae as the price of their union?
derivation: Janus, who sees what happens behind his back, caught the hiding nymph and granted her the ius cardinis - the aetiology of Carna's power over hinges. Short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: sic fatus spinam, qua tristes pellere posset a foribus noxas (haec erat alba) dedit.
question: Qualem spinam Ianus Carnae dedit, qua noxas tristes a foribus pelleret?
question_en: What kind of thorn did Janus give Carna to drive baleful harm from doorways?
derivation: The whitethorn (spina alba) given by Janus, the apotropaic branch against harm at the door - key to the striges-rite below. Answer verbatim (haec erat alba).

author: Ovid
source_text: nocte volant puerosque petunt nutricis egentes, et vitiant cunis corpora rapta suis; carpere dicuntur lactentia viscera rostris, et plenum poto sanguine guttur habent.
question: Quos striges, aves nocturnae, petere dicuntur?
question_en: Whom are the striges, the night-flying birds, said to attack?
answer_en: Infant children left without their nurse.
derivation: The strix-belief: night birds that seize unguarded infants from their cradles and tear their milk-fed innards. The screech-owl bogey is proverbial Roman folklore; answer verbatim (pueros... nutricis egentes).

author: Ovid
source_text: in thalamos venere Procae: Proca natus in illis praeda recens avium quinque diebus erat,
question: Quem regem infantem, quinque dies natum, striges praedam petiverunt?
question_en: Which future king, five days old, did the striges attack as fresh prey?
derivation: The victim of the striges in the aetiological tale is the infant Proca (the Alban king). Named person, with the five-day detail anchoring; verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: spargit aquis aditus (et aquae medicamen habebant) extaque de porca cruda bimenstre tenet, atque ita 'noctis aves, extis puerilibus' inquit 'parcite: pro parvo victima parva cadit. cor pro corde, precor, pro fibris sumite fibras: hanc animam vobis pro meliore damus.'
question: Cuius animalis exta strigibus pro extis puerilibus dantur, cum infans defenditur?
question_en: The entrails of what animal are given to the striges in place of the child's, when an infant is protected?
derivation: The substitution rite against the striges: raw entrails of a young sow offered with the formula 'heart for heart, fibres for fibres.' Answer verbatim (extaque de porca cruda bimenstre).

author: Ovid
source_text: virgaque Ianalis de spina subditur alba, qua lumen thalamis parva fenestra dabat.
question: Qualis virga fenestrae subditur, quae cunas infantis a strigibus tueatur?
question_en: What kind of rod is set at the window to guard the infant's cradle from the striges?
derivation: The close of the Proca rite: the whitethorn rod of Janus placed where the little window gave light - after which the birds harmed the cradle no more. Answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Pinguia cur illis gustentur larda Kalendis mixtaque cum calido sit faba farre rogas?
question: Qui cibi Kalendis Iuniis, die deae Carnae, gustantur?
answer: Larda pinguia et faba cum calido farre mixta.
question_en: What foods are tasted on the Kalends of June, the day of the goddess Carna?
answer_en: Fat bacon and beans mixed with hot spelt.
derivation: The meal of the Kalends of June (the 'bean Kalends'): fat bacon and bean-and-spelt mash, because Carna is an old goddess fed on the foods of former times. Food-fact verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: quae duo mixta simul sextis quicumque Kalendis ederit, huic laedi viscera posse negant.
question: Quid ei negant posse accidere qui fabam farri mixtam Kalendis Iuniis ederit?
question_en: What do they say cannot happen to one who eats beans mixed with spelt on the Kalends of June?
derivation: The folk-belief attached to the Kalendae fabariae: eating the two mixed foods on the sixth Kalends protects the viscera. Criterion 8's home ground; short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Arce quoque in summa Iunoni templa Monetae ex voto memorant facta, Camille, tuo.
question: Ex cuius voto templum Iunonis Monetae in summa arce factum esse memorant?
question_en: From whose vow do they record that the temple of Juno Moneta on the summit of the citadel was built?
derivation: Juno Moneta's temple on the Arx built from the vow of Camillus. Named founder and named cult; verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: ante domus Manli fuerat, qui Gallica quondam a Capitolino reppulit arma Iove.
question: Cuius viri domus ante in arce fuerat, ubi templum Monetae stat, qui Gallica arma a Iove Capitolino reppulit?
question_en: Whose house had earlier stood on the citadel where Moneta's temple stands - the man who drove the Gallic arms back from Capitoline Jupiter?
derivation: The site of Juno Moneta was the razed house of Manlius (Capitolinus), the defender of the Capitol against the Gauls. Name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: quam bene, di magni, pugna cecidisset in illa defensor solii, Iuppiter alte, tui! vixit, ut occideret damnatus crimine regni: hunc illi titulum longa senecta dabat.
question: Quo crimine damnatus Manlius, Capitolii defensor, occidit?
question_en: Condemned on what charge did Manlius, the defender of the Capitol, die?
answer_en: On the charge of aiming at kingship.
derivation: Manlius Capitolinus lived on only to die condemned on the charge of regnum - the celebrated reversal. Short answer verbatim (damnatus crimine regni).

author: Ovid
source_text: Lux eadem Marti festa est, quem prospicit extra adpositum Tectae porta Capena Viae.
question: Extra quam portam situm est templum Martis, Viae Tectae adpositum, cui Kalendae Iuniae festae sunt?
question_en: Outside which gate stands the temple of Mars beside the Via Tecta, whose festival falls on the Kalends of June?
derivation: The old temple of Mars extra portam Capenam, which the gate looks out upon beside the Covered Way; its day is June 1. Named landmark; verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: te quoque, Tempestas, meritam delubra fatemur, cum paene est Corsis obruta classis aquis.
question: Quibus in aquis classis Romana paene obruta est, unde dea Tempestas delubra merita est?
question_en: In what waters was the Roman fleet almost overwhelmed, whereby the goddess Tempestas earned her shrine?
derivation: The shrine of Tempestas vowed when the fleet was nearly lost off Corsica (Scipio's vow, 259 BC). Named goddess, named waters; verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: hac sacrata die Tusco Bellona duello dicitur, et Latio prospera semper adest. Appius est auctor, Pyrrho qui pace negata multum animo vidit
question: Quis auctor fuit templi Bellonae, Tusco duello sacrati?
question_en: Who was the founder of the temple of Bellona, consecrated in the Etruscan war?
answer_en: Appius (Claudius), the man who refused peace to Pyrrhus.
derivation: Bellona's temple vowed in the Tuscan war by Appius Claudius (Caecus), identified in the verse as the blind senator who denied Pyrrhus peace. Name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: prospicit a templo summum brevis area Circum: est ibi non parvae parva columna notae; hinc solet hasta manu, belli praenuntia, mitti, in regem et gentes cum placet arma capi.
question: Unde hasta, belli praenuntia, mitti solet, cum in regem et gentes arma capi placet?
answer: A parva columna ante templum Bellonae.
question_en: From where is the spear that heralds war customarily thrown, when it is resolved to take arms against a king or a people?
answer_en: From the little column before the temple of Bellona.
derivation: The columna bellica by Bellona's temple, from which the war-declaring spear is cast - the fetial rite in its later form. Landmark answer verbatim (parva columna... hinc solet hasta... mitti).

author: Ovid
source_text: Altera pars Circi Custode sub Hercule tuta est, quod deus Euboico carmine munus habet. muneris est tempus qui Nonas Lucifer ante est; si titulum quaeris, Sulla probavit opus.
question: Quis, ut titulus docet, opus aedis Herculis Custodis probavit?
question_en: Who, as the inscription records, approved the work of the temple of Hercules Custos?
derivation: Hercules Custos guards part of the Circus (Flaminius), an office assigned by the Euboean (Sibylline) verses; the inscription names Sulla. Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Quaerebam Nonas Sanco Fidione referrem an tibi, Semo pater; tum mihi Sancus ait: 'cuicumque ex istis dederis, ego munus habebo: nomina terna fero: sic voluere Cures.'
question: Quot nomina deus Sancus se ferre apud Ovidium dicit?
question_en: How many names does the god Sancus say he bears, in Ovid?
derivation: Semo Sancus Dius Fidius: the god himself declares he bears three names, as the men of Cures willed. Number-plus-names answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: hunc igitur veteres donarunt aede Sabini, inque Quirinali constituere iugo.
question: Quo in iugo veteres Sabini deo Sanco aedem constituerunt?
question_en: On which hill did the old Sabines establish the temple of the god Sancus?
derivation: The Sabines gave Sancus his temple on the Quirinal ridge (dedication day the Nones of June). Place answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: nam mihi sic coniunx sancta Dialis ait: 'donec ab Iliaca placidus purgamina Vesta detulerit flavis in mare Thybris aquis, non mihi detonso crinem depectere buxo, non ungues ferro subsecuisse licet, non tetigisse virum, quamvis Iovis ille sacerdos, quamvis perpetua sit mihi lege datus.
question: Quid Thybris in mare deferre debet, antequam flaminicae Diali crinem depectere, ungues secare, virum tangere liceat?
question_en: What must the Tiber carry down to the sea before the flaminica Dialis may comb her hair, cut her nails, or touch her husband?
derivation: The flaminica Dialis' own rule, told to Ovid: until the purgamina of Ilian Vesta go down the Tiber to the sea (June 15), she must not comb with the boxwood, cut nails with iron, or touch her husband though he is Jupiter's priest. Short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: tum mihi post sacras monstratus Iunius Idus utilis et nuptis, utilis esse viris, primaque pars huius thalamis aliena reperta est;
question: Quae pars mensis Iunii thalamis aliena reperta est?
question_en: What part of the month of June was found unsuited to marriage?
answer_en: The first part, before the sacred Ides.
derivation: Wedding-calendar lore: June is good for brides and husbands only after the sacred Ides; its first part is alien to the marriage-bed. Companion to the May proverb taken from liber V; answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: tunc ego me memini ludos in gramine Campi aspicere et dici, lubrice Thybri, tuos. festa dies illis qui lina madentia ducunt, quique tegunt parvis aera recurva cibis.
question: Quorum hominum festa dies est, cum ludi Tiberis in gramine Campi aguntur?
question_en: For what men is it a festival day, when the games of the Tiber are held on the grass of the Campus?
answer_en: For the fishermen, who draw the dripping nets.
derivation: The ludi piscatorii: the Tiber's games on the Campus are the holiday of those who draw wet nets and bait the curved bronze hooks - the fishermen's guild. Answer supported by the defining verbatim periphrasis.

author: Ovid
source_text: Mens quoque numen habet: Mentis delubra videmus vota metu belli, perfide Poene, tui. Poene, rebellaras, et leto consulis omnes attoniti Mauras pertimuere manus. spem metus expulerat, cum Menti vota senatus suscipit, et melior protinus illa venit.
question: Quo metu senatus delubra deae Menti vovit?
question_en: Out of fear of what did the senate vow a shrine to the goddess Mens?
answer_en: Out of fear of the Punic war.
derivation: The shrine of Mens vowed by the senate in the terror after a consul's death in the Punic war (Flaminius at Trasimene, 217 BC). Short answer verbatim (vota metu belli... Poene... vota senatus suscipit).

author: Ovid
source_text: dena quater memorant habuisse Parilia Romam, cum flammae custos aede recepta dea est,
question: Quot Parilia Roma habuisse memoratur, cum Vesta, flammae custos, aede recepta est?
question_en: How many Parilia (birthdays) is Rome recorded to have kept when Vesta, guardian of the flame, was received in her temple?
derivation: Rome was forty years old (forty Parilia) when Vesta's temple was founded. Number answer verbatim (dena quater... Parilia).

author: Ovid
source_text: regis opus placidi, quo non metuentius ullum numinis ingenium terra Sabina tulit. quae nunc aere vides, stipula tum tecta videres, et paries lento vimine textus erat. hic locus exiguus, qui sustinet Atria Vestae, tunc erat intonsi regia magna Numae;
question: Cuius regis opus fuit prima aedes Vestae?
question_en: Of which king was the first temple of Vesta the work?
derivation: Vesta's temple as the work of the god-fearing Sabine king, whose great palace stood where the Atria Vestae now are - Numa, named in the quoted lines. Single-name answer.

author: Ovid
source_text: quae nunc aere vides, stipula tum tecta videres, et paries lento vimine textus erat.
question: Quibus rebus prima aedes Vestae tecta et saepta erat?
question_en: With what was the first temple of Vesta roofed and walled?
answer_en: Roofed with straw, its wall woven of pliant wattle.
derivation: The antiquarian contrast: what is now bronze was once thatch and wattle - the primitive temple of Vesta. Two-item answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Vesta eadem est et terra: subest vigil ignis utrique: significant sedem terra focusque suam.
question: Cui rei eandem esse Vestam Ovidius docet?
question_en: With what does Ovid teach that Vesta is identical?
derivation: The theological identification Vesta = terra, both with the watchful fire beneath. This equation grounds the round temple and the punishment of the unchaste priestess later in the book; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: et quantum a summis, tantum secessit ab imis terra; quod ut fiat forma rotunda facit. par facies templi; nullus procurrit in illo angulus, a pluvio vindicat imbre tholus.
question: Qua forma est templum Vestae, cui nullus angulus procurrit?
question_en: Of what shape is the temple of Vesta, from which no corner juts out?
derivation: The round temple of Vesta mirrors the round earth (par facies templi), with its dome and no corners. Shape answer verbatim (forma rotunda... par facies templi).

author: Ovid
source_text: ex Ope Iunonem memorant Cereremque creatas semine Saturni; tertia Vesta fuit.
question: Quae tres deae ex Ope semine Saturni creatae esse memorantur?
question_en: Which three goddesses are recorded to have been born of Ops by the seed of Saturn?
derivation: The three daughters of Ops and Saturn, with Vesta the third. Canonical genealogy; three-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: ex Ope Iunonem memorant Cereremque creatas semine Saturni; tertia Vesta fuit. utraque nupserunt, ambae peperisse feruntur; de tribus impatiens restitit una viri.
question: Quae de tribus Saturni filiabus sola, impatiens viri, virgo restitit?
question_en: Which of Saturn's three daughters alone remained a virgin, refusing a husband?
derivation: Of the three sisters, the other two married and bore children; Vesta alone withstood a husband - why virgins serve her. Single-name answer supported verbatim (tertia Vesta... restitit una).

author: Ovid
source_text: esse diu stultus Vestae simulacra putavi, mox didici curvo nulla subesse tholo. ignis inexstinctus templo celatur in illo: effigiem nullam Vesta nec ignis habet.
question: Quot simulacra Vestae sub curvo tholo templi eius sunt, ut Ovidius tandem didicit?
question_en: How many statues of Vesta stand beneath the curved dome of her temple, as Ovid at last learned?
derivation: The famous fact that Vesta's temple holds no cult statue - Ovid confesses he long believed otherwise. One-word answer verbatim (nulla subesse... effigiem nullam).

author: Ovid
source_text: ignis inexstinctus templo celatur in illo: effigiem nullam Vesta nec ignis habet.
question: Quid in templo Vestae pro effigie celatur?
question_en: What is kept hidden in the temple of Vesta in place of any image?
derivation: The undying fire concealed within Vesta's temple, itself without effigy - the hearth as the goddess. Answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: venit in hos annos aliquid de more vetusto: fert missos Vestae pura patella cibos.
question: Cui deae, de more vetusto, pura patella cibos missos fert?
question_en: To which goddess, by ancient custom, does a clean dish carry the food that is sent?
derivation: A surviving table-custom: food sent to Vesta on a clean patella, relic of the age when the hearth was the gods' seat at meals. Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Ecce coronatis panis dependet asellis, et velant scabras florida serta molas.
question: Quibus animalibus coronatis panis festo Vestae die dependet?
question_en: From what garlanded animals does bread hang on Vesta's festival day?
derivation: The signature image of the Vestalia: loaves hung on garlanded asses, flower wreaths veiling the rough millstones. Answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: inde focum servat pistor dominamque focorum et quae pumiceas versat asella molas.
question: Quis opifex focum dominamque focorum Vestalibus colit?
question_en: Which craftsman honors the hearth and the mistress of hearths at the Vestalia?
derivation: The Vestalia as the holiday of the pistores: the baker keeps the hearth, the mistress of hearths (Vesta), and the she-ass that turns the pumice mills. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: forte senex, quo vectus erat, Silenus asellum liquerat ad ripas lene sonantis aquae; ibat ut inciperet longi deus Hellesponti, intempestivo cum rudit ille sono. territa voce gravi surgit dea; convolat omnis turba, per infestas effugit ille manus.
question: Cuius animalis voce Vesta dormiens a Priapo servata est?
question_en: By the voice of what animal was the sleeping Vesta saved from Priapus?
answer_en: Of the little ass on which Silenus had ridden.
derivation: The aetiology of the ass's honor at the Vestalia: Silenus' ass brayed at the wrong moment and woke Vesta as the god of the Hellespont (Priapus) crept up. Distinct from the Lotis version taken from liber I; answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: quem tu, diva, memor de pane monilibus ornas; cessat opus, vacuae conticuere molae.
question: Quo statu molae sunt die Vestae, cum asellus panis monilibus ornatur?
question_en: In what state are the mills on Vesta's day, when the ass is adorned with necklaces of bread?
derivation: The millers' holiday: Vesta, mindful, adorns the ass with bread-necklaces, work stops, the mills fall silent. Short answer verbatim (cessat opus, vacuae conticuere molae).

author: Ovid
source_text: Nomine quam pretio celebratior arce Tonantis dicam Pistoris quid velit ara Iovis.
question: Quo in loco stat ara Iovis Pistoris?
question_en: Where does the altar of Jupiter Pistor stand?
answer_en: On the citadel of the Thunderer (the Capitol).
derivation: The altar of Jupiter Pistor ('the Baker') on the Capitoline citadel, better known by its name than its cost. Place answer verbatim (arce Tonantis).

author: Ovid
source_text: somnus abit, quaeruntque, novis ambagibus acti, tradere quam nolint et iubeantur opem. esse Ceres visa est; iaciunt Cerialia dona: iacta super galeas scutaque longa sonant.
question: Quid Romani, in Capitolio a Gallis obsessi, Iove monente in hostes iecerunt?
question_en: What did the Romans, besieged on the Capitol by the Gauls, throw down upon the enemy at Jupiter's prompting?
answer_en: The gifts of Ceres (loaves of bread).
derivation: The famous stratagem behind Jupiter Pistor: the besieged threw their bread onto the Gauls' helmets and shields, killing the hope of starving them out. Answer verbatim (iaciunt Cerialia dona).

author: Ovid
source_text: posse fame vinci spes excidit: hoste repulso candida Pistori ponitur ara Iovi.
question: Cui Iovi candida ara posita est, hoste Gallico repulso?
question_en: To Jupiter under what title was the white altar set up, once the Gallic enemy was repulsed?
derivation: The cult title Pistor earned by the bread-stratagem: the shining altar set up when the enemy was driven off. Title answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Forte revertebar festis Vestalibus illa quae Nova Romano nunc Via iuncta foro est: huc pede matronam nudo descendere vidi;
question: Quo pede matrona festis Vestalibus per Novam Viam descendit, ut Ovidius ipse vidit?
question_en: With what kind of foot did Ovid himself see a matron descending by the Nova Via at the festival of Vesta?
derivation: The barefoot descent of matrons to Vesta's shrine at the Vestalia, an old custom surviving from the marshland days (mos tamen ille manet). Eyewitness rite-fact; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: hoc, ubi nunc fora sunt, udae tenuere paludes; amne redundatis fossa madebat aquis.
question: Quid olim fuit ubi nunc fora Romana sunt, ut anus apud Ovidium narrat?
question_en: What was once there, where the Roman fora now are, as the old woman tells in Ovid?
derivation: Shared antiquarian knowledge of the city: the ground of the fora was once marsh flooded by the river. Short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Curtius ille lacus, siccas qui sustinet aras, nunc solida est tellus, sed lacus ante fuit;
question: Quid ante fuit Curtius ille lacus, qui nunc solida tellus est et siccas aras sustinet?
question_en: What was the Lacus Curtius formerly, which is now solid ground bearing dry altars?
derivation: The Lacus Curtius in the Forum, now dry land with altars, was once a real lake. Famous landmark; answer verbatim (lacus ante fuit).

author: Ovid
source_text: creditur armiferae signum caeleste Minervae urbis in Iliacae desiluisse iuga. cura videre fuit: vidi templumque locumque; hoc superest illi, Pallada Roma tenet.
question: Cuius deae signum caeleste in iuga urbis Iliacae desiluisse creditur?
question_en: The heavenly image of which goddess is believed to have leapt down onto the heights of the Trojan city?
derivation: The Palladium: the heaven-sent image of armed Minerva that fell on Ilus' new city - and which Rome now holds (Pallada Roma tenet). Name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: 'aetheriam servate deam, servabitis urbem: imperium secum transferet illa loci.'
question: Quid signum caeleste Minervae secum transferre Smintheus vaticinatus est?
question_en: What did Apollo Smintheus prophesy that the heavenly image of Minerva would carry with it?
derivation: The oracle on the Palladium: keep the goddess and you keep the city, for she transfers empire with her - the doctrine that made the Palladium Rome's pledge of rule. Short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: auctor in incerto, res est Romana: tuetur Vesta, quod assiduo lumine cuncta videt.
question: Quae dea Romae Palladium tuetur, quod assiduo lumine cuncta videt?
question_en: Which goddess guards the Palladium at Rome, because she sees all things by her unfailing light?
derivation: Whoever stole it from Troy, the thing is now Roman and Vesta guards it - the Palladium kept in Vesta's temple. Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: provolat in medium, et magna 'succurrite' voce, 'non est auxilium flere' Metellus ait. 'pignora virgineis fatalia tollite palmis: non ea sunt voto, sed rapienda manu.
question: Quis, ardente aede Vestae, pignora fatalia e flammis eripienda curavit?
question_en: Who, when the temple of Vesta was burning, saw to it that the fateful pledges were snatched from the flames?
derivation: The fire of 241 BC: the pontifex maximus Metellus rushed in, bade the Vestals seize the fatal pledges, and himself broke in and saved the sacra (dixit, et inrupit... pontificisque sui munere tuta fuit). Celebrated exemplum; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: nullaque dicetur vittas temerasse sacerdos hoc duce, nec viva defodietur humo: sic incesta perit, quia, quam violavit, in illam conditur: est Tellus Vestaque numen idem.
question: Quo supplicio sacerdos Vestae incesta perire solet?
question_en: By what punishment does an unchaste priestess of Vesta die?
answer_en: She is buried alive in the earth.
derivation: The famous penalty of the unchaste Vestal: burial alive, because she is laid into the very deity she violated - Tellus and Vesta being one. Answer verbatim (viva defodietur humo... in illam conditur).

author: Ovid
source_text: Tum sibi Callaico Brutus cognomen ab hoste fecit et Hispanam sanguine tinxit humum.
question: Unde Brutus, Hispana humo sanguine tincta, cognomen sibi fecit?
question_en: From what did Brutus, having stained the Spanish soil with blood, win his cognomen?
derivation: Decimus Iunius Brutus took the cognomen Callaicus from the conquered Callaeci of Spain. Name-origin fact stated verbatim; translatable because the fact is the victory-title, not wordplay.

author: Ovid
source_text: Crassus ad Euphraten aquilas natumque suosque perdidit, et leto est ultimus ipse datus.
question: Ad quod flumen Crassus aquilas natumque suosque perdidit?
question_en: At what river did Crassus lose his eagles, his son, and his men?
derivation: The disaster of Carrhae dated to this day: Crassus lost the eagles, his son, and his army at the Euphrates, and died last himself. River answer verbatim; the standards' recovery is a separate pair in the liber V file.

author: Ovid
source_text: ite, bonae matres (vestrum Matralia festum), flavaque Thebanae reddite liba deae.
question: Quarum festum sunt Matralia?
question_en: Whose festival is the Matralia?
derivation: The Matralia (June 11) as the festival of the bonae matres, the respectable married women. Festival-owner fact verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: ite, bonae matres (vestrum Matralia festum), flavaque Thebanae reddite liba deae.
question: Quid bonae matres Matralibus Thebanae deae reddunt?
question_en: What do the good mothers offer to the Theban goddess at the Matralia?
derivation: The offering of the Matralia: yellow (toasted) liba to the Theban goddess (Ino/Mater Matuta) - libaque tosta at 6.482 confirms they are toasted. Food-offering answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: pontibus et magno iuncta est celeberrima Circo area, quae posito de bove nomen habet.
question: Unde nomen habet area celeberrima, magno Circo iuncta, in qua Matuta colitur?
question_en: From what does the much-frequented area joined to the great Circus, where Matuta is worshipped, take its name?
answer_en: From the ox set up there (the Forum Boarium, the Cattle Market).
derivation: The site of Matuta's temple: the famous area named from the ox - the Forum Boarium. Place-name aetiology stated verbatim; translatable as a landmark fact.

author: Ovid
source_text: hac ibi luce ferunt Matutae sacra parenti sceptriferas Servi templa dedisse manus.
question: Cuius regis manus templa Matri Matutae dedisse feruntur?
question_en: The scepter-bearing hands of which king are said to have dedicated the temple to Mother Matuta?
derivation: Servius Tullius as dedicator of Mater Matuta's temple in the Forum Boarium on this day. King-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: quae dea sit, quare famulas a limine templi arceat (arcet enim) libaque tosta petat,
question: Quas Mater Matuta a limine templi sui arcet?
question_en: Whom does Mother Matuta bar from the threshold of her temple?
derivation: The exclusion of slave-women from the Matralia (arcet enim, Ovid insists). The aetiology: a slave-girl was her husband Athamas' secret love and betrayed the toasted-seed trick (6.551-558) - the roasted-seed fact itself was already taken from liber III. Answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: arserat obsequio Semele Iovis: accipit Ino te, puer, et summa sedula nutrit ope.
question: Quae soror Semeles puerum Bacchum accepit et sedula nutrivit?
question_en: Which sister of Semele took in the boy Bacchus and diligently nursed him?
derivation: Ino as nurse of the infant Bacchus after Semele's fiery death - the start of the Matralia's founding myth. Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: hinc agitur furiis Athamas et imagine falsa, tuque cadis patria, parve Learche, manu;
question: Cuius manu parvus Learchus cecidit?
question_en: By whose hand did little Learchus fall?
derivation: Athamas, driven mad by the Furies and a false vision, killed his son Learchus. Canonical myth; answer verbatim (patria... manu, Athamas named in the couplet).

author: Ovid
source_text: adpulerat ripae vaccas Oetaeus Hiberas; audit, et ad vocem concitus urget iter: Herculis adventu quae vim modo ferre parabant turpia femineae terga dedere fugae.
question: Cuius adventu maenades Ausoniae, Inoni vim parantes, in fugam versae sunt?
question_en: At whose arrival were the Ausonian maenads, preparing violence against Ino, turned to flight?
derivation: Hercules, driving the Iberian cattle (of Geryon) past the Tiber bank, heard Ino's cry and scattered the maenads whom Juno had incited. Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: hospita Carmentis fidos intrasse penates diceris et longam deposuisse famem. liba sua properata manu Tegeaea sacerdos traditur in subito cocta dedisse foco. nunc quoque liba iuvant festis Matralibus illam; rustica sedulitas gratior arte fuit.
question: Quae sacerdos Tegeaea Inoni liba subito cocta dedit, unde liba festis Matralibus grata sunt?
question_en: Which Tegean priestess gave Ino cakes hastily baked on a sudden hearth, whence cakes please her at the Matralia?
derivation: The aetiology of the Matralia cakes: Carmentis (the Arcadian, 'Tegean' prophetess) baked liba in haste for her guest Ino, and such cakes delight the goddess still. Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: numen eris pelagi: natum quoque pontus habebit. in vestris aliud sumite nomen aquis: Leucothea Grais, Matuta vocabere nostris; in portus nato ius erit omne tuo,
question: Quibus nominibus Ino, numen pelagi facta, a Grais et a nostris vocatur?
question_en: By what names is Ino called, once made a sea-divinity, among the Greeks and among us (the Romans)?
answer_en: Leucothea among the Greeks, Matuta among the Romans.
derivation: Carmentis' prophecy: Ino becomes the sea-goddess called Leucothea in Greek and Matuta in Latin - the double identity behind the Matralia. Two-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: in portus nato ius erit omne tuo, quem nos Portunum, sua lingua Palaemona dicet. ite, precor, nostris aequus uterque locis.'
question: Quo nomine Romani Melicertam, Inus natum, dicunt, cui omne in portus ius est?
question_en: By what name do the Romans call Melicertes, Ino's son, who holds all right over harbors?
derivation: Ino's son (Melicertes, named at 6.494) becomes the harbor-god: Portunus to the Romans, Palaemon in his own (Greek) tongue. Name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: non tamen hanc pro stirpe sua pia mater adoret: ipsa parum felix visa fuisse parens. alterius prolem melius mandabitis illi: utilior Baccho quam fuit illa suis.
question: Pro cuius prole pia mater Matutam Matralibus adorare debet?
answer: Pro alterius prole, non pro sua.
question_en: For whose offspring ought a devoted mother to pray to Matuta at the Matralia?
answer_en: For another's offspring, not her own.
derivation: The striking rule of the Matralia: pray to Matuta for another's children (nephews and nieces), not one's own, since Ino was an unlucky parent to hers but served Bacchus well. Answer verbatim (alterius prolem melius mandabitis illi).

author: Ovid
source_text: hanc tibi 'quo properas?' memorant dixisse, Rutili, 'luce mea Marso consul ab hoste cades.' exitus accessit verbis, flumenque Toleni purpureum mixtis sanguine fluxit aquis.
question: A quo hoste consul Rutilius luce Matutae cecidit?
question_en: By what enemy did the consul Rutilius fall on Matuta's day?
derivation: On Matuta's day the consul Rutilius fell to the Marsi (Social War, 90 BC) and the Tolenus ran purple with blood. Named consul, named enemy; verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Lux eadem, Fortuna, tua est, auctorque locusque; sed superiniectis quis latet iste togis? Servius est, hoc constat enim:
question: Quis sub superiniectis togis in aede Fortunae latet?
question_en: Who lies hidden beneath the heaped-up togas in the temple of Fortuna?
derivation: The veiled statue in Fortuna's temple is Servius - 'hoc constat enim,' Ovid says; only the reason for the veiling is disputed. Famous cult curiosity; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: nocte domum parva solita est intrare fenestra, unde Fenestellae nomina porta tenet.
question: Quae porta Romae nomen ab fenestra tenet, qua Fortuna ad Servium regem nocte intrabat?
question_en: Which gate at Rome keeps its name from the little window through which Fortuna used to enter to king Servius by night?
derivation: Fortuna's love for Servius: she entered his house by night through a small window, whence the Porta Fenestella has its name. Landmark aetiology verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: hinc cruor et caedes, infirmaque vincitur aetas: sceptra gener socero rapta Superbus habet.
question: Quis gener Servio socero sceptra rapuit?
question_en: Which son-in-law seized the scepter torn from his father-in-law Servius?
derivation: Tarquinius Superbus, Servius' son-in-law, holds the scepter snatched from the murdered old king. Relation-and-name fact verbatim (sceptra gener socero rapta Superbus habet).

author: Ovid
source_text: ipse sub Esquiliis, ubi erat sua regia, caesus concidit in dura sanguinulentus humo.
question: Quo loco Servius rex caesus concidit?
answer: Sub Esquiliis, ubi regia eius erat.
question_en: In what place was king Servius cut down?
answer_en: Below the Esquiline, where his palace was.
derivation: Servius Tullius murdered below the Esquiline by his own palace. Place answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: filia carpento, patrios initura penates, ibat per medias alta feroxque vias. corpus ut aspexit, lacrimis auriga profusis restitit; hunc tali corripit illa sono: 'vadis, an exspectas pretium pietatis amarum? duc, inquam, invitas ipsa per ora rotas.' certa fides facti: dictus Sceleratus ab illa vicus, et aeterna res ea pressa nota.
question: Qui vicus Romae ab facto Tulliae, quae carpentum per patris corpus egit, nomen accepit?
question_en: Which street at Rome took its name from the deed of Tullia, who drove her carriage over her father's body?
derivation: Tullia (the 'filia,' named at 6.587) forced the wheels over Servius' corpse; from her the street is called Sceleratus, branded forever. Landmark answer verbatim (dictus Sceleratus ab illa vicus).

author: Ovid
source_text: arserat hoc templum: signo tamen ille pepercit ignis; opem nato Mulciber ipse tulit.
question: Cui signo ignis, aede Fortunae ardente, pepercit, Mulcibere opem ferente?
question_en: What statue did the fire spare when the temple of Fortuna burned, Mulciber himself bringing aid?
derivation: When Fortuna's temple burned, the fire spared Servius' statue: Vulcan (Mulciber) helped his own son. The 'signum' is Servius' veiled statue of the preceding lines; supported by 'opem nato Mulciber... tulit.'

author: Ovid
source_text: namque pater Tulli Volcanus, Ocresia mater praesignis facie Corniculana fuit.
question: Quis pater et quae mater Servi Tulli fuisse dicuntur?
question_en: Who are said to have been the father and the mother of Servius Tullius?
answer_en: Vulcan his father, Ocresia (of Corniculum) his mother.
derivation: The birth-legend of Servius: son of Vulcan and the beautiful Corniculan captive Ocresia, conceived from the form that appeared in the hearth-ashes. Two-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: signa dedit genitor tunc cum caput igne corusco contigit, inque comis flammeus arsit apex.
question: Quod signum Volcanus genitor Servio puero dedit?
question_en: What sign did his father Vulcan give the boy Servius?
answer_en: A crest of flame blazed in his hair.
derivation: The flame that played harmlessly on Servius' head - his father's sign, canonical omen of his kingship. Short answer verbatim (in comis flammeus arsit apex).

author: Ovid
source_text: Te quoque magnifica, Concordia, dedicat aede Livia, quam caro praestitit ipsa viro.
question: Quae femina Concordiam magnifica aede dedicavit, caro viro praestitam?
question_en: Which woman dedicated Concordia with a magnificent shrine, offered for her dear husband?
derivation: Livia's dedication of the shrine of Concordia (in the Porticus Liviae) for Augustus. Distinct from Camillus' temple of Concord taken from liber I; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: disce tamen, veniens aetas: ubi Livia nunc est porticus, immensae tecta fuere domus; urbis opus domus una fuit spatiumque tenebat quo brevius muris oppida multa tenent. haec aequata solo est, nullo sub crimine regni, sed quia luxuria visa nocere sua. sustinuit tantas operum subvertere moles totque suas heres perdere Caesar opes:
question: Quid nunc stat ubi immensae domus tecta fuerunt, quas Caesar heres solo aequavit ob luxuriam?
question_en: What now stands where the roofs of an immense house once were, which Caesar as heir leveled to the ground because of its luxury?
derivation: The Porticus Liviae built where one house as big as a town (Vedius Pollio's) was razed by its heir Caesar (Augustus) as a censorial example against luxury. Landmark answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nulla nota est veniente die, quam dicere possis; Idibus Invicto sunt data templa Iovi.
question: Cui deo Idibus Iuniis templa data sunt?
question_en: To which god were temples given on the Ides of June?
derivation: The Ides of June are the dedication day of Jupiter Invictus. God-plus-title answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: 'temporibus veterum tibicinis usus avorum magnus et in magno semper honore fuit: cantabat fanis, cantabat tibia ludis, cantabat maestis tibia funeribus;
question: Quibus in rebus tibia apud veteres Romanos canebat, ut Minerva apud Ovidium docet?
question_en: On what occasions did the flute play among the old Romans, as Minerva teaches in Ovid?
answer_en: In temples, at games, and at funerals.
derivation: The three employments of the tibicen in old Rome - shrines, games, funerals - the background of the flute-players' guild and its festival. Triple answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: adde quod aedilis, pompam qui funeris irent, artifices solos iusserat esse decem.
question: Quot solos artifices tibicines aedilis pompam funeris ire iusserat?
question_en: How many musicians only did the aedile order to attend a funeral procession?
derivation: The aedile's restriction that provoked the pipers' secession: no more than ten artificers at a funeral train. Number answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: exilio mutant Urbem Tiburque recedunt: exilium quodam tempore Tibur erat.
question: Quo tibicines, Urbe relicta, exilii causa recesserunt?
question_en: To where did the flute-players withdraw in exile, abandoning the City?
derivation: The famous secession of the tibicines to Tibur (311 BC) - when Tibur still counted as exile. Place answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: at dominus "discedite" ait, plaustroque morantes sustulit; in plaustro scirpea lata fuit. adliciunt somnos tempus motusque merumque, potaque se Tibur turba redire putat. iamque per Esquilias Romanam intraverat urbem, et mane in medio plaustra fuere foro.
question: Quo vecti tibicines, vino sopiti, mane in medio foro Romano inventi sunt?
question_en: On what conveyance were the flute-players, lulled asleep by wine, found at morning in the middle of the Roman Forum?
derivation: The trick that brought the pipers home: their Tiburtine host loaded the drunken company on a wagon which rolled through the Esquiline into the Forum by dawn. Answer verbatim (plaustro... mane in medio plaustra fuere foro).

author: Ovid
source_text: Plautius, ut posset specie numeroque senatum fallere, personis imperat ora tegi, admiscetque alios et, ut hunc tibicina coetum augeat, in longis vestibus esse iubet;
question: Quis tibicinibus reducibus personis ora tegi longisque vestibus uti imperavit?
question_en: Who ordered the returning flute-players to cover their faces with masks and to wear long garments?
derivation: Plautius' device to deceive the senate about the returned exiles: masks over the faces, long robes to swell the company - the origin of the guild's costume. Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: 'cur vagus incedit tota tibicen in Urbe? quid sibi personae, quid stola longa volunt?'
question: Quo cultu tibicines Quinquatribus minoribus tota Urbe vagantur?
question_en: In what costume do the flute-players roam through the whole City at the lesser Quinquatrus?
answer_en: Masked and clad in the long robe.
derivation: The rite Ovid sets out to explain: at the lesser Quinquatrus (from the Ides of June) the tibicen wanders the whole city in mask and long stola, a license confirmed at 6.691-692 (cultuque novo licet Idibus uti). Answer drawn verbatim from personae and stola longa.

author: Ovid
source_text: prima, terebrato per rara foramina buxo, ut daret, effeci, tibia longa sonos. vox placuit: faciem liquidis referentibus undis vidi virgineas intumuisse genas. "ars mihi non tanti est; valeas, mea tibia" dixi: excipit abiectam caespite ripa suo.
question: Quae dea tibiam primam effecit et abiecit, cum genas suas in aqua intumuisse vidisset?
question_en: Which goddess made the first flute and threw it away when she saw in the water that her cheeks had swollen?
derivation: Minerva's invention and rejection of the tibia - she saw her maiden cheeks puffed out in the water's mirror and cast the pipe away. The speaker of the quoted lines is Minerva (Tritonia, 6.655). Canonical myth; single-name answer.

author: Ovid
source_text: inventam satyrus primum miratur, et usum nescit, et inflatam sentit habere sonum; et modo dimittit digitis, modo concipit auras, iamque inter nymphas arte superbus erat: provocat et Phoebum. Phoebo superante pependit; caesa recesserunt a cute membra sua.
question: Quo deo superante satyrus, qui tibiam abiectam invenerat, pependit cute caesa?
question_en: Which god's victory left the satyr who had found the discarded flute hanging, his limbs stripped of their skin?
derivation: The satyr (Marsyas) who found Minerva's discarded pipe challenged Phoebus and, defeated, was hung up and flayed. The god's name is verbatim; the satyr's name, absent from the text, is left to the derivation.

author: Ovid
source_text: scilicet hic olim Volscos Aequosque fugatos viderat in campis, Algida terra, tuis; unde suburbano clarus, Tuberte, triumpho vectus es in niveis postmodo victor equis.
question: Quibus hostibus in Algida terra fugatis Tubertus suburbano triumpho clarus factus est?
question_en: By routing which enemies on the soil of Algidus did Tubertus win fame with a triumph from the suburbs?
derivation: The victory of (Postumius) Tubertus over the Volsci and Aequi at Algidus, celebrated with the near-Rome triumph drawn by snow-white horses. Two-people answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: sol abit a Geminis, et Cancri signa rubescunt: coepit Aventina Pallas in arce coli.
question: Qua in arce Pallas coli coepit, sole a Geminis abeunte?
question_en: On what height did Pallas begin to be worshipped, as the sun leaves Gemini?
derivation: The Aventine cult of Pallas (Minerva) began on this June day. Distinct from the Caelian shrine of Minerva Capta taken from liber III; place answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: reddita, quisquis is est, Summano templa feruntur, tum cum Romanis, Pyrrhe, timendus eras.
question: Quo tempore Summano templa data esse feruntur?
question_en: At what time is the temple said to have been rendered to Summanus?
answer_en: When Pyrrhus was a terror to the Romans.
derivation: The temple of Summanus - 'whoever he is,' says Ovid of the faded night-lightning god - dates from the war with Pyrrhus. Time-anchor answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: reddideratque animam, multum indignante Diana. 'nulla' Coronides 'causa doloris' ait: 'namque pio iuveni vitam sine volnere reddam, et cedent arti tristia fata meae.'
question: Quis Hippolyto, equis lacerato, vitam sine volnere reddidit?
question_en: Who gave back life, without a wound, to Hippolytus after he was torn by his horses?
derivation: Aesculapius (Coronides) restored Hippolytus to life with his healing herbs, to Diana's comfort. The reviver's identity is the fact; patronymic verbatim. The Arician grove fact was taken from liber III; the revival is new.

author: Ovid
source_text: lucus eum nemorisque sui Dictynna recessu celat: Aricino Virbius ille lacu.
question: Quo nomine Hippolytus, in nemore suo a Dictynna celatus, ad lacum Aricinum vocatur?
question_en: By what name is Hippolytus called at the Arician lake, hidden by Dictynna in the recess of her grove?
derivation: The revived Hippolytus lives on as Virbius by the lake of Aricia - the Roman identity of the Greek hero in Diana's grove. Name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Iuppiter, exemplum veritus, derexit in ipsum fulmina qui nimiae moverat artis opem.
question: Quid Iuppiter in eum direxit qui Hippolyto vitam nimia arte reddiderat?
question_en: What did Jupiter aim at the one who had restored Hippolytus' life by too great an art?
derivation: Jupiter, fearing the precedent, blasted with the thunderbolt the healer (Aesculapius) who wielded too potent an art. Canonical myth; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Non ego te, quamvis properabis vincere, Caesar, si vetet auspicium, signa movere velim. sint tibi Flaminius Trasimenaque litora testes per volucres aequos multa monere deos.
question: Quis dux, cum Trasimenis litoribus, testis est deos per aves iustos multa monere?
question_en: Which commander, together with the shores of Trasimene, stands witness that the just gods give many warnings through the birds?
derivation: Flaminius and the shores of Trasimene as the standing proof of neglected auspices (the disaster of 217 BC, dated in the next couplet). Name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: postera lux melior: superat Masinissa Syphacem, et cecidit telis Hasdrubal ipse suis.
