question: Quem regem Masinissa superavit, ut Ovidius die meliore notat?
question_en: Which king did Masinissa defeat, as Ovid notes on the luckier day?
derivation: The luckier day after Trasimene's anniversary: Masinissa's victory over Syphax. Two named kings; answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: postera lux melior: superat Masinissa Syphacem, et cecidit telis Hasdrubal ipse suis.
question: Quibus telis Hasdrubal cecidit, ut Ovidius in Fastis tradit?
question_en: By whose weapons did Hasdrubal fall, as Ovid records in the Fasti?
derivation: Hasdrubal fell by his own weapons (the self-sought death in the tradition Ovid follows). Short answer verbatim (telis... ipse suis).

author: Ovid
source_text: ite, deam laeti Fortem celebrate, Quirites: in Tiberis ripa munera regis habet.
question: Quo in loco dea Fors Fortuna templa, munera regis, habet?
question_en: Where does the goddess Fors Fortuna have her temple, a king's gift?
answer_en: On the bank of the Tiber.
derivation: Fors Fortuna's temple across on the Tiber bank, the gift of a king (Servius, named below). Place answer verbatim; her day falls seven days before June's end (June 24).

author: Ovid
source_text: pars pede, pars etiam celeri decurrite cumba, nec pudeat potos inde redire domum.
question: Quibus modis Quirites ad festum Fortis Fortunae decurrunt?
question_en: By what means do the Quirites hurry down to the festival of Fors Fortuna?
answer_en: Some on foot, some by swift skiff.
derivation: The people's outing to Fors Fortuna: down the Tiber on foot or by fast boat. Two-part answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: pars pede, pars etiam celeri decurrite cumba, nec pudeat potos inde redire domum. ferte coronatae iuvenum convivia, lintres, multaque per medias vina bibantur aquas.
question: Quo statu a festo Fortis Fortunae domum redire Quirites non pudet?
question_en: In what condition are the Quirites not ashamed to return home from the festival of Fors Fortuna?
derivation: The famous license of the day: no shame in coming home drunk, garlanded boats carrying the young men's parties, wine drunk in midstream. One-word answer verbatim (potos).

author: Ovid
source_text: plebs colit hanc, quia qui posuit de plebe fuisse fertur, et ex humili sceptra tulisse loco. convenit et servis, serva quia Tullius ortus constituit dubiae templa propinqua deae.
question: Quis, de plebe ortus, templa Fortis Fortunae posuisse fertur?
question_en: Who, sprung from the plebs, is said to have founded the temple of Fors Fortuna?
derivation: Why the plebs keeps this feast: its founder is said to have been of the plebs, raised from a lowly place to the scepter - Tullius, named in the quoted lines. Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: convenit et servis, serva quia Tullius ortus constituit dubiae templa propinqua deae.
question: Qua matre Tullius ortus est, unde festum Fortis Fortunae etiam servis convenit?
question_en: Of what mother was Tullius born, whence the festival of Fors Fortuna suits even slaves?
derivation: The festival suits slaves too because Tullius was born of a slave - consistent with Ocresia the captive in the birth-legend earlier in the book. One-word answer verbatim (serva... ortus).

author: Ovid
source_text: tempus idem Stator aedis habet, quam Romulus olim ante Palatini condidit ora iugi.
question: Quis aedem Iovis Statoris ante ora Palatini iugi condidit?
question_en: Who founded the temple of Jupiter Stator before the front of the Palatine ridge?
derivation: The aedes of (Jupiter) Stator founded of old by Romulus facing the Palatine - the vow of the Sabine battle. Founder answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tot restant de mense dies quot nomina Parcis, cum data sunt trabeae templa, Quirine, tuae.
question: Cui deo trabeato templa data sunt, cum tot dies de Iunio restarent quot nomina Parcis?
question_en: To which god of the trabea were temples given, when as many days remained of June as the Parcae have names?
derivation: Quirinus' temple day, dated by the riddle 'as many days left as the Parcae's names' (three - June 29). God-name answer verbatim; the deified Romulus = Quirinus was taken in liber II, this is the temple-day fact.

author: Ovid
source_text: sic ego. sic Clio: 'clari monimenta Philippi aspicis, unde trahit Marcia casta genus, Marcia, sacrifico deductum nomen ab Anco, in qua par facies nobilitate sua.
question: A quo rege Marcia casta nomen genusque deducit, ut Clio apud Ovidium canit?
question_en: From which king does the chaste Marcia derive her name and descent, as Clio sings in Ovid?
derivation: Closing the book: Marcia (of the monuments of Philippus, the aedes Herculis Musarum) traces her name and line from king Ancus Marcius, 'sacrificus' for his attention to rites. King answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Ante mare et terras et quod tegit omnia caelum unus erat toto naturae vultus in orbe, quem dixere chaos: rudis indigestaque moles nec quicquam nisi pondus iners congestaque eodem non bene iunctarum discordia semina rerum.
question: Quo nomine, ut narrat Ovidius in primo Metamorphoseon libro, appellabatur ille unus naturae vultus, rudis indigestaque moles, ante mare et terras et caelum?
question_en: By what name, as Ovid tells in the first book of the Metamorphoses, was that single face of nature called — a rough and unordered mass — before sea and lands and sky existed?
derivation: The opening cosmogonic fact of the Metamorphoses: the primordial state was named Chaos (quem dixere chaos). Anchored to Ovid + Metamorphoses book 1; one-name answer supported verbatim; canonical shared myth every Latin reader carries.

author: Ovid
source_text: Hanc deus et melior litem natura diremit.
question: Quis apud Ovidium litem elementorum in chao inter se pugnantium diremit mundumque ordinavit?
question_en: Who, in Ovid, resolved the strife of the elements fighting with one another in chaos and set the world in order?
derivation: The famous phrase 'deus et melior natura' (1.21) names the orderer of chaos — one of the most quoted lines of the cosmogony. Anchored to Ovid's chaos; short answer verbatim in the source.

author: Ovid
source_text: quam satus Iapeto, mixtam pluvialibus undis, finxit in effigiem moderantum cuncta deorum
question: Quis, ut tradit Ovidius, hominem e terra pluvialibus undis mixta in effigiem deorum finxit?
question_en: Who, as Ovid relates, fashioned man from earth mixed with rainwater in the image of the gods?
derivation: Ovid credits the making of man to 'satus Iapeto' — the son of Iapetus, i.e. Prometheus, a standard identification every reader carries. Anchored to Ovid + the creation of man; single-name answer supported by the quoted line.

author: Ovid
source_text: Aurea prima sata est aetas, quae vindice nullo, sponte sua, sine lege fidem rectumque colebat.
question: Quae aetas hominum apud Ovidium prima fuit, quae sine lege ac vindice sponte sua fidem rectumque colebat?
question_en: Which age of mankind in Ovid came first, cultivating faith and right of its own accord, without law or enforcer?
derivation: The golden age as first of the ages, needing no laws — the canonical myth of the ages (1.89-90). Anchored to Ovid's scheme of the ages; short noun-phrase answer verbatim (Aurea prima sata est aetas).

author: Ovid
source_text: ver erat aeternum, placidique tepentibus auris mulcebant zephyri natos sine semine flores;
question: Quod anni tempus aetate aurea, ut canit Ovidius, aeternum erat?
question_en: Which season of the year, as Ovid sings, was everlasting in the golden age?
derivation: 'Ver erat aeternum' — the eternal spring of the golden age, a proverbial feature of the myth. Anchored to the golden age in Ovid; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Postquam Saturno tenebrosa in Tartara misso sub Iove mundus erat, subiit argentea proles, auro deterior, fulvo pretiosior aere.
question: Quae proles hominum apud Ovidium successit, postquam Saturno in Tartara misso mundus sub Iove erat?
question_en: Which race of men in Ovid followed, after Saturn was sent to Tartarus and the world came under Jove?
derivation: The succession of the ages: the golden age belongs to Saturn, and when Jove takes the world the silver race follows. Anchored to Saturn/Jove; short answer verbatim (subiit argentea proles).

author: Ovid
source_text: Iuppiter antiqui contraxit tempora veris perque hiemes aestusque et inaequalis autumnos et breve ver spatiis exegit quattuor annum.
question: Quis deus, ut narrat Ovidius, antiqui veris tempora contraxit et annum quattuor spatiis primum distinxit?
question_en: Which god, as Ovid tells, shortened the ancient spring and first divided the year into four seasons?
derivation: Jupiter ends the eternal spring and institutes the four seasons at the start of the silver age — a canonical aetiology within the ages myth. Anchored to the seasons + Ovid; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tertia post illam successit aenea proles, saevior ingeniis et ad horrida promptior arma, non scelerata tamen; de duro est ultima ferro.
question: Ex quo metallo ultima hominum aetas apud Ovidium nomen ducit?
question_en: From which metal does the last age of mankind in Ovid take its name?
derivation: 'De duro est ultima ferro' — the iron age as the last and worst of the four. Anchored to Ovid's ages; one-word metal answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: victa iacet pietas, et virgo caede madentis ultima caelestum terras Astraea reliquit.
question: Quae virgo caelestis, ut narrat Ovidius, ultima deorum terras aetate ferrea reliquit?
question_en: Which celestial maiden, as Ovid tells, was the last of the gods to abandon the earth in the age of iron?
derivation: Astraea (Justice) as the last divinity to leave the blood-soaked earth of the iron age — a celebrated mythological fact, later tied to the constellation Virgo. Anchored to the iron age + Ovid; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: obruta mole sua cum corpora dira iacerent, perfusam multo natorum sanguine Terram immaduisse ferunt calidumque animasse cruorem et, ne nulla suae stirpis monimenta manerent, in faciem vertisse hominum;
question: Ex quo Terra, ut ferunt apud Ovidium, novam stirpem in faciem hominum animavit, postquam gigantes montibus obruti sunt?
question_en: From what, according to the tale in Ovid, did Earth animate a new stock in human shape after the Giants were crushed beneath the mountains?
answer_en: From the blood of the Giants.
derivation: The blood-born men: Earth soaks up the Giants' blood and turns it into a violent human race. Anchored to Terra + the Giants; short answer supported verbatim (natorum sanguine ... animasse cruorem ... in faciem vertisse hominum).

author: Ovid
source_text: adfectasse ferunt regnum caeleste gigantas altaque congestos struxisse ad sidera montis. tum pater omnipotens misso perfregit Olympum fulmine et excussit subiecto Pelion Ossae.
question: Qui, ut ferunt apud Ovidium, regnum caeleste adfectaverunt montibus in altum congestis, donec Iuppiter eos fulmine perfregit?
question_en: Who, according to the tale in Ovid, aimed at the kingdom of heaven by piling mountains on high, until Jupiter shattered them with his thunderbolt?
derivation: The Gigantomachy: the Giants pile Pelion on Ossa toward the stars and are struck down by Jove's bolt — canonical shared myth. Anchored to the assault on heaven + Jupiter; one-name answer verbatim (gigantas).

author: Ovid
source_text: Est via sublimis, caelo manifesta sereno; lactea nomen habet, candore notabilis ipso. hac iter est superis ad magni tecta Tonantis regalemque domum:
question: Qua via superi apud Ovidium ad regiam magni Tonantis iter faciunt?
question_en: By what road, in Ovid, do the gods travel to the royal palace of the great Thunderer?
derivation: The Milky Way as the road of the gods to Jove's palace — a canonical mythological picture (lactea nomen habet). Anchored to the Thunderer's palace + Ovid; short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tertia post illam successit aenea proles, saevior ingeniis et ad horrida promptior arma, non scelerata tamen; de duro est ultima ferro.
question: Quota inter aetates hominum apud Ovidium fuit aenea proles?
question_en: Which in order among the ages of mankind in Ovid was the bronze race?
derivation: The bronze race as third of the four ages (Tertia ... aenea proles) — part of the canonical gold-silver-bronze-iron sequence. Anchored to Ovid's ages; one-word ordinal answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Arcadis hinc sedes et inhospita tecta tyranni ingredior, traherent cum sera crepuscula noctem. signa dedi venisse deum, vulgusque precari coeperat: inridet primo pia vota Lycaon,
question: Cuius terrae tyrannus erat Lycaon, cuius tecta Iuppiter humana sub imagine intravit?
question_en: Of what land was Lycaon the tyrant, whose house Jupiter entered in human guise?
derivation: Lycaon as the Arcadian tyrant (Arcadis ... tecta tyranni) visited by Jove in disguise. Anchored to Lycaon + Jupiter; one-place answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: nec contentus eo, missi de gente Molossa obsidis unius iugulum mucrone resolvit atque ita semineces partim ferventibus artus mollit aquis, partim subiecto torruit igni. quod simul inposuit mensis, ego vindice flamma in domino dignos everti tecta penates;
question: Quales epulas Lycaon Iovi hospiti in mensis apposuit, ut deum experiretur?
question_en: What sort of feast did Lycaon set on the table before his guest Jupiter, to put the god to the test?
answer_en: Human flesh — the limbs of a Molossian hostage.
derivation: Lycaon's crime: he cooks and serves the flesh of a Molossian hostage to test whether his guest is a god. The story every reader knows as the cause of the flood. Anchored to Lycaon + Jove; short answer supported verbatim (obsidis ... artus ... inposuit mensis).

author: Ovid
source_text: in villos abeunt vestes, in crura lacerti: fit lupus et veteris servat vestigia formae; canities eadem est, eadem violentia vultus, idem oculi lucent, eadem feritatis imago est.
question: In quod animal Lycaon, tyrannus Arcadiae, apud Ovidium mutatus est?
question_en: Into what animal was Lycaon, the tyrant of Arcadia, transformed in Ovid?
derivation: The first great transformation of the poem: Lycaon becomes a wolf (fit lupus), keeping traces of his old savagery. Anchored to Lycaon; one-word animal answer verbatim. Canonical myth (and the ambient etymological association with Greek lykos).

author: Ovid
source_text: tela reponuntur manibus fabricata cyclopum; poena placet diversa, genus mortale sub undis perdere et ex omni nimbos demittere caelo.
question: Qua poena Iuppiter, scelere Lycaonis cognito, genus mortale perdere statuit?
answer: Diluvio: sub undis nimbisque de caelo demissis.
question_en: With what punishment did Jupiter, once Lycaon's crime was known, decide to destroy the mortal race?
answer_en: With a flood: beneath the waters, with storm-clouds sent down from the sky.
derivation: Jove sets aside the thunderbolt and chooses the flood — the pivot of the whole flood myth (poena placet diversa, genus mortale sub undis perdere). Anchored to Jupiter + Lycaon; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: tela reponuntur manibus fabricata cyclopum;
question: Quorum manibus fulmina Iovis fabricata esse dicuntur apud Ovidium?
question_en: By whose hands are Jupiter's thunderbolts said, in Ovid, to have been forged?
answer_en: By the hands of the Cyclopes.
derivation: The Cyclopes as forgers of Jove's bolts — a canonical mythological attribute (tela ... fabricata cyclopum). Anchored to Jupiter's weapons; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Protinus Aeoliis Aquilonem claudit in antris et quaecumque fugant inductas flamina nubes emittitque Notum. madidis Notus evolat alis,
question: Quem ventum Iuppiter emisit, ut nimbis terras diluvio obrueret, Aquilone in antris Aeoliis cluso?
question_en: Which wind did Jupiter let loose to overwhelm the lands with rain in the flood, after shutting Aquilo in the Aeolian caves?
derivation: The rain-bringing south wind Notus released (and the cloud-chasing north wind imprisoned) to start the deluge — the winds' canonical characters. Anchored to Jupiter + the flood; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nec caelo contenta suo est Iovis ira, sed illum caeruleus frater iuvat auxiliaribus undis.
question: Quis deus, frater Iovis, iram eius in diluvio auxiliaribus undis iuvit?
question_en: Which god, Jupiter's brother, aided his wrath in the flood with auxiliary waters?
derivation: Neptune ('caeruleus frater', the rector pelagi of the following lines) joins the flood with his waters — the standard identification of Jove's sea-god brother. Anchored to Jupiter + the flood; one-name answer.

author: Ovid
source_text: Ipse tridente suo terram percussit, at illa intremuit motuque vias patefecit aquarum.
question: Quo telo Neptunus terram percussit, ut vias aquarum diluvio patefaceret?
question_en: With what weapon did Neptune strike the earth, to open the ways of the waters for the flood?
derivation: Neptune strikes the earth with his trident and the waters break out — the god's canonical attribute in action. Anchored to Neptune + the flood; one-word answer verbatim (tridente suo).

author: Ovid
source_text: nec maris ira manet, positoque tricuspide telo mulcet aquas rector pelagi supraque profundum exstantem atque umeros innato murice tectum caeruleum Tritona vocat conchaeque sonanti inspirare iubet fluctusque et flumina signo iam revocare dato:
question: Quis deus, a rectore pelagi vocatus, concha sonanti fluctus et flumina post diluvium receptui cecinit?
question_en: Which god, summoned by the ruler of the sea, sounded the retreat for the waves and rivers after the flood on his echoing conch?
derivation: Triton and his conch-trumpet recall the waters at the end of the flood — the canonical image of the sea-god's herald. Anchored to Neptune (rector pelagi) + the flood's end; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: mons ibi verticibus petit arduus astra duobus, nomine Parnasos, superantque cacumina nubes. hic ubi Deucalion (nam cetera texerat aequor) cum consorte tori parva rate vectus adhaesit,
question: In quo monte Deucalion cum Pyrrha coniuge, parva rate vectus, post diluvium adhaesit?
question_en: On what mountain did Deucalion with his wife Pyrrha, borne on a little raft, come to rest after the flood?
derivation: The sole survivors of the flood land on Parnassus — a core fact of the Deucalion myth. Anchored to Deucalion + Pyrrha; one-place answer verbatim (nomine Parnasos ... hic ubi Deucalion ... adhaesit).

author: Ovid
source_text: mons ibi verticibus petit arduus astra duobus, nomine Parnasos, superantque cacumina nubes.
question: Quot verticibus mons Parnasos, ut describit Ovidius, arduus astra petit?
question_en: With how many peaks does Mount Parnassus, as Ovid describes it, rise steep toward the stars?
derivation: The twin peaks of Parnassus — a stock geographical fact about the mountain of Apollo and the Muses. Anchored to Parnassus by name; one-number answer verbatim (verticibus ... duobus).

author: Ovid
source_text: Separat Aonios Oetaeis Phocis ab arvis, terra ferax, dum terra fuit, sed tempore in illo pars maris et latus subitarum campus aquarum. mons ibi verticibus petit arduus astra duobus, nomine Parnasos, superantque cacumina nubes.
question: In qua terra situs est mons Parnasos, ubi Deucalion post diluvium adhaesit?
question_en: In what land is Mount Parnassus situated, where Deucalion came to rest after the flood?
derivation: Parnassus stands in Phocis, the land between the Aonian (Boeotian) and Oetaean fields — standard Greek geography every reader of the Delphi myths carries. Anchored to Parnassus + Deucalion; one-place answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Corycidas nymphas et numina montis adorant fatidicamque Themin, quae tunc oracla tenebat:
question: Quae dea fatidica oracula Parnasia tunc tenebat, cum Deucalion et Pyrrha post diluvium eam adirent?
question_en: Which prophetic goddess then held the oracle at Parnassus, when Deucalion and Pyrrha approached her after the flood?
derivation: Themis holds the oracle (later Apollo's Delphi) at the time of the flood — a canonical piece of oracle-history (quae tunc oracla tenebat). Anchored to Deucalion + Pyrrha + Parnassus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Mota dea est sortemque dedit: 'discedite templo et velate caput cinctasque resolvite vestes ossaque post tergum magnae iactate parentis!'
question: Quid Themis oraculo Deucalioni et Pyrrhae post tergum iactare iussit, ut genus humanum repararetur?
question_en: What did Themis by her oracle order Deucalion and Pyrrha to throw behind their backs, so that the human race might be restored?
answer_en: The bones of their great mother.
derivation: The riddling oracle of Themis — throw the great mother's bones behind you — the hinge of the Deucalion myth. Anchored to Themis + Deucalion + Pyrrha; short answer verbatim (ossaque post tergum magnae iactate parentis).

author: Ovid
source_text: magna parens terra est: lapides in corpore terrae ossa reor dici; iacere hos post terga iubemur.'
question: Quae esse 'ossa magnae parentis' Deucalion sortem Themidis interpretatus est?
question_en: What did Deucalion interpret the 'bones of the great mother' in Themis's oracle to be?
answer_en: The stones in the body of the earth.
derivation: Deucalion solves the riddle: the great mother is Earth, her bones are stones. The famous interpretation that saves mankind. Anchored to Deucalion + the oracle; short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: inque brevi spatio superorum numine saxa missa viri manibus faciem traxere virorum et de femineo reparata est femina iactu.
question: Post diluvium, de cuius iactu saxa in feminas versa sunt, cum saxa a Deucalione missa virorum faciem traherent?
question_en: After the flood, from whose throw were the stones turned into women, while the stones cast by Deucalion took on the form of men?
derivation: The double aetiology: men from the man's stones, women from the woman's (de femineo reparata est femina iactu). Anchored to Deucalion + Pyrrha; short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: inde Promethides placidis Epimethida dictis mulcet et 'aut fallax' ait 'est sollertia nobis,
question: Cuius filius erat Deucalion, qui solus cum coniuge diluvio superfuit?
question_en: Whose son was Deucalion, who alone with his wife survived the flood?
derivation: Ovid calls Deucalion 'Promethides' — son of Prometheus — the standard genealogy of the flood-survivor. Anchored to Deucalion; one-name answer supported by the patronymic.

author: Ovid
source_text: inde Promethides placidis Epimethida dictis mulcet et 'aut fallax' ait 'est sollertia nobis,
question: Cuius filia erat Pyrrha, coniunx Deucalionis?
question_en: Whose daughter was Pyrrha, the wife of Deucalion?
derivation: Ovid calls Pyrrha 'Epimethis' — daughter of Epimetheus (brother of Prometheus) — the standard genealogy. Anchored to Pyrrha + Deucalion; one-name answer supported by the patronymic.

author: Ovid
source_text: ergo ubi diluvio tellus lutulenta recenti solibus aetheriis altoque recanduit aestu, edidit innumeras species; partimque figuras rettulit antiquas, partim nova monstra creavit. Illa quidem nollet, sed te quoque, maxime Python, tum genuit, populisque novis, incognita serpens, terror eras:
question: Unde natus est Python, ingens ille serpens, novorum populorum terror?
question_en: From what was Python born, that huge serpent, the terror of the new peoples?
answer_en: From the Earth, after the flood.
derivation: Python as earth-born from the mud left by the flood — the canonical origin of the Delphic serpent. Anchored to Python by name; short answer supported verbatim (tellus ... te quoque, maxime Python, tum genuit).

author: Ovid
source_text: hunc deus arcitenens, numquam letalibus armis ante nisi in dammis capreisque fugacibus usus, mille gravem telis exhausta paene pharetra perdidit effuso per vulnera nigra veneno.
question: Quis deus Pythona serpentem mille telis, exhausta paene pharetra, perdidit?
question_en: Which god destroyed the serpent Python with a thousand arrows, his quiver almost emptied?
derivation: Apollo's slaying of Python with his arrows — one of the most canonical of all myths, the foundation-story of Delphi. Anchored to Python; one-name answer (deus arcitenens = Apollo, the standard epithet).

author: Ovid
source_text: neve operis famam posset delere vetustas, instituit sacros celebri certamine ludos, Pythia de domitae serpentis nomine dictos.
question: Quos ludos sacros Apollo instituit, ne fama Pythonis domiti vetustate deleretur?
answer: Ludos Pythios, de nomine serpentis dictos.
question_en: What sacred games did Apollo found, so that the fame of his conquest of Python should not fade with time?
answer_en: The Pythian games, named after the serpent.
derivation: The aetiology of the Pythian games: founded by Apollo as a memorial of the slain serpent and named for it (Pythia de domitae serpentis nomine dictos). Anchored to Apollo + Python; short answer verbatim. A cult fact of the shared Greco-Roman calendar of games.

author: Ovid
source_text: hic iuvenum quicumque manu pedibusve rotave vicerat, aesculeae capiebat frondis honorem. nondum laurus erat, longoque decentia crine tempora cingebat de qualibet arbore Phoebus.
question: Cuius arboris fronde victores ludorum Pythiorum primo coronabantur, cum laurus nondum esset?
question_en: With the foliage of what tree were the victors of the Pythian games first crowned, when the laurel did not yet exist?
derivation: Before Daphne became the laurel, the Pythian prize was oak foliage (aesculeae frondis honorem; nondum laurus erat) — the detail that sets up the Daphne aetiology. Anchored to the Pythian games; one-word tree answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Primus amor Phoebi Daphne Peneia, quem non fors ignara dedit, sed saeva Cupidinis ira,
question: Quis fuit primus amor Phoebi, ut narrat Ovidius in primo Metamorphoseon libro?
question_en: Who was the first love of Phoebus, as Ovid tells in the first book of the Metamorphoses?
derivation: The programmatic opening of the Daphne episode: 'Primus amor Phoebi Daphne Peneia.' Anchored to Phoebus + Ovid; one-name answer verbatim. The centerpiece myth of the book.

author: Ovid
source_text: Primus amor Phoebi Daphne Peneia, quem non fors ignara dedit, sed saeva Cupidinis ira,
question: Cuius dei saeva ira, non fors, amorem Phoebi in Daphnen excitavit?
question_en: Whose fierce divine anger — not chance — kindled Phoebus's love for Daphne?
derivation: The cause of the whole episode: not blind chance but the wrath of Cupid, whom Apollo had mocked after slaying Python. Anchored to Phoebus + Daphne; one-name answer verbatim (saeva Cupidinis ira).

author: Ovid
source_text: dixit et eliso percussis aere pennis inpiger umbrosa Parnasi constitit arce
question: In cuius montis arce Cupido constitit, cum tela sua in Phoebum Daphnenque directurus esset?
question_en: On the summit of what mountain did Cupid take his stand, when about to aim his arrows at Phoebus and Daphne?
derivation: Cupid shoots his two arrows from the shady citadel of Parnassus — the staging of the Daphne myth. Anchored to Cupid + Phoebus + Daphne; one-place answer verbatim (umbrosa Parnasi ... arce).

author: Ovid
source_text: eque sagittifera prompsit duo tela pharetra diversorum operum: fugat hoc, facit illud amorem; quod facit, auratum est et cuspide fulget acuta, quod fugat, obtusum est et habet sub harundine plumbum.
question: Ex quo metallo factum erat telum Cupidinis quod amorem facit?
question_en: Of what metal was Cupid's arrow made that causes love?
derivation: Cupid's two arrows of opposite powers: the love-making one is golden and sharp. One of the most famous images in Latin poetry. Anchored to Cupid's arrows; one-word metal answer verbatim (quod facit, auratum est).

author: Ovid
source_text: eque sagittifera prompsit duo tela pharetra diversorum operum: fugat hoc, facit illud amorem; quod facit, auratum est et cuspide fulget acuta, quod fugat, obtusum est et habet sub harundine plumbum.
question: Quod metallum habet sub harundine telum Cupidinis quod amorem fugat?
question_en: What metal does Cupid's arrow that puts love to flight carry beneath its shaft?
derivation: The counterpart arrow: blunt and leaden, it repels love. Anchored to Cupid's arrows; one-word metal answer verbatim (obtusum est et habet sub harundine plumbum).

author: Ovid
source_text: hoc deus in nympha Peneide fixit, at illo laesit Apollineas traiecta per ossa medullas;
question: Utrum telum, plumbeumne an auratum, Cupido in Daphnen nympham Peneida fixit?
question_en: Which arrow, the leaden or the golden, did Cupid plant in Daphne, the nymph daughter of Peneus?
answer_en: The leaden one, which puts love to flight.
derivation: The mechanism of the myth: the lead (love-fleeing) arrow strikes Daphne, the gold one pierces Apollo — hence pursuit and flight. Anchored to Cupid + Daphne; short answer supported verbatim (hoc = quod fugat, in nympha Peneide fixit).

author: Ovid
source_text: 'da mihi perpetua, genitor carissime,' dixit 'virginitate frui! dedit hoc pater ante Dianae.'
question: Quid Daphne a genitore suo Peneo petivit, exemplum Dianae secuta?
question_en: What did Daphne ask of her father Peneus, following the example of Diana?
derivation: Daphne's wish for perpetual virginity like Diana's, granted (in word) by her father — a core element of the myth (dedit hoc pater ante Dianae; cf. innuptaeque aemula Phoebes, 1.476). Anchored to Daphne + Peneus + Diana; short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: mihi Delphica tellus et Claros et Tenedos Patareaque regia servit; Iuppiter est genitor;
question: Cui deo serviunt Delphica tellus et Claros et Tenedos Patareaque regia, ut ipse apud Ovidium gloriatur?
question_en: Which god do the Delphic land, Claros, Tenedos, and the royal seat of Patara serve, as he himself boasts in Ovid?
derivation: Apollo's canonical oracle-seats, listed by the god himself in his plea to Daphne (the speaker, son of Jupiter, is Phoebus). Anchored by the four named cult places; one-name answer. Shared religious geography of the Apollo cult.

author: Ovid
source_text: inventum medicina meum est, opiferque per orbem dicor, et herbarum subiecta potentia nobis.
question: Cuius dei inventum medicina est, qui 'opifer' per orbem dicitur, ut apud Ovidium legimus?
question_en: Which god's invention is medicine — the god called 'help-bringer' throughout the world, as we read in Ovid?
derivation: Apollo as inventor of medicine and lord of herbs, with the cult epithet 'opifer' — spoken by the god himself in the Daphne episode. A canonical divine attribute; one-name answer. Anchored by the epithet + the invention of medicine.

author: Ovid
source_text: viribus absumptis expalluit illa citaeque victa labore fugae spectans Peneidas undas 'fer, pater,' inquit 'opem! si flumina numen habetis, qua nimium placui, mutando perde figuram!'
question: Quem Daphne, victa labore fugae, oravit ut opem ferret figuramque suam mutando perderet?
question_en: Whom did Daphne, overcome by the effort of her flight, beg to bring help and destroy her beauty by changing it?
derivation: Daphne's prayer at the climax of the chase, addressed to her father the river ('fer, pater... opem', gazing at the Peneian waters) — the prayer that triggers the transformation. Anchored to Daphne; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: cui deus 'at, quoniam coniunx mea non potes esse, arbor eris certe' dixit 'mea! semper habebunt te coma, te citharae, te nostrae, laure, pharetrae;
question: In quam arborem Daphne, Penei filia, Apollinem fugiens mutata est?
question_en: Into what tree was Daphne, the daughter of Peneus, transformed as she fled Apollo?
derivation: THE central fact of the episode: Daphne becomes the laurel — Apollo addresses the new tree as 'laure'. The paradigm 'who was turned into what' cultural fact (cited in issue #2 itself). Anchored to Daphne + Apollo; one-word tree answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: cui deus 'at, quoniam coniunx mea non potes esse, arbor eris certe' dixit 'mea! semper habebunt te coma, te citharae, te nostrae, laure, pharetrae;
question: Quae tria Apollinis laurum semper habitura esse deus ipse Daphnae in arborem mutatae promisit?
question_en: What three things of Apollo's did the god himself promise would always bear the laurel, when Daphne had been changed into the tree?
answer_en: His hair, his lyres, and his quivers.
derivation: Apollo's adoption of the laurel for his hair, lyre, and quiver — the aetiology of the god's most familiar attribute. Anchored to Apollo + the laurel; brief three-item answer verbatim (te coma, te citharae, te nostrae, laure, pharetrae).

author: Ovid
source_text: tu ducibus Latiis aderis, cum laeta Triumphum vox canet et visent longas Capitolia pompas;
question: Quae arbor ducibus Latiis in triumphis adest, cum laeta vox Triumphum canit et Capitolia longas pompas visunt?
question_en: What tree attends Latin generals in their triumphs, when the joyful voice sings 'Triumphus' and the Capitol beholds the long processions?
derivation: The laurel of the Roman triumph, prophesied by Apollo to the new-made tree — the prime culture-fact linking the Daphne myth to Roman civic religion. Anchored to the triumph + the Capitol; one-word answer (the addressee is the laurel of 1.559).

author: Ovid
source_text: postibus Augustis eadem fidissima custos ante fores stabis mediamque tuebere quercum,
question: Ante cuius fores laurus, ut Apollo apud Ovidium praedixit, fidissima custos stat?
question_en: Before whose doors, as Apollo foretold in Ovid, does the laurel stand as most faithful guardian?
derivation: The laurels flanking Augustus' doorposts (postibus Augustis) — a celebrated honor of 27 BC, woven by Ovid into the Daphne aetiology. Anchored to the laurel + Augustus; short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: postibus Augustis eadem fidissima custos ante fores stabis mediamque tuebere quercum,
question: Quam arborem mediam laurus ante fores Augusti custodit, ut Apollo praedixit?
question_en: What tree in the middle does the laurel guard before the doors of Augustus, as Apollo foretold?
derivation: The oak wreath (corona civica, 'ob cives servatos') over Augustus' door, flanked by the laurels — the paired honors of 27 BC known to every Roman. Anchored to Augustus' doors + the laurel; one-word answer verbatim (mediam ... quercum).

author: Ovid
source_text: utque meum intonsis caput est iuvenale capillis, tu quoque perpetuos semper gere frondis honores!'
question: Quales frondis honores laurus, Apolline iubente, semper gerit, sicut caput dei intonsis capillis iuvenale est?
question_en: What kind of honors of foliage does the laurel always wear, at Apollo's command, just as the god's head is youthful with unshorn hair?
derivation: The aetiology of the evergreen laurel: Apollo grants it perpetual foliage matching his own unshorn, ever-young hair. Anchored to Apollo + the laurel; short answer verbatim (perpetuos semper gere frondis honores).

author: Ovid
source_text: Est nemus Haemoniae, praerupta quod undique claudit silva: vocant Tempe; per quae Peneos ab imo effusus Pindo spumosis volvitur undis
question: Quod nemus Haemoniae, silva praerupta undique clausum, Peneos amnis perfluit?
question_en: What grove of Haemonia (Thessaly), shut in on every side by steep forest, does the river Peneus flow through?
derivation: The vale of Tempe in Thessaly, through which the Peneus flows — proverbial beauty-spot of ancient geography (vocant Tempe). Anchored to Haemonia + the Peneus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Est nemus Haemoniae, praerupta quod undique claudit silva: vocant Tempe; per quae Peneos ab imo effusus Pindo spumosis volvitur undis
question: Ex quo monte effusus Peneos amnis per Tempe spumosis undis volvitur?
question_en: From what mountain does the river Peneus pour forth and roll through Tempe with foaming waters?
derivation: The Peneus rises from Mount Pindus and flows through Tempe — standard Thessalian geography carried by every reader of the poets. Anchored to the Peneus + Tempe; one-place answer verbatim (ab imo effusus Pindo).

author: Ovid
source_text: Inachus unus abest imoque reconditus antro fletibus auget aquas natamque miserrimus Io luget ut amissam:
question: Cuius amnis filia erat Io, quam Iuppiter amavit?
question_en: Of what river was Io, whom Jupiter loved, the daughter?
derivation: Io as daughter of the Argive river-god Inachus (natam ... Io) — the canonical genealogy that opens the episode. Anchored to Io + Jupiter; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: cum deus inducta latas caligine terras occuluit tenuitque fugam rapuitque pudorem.
question: Qua re inducta Iuppiter terras occuluit, cum Io fugientem comprehendit?
question_en: By spreading what did Jupiter hide the lands, when he caught the fleeing Io?
derivation: Jove's covering cloud — the sudden darkness over Argos that Juno immediately notices — the signature device of the Io story. Anchored to Jupiter + Io; one-word answer verbatim (inducta ... caligine).

author: Ovid
source_text: coniugis adventum praesenserat inque nitentem Inachidos vultus mutaverat ille iuvencam;
question: In quod animal Iuppiter Io, Inachi filiam, mutavit, cum adventum Iunonis praesensisset?
question_en: Into what animal did Jupiter change Io, the daughter of Inachus, when he had sensed Juno's approach?
derivation: The central transformation of the Io myth: Jupiter himself turns her into a shining heifer to hide his affair from Juno. Anchored to Io + Jupiter + Juno; one-word animal answer verbatim (nitentem ... iuvencam).

author: Ovid
source_text: Iuppiter e terra genitam mentitur, ut auctor desinat inquiri: petit hanc Saturnia munus.
question: Quod munus Iuno Saturnia a Iove petivit, cum Io in vaccam formosam mutata esset?
question_en: What gift did Saturnian Juno demand of Jupiter, when Io had been changed into a beautiful cow?
derivation: Juno's cunning counter-move: she asks for the heifer as a present, and Jove cannot refuse without betraying himself. Anchored to Juno + Jupiter + the transformed Io; short answer verbatim (petit hanc Saturnia munus).

author: Ovid
source_text: Paelice donata non protinus exuit omnem diva metum timuitque Iovem et fuit anxia furti, donec Arestoridae servandam tradidit Argo.
question: Cui custodi Iuno vaccam Io servandam tradidit?
question_en: To what guardian did Juno hand over the cow Io to be kept?
derivation: Juno entrusts Io to Argus (the patronymic Arestorides gives his father Arestor) — the watchman of the canonical tale. Anchored to Juno + Io; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: centum luminibus cinctum caput Argus habebat inde suis vicibus capiebant bina quietem, cetera servabant atque in statione manebant.
question: Quot luminibus cinctum caput habebat Argus, custos Ius a Iunone datus?
question_en: With how many eyes was the head of Argus ringed, the guard set over Io by Juno?
derivation: The hundred eyes of Argus — his defining canonical attribute (centum luminibus cinctum caput). Anchored to Argus + Io; one-number answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: centum luminibus cinctum caput Argus habebat inde suis vicibus capiebant bina quietem, cetera servabant atque in statione manebant.
question: Quot oculi Argi centoculi suis vicibus simul quietem capiebant, ceteris in statione manentibus?
question_en: How many of hundred-eyed Argus's eyes took their rest at a time in turn, while the rest stayed on watch?
derivation: The famous detail that only two of Argus's hundred eyes slept at a time, the rest keeping watch — why he was the perfect guard. Anchored to Argus; one-number answer verbatim (capiebant bina quietem).

author: Ovid
source_text: littera pro verbis, quam pes in pulvere duxit, corporis indicium mutati triste peregit.
question: Quo modo Io in vaccam mutata patri Inacho, quae esset, indicavit?
question_en: How did Io, changed into a cow, reveal to her father Inachus who she was?
answer_en: By letters traced in the dust with her hoof.
derivation: The pathetic recognition scene: mute Io writes her name in the dust with her hoof (littera ... quam pes in pulvere duxit). A celebrated moment of the myth. Anchored to Io + Inachus; short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nec superum rector mala tanta Phoronidos ultra ferre potest natumque vocat, quem lucida partu Pleias enixa est letoque det imperat Argum.
question: Quem filium Iuppiter vocavit, cum imperaret ut Argus, custos Ius, leto daretur?
question_en: Which son did Jupiter summon, when he ordered that Argus, Io's guard, be put to death?
derivation: Jove sends Mercury — 'the son whom the bright Pleiad bore' (Maia) — to kill Argus. The identification of the Pleiad's son as Mercury is canonical shared knowledge. Anchored to Jupiter + Argus + Io; one-name answer.

author: Ovid
source_text: parva mora est alas pedibus virgamque potenti somniferam sumpsisse manu tegumenque capillis.
question: Quae tria Mercurius sumpsit, ad Argum necandum a Iove missus?
answer: Alas pedibus, virgam somniferam, tegumen capillis.
question_en: What three things did Mercury take up, when sent by Jupiter to kill Argus?
answer_en: Wings for his feet, the sleep-bringing wand, and the cap for his hair.
derivation: Mercury's canonical kit — the winged sandals (talaria), the sleep-bringing wand (caduceus/virga somnifera), and the traveler's cap (petasus) — assumed for the Argus mission. Anchored to Mercury + Argus; brief three-item answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: parte tamen vigilat. quaerit quoque (namque reperta fistula nuper erat), qua sit ratione reperta. Tum deus 'Arcadiae gelidis sub montibus' inquit 'inter hamadryadas celeberrima Nonacrinas naias una fuit: nymphae Syringa vocabant.
question: De qua nympha Mercurius Argo fabulam narrare coepit, ut servantia lumina somno evinceret?
question_en: About which nymph did Mercury begin to tell Argus a tale, in order to overcome his watching eyes with sleep?
derivation: The tale-within-the-tale: Mercury lulls Argus with the story of Pan and Syrinx, prompted by Argus's question about the newly invented pipe. Anchored to Mercury + Argus; one-name answer verbatim (nymphae Syringa vocabant).

author: Ovid
source_text: Tum deus 'Arcadiae gelidis sub montibus' inquit 'inter hamadryadas celeberrima Nonacrinas naias una fuit: nymphae Syringa vocabant.
question: Cuius terrae nympha erat Syrinx, inter hamadryadas Nonacrinas celeberrima naias?
question_en: Of what land was Syrinx a nymph, the most famous naiad among the Nonacrian hamadryads?
derivation: Syrinx as an Arcadian naiad (from Nonacris, under Arcadia's cold mountains), a devotee of Diana like Daphne. Anchored to Syrinx by name; one-place answer verbatim (Arcadiae gelidis sub montibus).

author: Ovid
source_text: et precibus spretis fugisse per avia nympham, donec harenosi placidum Ladonis ad amnem venerit;
question: Ad quem amnem Syrinx nympha, Pana et preces eius fugiens, tandem pervenit?
question_en: To what river did the nymph Syrinx at last come, fleeing Pan and his entreaties?
derivation: The sandy Ladon (an Arcadian river) halts Syrinx's flight — the setting of her transformation. Anchored to Syrinx + Pan; one-name river answer verbatim (harenosi ... Ladonis ad amnem).

author: Ovid
source_text: hic illam cursum inpedientibus undis ut se mutarent liquidas orasse sorores, Panaque cum prensam sibi iam Syringa putaret, corpore pro nymphae calamos tenuisse palustres,
question: In quas res Syrinx mutata est, cum Pan eam iam prensam se tenere putaret?
question_en: Into what was Syrinx changed, when Pan thought he already held her in his grasp?
derivation: The transformation at the heart of the panpipe aetiology: Pan grasps reeds instead of the nymph (corpore pro nymphae calamos ... palustres). Anchored to Syrinx + Pan; short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: atque ita disparibus calamis conpagine cerae inter se iunctis nomen tenuisse puellae.
question: Cuius puellae nomen tenet fistula, quam Pan disparibus calamis cera inter se iunctis composuit?
question_en: Whose name does the pipe keep, which Pan made of unequal reeds joined together with wax?
derivation: The aetiology of the panpipes (syrinx/fistula): unequal reeds bound with wax, keeping the name of the girl. A canonical culture-fact about the shepherd's instrument. Anchored to Pan + the pipe; one-name answer verbatim (nomen tenuisse puellae).

author: Ovid
source_text: talia dicturus vidit Cyllenius omnes subcubuisse oculos adopertaque lumina somno; supprimit extemplo vocem firmatque soporem languida permulcens medicata lumina virga. nec mora, falcato nutantem vulnerat ense, qua collo est confine caput, saxoque cruentum deicit et maculat praeruptam sanguine rupem.
question: Quis deus Argum centoculum, omnibus oculis somno victis, occidit?
question_en: Which god killed hundred-eyed Argus, when all his eyes had been overcome by sleep?
derivation: Mercury (Cyllenius, from his birthplace Mount Cyllene) beheads the sleeping Argus — the resolution of the watchman tale, hence his epithet Argiphontes. Anchored to Argus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: nec mora, falcato nutantem vulnerat ense, qua collo est confine caput,
question: Quali ense Mercurius Argum nutantem vulneravit, qua collo caput confine est?
question_en: With what kind of sword did Mercury strike the nodding Argus, where the head borders on the neck?
derivation: The falcatus ensis — the curved harpe of Mercury (the same blade type Perseus later wields) — used to behead Argus. Anchored to Mercury + Argus; one-word answer verbatim (falcato ... ense).

author: Ovid
source_text: Excipit hos volucrisque suae Saturnia pennis collocat et gemmis caudam stellantibus inplet.
question: In cuius avis pennis Iuno centum oculos Argi occisi collocavit?
question_en: On the feathers of what bird did Juno place the hundred eyes of the slain Argus?
answer_en: On the feathers of the peacock, her own bird.
derivation: The aetiology of the peacock's starry tail: Juno sets Argus's eyes on the feathers of 'her bird' — the peacock, Juno's canonical bird. Anchored to Juno + Argus; the identification volucris sua = pavo is the shared knowledge the question tests.

author: Ovid
source_text: protinus exarsit nec tempora distulit irae horriferamque oculis animoque obiecit Erinyn paelicis Argolicae stimulosque in pectore caecos condidit et profugam per totum exercuit orbem.
question: Quam ultricem Iuno, Argo occiso, oculis animoque Ius obiecit, ut eam profugam per totum orbem ageret?
question_en: What avenging spirit did Juno, after Argus was killed, set before the eyes and mind of Io, to drive her as a fugitive over the whole world?
derivation: In Ovid's version Juno torments Io with a horrifying Erinys and blind goads, driving her across the world (the gadfly of the Greek tradition). Anchored to Juno + Io; one-name answer verbatim (obiecit Erinyn).

author: Ovid
source_text: ultimus inmenso restabas, Nile, labori; quem simulac tetigit, positisque in margine ripae procubuit genibus resupinoque ardua collo,
question: Quod flumen ultimum inmenso labori Ius profugae restabat?
question_en: What river remained as the last stage of the fugitive Io's immense toil?
derivation: Io's wanderings end at the Nile — the canonical link of the Argive heifer to Egypt, where she becomes a goddess. Anchored to Io; one-name river answer verbatim (ultimus ... restabas, Nile, labori).

author: Ovid
source_text: finiat ut poenas tandem, rogat 'in' que 'futurum pone metus' inquit: 'numquam tibi causa doloris haec erit,' et Stygias iubet hoc audire paludes.
question: Quas paludes Iuppiter audire iussit, cum Iunoni promitteret Io numquam posthac causam doloris futuram esse?
question_en: What waters did Jupiter order to hear his words, when he promised Juno that Io would never again be a cause of grief?
derivation: Jove seals his promise by calling the Stygian waters to witness — the inviolable oath of the gods by the Styx, a canonical piece of divine custom. Anchored to Jupiter + Juno + Io; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Ut lenita dea est, vultus capit illa priores fitque, quod ante fuit: fugiunt e corpore saetae, cornua decrescunt, fit luminis artior orbis, contrahitur rictus, redeunt umerique manusque, ungulaque in quinos dilapsa absumitur ungues: de bove nil superest formae nisi candor in illa.
question: Quid unum de bove in Io, formae pristinae redditae, superfuit?
question_en: What single trace of the cow remained in Io, when she was restored to her former shape?
derivation: Io's restoration once Juno is appeased: everything bovine vanishes except her radiant whiteness (de bove nil superest formae nisi candor). Anchored to Io; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nunc dea linigera colitur celeberrima turba.
question: A quali turba Io, dea facta, nunc celeberrima colitur, ut Ovidius scribit?
question_en: By what sort of throng is Io, now made a goddess, worshipped most famously, as Ovid writes?
answer_en: By the linen-wearing throng (the Egyptian worshippers of Isis).
derivation: Io restored and worshipped as a goddess by the linen-clad crowd — the linen-wearing (linigera) devotees mark the Egyptian cult of Isis, with whom Io was identified. Anchored to Io + her deification; short answer verbatim. A cult fact of shared Greco-Roman religion.

author: Ovid
source_text: huic Epaphus magni genitus de semine tandem creditur esse Iovis perque urbes iuncta parenti templa tenet.
question: Quis filius Ius de semine magni Iovis genitus esse creditur, qui per urbes templa iuncta matri tenet?
question_en: Which son of Io is believed to have been begotten of great Jupiter's seed, holding temples in the cities joined to his mother's?
derivation: Epaphus, son of Io by Jove, worshipped in temples beside his mother's — the genealogical bridge to the Phaethon story. Anchored to Io + Jupiter; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: fuit huic animis aequalis et annis Sole satus Phaethon, quem quondam magna loquentem nec sibi cedentem Phoeboque parente superbum
question: Quo patre satus esse ferebatur Phaethon, Epapho animis annisque aequalis?
question_en: Of what father was Phaethon, the equal of Epaphus in spirit and years, said to be born?
derivation: Phaethon as son of the Sun (Sole satus), proud of his father Phoebus — the premise of the story that spills into book 2. Anchored to Phaethon + Epaphus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: quem quondam magna loquentem nec sibi cedentem Phoeboque parente superbum non tulit Inachides 'matri' que ait 'omnia demens credis et es tumidus genitoris imagine falsi.'
question: Quis Phaethonti, Phoebo parente superbo, obiecit eum imagine falsi genitoris tumidum esse?
question_en: Who taunted Phaethon, proud of his father Phoebus, that he was puffed up with the image of a false father?
derivation: The taunt of Epaphus (called Inachides, grandson of Inachus through Io) that sets Phaethon on his fatal quest. Anchored to Phaethon + Phoebus; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: erubuit Phaethon iramque pudore repressit et tulit ad Clymenen Epaphi convicia matrem
question: Quae erat mater Phaethontis, ad quam convicia Epaphi rettulit?
question_en: Who was the mother of Phaethon, to whom he carried back the insults of Epaphus?
derivation: Clymene as Phaethon's mother, to whom the boy brings Epaphus's taunt and who swears by the Sun that the Sun is his father. Anchored to Phaethon + Epaphus; one-name answer verbatim (ad Clymenen ... matrem).

author: Ovid
source_text: emicat extemplo laetus post talia matris dicta suae Phaethon et concipit aethera mente Aethiopasque suos positosque sub ignibus Indos sidereis transit patriosque adit inpiger ortus.
question: Quas gentes Phaethon transiit, cum ad patrios Solis ortus profectus esset?
question_en: What peoples did Phaethon pass through, when he set out for the rising-place of his father the Sun?
derivation: The close of book 1: Phaethon crosses his Ethiopians and the Indians beneath the starry fires to reach his father's rising-place (the palace of the Sun, where book 2 opens). Anchored to Phaethon + the Sun; brief two-name answer verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Trimalchio, lautissimus homo. Horologium in triclinio et bucinatorem habet subornatum, ut subinde sciat quantum de vita perdiderit!
question: Quae duo instrumenta Trimalchio in triclinio suo habebat, ut quantum de vita perdidisset subinde sciret?
question_en: What two devices did Trimalchio keep in his dining room so that he might constantly know how much of his life he had lost?
derivation: One of the most famous introductory details of the Cena Trimalchionis: the clock and the liveried trumpeter in the triclinium. Anchored to the named Trimalchio; two-item answer supported verbatim. The Cena is canonical ambient knowledge for the well-read (criterion 8).

author: Petronius
source_text: cum subito videmus senem calvum, tunica vestitum russea, inter pueros capillatos ludentem pila. Nec tam pueri nos, quamquam erat operae pretium, ad spectaculum duxerant, quam ipse pater familiae, qui soleatus pila prasina exercebatur.
question: Quo colore erat pila, qua Trimalchio senex calvus ante cenam se exercebat?
question_en: What color was the ball with which the bald old Trimalchio exercised before dinner?
derivation: The celebrated first appearance of Trimalchio: a bald old man in a russet tunic playing with a green (prasina) ball. Anchored to Trimalchio; single color answer supported verbatim ('pila prasina exercebatur'). The green ball is a stock detail of the Cena.

author: Petronius
source_text: QVISQVIS SERVVS SINE DOMINICO IVSSV FORAS EXIERIT ACCIPIET PLAGAS CENTVM.
question: Quot plagas, secundum libellum in poste ianuae Trimalchionis fixum, accepturus erat servus qui sine iussu domini foras exisset?
question_en: According to the notice fixed on Trimalchio's doorpost, how many lashes would a slave receive who went out of doors without his master's order?
derivation: The posted household edict at Trimalchio's door: 100 lashes for any slave leaving without permission. Anchored to Trimalchio's house; single number answer supported verbatim by the quoted inscription.

author: Petronius
source_text: Ad sinistram enim intrantibus non longe ab ostiarii cella canis ingens, catena vinctus, in pariete erat pictus superque quadrata littera scriptum CAVE CANEM.
question: Quae verba supra canem pictum in pariete domus Trimalchionis quadrata littera scripta erant?
question_en: What words were written in square capitals above the painted dog on the wall of Trimalchio's house?
derivation: The most famous single detail of the Satyricon: the painted chained dog with the warning CAVE CANEM at Trimalchio's entrance, matching the real mosaic from Pompeii. Anchored to Trimalchio's house; the two-word answer is quoted verbatim. Quintessential shared Roman daily-life knowledge.

author: Petronius
source_text: Erat autem venalicium cum titulis pictis, et ipse Trimalchio capillatus caduceum tenebat Minervamque ducente Romam intrabat.
question: Qua dea ducente Trimalchio in pictura parietis domus suae Romam intrabat?
question_en: Led by which goddess did Trimalchio enter Rome in the wall-painting of his own house?
derivation: The biographical fresco in Trimalchio's portico: the young long-haired Trimalchio, holding the caduceus, enters Rome led by Minerva. Anchored to Trimalchio + Rome; single named-deity answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Interrogare ergo atriensem coepi, quas in medio picturas haberent. Iliada et Odyssian, inquit, ac Laenatis gladiatorium munus.
question: Praeter Iliada et Odyssian, quae pictura in medio domus Trimalchionis erat, ut atriensis narravit?
question_en: Besides the Iliad and the Odyssey, what painting was in the middle of Trimalchio's house, as the steward reported?
derivation: The atriensis lists the middle paintings: the Iliad, the Odyssey, and Laenas' gladiatorial games — Homer beside the arena, a signature joke about freedman taste. Anchored to Trimalchio's house; short named answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: in postibus triclinii fasces erant cum securibus fixi, quorum imam partem quasi embolum navis aeneum finiebat, in quo erat scriptum: C. POMPEIO TRIMALCHIONI SEVIRO AVGVSTALI CINNAMVS DISPENSATOR.
question: Quo sacerdotio sive honore Trimalchio in titulo postibus triclinii fixo ornatur?
question_en: With what priesthood or office is Trimalchio honored in the inscription fixed on his dining-room doorposts?
derivation: Trimalchio's proudest title, sevir Augustalis — the civic-religious office open to rich freedmen — displayed with fasces at his triclinium door. Anchored to Trimalchio; single-office answer supported verbatim by the quoted dedication of Cinnamus the steward.

author: Petronius
source_text: His repleti voluptatibus cum conaremur in triclinium intrare, exclamavit unus ex pueris, qui super hoc officium erat positus: 'Dextro pede!'
question: Quo pede convivae limen triclinii Trimalchionis transire iubebantur, ne omen malum fieret?
question_en: With which foot were guests ordered to cross the threshold of Trimalchio's dining room, lest it be a bad omen?
derivation: The famous Roman threshold superstition: a slave posted at Trimalchio's door cries 'Dextro pede!' — enter right foot first. Anchored to Trimalchio's triclinium; single answer supported verbatim. A shared Roman luck-belief, criterion 8's home turf.

author: Petronius
source_text: Ceterum in promulsidari asellus erat Corinthius cum bisaccio positus, qui habebat olivas in altera parte albas, in altera nigras.
question: Quid asellus Corinthius in promulsidari cenae Trimalchionis in bisaccio suo gerebat?
answer: Olivas, in altera parte albas, in altera nigras.
question_en: What did the Corinthian bronze donkey on the hors-d'oeuvre tray at Trimalchio's dinner carry in its saddle-bags?
answer_en: Olives — white in one side, black in the other.
derivation: The opening dish of the Cena: a Corinthian-bronze donkey with double panniers of white and black olives. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; short answer supported verbatim. Named-dish food culture (criterion 8).

author: Petronius
source_text: Ponticuli etiam ferruminati sustinebant glires melle ac papavere sparsos.
question: Quibus rebus aspersi glires in gustatione cenae Trimalchionis appositi sunt?
question_en: With what were the dormice sprinkled that were served among the hors-d'oeuvres at Trimalchio's dinner?
derivation: Dormice with honey and poppy-seed — the emblematic Roman delicacy, attested here at the Cena. Anchored to Trimalchio's gustatio; two-ingredient answer supported verbatim. Classic cibus fact.

author: Petronius
source_text: Pallio enim coccineo adrasum excluserat caput, circaque oneratas veste cervices laticlaviam immiserat mappam fimbriis hinc atque illinc pendentibus.
question: Quo colore erat pallium, quo Trimalchio in cenam suam allatus caput adrasum excluserat?
question_en: What color was the cloak from which Trimalchio, carried in to his own dinner, thrust his close-shaven head?
derivation: Trimalchio's grand entrance: the scarlet pallium and a napkin with a broad purple stripe (a mock laticlavus). Anchored to Trimalchio; single color answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Sequebatur puer cum tabula terebinthina et crystallinis tesseris, notavique rem omnium delicatissimam. Pro calculis enim albis ac nigris aureos argenteosque habebat denarios.
question: Quibus rebus pro calculis albis ac nigris Trimalchio in lusu suo utebatur?
question_en: What did Trimalchio use in his board game instead of white and black counters?
derivation: Trimalchio plays his game with gold and silver coins for counters — the celebrated emblem of his vulgar wealth. Anchored to Trimalchio; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Amici, ait, pavonis ova gallinae iussi supponi. Et mehercules timeo ne iam concepti sint. Temptemus tamen, si adhuc sorbilia sunt.
question: Cuius avis ova Trimalchio gallinae supponi iussit, ut convivis in gustatione apponerentur?
question_en: Which bird's eggs did Trimalchio order to be placed under a hen, to be served to his guests as an appetizer?
derivation: The peahen-egg course: eggs 'of a peacock' set under a wooden hen, each containing a fig-pecker in peppered yolk. Anchored to Trimalchio; single-bird answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Accipimus nos cochlearia non minus selibras pendentia, ovaque ex farina pingui figurata pertundimus. Ego quidem paene proieci partem meam ... persecutus putamen manu, pinguissimam ficedulam inveni piperato vitello circumdatam.
question: Quae avicula intra ova ficta in cena Trimalchionis apposita, piperato vitello circumdata, inventa est?
question_en: What little bird was found inside the imitation eggs served at Trimalchio's dinner, surrounded by peppered yolk?
derivation: The surprise inside the pastry 'peahen eggs': a ficedula (fig-pecker, a prized table bird) in peppered egg-yolk. Anchored to the Cena's famous egg course; single answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Statim allatae sunt amphorae vitreae diligenter gypsatae, quarum in cervicibus pittacia erant affixa cum hoc titulo: FALERNVM OPIMIANVM ANNORVM CENTVM.
question: Quod vinum et quot annorum in amphoris gypsatis apud Trimalchionem titulo inscriptum apponebatur?
question_en: What wine, and of what age, was served at Trimalchio's with a label inscribed on the plastered amphorae?
answer_en: Falernian of Opimius' vintage, one hundred years old.
derivation: The famous wine label FALERNUM OPIMIANUM ANNORUM CENTUM — Falernian of the legendary Opimian vintage (121 BC), absurdly labeled a round hundred years old. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; answer quoted verbatim from the titulus. Falernian and the Opimian vintage are canonical Roman wine culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Potantibus ergo nobis et accuratissime lautitias mirantibus larvam argenteam attulit servus sic aptatam ut articuli eius vertebraeque laxatae in omnem partem flecterentur.
question: Cuius rei imaginem argenteam, articulis in omnem partem flexilibus, servus inter pocula in mensam Trimalchionis attulit?
question_en: What silver figure, with joints flexible in every direction, did a slave bring to Trimalchio's table during the drinking?
derivation: The silver skeleton (larva argentea) thrown on the table with the carpe-diem verses 'Ergo vivamus, dum licet esse bene' — a celebrated Roman memento mori at banquets. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; single-object answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Rotundum enim repositorium duodecim habebat signa in orbe disposita, super quae proprium convenientemque materiae structor imposuerat cibum: super arietem cicer arietinum, super taurum bubulae frustum, super geminos testiculos ac rienes ... super aquarium anserem, super pisces duos mullos.
question: Quot signa caelestia in orbe disposita rotundum illud repositorium cenae Trimalchionis habebat, super quae singulis conveniens cibus impositus erat?
question_en: How many celestial signs, arranged in a circle, did the famous round dish at Trimalchio's dinner bear, with an appropriate food placed on each?
derivation: The zodiac dish: a round tray with the twelve signs, each topped by a punningly appropriate food (chickpea on the Ram, beef on the Bull, mullets on the Fishes...). Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; single number answer supported verbatim ('duodecim habebat signa').

author: Petronius
source_text: super arietem cicer arietinum, super taurum bubulae frustum, super geminos testiculos ac rienes, super cancrum coronam, super leonem ficum Africanam.
question: Quis cibus in repositorio zodiaco Trimalchionis super signum arietis impositus erat?
question_en: What food was placed over the sign of the Ram on Trimalchio's zodiac dish?
derivation: The pun-dish of the zodiac tray: chickpea (cicer arietinum, 'ram chickpea') on Aries. Anchored to the famous zodiac repositorium; single answer supported verbatim; the joke survives translation because the botanical name itself carries it.

author: Petronius
source_text: Haec ut dixit, ad symphoniam quattuor tripudiantes procurrerunt superioremque partem repositorii abstulerunt. Quo facto, videmus infra altilia et sumina leporemque in medio pinnis subornatum, ut Pegasus videretur.
question: Quod animal fabulosum lepus pinnis subornatus in medio ferculo Trimalchionis imitabatur?
question_en: What mythical creature did the hare fitted with wings in the middle of Trimalchio's dish represent?
derivation: Under the zodiac lid: fattened fowls, sow's udders, and a hare with wings 'so that it looked like Pegasus'. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; single mythological-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Notavimus etiam circa angulos repositorii Marsyas quattuor, ex quorum utriculis garum piperatum currebat super pisces, qui tamquam in euripo natabant.
question: Quod liquamen ex utriculis quattuor Marsyarum super pisces in ferculo Trimalchionis currebat?
question_en: What sauce ran from the little wineskins of the four Marsyas figures over the fish on Trimalchio's dish?
derivation: Four Marsyas figures at the tray's corners pour peppered garum — the staple Roman fish sauce — over fish swimming as in a channel. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; named-sauce answer supported verbatim. Garum is core Roman food culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Vides illum, inquit, qui obsonium carpit: Carpus vocatur. Ita quotiescumque dicit 'Carpe', eodem verbo et vocat et imperat.
question: Quo nomine scissor ille apud Trimalchionem vocabatur, ut dominus uno verbo 'Carpe' et vocaret et imperaret?
question_en: What was the name of the carver at Trimalchio's, so that his master with the single word 'Carpe' both called him and gave the order?
derivation: The Carpe/Carpus joke: the carver is named Carpus so 'Carpe!' is at once vocative and imperative. Anchored to Trimalchio's household; single-name answer supported verbatim. One of the most-cited jokes of the Cena; the point (a servant named so that calling him is the command to carve) survives translation as a fact about the name.

author: Petronius
source_text: Vxor, inquit, Trimalchionis, Fortunata appellatur, quae nummos modio metitur.
question: Quo nomine uxor Trimalchionis appellabatur?
question_en: What was the name of Trimalchio's wife?
derivation: Fortunata, Trimalchio's wife, 'who measures her money by the peck' — a principal character of the Cena. Anchored to Trimalchio; single-name answer supported verbatim. Core ambient knowledge of the Satyricon.

author: Petronius
source_text: Ad summam, parum illi bona lana nascebatur; arietes a Tarento emit, et eos culavit in gregem. Mel Atticum ut domi nasceretur, apes ab Athenis iussit afferri.
question: Vnde Trimalchio apes afferri iussit, ut mel Atticum domi sibi nasceretur?
question_en: From where did Trimalchio order bees to be brought, so that Attic honey might be produced on his own estate?
derivation: Trimalchio's 'everything home-grown' boast: rams from Tarentum, bees from Athens for Attic honey. Anchored to Trimalchio; single place answer supported verbatim. Attic honey as the proverbial best is shared Roman food culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: In cancro ego natus sum: ideo multis pedibus sto, et in mari et in terra multa possideo; nam cancer et hoc et illoc quadrat.
question: Quo signo caelesti Trimalchio se natum esse convivis suis dixit?
question_en: Under which sign of the zodiac did Trimalchio tell his guests he had been born?
derivation: In his astrological lecture on the zodiac dish Trimalchio declares 'In cancro ego natus sum' — hence he stands on many feet and owns property on land and sea. Anchored to Trimalchio; single-sign answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Secutum est hos repositorium, in quo positus erat primae magnitudinis aper, et quidem pilleatus, e cuius dentibus sportellae dependebant duae palmulis textae, altera caryatis, altera thebaicis repleta.
question: Quo capitis ornamento aper ille primae magnitudinis in cena Trimalchionis allatus insignis erat?
question_en: What head-covering distinguished the huge boar brought in at Trimalchio's dinner?
derivation: The boar served wearing the pilleus, the cap of liberty — one of the Cena's most famous conceits. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; single-object answer supported verbatim ('aper, et quidem pilleatus').

author: Petronius
source_text: Hic aper, cum heri summa cena eum vindicasset, a conviviis dimissus est; itaque hodie tamquam libertus in convivium revertitur.
question: Cur aper in cena Trimalchionis pilleatus allatus est, ut convivae interpretati sunt?
answer: Quia heri a cena dimissus hodie tamquam libertus revertebatur.
question_en: Why was the boar at Trimalchio's dinner brought in wearing a freedman's cap, as the guests explained?
answer_en: Because, sent away from dinner the day before, it returned today as a freedman.
derivation: The riddle of the pilleated boar solved: it had been 'dismissed' by yesterday's diners, so today it returns as a freed slave — freedman culture turned into a table joke. Anchored to the famous boar of the Cena; the explanation is a short checkable point stated verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: strictoque venatorio cultro latus apri vehementer percussit, ex cuius plaga turdi evolaverunt.
question: Quae aves ex latere apri percusso in cena Trimalchionis evolaverunt?
question_en: What birds flew out of the boar's side when it was struck open at Trimalchio's dinner?
derivation: The carver strikes the boar and live thrushes fly out, to be caught by waiting fowlers — a celebrated coup de theatre of the Cena. Anchored to the boar course; single answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: puer speciosus, vitibus hederisque redimitus ... Ad quem sonum conversus Trimalchio: 'Dionyse, inquit, liber esto.' Puer detraxit pilleum apro capitique suo imposuit.
question: Quibus verbis Trimalchio puerum Dionysum appellatum manumisisse ioco visus est?
question_en: With what words did Trimalchio jokingly appear to free the slave-boy named Dionysus?
derivation: The Liber/liber pun: Trimalchio tells the boy costumed as Bacchus 'Dionyse, liber esto', then boasts he has 'Liberum patrem'. Anchored to Trimalchio + the named boy; the two-word formula (also the legal manumission formula) is quoted verbatim and its double sense is a canonical joke of the Cena.

author: Petronius
source_text: Homo bellus, tam bonus Chrysanthus animam ebulliit. Modo, modo me appellavit. Videor mihi cum illo loqui. Heu, eheu! Vtres inflati ambulamus.
question: Quis homo, ut Seleucus in cena Trimalchionis narravit, nuper animam ebulliit, cuius in funere ipse fuerat?
question_en: Who, as Seleucus related at Trimalchio's dinner, had just 'bubbled out his soul', at whose funeral he had been?
derivation: Seleucus' funeral gossip: the death of Chrysanthus ('animam ebulliit', a famous colloquialism) after a five-day fast against his doctors. Anchored to the named Chrysanthus + Seleucus at the Cena; single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Et quot putas illum annos secum tulisse? Septuaginta et supra. Sed corneolus fuit, aetatem bene ferebat, niger tanquam corvus.
question: Quot annos Chrysanthus, cuius mors in cena Trimalchionis narratur, secum tulisse dicitur?
question_en: How many years is Chrysanthus, whose death is discussed at Trimalchio's dinner, said to have carried with him?
derivation: Phileros' obituary of Chrysanthus: he died at over seventy, still hale, 'black as a crow'. Anchored to the named Chrysanthus; number answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Aediles male eveniat, qui cum pistoribus colludunt: 'Serva me, servabo te.' Itaque populus minutus laborat; nam isti maiores maxillae semper Saturnalia agunt.
question: Cum quibus opificibus aediles, ut Ganymedes apud Petronium queritur, de annona colludebant?
question_en: With which tradesmen, as Ganymedes complains in Petronius, did the aediles collude over the grain supply?
derivation: Ganymedes' bread-price tirade: the aediles are in league with the bakers ('Serva me, servabo te'), so the little man starves. Anchored to the aediles + the named speaker at the Cena; single answer supported verbatim. Everyday municipal-corruption culture, with the proverbial 'you scratch my back'.

author: Petronius
source_text: Et ecce habituri sumus munus excellente in triduo die festa; familia non lanisticia, sed plurimi liberti. Et Titus noster magnum animum habet, et est caldicerebrius.
question: Quis apud Petronium munus gladiatorium excellens in triduo editurus erat, ut Echion centonarius narrat?
question_en: Who, according to the rag-dealer Echion in Petronius, was about to give an excellent three-day gladiatorial show?
derivation: Echion's gladiator gossip: Titus will give a splendid munus over three festival days, with cold steel and no running away. Anchored to the named Titus + Echion; single-name answer supported verbatim. Spectacle culture of the colonial town.

author: Petronius
source_text: Iam Manios aliquot habet et mulierem essedariam et dispensatorem Glyconis, qui deprehensus est cum dominam suam delectaretur.
question: Cuius generis gladiatorem feminam Titus ille apud Petronium in munus suum comparaverat?
question_en: What type of female gladiator had Titus in Petronius acquired for his show?
derivation: Among Titus' attractions: a woman who fights from a British war-chariot (essedaria) — a named gladiator type. Anchored to Titus' munus; single-type answer supported verbatim. Gladiatorial realia (criterion 8).

author: Petronius
source_text: Glyco autem, sestertiarius homo, dispensatorem ad bestias dedit. Hoc est se ipsum traducere.
question: Quo supplicio Glyco apud Petronium dispensatorem suum, cum domina deprehensum, affecit?
question_en: With what punishment did Glyco in Petronius visit his steward, caught with his mistress?
answer_en: He gave him to the beasts.
derivation: Glyco condemns his steward to the beasts for adultery with his wife — damnatio ad bestias as a master's revenge, aired as town gossip. Anchored to the named Glyco; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: 'Munus tamen, inquit, tibi dedi — et ego tibi plodo. Computa, et tibi plus do quam accepi. Manus manum lavat.'
question: Quod proverbium de mutuis officiis Echion apud Petronium de munerario et populo profert?
question_en: What proverb about mutual services does Echion quote in Petronius concerning the giver of games and the people?
answer_en: 'One hand washes the other' (manus manum lavat).
derivation: The proverb manus manum lavat, preserved verbatim in Echion's speech — one of the most famous Latin sayings, here in its locus classicus. Anchored to Petronius as the attesting text; the three-word answer is quoted verbatim and its point survives translation.

author: Petronius
source_text: Emi ergo nunc puero aliquot libra rubricata, quia volo illum ad domusionem aliquid de iure gustare. Habet haec res panem. ... Litterae thesaurum est, et artificium nunquam moritur.
question: Quam sententiam de litteris Echion centonarius apud Petronium profert, cum de filio suo erudiendo loquitur?
question_en: What maxim about letters does the rag-dealer Echion pronounce in Petronius when speaking of his son's education?
derivation: Echion's famous (solecistic) maxim 'litterae thesaurum est' with its pendant 'artificium nunquam moritur'. Anchored to the named Echion at the Cena; short quotable answer supported verbatim. A celebrated saying the text itself made proverbial.

author: Petronius
source_text: Nam mundatis ad symphoniam mensis tres albi sues in triclinium adducti sunt capistris et tintinnabulis culti, quorum unum bimum nomenculator esse dicebat, alterum trimum, tertium vero iam sexennem.
question: Quot sues albi vivi, capistris et tintinnabulis culti, in triclinium Trimalchionis adducti sunt?
question_en: How many live white pigs, decked with muzzles and bells, were led into Trimalchio's dining room?
derivation: Three white pigs of two, three, and six years are paraded so the guests may choose their dinner. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; single number supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Et ne me putes studia fastiditum, tres bybliothecas habeo, unam Graecam, alteram Latinam.
question: Quot bybliothecas se habere Trimalchio gloriatus est?
question_en: How many libraries did Trimalchio boast that he owned?
derivation: The famous arithmetic joke: 'I have three libraries, one Greek, the other Latin.' Anchored to Trimalchio; single number supported verbatim; the count (three announced, two listed) is the joke every reader of the Cena carries.

author: Petronius
source_text: Nam Sibyllam quidem Cumis ego ipse oculis meis vidi in ampulla pendere, et cum illi pueri dicerent: 'Sibilla, ti thelis?', respondebat illa: 'apothanin thelo'.
question: Quid Sibylla Cumana, in ampulla pendens, pueris interrogantibus se velle respondebat, ut Trimalchio narrat?
question_en: What did the Cumaean Sibyl, hanging in her jar, answer that she wanted when the boys questioned her, as Trimalchio tells it?
answer_en: That she wanted to die ('apothanein thelo').
derivation: The celebrated Sibyl-in-the-bottle story: at Cumae she hangs in an ampulla and, asked 'Sibyl, what do you want?', answers 'I want to die.' Anchored to the Cumaean Sibyl + Trimalchio as narrator; short answer supported verbatim by the quoted Greek. Canonical myth-fact (famous also as the epigraph of The Waste Land).

author: Petronius
source_text: Cum constitisset ad mensam cocus tristis et diceret se oblitum esse exinterare ... 'Ergo, inquit, quia tam malae memoriae es, palam nobis illum exintera.' Recepta cocus tunica cultrum arripuit, porcique ventrem hinc atque illinc timida manu secuit. Nec mora, ex plagis ponderis inclinatione crescentibus tomacula cum botulis effusa sunt.
question: Quae obsonia ex ventre porci non exinterati coram convivis Trimalchionis secti effusa sunt?
question_en: What delicacies poured out of the belly of the 'ungutted' pig when it was cut open before Trimalchio's guests?
derivation: The mock-punished cook's trick: the pig 'forgotten to be gutted' spills out tomacula and botuli when slit. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; two-item answer supported verbatim. Named Roman sausage types are food culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Et forsitan, inquit, quaeris quare solus Corinthea vera possideam: quia scilicet aerarius, a quo emo, Corinthus vocatur.
question: Cur Trimalchio solus vera Corinthea vasa possidere se iactabat?
answer: Quia aerarius, a quo emebat, Corinthus vocabatur.
question_en: Why did Trimalchio boast that he alone possessed genuine Corinthian bronze?
answer_en: Because the bronzesmith he bought from was named Corinthus.
derivation: The Corinthus joke: his bronzes are 'Corinthian' because his dealer is named Corinthus. Anchored to Trimalchio; the checkable point (the dealer's name) is stated verbatim. One of the Cena's most quoted witticisms; Corinthian bronze itself is shared Roman luxury culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Fuit tamen faber qui fecit phialam vitream, quae non frangebatur. ... Postquam negavit, iussit illum Caesar decollari: quia enim, si scitum esset, aurum pro luto haberemus.
question: Quid Caesar de fabro fecit, qui phialam vitream infrangibilem invenerat, ut Trimalchio narrat?
