question_en: What did Caesar do with the craftsman who had invented unbreakable glass, as Trimalchio tells the story?
derivation: The famous legend of unbreakable (flexible) glass: the inventor shows Caesar a phiala that will not shatter, admits no one else knows the secret, and is beheaded lest gold become as cheap as mud. Anchored to Caesar + the story as Trimalchio tells it; short answer supported verbatim. A celebrated anecdote also in Pliny — canonical ambient knowledge.

author: Petronius
source_text: Nam Hermerotis pugnas et Petraitis in poculis habeo, omnia ponderosa; meum enim intelligere nulla pecunia vendo.
question: Quorum duorum gladiatorum pugnas Trimalchio in poculis suis caelatas habebat?
question_en: The fights of which two gladiators did Trimalchio have engraved on his cups?
derivation: Trimalchio's cups show the bouts of the gladiators Hermeros and Petraites (Petraites recurs on his tomb reliefs, 71). Anchored to Trimalchio; two-name answer supported verbatim. Gladiator fandom on tableware is spectacle culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Et 'Aquam foras, vinum intro' clamavit Trimalchio.
question: Quibus verbis Trimalchio inter pocula clamavit, aquam eici et vinum induci iubens?
question_en: With what words did Trimalchio cry out over the cups, ordering water out and wine in?
answer_en: 'Water out, wine in!' (aquam foras, vinum intro).
derivation: The convivial cry 'Aquam foras, vinum intro' — a drinking-culture tag the Cena made proverbial. Anchored to Trimalchio; the formula is quoted verbatim and its sense survives translation.

author: Petronius
source_text: actuarius, qui tanquam Vrbis acta recitavit: 'VII kalendas Sextiles: in praedio Cumano, quod est Trimalchionis, nati sunt pueri XXX, puellae XL.'
question: Quot pueri et quot puellae uno die in praedio Cumano Trimalchionis nati esse in actis recitati sunt?
question_en: How many boys and how many girls were reported in the estate record as born in a single day on Trimalchio's Cumaean property?
derivation: The estate gazette read out like the acta Urbis: 30 boys and 40 girls born in one day on the Cumaean estate — the celebrated absurd index of Trimalchio's wealth. Anchored to Trimalchio's praedium Cumanum; two-number answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Mirabatur haec solus Trimalchio dicebatque ingratum artificium esse: ceterum duo esse in rebus humanis, quae libentissime spectaret, petauristarios et cornicines.
question: Quae duo acroamata Trimalchio libentissime se spectare dicebat?
question_en: What two kinds of entertainers did Trimalchio say he most enjoyed watching?
derivation: Trimalchio's stated taste in entertainment: acrobats and horn-blowers alone please him. Anchored to Trimalchio; two-item answer supported verbatim. Leisure culture of the Cena.

author: Petronius
source_text: in vicem enim poenae venit decretum Trimalchionis, quo puerum iussit liberum esse, ne quis posset dicere tantum virum esse a servo vulneratum.
question: Quid Trimalchio de puero decrevit, qui in brachium eius e scalis ceciderat?
question_en: What did Trimalchio decree concerning the boy who had fallen from the ladder onto his arm?
answer_en: He ordered him to be freed.
derivation: The acrobat who falls on Trimalchio is freed by decree — 'lest anyone say so great a man was wounded by a slave.' Anchored to Trimalchio + the falling boy; short answer supported verbatim. A famous set-piece of the Cena on manumission as display.

author: Petronius
source_text: Rogo, inquit, magister, quid putas inter Ciceronem et Publilium interesse? Ego alterum puto disertiorem fuisse, alterum honestiorem.
question: Quos duos scriptores Trimalchio inter se comparavit, alterum disertiorem, alterum honestiorem iudicans?
question_en: Which two writers did Trimalchio compare, judging the one more eloquent and the other more upright?
derivation: Trimalchio's literary verdict: Cicero the more eloquent, Publilius the more honest — the Cena's famous mock-criticism. Anchored to the two named authors + Trimalchio; two-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Quod autem, inquit, putamus secundum litteras difficillimum esse artificium? Ego puto medicum et nummularium.
question: Quae duo artificia Trimalchio post litteras difficillima esse putabat?
question_en: Which two trades did Trimalchio consider the most difficult after letters?
derivation: Trimalchio's table-philosophy: after literature the hardest trades are medicine and money-changing (the one sees inside men, the other sees the bronze through the silver). Anchored to Trimalchio; two-item answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: cum pittacia in scypho circumferri coeperunt, puerque super hoc positus officium apophoreta recitavit. 'Argentum sceleratum': allata est perna, supra quam acetabula erant posita.
question: Quo nomine dona vocabantur, quae convivae Trimalchionis sortibus ductis secum auferebant?
question_en: What was the name of the gifts which Trimalchio's guests drew by lot and carried away with them?
derivation: The lottery of punning apophoreta (take-home party gifts) at the Cena — the same convivial institution Martial's book 14 is named for. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; single-term answer supported verbatim; the custom, not the Latin word-play of individual lots, is the fact.

author: Petronius
source_text: Glebulas emi, lamellulas paravi; viginti ventres pasco et canem; contubernalem meam redemi, ne qui in illius capillis manus tergeret; mille denarios pro capite solvi; sevir gratis factus sum.
question: Quot denarios Hermeros conlibertus Trimalchionis pro capite contubernalis suae redimendae se solvisse iactat?
question_en: How many denarii does Hermeros, Trimalchio's fellow freedman, boast he paid to buy his mate's freedom?
derivation: Hermeros' self-defense: he bought his contubernalis free for 1000 denarii and became sevir without paying. Anchored to the named Hermeros; single number answer supported verbatim. Freedman economics — the price of a person — is core cultural realia.

author: Petronius
source_text: Quare ergo servivisti? Quia ipse me dedi in servitutem et malui civis Romanus esse quam tributarius.
question: Cur Hermeros apud Petronium se ipsum in servitutem dedisse dicit?
answer: Quia maluit civis Romanus esse quam tributarius.
question_en: Why does Hermeros in Petronius say he sold himself into slavery?
answer_en: Because he preferred to become a Roman citizen rather than a provincial tribute-payer.
derivation: Hermeros' famous paradox: he entered slavery voluntarily because manumission would make him a Roman citizen, better than a free tributarius. Anchored to the named speaker; the reason is a short checkable clause quoted verbatim — a much-cited fact about the Roman freedman route to citizenship.

author: Petronius
source_text: Plane qualis dominus, talis et servus.
question: Quod proverbium de domino et servo Hermeros apud Petronium in Gitonem ridentem torquet?
question_en: What proverb about master and slave does Hermeros hurl at the laughing Giton in Petronius?
answer_en: 'Like master, like slave' (qualis dominus, talis et servus).
derivation: The proverb 'qualis dominus, talis et servus', preserved verbatim in Hermeros' tirade — its locus classicus. Anchored to Petronius; the saying is the answer, quoted verbatim, and its point survives translation.

author: Petronius
source_text: O? Saturnalia? rogo, mensis December est? Quando vicesimam numerasti?
question: Quo mense Saturnalia agi solita esse Hermeros apud Petronium significat, cum Gitonem tanquam intempestive lascivientem obiurgat?
question_en: In what month does Hermeros in Petronius imply the Saturnalia were held, when he scolds Giton for untimely frolicking?
derivation: Hermeros' jibe 'Saturnalia? rogo, mensis December est?' attests the shared calendar fact that the license of the Saturnalia belongs to December. Anchored to the named festival; single-month answer supported verbatim. Core festival culture (criterion 8).

author: Petronius
source_text: clamorem Homeristae sustulerunt, interque familiam discurrentem vitulus in lance ducenaria elixus allatus est, et quidem galeatus. Secutus est Aiax strictoque gladio, tanquam insaniret, concidit.
question: Quis heros, dum Homeristae apud Trimalchionem fabulam agunt, vitulum galeatum stricto gladio tanquam insaniens concidit?
question_en: Which hero, while the Homeric performers acted at Trimalchio's, hacked up the helmeted boiled calf with drawn sword as if mad?
derivation: The Homeristae show: a boiled calf wearing a helmet is carved by a performer playing the mad Ajax. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena + the named hero; single-name answer supported verbatim. Ajax's madness is canonical myth used as dinner theater.

author: Petronius
source_text: Inter haec tres pueri candidas succincti tunicas intraverunt, quorum duo Lares bullatos super mensam posuerunt ... Aiebat autem unum Cerdonem, alterum Felicionem, tertium Lucronem vocari.
question: Quibus nominibus Lares domus Trimalchionis vocabantur?
question_en: By what names were the Lares of Trimalchio's household called?
derivation: Trimalchio's household gods bear money-names: Cerdo, Felicio, Lucro — the famous satiric emblem of freedman piety toward profit. Anchored to Trimalchio's Lares; three-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Rati ergo sacrum esse fericulum tam religioso apparatu perfusum, consurreximus altius et 'Augusto, patri patriae, feliciter' diximus.
question: Quibus verbis convivae Trimalchionis, sacrum esse fericulum rati, consurrexerunt et acclamaverunt?
question_en: With what words did Trimalchio's guests, thinking the dish sacred, rise and acclaim?
answer_en: 'Good fortune to Augustus, father of his country!'
derivation: The loyal acclamation 'Augusto, patri patriae, feliciter' at the saffron-spurting dessert — imperial-cult etiquette at a private table. Anchored to the emperor's title; the formula is quoted verbatim and its content survives translation.

author: Petronius
source_text: At ille circumminxit vestimenta sua, et subito lupus factus est. ... Intellexi illum versipellem esse, nec postea cum illo panem gustare potui, non si me occidisses.
question: Quis conviva Trimalchionis fabulam de milite narravit, qui inter monimenta lupus factus est?
question_en: Which of Trimalchio's guests told the story of the soldier who turned into a wolf among the tombs?
derivation: The werewolf tale of the Cena: Niceros tells how his companion, a soldier, urinated a circle around his clothes among the tombstones and became a wolf. Anchored to the named narrator + the famous story; single-name answer; the frame (61 'Trimalchio ad Nicerotem respexit... narra illud') and the quoted transformation support it. The most famous werewolf story in classical literature.

author: Petronius
source_text: Deinde ut respexi ad comitem, ille exuit se et omnia vestimenta secundum viam posuit. ... At ille circumminxit vestimenta sua, et subito lupus factus est. ... deinde accessi, ut vestimenta eius tollerem: illa autem lapidea facta sunt.
question: Quid de vestimentis militis versipellis in fabula Nicerotis factum est, postquam ille lupus abiit?
question_en: What happened to the werewolf soldier's clothes in Niceros' story after he ran off as a wolf?
derivation: The signature detail of the werewolf story: the clothes, ringed with urine, turn to stone, proving the magic. Anchored to Niceros' famous tale; short answer supported verbatim ('illa autem lapidea facta sunt').

author: Petronius
source_text: lupus enim villam intravit et omnia pecora tanquam lanius sanguinem illis misit. Nec tamen derisit, etiamsi fugit; senius enim noster lancea collum eius traiecit. ... iacebat miles meus in lecto tanquam bovis, et collum illius medicus curabat. Intellexi illum versipellem esse.
question: Quo indicio Niceros militem illum versipellem fuisse intellexit, cum domum rediit?
answer: Quod medicus collum eius curabat, quo loco lupus lancea traiectus erat.
question_en: By what sign did Niceros realize the soldier was a werewolf when he returned home?
answer_en: A doctor was treating his neck, where the wolf had been run through with a lance.
derivation: The proof of the versipellis: the wolf speared in the neck at the farm, the soldier found in bed with a neck wound. Anchored to Niceros' tale; the sympathetic-wound motif is the story's checkable point, supported verbatim. 'Versipellis' names the werewolf — the Latin term the passage made canonical.

author: Petronius
source_text: scilicet iam puerum strigae involaverant et supposuerant stramenticium vavatonem. Rogo vos, oportet credatis, sunt mulieres plussciae, sunt Nocturnae, et quod sursum est, deorsum faciunt.
question: Quid strigae in fabula Trimalchionis pro puero mortuo, quem involaverant, supposuerunt?
question_en: What did the witches in Trimalchio's story substitute for the dead boy they had carried off?
derivation: Trimalchio's striga story: the witches steal the boy's corpse and leave a straw changeling with no heart or innards. Anchored to Trimalchio's famous tale; short answer supported verbatim. The strigae (night-witches) are core Roman folklore.

author: Petronius
source_text: Quo admonitus officio Trimalchio Scylacem iussit adduci 'praesidium domus familiaeque'. Nec mora, ingentis formae adductus est canis catena vinctus.
question: Quo nomine canis ingens Trimalchionis, praesidium domus familiaeque, vocabatur?
question_en: What was the name of Trimalchio's huge dog, the 'guardian of house and household'?
derivation: Trimalchio's chained watchdog Scylax ('Puppy' in Greek), styled guardian of house and familia. Anchored to Trimalchio; single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Habinnas sevir est idemque lapidarius, qui videtur monumenta optime facere.
question: Quod artificium Habinnas sevir, amicus Trimalchionis, exercebat?
question_en: What trade did the sevir Habinnas, Trimalchio's friend, practice?
answer_en: He was a stonemason, a maker of tomb monuments.
derivation: Habinnas, sevir and monument-mason 'who makes tombstones best' — the friend later commissioned for Trimalchio's tomb. Anchored to the named Habinnas; single-trade answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Scissa lautum novendialem servo suo misello faciebat, quem mortuum manu miserat. Et, puto, cum vicensimariis magnam mantissam habet; quinquaginta enim millibus aestimant mortuum.
question: Quod convivium funebre Scissa servo suo mortuo faciebat, de quo Habinnas ad cenam Trimalchionis venit?
question_en: What funeral feast was Scissa holding for his dead slave, from which Habinnas came to Trimalchio's dinner?
derivation: Habinnas arrives from a novendialis — the Roman ninth-day funeral banquet — held by Scissa for a slave freed on his deathbed (with the 5% manumission tax, vicesima, in play). Anchored to the named Scissa; single-term answer supported verbatim. Funeral custom is core mores.

author: Petronius
source_text: Habuimus tamen in primo porcum botulo coronatum et circa sangunculum et gizeria optime facta et certe betam et panem autopyrum de suo sibi, quem ego malo quam candidum; nam et vires facit, et cum mea re causa facio, non ploro.
question: Quale panem Habinnas candido praeferre se dixit, cum cenam apud Scissam narraret?
question_en: What kind of bread did Habinnas say he prefers to white, when describing the dinner at Scissa's?
derivation: Habinnas prefers panis autopyrus (whole-wheat) to white bread because 'it gives strength'. Anchored to the named Habinnas; single answer supported verbatim. Named bread types are Roman food culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Venit ergo galbino succincta cingillo, ita ut infra cerasina appareret tunica et periscelides tortae phaecasiaeque inauratae.
question: Quo colore erat cingillum, quo Fortunata in cenam veniens succincta erat?
question_en: What color was the little belt with which Fortunata was girt when she came in to the dinner?
derivation: Fortunata's celebrated get-up: yellow-green sash over a cherry-red tunic, with twisted anklets and gilt slippers. Anchored to the named Fortunata; single-color answer supported verbatim. Dress culture of the freedman milieu.

author: Petronius
source_text: Nec ullus tot malorum finis fuisset, nisi epidipnis esset allata, turdi siliginei uvis passis nucibusque farsi.
question: Quibus rebus farsi erant turdi siliginei, qui in epidipnide cenae Trimalchionis allati sunt?
question_en: With what were the pastry thrushes stuffed that were brought in as the dessert course at Trimalchio's dinner?
derivation: The epidipnis (dessert course): imitation thrushes of fine wheat pastry stuffed with raisins and nuts. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; two-item answer supported verbatim. Named-dish food culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Non potest esse pretiosior homo. Volueris, de vulva faciet piscem, de lardo palumbam, de perna turturem, de colaepio gallinam. Et ideo ingenio meo impositum est illi nomen bellissimum; nam Daedalus vocatur.
question: Quo nomine cocus ille Trimalchionis vocabatur, qui de porco quidvis fingere poterat?
question_en: What was the name of Trimalchio's cook, who could fashion anything out of pork?
derivation: The virtuoso cook named Daedalus — after the mythical craftsman — because he makes fish from sow's womb, pigeon from bacon, turtledove from ham. Anchored to Trimalchio's household; single-name answer supported verbatim. A signature Cena fact.

author: Petronius
source_text: Et quia bonam mentem habet, attuli illi Roma munus cultros Norico ferro.
question: Ex quo ferro facti erant cultri, quos Trimalchio coco suo Daedalo Roma munus attulit?
question_en: Of what iron were the knives made that Trimalchio brought from Rome as a gift for his cook Daedalus?
derivation: The gift knives of Noric iron — Noricum's steel was proverbially the best (cf. Horace). Anchored to Trimalchio + Daedalus; single answer supported verbatim. Shared Roman knowledge of regional products.

author: Petronius
source_text: Permitto, inquit, Philargyre et Cario, etsi prasinianus es famosus, dic et Menophilae, contubernali tuae, discumbat.
question: Cuius factionis circensis fautor erat Philargyrus servus Trimalchionis?
question_en: Of which circus faction was Trimalchio's slave Philargyrus a partisan?
derivation: Philargyrus is a notorious partisan of the Green faction (prasina) of the circus; the cook likewise bets on the Greens at the next races (70 fin.). Anchored to the named slave + Trimalchio's household; single-faction answer supported verbatim. Chariot-faction fandom is core ludi culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Amici, inquit, et servi homines sunt et aeque unum lactem biberunt, etiam si illos malus fatus oppresserit. Tamen me salvo cito aquam liberam gustabunt. Ad summam, omnes illos in testamento meo manu mitto.
question: Quid Trimalchio de omnibus servis suis in testamento suo cavisse se publicavit?
question_en: What did Trimalchio announce he had provided for all his slaves in his will?
derivation: Trimalchio's testamentary manumission of all his slaves, proclaimed at table with the famous dictum 'et servi homines sunt'. Anchored to Trimalchio; short answer supported verbatim. Testamentary manumission is a core Roman institution.

author: Petronius
source_text: Nam Fortunatam meam heredem facio, et commendo illam omnibus amicis meis.
question: Quem heredem Trimalchio testamento suo, quod in cena recitavit, faciebat?
question_en: Whom did Trimalchio make his heir in the will he read out at dinner?
derivation: Trimalchio names Fortunata his heir and reads the whole will aloud at his own dinner. Anchored to Trimalchio + Fortunata; single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: praeterea ut sint in fronte pedes centum, in agrum pedes ducenti.
question: Quot pedes in fronte et quot in agrum monumentum Trimalchionis habere debebat?
answer: In fronte centum, in agrum ducentos.
question_en: How many feet of frontage and how many of depth was Trimalchio's tomb-plot to have?
answer_en: A hundred feet of frontage, two hundred of depth.
derivation: Trimalchio's tomb order to Habinnas uses the standard epigraphic plot formula (IN FRONTE P. C, IN AGRO P. CC), at absurd scale. Anchored to Trimalchio's monument; two-number answer supported verbatim. The formula itself is shared epigraphic culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Et ideo ante omnia adici volo: HOC MONUMENTUM HEREDEM NON SEQUATUR.
question: Quae formula sepulcralis ante omnia in monumento Trimalchionis adici debebat, ne sepulcrum ad heredem transiret?
question_en: What funerary formula did Trimalchio want added to his monument above all, so the tomb would not pass to his heir?
answer_en: 'This monument does not pass to the heir' (H.M.H.N.S.).
derivation: The standard Roman epitaph clause HMHNS ordered by Trimalchio for his tomb. Anchored to Trimalchio; the formula (a real, ubiquitous epigraphic clause) is quoted verbatim. Exactly the epitaph-formula culture of criterion 8.

author: Petronius
source_text: Horologium in medio, ut quisquis horas inspiciet, velit nolit, nomen meum legat.
question: Quid in medio monumento suo poni Trimalchio iussit, ut quisquis horas inspiceret nomen eius legeret?
question_en: What did Trimalchio order to be placed in the middle of his monument, so that whoever checked the time would read his name?
derivation: The sundial at the center of the tomb, forcing every passer-by to read Trimalchio's name — one of the most quoted touches of the Cena. Anchored to Trimalchio's monument; single-object answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: C. POMPEIVS TRIMALCHIO MAECENATIANVS HIC REQVIESCIT HVIC SEVIRATVS ABSENTI DECRETVS EST CVM POSSET IN OMNIBVS DECVRIIS ROMAE ESSE TAMEN NOLVIT PIVS FORTIS FIDELIS EX PARVO CREVIT SESTERTIVM RELIQVIT TRECENTIES NEC VNQVAM PHILOSOPHVM AVDIVIT VALE ET TV
question: Quot sestertium Trimalchio in epitaphio suo se reliquisse gloriatur?
answer: Trecenties (sestertium trecenties, id est triginta miliones sestertiorum).
question_en: How large a fortune does Trimalchio boast in his epitaph that he left?
derivation: The famous self-composed epitaph: 'EX PARVO CREVIT, SESTERTIVM RELIQVIT TRECENTIES'. Anchored to Trimalchio's epitaph; single sum answer supported verbatim. The epitaph is among the most quoted texts in the Satyricon.

author: Petronius
source_text: NEC VNQVAM PHILOSOPHVM AVDIVIT VALE ET TV
question: Quid Trimalchio in epitaphio suo se nunquam audivisse gloriatur?
question_en: What does Trimalchio boast in his epitaph that he never listened to?
derivation: The epitaph's crowning boast: 'and he never listened to a philosopher.' Anchored to Trimalchio's epitaph; one-word answer supported verbatim. A celebrated satiric line every reader of the Cena carries.

author: Petronius
source_text: C. POMPEIVS TRIMALCHIO MAECENATIANVS HIC REQVIESCIT
question: Quo agnomine Trimalchio in epitaphio suo praeter nomina C. Pompei ornatur?
question_en: What surname adorns Trimalchio in his epitaph besides the names C. Pompeius?
derivation: The epitaph's full name C. Pompeius Trimalchio Maecenatianus — the agnomen advertising a former master or patron Maecenas. Anchored to the famous epitaph; single-name answer quoted verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: ducente per porticum Gitone ad ianuam venimus, ubi canis catenarius tanto nos tumultu excepit, ut Ascyltos etiam in piscinam ceciderit. Nec non ego quoque ebrius, qui etiam pictum timueram canem, dum natanti opem fero, in eundem gurgitem tractus sum.
question: Nonne verus canis erat, quem Encolpius in aditu domus Trimalchionis primo timuerat?
question_en: Was the dog that Encolpius first feared at the entrance of Trimalchio's house a real one?
answer_en: No; it was painted on the wall.
derivation: The paired joke of the Cena: the terrifying entrance dog is a painting (CAVE CANEM), while a real chain-dog later knocks Ascyltos into the fishpond. Anchored to Encolpius + Trimalchio's house; short answer supported verbatim ('qui etiam pictum timueram canem'). The painted-dog gag is canonical.

author: Petronius
source_text: Erras, inquit, si putas te exire hac posse, qua venisti. Nemo unquam convivarum per eandem ianuam emissus est; alia intrant, alia exeunt.
question: Qua consuetudine convivae e domo Trimalchionis emittebantur, ut atriensis exponit?
question_en: By what house rule were guests let out of Trimalchio's home, as the porter explains?
answer_en: They entered by one door and left by another.
derivation: The labyrinth rule of Trimalchio's house: no guest ever leaves by the door he entered. Anchored to Trimalchio's house; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Haec dicente eo gallus gallinaceus cantavit. Qua voce confusus Trimalchio vinum sub mensa iussit effundi lucernamque etiam mero spargi. Immo anulum traiecit in dexteram manum et: 'Non sine causa, inquit, hic bucinus signum dedit; nam aut incendium oportet fiat, aut aliquis in vicinia animam abiciat.'
question: Quid portendere Trimalchio credidit gallum gallinaceum, qui inter cenam intempestive cantavit?
answer: Aut incendium aut mortem alicuius in vicinia.
question_en: What did Trimalchio believe the rooster that crowed untimely during dinner portended?
answer_en: Either a fire or a death in the neighborhood.
derivation: The rooster-crow omen: Trimalchio spills wine under the table, sprinkles the lamp, shifts his ring to the right hand, and has the offending cock cooked. Anchored to Trimalchio; two-item answer supported verbatim. Roman omen-lore of the Cena.

author: Petronius
source_text: coheredem me Caesari fecit, et accepi patrimonium laticlavium. Nemini tamen nihil satis est. Concupivi negotiari. Ne multis vos morer, quinque naves aedificavi, oneravi vinum — et tunc erat contra aurum — misi Romam. ... omnes naves naufragarunt. Factum, non fabula. Vno die Neptunus trecenties sestertium devoravit.
question: Quot naves Trimalchio, ut ipse de vita sua narrat, primum aedificavit et vino oneratas Romam misit?
question_en: How many ships, as Trimalchio tells his own life story, did he first build and send to Rome laden with wine?
derivation: Trimalchio's rags-to-riches autobiography: five wine-ships built, all wrecked, thirty million lost in a day ('Neptunus trecenties sestertium devoravit'), then the greater second fleet. Anchored to Trimalchio; single number supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Hoc loco Fortunata rem piam fecit: omne enim aurum suum, omnia vestimenta vendidit et mi centum aureos in manu posuit. Hoc fuit peculii mei fermentum.
question: Quot aureos Fortunata, venditis auro suo et vestimentis, Trimalchioni post naufragium in manu posuit?
question_en: How many gold pieces did Fortunata, having sold her gold and clothes, put in Trimalchio's hand after the shipwreck?
derivation: Fortunata's pious act, the 'yeast' of Trimalchio's fortune: she sold all her gold and clothing and gave him 100 aurei. Anchored to Fortunata + Trimalchio; single number supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: exhortavit mathematicus, qui venerat forte in coloniam nostram, Graeculio, Serapa nomine, consiliator deorum.
question: Quo nomine mathematicus ille Graeculus vocabatur, qui Trimalchioni fata eius exposuit?
question_en: What was the name of the little Greek astrologer who expounded Trimalchio's destiny to him?
derivation: The astrologer Serapa, 'counselor of the gods', who told Trimalchio his past and future. Anchored to Trimalchio; single-name answer supported verbatim. Astrologer-consulting is shared Roman practice.

author: Petronius
source_text: etiam nunc mi restare vitae annos triginta et menses quattuor et dies duos.
question: Quot annos, menses, dies vitae sibi restare Trimalchio ex responso mathematici Serapae credidit?
answer: Annos triginta, menses quattuor, dies duos.
question_en: How many years, months, and days of life did Trimalchio believe remained to him according to the astrologer Serapa's reckoning?
answer_en: Thirty years, four months, and two days.
derivation: The absurdly precise horoscope: 30 years, 4 months, 2 days left to live. Anchored to Trimalchio + Serapa; three-number answer supported verbatim. A famous satiric detail of astrological credulity.

author: Petronius
source_text: Credite, mihi: assem habeas, assem valeas; habes, habeberis. Sic amicus vester, qui fuit rana, nunc est rex.
question: Quam sententiam de asse et pretio hominis Trimalchio in fine cenae suae profert?
question_en: What maxim about the penny and a man's worth does Trimalchio pronounce at the end of his dinner?
answer_en: 'Have a penny, and you are worth a penny' (assem habeas, assem valeas).
derivation: Trimalchio's money-creed 'assem habeas, assem valeas; habes, habeberis', capped by 'qui fuit rana, nunc est rex' — sayings this text made famous. Anchored to Trimalchio; the proverb is quoted verbatim and its point survives translation.

author: Petronius
source_text: Consonuere cornicines funebri strepitu. Vnus praecipue servus libitinarii illius ... tam valde intonuit, ut totam concitaret viciniam. Itaque vigiles, qui custodiebant vicinam regionem, rati ardere Trimalchionis domum, effregerunt ianuam subito et cum aqua securibusque tumultuari suo iure coeperunt.
question: Qui, cornicinum funebri strepitu exciti, domum Trimalchionis ardere rati ianuam effregerunt?
question_en: Who, roused by the funereal blast of the horn-players, broke down Trimalchio's door thinking the house was on fire?
derivation: The finale of the Cena: Trimalchio stages his own funeral, the horns blare, and the vigiles — the fire brigade/night watch — burst in with water and axes. Anchored to Trimalchio's mock funeral; single answer supported verbatim. The vigiles are a real Roman institution, and this scene is canonical.

author: Petronius
source_text: Trimalchio ... extendit se super torum extremum et: 'Fingite me, inquit, mortuum esse. Dicite aliquid belli.' Consonuere cornicines funebri strepitu.
question: Quid Trimalchio in fine cenae convivas facere iussit, cum super torum tanquam mortuus extenderetur?
answer: Vt fingerent eum mortuum esse et aliquid belli dicerent.
question_en: What did Trimalchio order his guests to do at the end of the dinner, when he stretched out on the couch as if dead?
answer_en: To pretend he was dead and say something nice about him.
derivation: Trimalchio's mock funeral: 'Fingite me mortuum esse' — he rehearses his own laudatio with horns playing. Anchored to Trimalchio; the command is quoted verbatim. The mock-funeral is one of the most celebrated scenes in Latin literature.

author: Petronius
source_text: Iam enim faxo sciatis non viduae hanc insulam esse sed Marci Mannicii.
question: Cuius esse insulam deversitor apud Petronium iactat, cum Eumolpum ceterosque rixantes obiurgat?
question_en: Whose apartment block does the innkeeper in Petronius declare it to be when he scolds Eumolpus and the other brawlers?
derivation: The innkeeper invokes the name of the insula's owner, M. Mannicius — urban lodging under a named proprietor, the tenement (insula) system in action. Anchored to the named owner; single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Imperavi Gitoni ut raptim grabatum subiret annecteretque pedes et manus institis, quibus sponda culcitam ferebat, ac sic ut olim Vlixes pro arieti adhaesisset, extentus infra grabatum scrutantium eluderet manus.
question: Cuius herois astum Giton imitatus est, cum sub grabato pendens quaerentium manus eluderet?
question_en: Which hero's trick did Giton imitate when, clinging under the bed, he eluded the hands of his searchers?
answer_en: Ulysses' (who escaped the Cyclops under the ram).
derivation: Giton hides under the bed 'as Ulysses once clung beneath the ram' — the Odyssey's Cyclops escape used as shared story. Anchored to Giton + Ulysses; single-name answer supported verbatim. Myth as ambient knowledge.

author: Petronius
source_text: Audio enim non licere cuiquam mortalium in nave neque ungues neque capillos deponere, nisi cum pelago ventus irascitur.
question: Quando solum, secundum religionem nautarum apud Petronium, licet in nave ungues capillosque deponere?
question_en: When alone, according to the sailors' superstition in Petronius, is it permitted to cut nails or hair aboard ship?
answer_en: When the wind is raging against the sea (in a storm).
derivation: The sailors' taboo: no one may cut hair or nails at sea except in a storm — hence the fury when Encolpius and Giton are shaved on board. Anchored to the ship-custom stated as a general rule; short answer supported verbatim. A named nautical superstition, shared maritime culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Itaque ut Tutela navis expiaretur, placuit quadragenas utrique plagas imponi.
question: Quot plagas Encolpio et Gitoni in nave Lichae imponi placuit, ut Tutela navis expiaretur?
question_en: How many lashes each were to be laid on Encolpius and Giton aboard Lichas' ship, to expiate the ship's guardian deity?
derivation: Forty lashes each to appease the ship's Tutela after the hair-cutting sacrilege. Anchored to the named ship of Lichas; single number supported verbatim; the Tutela (guardian deity of a ship) is real nautical religion.

author: Petronius
source_text: aegre expugnavit gubernator ut caduceatoris more Tryphaena indutias faceret. Data ergo acceptaque ex more patrio fide, protendit ramum oleae a Tutela navigii raptum.
question: Cuius arboris ramum Tryphaena protendit, cum in nave indutias caduceatoris more faceret?
question_en: The branch of what tree did Tryphaena hold out when she made a truce, herald-fashion, on the ship?
derivation: The olive branch, snatched from the ship's Tutela, extended as the sign of truce 'in the manner of a herald'. Anchored to the named Tryphaena; single-tree answer supported verbatim. The olive as peace-token is shared ancient culture attested here.

author: Petronius
source_text: Matrona quaedam Ephesi tam notae erat pudicitiae, ut vicinarum quoque gentium feminas ad spectaculum sui evocaret.
question: Qua virtute matrona illa Ephesi, de qua Eumolpus fabulam celeberrimam narrat, imprimis nota erat?
question_en: For what virtue was the matron of Ephesus, about whom Eumolpus tells his most famous tale, especially renowned?
derivation: The opening fact of the Widow of Ephesus tale: her chastity was so famous that women came from neighboring lands to see her. Anchored to the matron of Ephesus (a canonical story); single answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: complorataque singularis exempli femina ab omnibus quintum iam diem sine alimento trahebat. ... cum interim imperator provinciae latrones iussit crucibus affigi secundum illam casulam, in qua recens cadaver matrona deflebat.
question: Quos imperator provinciae iuxta conditorium matronae Ephesiae crucibus affigi iussit?
question_en: Whom did the governor of the province order crucified next to the tomb-vault of the matron of Ephesus?
derivation: The crucified robbers beside the widow's tomb — the plot hinge of the celebrated tale, and an attestation of crucifixion of latrones with a soldier posted to prevent removal of the bodies. Anchored to the matron of Ephesus; single answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Proxima ergo nocte, cum miles, qui cruces asservabat, ne quis ad sepulturam corpus detraheret, notasset sibi lumen inter monumenta clarius fulgens ... Quibus blanditiis impetraverat miles ut matrona vellet vivere, iisdem etiam pudicitiam eius aggressus est.
question: Quis matronam Ephesiam in conditorio lugentem et cibum sumere et amori suo cedere persuasit?
question_en: Who persuaded the mourning matron of Ephesus in the tomb both to take food and to yield to his love?
answer_en: The soldier who was guarding the crosses.
derivation: The soldier of the Ephesus tale: posted to guard the crosses, he wins the widow first to food, then to love. Anchored to the matron of Ephesus; single answer supported verbatim. The story's celebrated core.

author: Petronius
source_text: Itaque unius cruciarii parentes ut viderunt laxatam custodiam, detraxere nocte pendentem supremoque mandaverunt officio. ... iubet ex arca corpus mariti sui tolli atque illi, quae vacabat, cruci affigi.
question: Quid matrona Ephesia de corpore mariti sui fieri iussit, cum corpus unius cruciarii a parentibus subductum esset?
answer: Ex arca tolli et vacanti cruci affigi.
question_en: What did the matron of Ephesus order done with her husband's body when the corpse of one of the crucified men had been stolen by his relatives?
answer_en: To be taken from the coffin and fastened to the empty cross.
derivation: The famous denouement: the widow gives her husband's corpse to replace the stolen one on the cross — 'malo mortuum impendere quam vivum occidere.' Anchored to the matron of Ephesus; short answer supported verbatim. The story's punchline is canonical ambient knowledge.

author: Petronius
source_text: Usus est miles ingenio prudentissimae feminae, posteroque die populus miratus est qua ratione mortuus isset in crucem.
question: Quid populus postero die miratus est, cum fabula matronae Ephesiae finitur?
answer: Qua ratione mortuus in crucem isset.
question_en: What did the people marvel at the next day, at the close of the tale of the matron of Ephesus?
answer_en: How a dead man had climbed onto the cross.
derivation: The closing line of the Widow of Ephesus: the town wonders how a dead man got up on the cross. Anchored to the famous tale; the short answer is its verbatim final point.

author: Petronius
source_text: donec a vilico quodam Crotona esse cognovimus, urbem antiquissimam et aliquando Italiae primam.
question: Quae urbs apud Petronium antiquissima et aliquando Italiae prima appellatur, in quam naufragi perveniunt?
question_en: Which city is called in Petronius 'most ancient and once the first of Italy', where the shipwrecked party arrives?
derivation: Croton, 'urbs antiquissima et aliquando Italiae prima' — the historical Greek city of southern Italy, setting of the legacy-hunter episode. Anchored to the named city; single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: quoscunque homines in hac urbe videritis, scitote in duas partes esse divisos. Nam aut captantur aut captant. In hac urbe nemo liberos tollit, quia quisquis suos heredes habet, non ad cenas, non ad spectacula admittitur, sed omnibus prohibetur commodis, inter ignominiosos latitat.
question: In quas duas partes homines Crotoniatae apud Petronium divisi esse dicuntur?
question_en: Into what two classes are the people of Croton said in Petronius to be divided?
answer_en: Those who are preyed upon (by legacy-hunters) and those who prey.
derivation: The vilicus' famous description of Croton: everyone is either captator or prey, and no one rears children because heirs disqualify a man from dinners and favors. Anchored to Croton; two-part answer supported verbatim. Legacy-hunting (captatio) is a stock Roman social institution.

author: Petronius
source_text: Itaque ut duraret inter omnes tutum mendacium, in verba Eumolpi sacramentum iuravimus: uri, vinciri, verberari ferroque necari, et quicquid aliud Eumolpus iussisset. Tanquam legitimi gladiatores domino corpora animasque religiosissime addicimus.
question: Quibus verbis gladiatorii sacramenti Encolpius sociique in verba Eumolpi apud Petronium iuraverunt?
question_en: In what words of the gladiatorial oath did Encolpius and his companions swear allegiance to Eumolpus in Petronius?
answer_en: 'To be burned, bound, beaten, and slain by the sword.'
derivation: The auctoramentum, the real gladiator's oath ('uri, vinciri, verberari ferroque necari'), sworn 'like true gladiators' to Eumolpus. Anchored to the named characters + the gladiatorial institution; the formula is quoted verbatim and is core spectacle-culture knowledge.

author: Petronius
source_text: Homerus testis et lyrici, Romanusque Vergilius et Horatii curiosa felicitas.
question: Cuius poetae 'curiosam felicitatem' Eumolpus apud Petronium laudat?
question_en: Whose 'studied felicity' does Eumolpus praise in Petronius?
derivation: The famous critical tag 'Horatii curiosa felicitas' — Petronius' phrase about Horace that became a standard judgment in literary history. Anchored to the named Horace; single-name answer supported verbatim. A crisp checkable fact from the poetics chapter (the rest of the theory is dropped).

author: Petronius
source_text: Crassum Parthus habet, Libyco iacet aequore Magnus, Iulius ingratam perfudit sanguine Romam, et quasi non posset tot tellus ferre sepulcra, divisit cineres.
question: Vbi, secundum carmen de bello civili apud Petronium, tres illi duces — Crassus, Magnus, Iulius — sepulti iacent?
answer: Crassus apud Parthos, Pompeius in Libyco aequore, Caesar Romae.
question_en: Where, according to the civil-war poem in Petronius, do the three great leaders — Crassus, Pompey, and Julius — lie buried?
answer_en: Crassus among the Parthians, Pompey on the Libyan shore, Caesar at Rome.
derivation: The poem's epigram on the triumvirs' scattered graves: Parthia holds Crassus, Magnus lies on the Libyan sea, Julius drenched Rome with his blood — the earth 'divided their ashes'. Anchored to three named principals; supported verbatim. Famous shared history in a quotable form (the one crisp fact kept from the Bellum civile inset).

author: Petronius
source_text: Ex hac nota domina est mea; usque ab orchestra quattuordecim transilit, et in extrema plebe quaerit quod diligat.
question: Quot ordines ab orchestra transilire dicitur Circe, cum in extrema plebe amatores quaereret?
question_en: How many rows from the orchestra is Circe said to leap over when seeking lovers among the lowest commons?
derivation: Chrysis on her mistress: she 'jumps the fourteen rows' — the fourteen rows of theater seats reserved for the equites by the lex Roscia. Anchored to the named Circe; single number supported verbatim. The XIV ordines are canonical Roman civic culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Ita, inquit, non dixit tibi ancilla mea Circen me vocari? Non sum quidem Solis progenies, nec mea mater, dum placet, labentis mundi cursum detinuit.
question: Quo nomine matrona illa Crotoniensis vocabatur, quae Polyaenum (Encolpium) in platanona adamavit?
question_en: What was the name of the lady of Croton who fell in love with 'Polyaenus' (Encolpius) in the plane-tree grove?
derivation: The Croton episode's heroine Circe, paired with Encolpius' alias Polyaenus (both names from the Odyssey: 'Circe loves Polyaenus'). Anchored to the named characters; single-name answer supported verbatim. The Homeric name-play is part of the novel's celebrated design.

author: Petronius
source_text: Hoc peracto carmine ter me iussit expuere terque lapillos conicere in sinum, quos ipsa praecantatos purpura involuerat.
question: Quotiens anus illa apud Petronium Encolpium expuere et lapillos praecantatos in sinum conicere iussit?
question_en: How many times did the old woman in Petronius order Encolpius to spit and to cast the charmed pebbles into his breast?
derivation: The healing charm of Proselenos: threefold spitting and thrice-thrown enchanted pebbles wrapped in purple. Anchored to the named episode; single number supported verbatim. Triple ritual actions and spitting against harm are shared Roman magic-lore.

author: Petronius
source_text: Scelerate, inquit, etiam loqueris? Nescis quam magnum flagitium admiseris: occidisti Priapi delicias, anserem omnibus matronis acceptissimum.
question: Cuius dei delicias Encolpius occidisse dicitur, cum anserem sacrum ad casam Oenotheae elisit?
question_en: Whose divine pet is Encolpius said to have killed when he struck down the sacred goose at Oenothea's cottage?
derivation: The slain sacred goose is 'Priapi delicias' — Priapus, whose wrath drives the whole novel, here in his cult at Oenothea's shrine. Anchored to the named god + episode; single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Quisquis habet nummos, secura naviget aura fortunamque suo temperet arbitrio. ... Multa loquor: quod vis, nummis praesentibus opta, et veniet. Clausum possidet arca Iovem.
question: Quis, secundum versus illos apud Petronium, secura aura navigat et fortunam suo arbitrio temperat?
question_en: Who, according to the famous verses in Petronius, sails with a favoring breeze and orders fortune at his own pleasure?
derivation: The money-epigram 'Quisquis habet nummos, secura naviget aura' ending 'Clausum possidet arca Iovem' — a proverbial statement of cash omnipotence. Anchored to Petronius' celebrated verses; the answer is their verbatim subject and the point survives translation.

author: Petronius
source_text: Omnes, qui in testamento meo legata habent, praeter libertos meos hac condicione percipient quae dedi, si corpus meum in partes conciderint et astante populo comederint.
question: Qua condicione legatarii testamenti Eumolpi apud Crotoniatas legata sua percepturi erant?
answer: Si corpus eius concisum astante populo comedissent.
question_en: On what condition were the legatees of Eumolpus' will at Croton to receive their legacies?
answer_en: If they cut up his corpse and ate it before the assembled people.
derivation: The novel's notorious ending: Eumolpus' will requires his legacy-hunters to eat his body in public to inherit. Anchored to Eumolpus + Croton's captatores; short answer supported verbatim. The cannibal-will is canonical ambient knowledge of the Satyricon.

author: Petronius
source_text: Quod si exemplis vis quoque probari consilium, Saguntini oppressi ab Hannibale humanas edere carnes, nec hereditatem expectabant. ... Cum esset Numantia a Scipione capta, inventae sunt matres, quae liberorum suorum tenerent semesa in sinu corpora.
question: Qui populus, ab Hannibale oppressus, humanas carnes edisse apud Petronium memoratur?
question_en: What people, besieged by Hannibal, are recalled in Petronius as having eaten human flesh?
derivation: The historical exempla cited to justify the cannibal will: Saguntum under Hannibal, Petelia, and Numantia taken by Scipio. Anchored to the named Saguntines + Hannibal; single-name answer supported verbatim. Saguntum's famine is celebrated shared history.

author: Petronius
source_text: Cum ego proclamarem, gladium strinxit et 'Si Lucretia es, inquit, Tarquinium invenisti'.
question: Quibus verbis Ascyltos, gladio stricto, Gitonem reluctantem apud Petronium compellavit?
question_en: With what words did Ascyltos, sword drawn, address the resisting Giton in Petronius?
answer_en: 'If you are Lucretia, you have found your Tarquin.'
derivation: The famous quip turning the Lucretia-Tarquin story into a threat. Anchored to the named Ascyltos + Giton; the answer is the verbatim mot, and its point rests on the canonical shared story of Lucretia and Tarquin (mythos/historia every Roman carried).

author: Petronius
source_text: Datum est cui datum est, non cui destinatum. Plane Fortunae filius. In manu illius plumbum aurum fiebat.
question: Quo cognomine Phileros apud Petronium hominem appellat, in cuius manu plumbum aurum fiebat?
question_en: By what nickname does Phileros in Petronius call the man in whose hand lead turned to gold?
derivation: The proverbial label Fortunae filius (cf. Horace) with its pendant image 'in manu illius plumbum aurum fiebat'. Anchored to the named speaker at the Cena; short answer supported verbatim; the expression is a shared Latin saying.

author: Petronius
source_text: Nunc populus est domi leones, foras vulpes.
question: Quo proverbio Ganymedes apud Petronium populum coloniae suae describit?
question_en: With what proverb does Ganymedes in Petronius describe the people of his town?
derivation: The preserved saying 'domi leones, foras vulpes' — bold at home, cowardly outside. Anchored to the named speaker; the proverb is the verbatim answer and its point survives translation.

author: Petronius
source_text: Quid servus peccavit, qui coactus est facere? Magis illa matella digna fuit quam taurus iactaret. Sed qui asinum non potest, stratum caedit.
question: Quod proverbium Echion profert de Glycone, qui servum pro uxore adultera punivit?
answer: Qui asinum non potest, stratum caedit.
question_en: What proverb does Echion quote about Glyco, who punished the slave instead of his adulterous wife?
answer_en: 'He who cannot beat the donkey beats the saddle.'
derivation: The proverb of misdirected punishment, preserved verbatim in Echion's speech about Glyco's steward. Anchored to the named Glyco affair; the saying is the answer and survives translation.

author: Petronius
source_text: Tu autem tam laboriosus es, ut post te non respicias! In alio peduclum vides, in te ricinum non vides.
question: Quod proverbium de vitiis alienis et suis Hermeros in Ascylton ridentem torquet?
answer: In alio peduclum vides, in te ricinum non vides.
question_en: What proverb about other people's faults and one's own does Hermeros hurl at the laughing Ascyltos?
answer_en: 'You see the louse on another, but not the tick on yourself.'
derivation: The mote-and-beam-type proverb in its Latin popular form, preserved verbatim in Hermeros' tirade. Anchored to the named speakers; the saying is the answer; the point survives translation.

author: Petronius
source_text: Super limen autem cavea pendebat aurea in qua pica varia intrantes salutabat.
question: Quae avis, in cavea aurea super limen pendens, intrantes in domum Trimalchionis salutabat?
question_en: What bird, hanging in a golden cage over the threshold, greeted those entering Trimalchio's house?
derivation: The talking magpie in a golden cage greeting guests at the door — part of the celebrated entrance sequence (with the CAVE CANEM dog). Anchored to Trimalchio's house; single-bird answer supported verbatim. Kept birds greeting visitors are Roman daily-life culture.

author: Petronius
source_text: Tandem ergo discubuimus, pueris Alexandrinis aquam in manus nivatam infundentibus.
question: Qualem aquam pueri Alexandrini in manus convivarum Trimalchionis discumbentium infuderunt?
question_en: What kind of water did the Alexandrian boys pour over the hands of Trimalchio's reclining guests?
derivation: Snow-cooled water (aqua nivata) for the hand-washing at table, poured by Alexandrian slave boys — Roman luxury dining practice. Anchored to Trimalchio's cena; single answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: In medio autem caespes cum herbis excisus favum sustinebat.
question: Quid in medio repositorio zodiaco Trimalchionis super caespitem positum erat?
question_en: What was placed on the cut turf in the middle of Trimalchio's zodiac dish?
derivation: The center of the zodiac dish: a turf of grass bearing a honeycomb — glossed by Trimalchio himself (39: the earth like an egg in the middle, holding all good things 'tanquam favus'). Anchored to the famous zodiac repositorium; single answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Cum Ilium captum est, Hannibal, homo vafer et magnus stelio, omnes statuas aeneas et aureas et argenteas in unum rogum congessit et eas incendit; factae sunt in unum aera miscellanea.
question: Quis, ut Trimalchio perperam docet, Ilio capto statuas aeneas aureas argenteasque in unum rogum congessit, unde Corinthea nata sint?
question_en: Who, as Trimalchio wrongly teaches, heaped the bronze, gold, and silver statues onto one pyre at the capture of Troy, whence Corinthian bronze was born?
derivation: Trimalchio's celebrated historical howler: Hannibal at the sack of Troy melting the statues into 'Corinthian' alloy. Anchored to Trimalchio + the named Hannibal; single-name answer supported verbatim; the question's 'perperam' frames it as his claim. The real aetiology (the sack of Corinth) makes the blunder the famous point.

author: Petronius
source_text: Diomedes et Ganymedes duo fratres fuerunt. Horum soror erat Helena. Agamemnon illam rapuit et Dianae cervam subiecit.
question: Quorum duorum fratrum sororem Helenam fuisse Trimalchio, fabulas perturbans, affirmat?
question_en: Of which two 'brothers' does Trimalchio, garbling the myths, declare Helen to have been the sister?
derivation: Trimalchio's famous mythological muddle introducing the Homeristae: Helen the sister of 'Diomedes and Ganymedes', seized by Agamemnon who palmed off a doe on Diana. Anchored to Trimalchio + named figures; two-name answer supported verbatim; the garbling itself is the celebrated point (the real brothers being Castor and Pollux).

author: Petronius
source_text: Ceterum, quemadmodum di volunt, dominus in domo factus sum, et ecce cepi ipsimi cerebellum. Quid multa? coheredem me Caesari fecit, et accepi patrimonium laticlavium.
question: Cum quo Trimalchio a patrono suo coheres testamento factus est?
question_en: With whom was Trimalchio made co-heir in his patron's will?
derivation: Trimalchio's master made him co-heir with the emperor — 'coheredem me Caesari fecit' — the origin of his 'senatorial' fortune (patrimonium laticlavium). Anchored to Trimalchio; single answer supported verbatim. Naming Caesar co-heir was real Roman testamentary prudence.

author: Petronius
source_text: Quidni? inquit Giton, etiam circumcide nos, ut Iudaei videamur, et pertunde aures, ut imitemur Arabes, et increta facies, ut suos Gallia cives putet.
question: Quo corporis signo Iudaei apud Petronium distingui dicuntur, cum Giton fugae consilia deridet?
question_en: By what bodily mark are the Jews said to be distinguished in Petronius, when Giton mocks the escape plans?
derivation: Giton's mock-disguise catalogue attests the shared ethnographic markers: circumcision for Jews, pierced ears for Arabs, chalked faces for Gauls. Anchored to the named peoples; single answer supported verbatim. Ethnic-custom knowledge every Roman carried.

author: Petronius
source_text: Ibit ad aras, Sancte, tuas hircus, pecoris pater; ibit ad aras corniger et querulae fetus suis, hostia lactens.
question: Quam hostiam praecipuam Encolpius Priapo, si fortuna arrisisset, ad aras se daturum vovit?
question_en: What chief victim did Encolpius vow to bring to Priapus' altars, should fortune smile on him?
answer_en: A he-goat, father of the flock.
derivation: Encolpius' votive prayer to Priapus promises the god's canonical victim, the goat (with a suckling pig). Anchored to Priapus + Encolpius; short answer supported verbatim. The goat as Priapus' sacrifice is shared cult knowledge.

author: Petronius
source_text: duae tabulae in utroque poste defixae, quarum altera, si bene memini, hoc habebat inscriptum: III ET PRIDIE KALENDAS IANVARIAS C. NOSTER FORAS CENAT, altera lunae cursum stellarumque septem imagines pictas; et qui dies boni quique incommodi essent, distinguente bulla notabantur.
question: Quid altera tabula in poste triclinii Trimalchionis defixa pictum habebat?
answer: Lunae cursum stellarumque septem imagines, distinctis bulla diebus bonis et incommodis.
question_en: What did the second tablet fixed on Trimalchio's dining-room doorpost display?
answer_en: The course of the moon and images of the seven stars (planets), with lucky and unlucky days marked by studs.
derivation: The household calendar-tablet: moon's course, the seven planets, and dies boni/incommodi marked with studs — Roman hemerology on display. Anchored to Trimalchio's triclinium; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Petronius
source_text: Itaque proxime cum hoc titulo proscripsit: C. POMPEIVS DIOGENES EX KALENDIS IVLIIS CENACVLVM LOCAT; IPSE ENIM DOMVM EMIT.
question: Cur C. Pompeius Diogenes, ut titulus apud Petronium testatur, cenaculum suum ex kalendis Iuliis locabat?
question_en: Why, as the posted notice in Petronius attests, was C. Pompeius Diogenes letting his garret from the first of July?
answer_en: Because he had bought a house himself.
derivation: The freedman's triumphant to-let notice: garret available from 1 July — 'for he has bought a house.' Anchored to the named C. Pompeius Diogenes; the reason is quoted verbatim. Rental culture (cenacula, July moving day) plus freedman social climbing.

author: Petronius
source_text: Sed quomodo dicunt — ego nihil scio, sed audivi — quom Incuboni pilleum rapuisset, et thesaurum invenit.
question: Quid, ut vulgo apud Petronium narratur, invenit qui Incuboni pilleum rapuit?
question_en: What, as the popular story in Petronius has it, did the man find who snatched the cap of an Incubo?
derivation: The folk-belief that seizing the cap of an Incubo (a treasure-guarding goblin) yields his treasure, told of a rich fellow freedman. Anchored to the named Incubo of Roman folklore; single answer supported verbatim. Shared superstition, criterion 8's core.

author: Petronius
source_text: Eodem die: Mithridates servus in crucem actus est, quia Gai nostri genio male dixerat.
question: Quam ob causam Mithridates servus, ut in actis Trimalchionis recitatum est, in crucem actus est?
question_en: For what reason, as read out in Trimalchio's estate gazette, was the slave Mithridates crucified?
answer_en: Because he had cursed the genius of Gaius (Trimalchio).
derivation: From the estate acta: the slave Mithridates crucified for cursing his master's genius. Anchored to the named slave + Trimalchio; the reason is quoted verbatim. The cult of the master's genius (sworn by, not cursed) is central Roman household religion.

author: Petronius
source_text: Puer autem lippus, sordidissimis dentibus, catellam nigram atque indecenter pinguem prasina involuebat fascia ... Scylax, canino scilicet usus ingenio, taeterrimo latratu triclinium implevit Margaritamque Croesi paene laceravit.
question: Quo nomine catella nigra Croesi, deliciarum Trimalchionis, vocabatur?
question_en: What was the name of the black lapdog belonging to Croesus, Trimalchio's pet boy?
derivation: The lapdog Margarita, wrapped by Croesus in a green ribbon and nearly torn apart by Scylax. Anchored to the named Croesus + Trimalchio's household; single-name answer supported verbatim. Pet-keeping culture of the Cena.

author: Petronius
source_text: Desperatum valde ingeniosus est: idem sutor est, idem cocus, idem pistor, omnis Musae mancipium. Duo tamen vitia habet, quae si non haberet, esset omnium numerum: recutitus est et stertit. ... Illum emi trecentis denariis.
question: Quanti Habinnas servum illum omnis Musae mancipium, qui Vergilium tam acide cantaverat, emisse se dixit?
question_en: For how much did Habinnas say he had bought that jack-of-all-trades slave who had recited Vergil so sourly?
derivation: Habinnas' price for his multi-talented slave: 300 denarii. Anchored to the named Habinnas; single sum supported verbatim. Slave prices are hard cultural realia; the scene (a slave mangling Aeneid 5.1 with Atellane verses) is a famous set piece.

author: Petronius
source_text: complorataque singularis exempli femina ab omnibus quintum iam diem sine alimento trahebat.
question: Quotum iam diem sine alimento matrona Ephesia in conditorio mariti lugens trahebat, cum miles eam invenit?
question_en: Which day without food was the matron of Ephesus dragging through, mourning in her husband's vault, when the soldier found her?
derivation: The widow's five-day fast in the tomb — the number fact of the celebrated tale. Anchored to the matron of Ephesus; single ordinal answer supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: faciam ut commixta sit: sit tragicomoedia. nam me perpetuo facere ut sit comoedia, reges quo veniant et di, non par arbitror. quid igitur? quoniam hic servos quoque partes habet, faciam sit, proinde ut dixi, tragicomoedia.
question: Quo novo nomine Mercurius in prologo Amphitruonis Plauti fabulam appellat, quia et di regesque et servus in ea partes habent?
question_en: By what new name does Mercury in the prologue of Plautus' Amphitruo call the play, because both gods and kings and a slave have roles in it?
derivation: Mercury's prologue coins the word 'tragicomoedia' — the first attested use in literature, a canonical literary fact every Latin reader carries. Anchored to Mercury + the Amphitruo prologue; single-word answer stated verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam meus pater intus nunc est eccum Iuppiter; in Amphitruonis vertit sese imaginem
question: Cuius viri imaginem Iuppiter in Amphitruone Plauti induit, ut Alcumena clam frueretur?
question_en: Whose form does Jupiter assume in Plautus' Amphitruo in order to enjoy Alcumena in secret?
answer_en: That of Amphitruo, the Theban commander.
derivation: The central myth of the play: Jupiter impersonates Amphitruo. Closed-book canonical story (the begetting of Hercules); anchored to Jupiter + Amphitruo.

author: Plautus
source_text: ego servi sumpsi Sosiae mi imaginem, qui cum Amphitruone abiit hinc in exercitum
question: Cuius servi formam Mercurius in Amphitruone Plauti sumpsit, ut patri amanti subserviret?
question_en: Which slave's form does Mercury take in Plautus' Amphitruo, to serve his father in his love affair?
derivation: Mercury doubles the slave Sosia — the famous 'double' plot that made 'sosie' a common noun for a lookalike. Anchored to Mercury + Sosia; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: et meus pater nunc intus hic cum illa cubat, et haec ob eam rem nox est facta longior
question: Quid nocti accidit, dum Iuppiter apud Alcumenam in Amphitruone Plauti cubat?
question_en: What happened to the night while Jupiter lay with Alcumena in Plautus' Amphitruo?
derivation: The famous 'long night' of the Amphitruo/Hercules myth — Jupiter lengthens the night for his tryst. Canonical shared story, stated verbatim (nox est facta longior).

author: Plautus
source_text: Haec urbs est Thebae. in illisce habitat aedibus Amphitruo
question: In qua urbe fabula Plauti quae Amphitruo inscribitur agitur?
question_en: In what city is Plautus' play Amphitruo set?
derivation: The setting of the play, declared in the prologue — part of the shared Amphitruo/Hercules story (Hercules born at Thebes). Anchored to the named play; one-place answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: quicum Alcumena est nupta, Electri filia.
question: Cuius filia fuit Alcumena, uxor Amphitruonis, ut Plautus tradit?
question_en: Whose daughter was Alcumena, the wife of Amphitruo, as Plautus records?
derivation: Genealogical myth-fact: Alcumena is daughter of Electrus (Greek Electryon). Anchored to Alcumena + Amphitruo; single-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc de Alcumena ut rem teneatis rectius, utrimque est gravida, et ex viro et ex summo Iove.
question: Ex quibus duobus Alcumena in Amphitruone Plauti simul gravida est?
answer: Ex Amphitruone viro et ex Iove.
question_en: By which two is Alcumena simultaneously pregnant in Plautus' Amphitruo?
answer_en: By her husband Amphitruo and by Jupiter.
derivation: The double paternity that yields the twins Hercules and Iphicles — canonical myth. Two-name answer stated verbatim (et ex viro et ex summo Iove).

author: Plautus
source_text: nam vos quidem id iam scitis concessum et datum mi esse ab dis aliis, nuntiis praesim et lucro
question: Quibus duabus rebus Mercurium deum praeesse prologus Amphitruonis dicit?
question_en: Over what two things does the prologue of the Amphitruo say the god Mercury presides?
derivation: Canonical divine attribute: Mercury as god of messengers and gain (commerce) — ambient Roman religious knowledge, stated verbatim by the god himself.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc internosse ut nos possitis facilius, ego has habebo usque in petaso pinnulas; tum meo patri autem torulus inerit aureus sub petaso: id signum Amphitruoni non erit.
question: Quo signo spectatores Iovem a vero Amphitruone in fabula Plauti dignoscere possunt?
question_en: By what token can the spectators distinguish Jupiter from the real Amphitruo in Plautus' play?
answer_en: By a little golden tuft under his hat.
derivation: Famous theatrical convention of the play: Mercury wears little wings on his petasus, Jupiter a golden tuft beneath his — the tokens announced to the audience. Anchored to Jupiter/Amphitruo; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quid faciam nunc, si tres viri me in carcerem compegerint?
question: Quos magistratus Sosia servus in Amphitruone Plauti timet, ne se noctu ambulantem in carcerem compingant?
question_en: Which magistrates does the slave Sosia in Plautus' Amphitruo fear may throw him into prison for walking about at night?
answer_en: The tresviri (the Roman board of three who policed the night).
derivation: Roman realia through the Greek mask: the tresviri capitales, Rome's night police with jail duty, invoked anachronistically in Theban 'Thebes'. Anchored to Sosia + the play; one-office answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sive adeo aediles perfidiose cui duint, sirempse legem iussit esse Iuppiter, quasi magistratum sibi alterive ambiverit.
question: Qui magistratus Romani, ut prologus Amphitruonis innuit, palmam histrionibus in ludis dabant?
question_en: Which Roman magistrates, as the prologue of the Amphitruo implies, awarded the palm to actors at the games?
derivation: Roman theatrical institution poking through the Greek dress: the aediles ran the ludi and judged the prize (palma) for actors. Anchored to the Amphitruo prologue; one-office answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: is nunc Amphitruo praefectust legionibus, nam cum Telobois bellum est Thebano poplo.
question: Contra quem populum Amphitruo, legionibus Thebanis praefectus, bellum gessit apud Plautum?
question_en: Against what people did Amphitruo, commander of the Theban legions, wage war in Plautus?
derivation: The war frame of the myth: Amphitruo commands Thebes against the Teloboae while Jupiter visits his wife. Anchored to Amphitruo + Thebes; one-people answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ipsusque Amphitruo regem Pterelam sua obtruncavit manu.
question: Quem regem Teloboarum Amphitruo sua manu occidit, ut in Amphitruone Plauti narratur?
question_en: Which king of the Teloboians did Amphitruo slay with his own hand, as told in Plautus' Amphitruo?
derivation: Named single combat of the myth: Amphitruo kills King Pterelas. Anchored to Amphitruo + the Teloboae; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: regique Thebano Creoni regnum stabilivit suom.
question: Quis Thebis regnabat, cum Amphitruo contra Teloboas pugnaret, ut Plautus tradit?
question_en: Who was reigning at Thebes when Amphitruo fought the Teloboians, as Plautus records?
derivation: Creon as king of Thebes in the Amphitruo/Hercules saga — canonical myth-figure. Anchored to Thebes + the Teloboan war; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: in illisce habitat aedibus Amphitruo, natus Argis ex Argo patre
question: Qua in urbe natum esse Amphitruonem prologus Plauti dicit?
question_en: In what city does Plautus' prologue say Amphitruo was born?
derivation: Plautus' particular claim about Amphitruo's origin (born at Argos of an Argive father) — attributed to the prologue, hence the 'dicit' frame. One-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: post ob virtutem ero Amphitruoni patera donata aurea est, qui Pterela potitare solitus est rex.
question: Quod donum Amphitruo dux ob virtutem, Telobois victis, accepit apud Plautum?
answer: Pateram auream, qua Pterela rex potitare solitus erat.
question_en: What gift did the commander Amphitruo receive for his valor after the defeat of the Teloboians, in Plautus?
answer_en: The golden bowl from which King Pterelas used to drink.
derivation: The famous stage property of the play — the patera aurea of King Pterelas, given to Amphitruo as prize of valor; it later drives the recognition plot. Anchored to Amphitruo + Pterelas; short noun-phrase answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Est in cistula; Amphitruonis obsignata signo est. Signi dic quid est? Cum quadrigis Sol exoriens.
question: Quod signum anulo Amphitruonis insculptum erat, quo patera aurea in Amphitruone Plauti obsignata est?
question_en: What device was engraved on Amphitruo's signet, with which the golden bowl was sealed in Plautus' Amphitruo?
answer_en: The rising Sun with his four-horse chariot.
derivation: Named seal-device of Amphitruo's signet (the rising Sun with quadriga), by which Mercury proves his false identity — a memorable checkable detail of the canonical play; also Roman sealing practice through the Greek mask. Speaker tags stripped per normalization.

author: Plautus
source_text: hodie illa pariet filios geminos duos alter decumo post mense nascetur puer quam seminatust, alter mense septumo; eorum Amphitruonis alter est, alter Iovis
question: Quot filios et quibus patribus Alcumena in Amphitruone Plauti paritura esse dicitur?
answer: Geminos duos, alterum Amphitruonis, alterum Iovis.
question_en: How many sons, and by what fathers, is Alcumena said to be about to bear in Plautus' Amphitruo?
answer_en: Twin sons, one Amphitruo's, one Jupiter's.
derivation: The canonical twin birth (Hercules and Iphicles) with double paternity, foretold by Mercury. Anchored to Alcumena + the two named fathers; short count-and-names answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: alter decumo post mense nascetur puer quam seminatust, alter mense septumo
question: Quoto mense post conceptum nasciturus est puer Iovis filius, ut Mercurius in Amphitruone praedicit?
question_en: In what month after conception will the boy who is Jupiter's son be born, as Mercury foretells in the Amphitruo?
derivation: Mercury's obstetric detail: the younger-conceived child (Jupiter's, i.e. Hercules) comes in the seventh month, the husband's in the tenth — the ancient seven-month/ten-month birth lore. Number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Sosiam vocant Thebani, Davo prognatum patre.
question: Quo patre natus est Sosia, servus Amphitruonis, apud Plautum?
question_en: Of what father was Sosia, Amphitruo's slave, born, according to Plautus?
derivation: Named filiation of the famous doubled slave: Sosia son of Davus (the stock comic slave name). Anchored to Sosia + Amphitruo; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc tibi hanc pateram, quae dono mi illi ob virtutem data est, Pterela rex qui potitavit, quem ego mea occidi manu, Alcumena, tibi condono.
question: Cui Iuppiter, Amphitruonis specie indutus, pateram auream Pterelae regis dono dedit apud Plautum?
question_en: To whom did Jupiter, wearing Amphitruo's likeness, present the golden bowl of King Pterelas, in Plautus?
derivation: Jupiter regifts Amphitruo's prize bowl to Alcumena — the act that later convicts the real Amphitruo of 'lying'. Anchored to Jupiter + the named patera; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ecastor te experior quanti facias uxorem tuam.
question: Quod iusiurandum, quo solae mulieres Romanae utebantur, Alcumena matrona in Amphitruone Plauti profert?
question_en: What oath, used only by Roman women, does the matron Alcumena utter in Plautus' Amphitruo?
derivation: Gendered Roman oath usage evidenced in the text: the matrona swears 'ecastor' (by Castor), the women-only oath, while the men swear edepol/hercle. Roman speech-custom through the Greek mask; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: virtus praemium est optimum; virtus omnibus rebus anteit profecto: libertas salus vita res et parentes, patria et prognati tutantur, servantur: virtus omnia in sese habet, omnia adsunt bona quem penest virtus.
question: Quid Alcumena in Amphitruone Plauti praemium optimum esse et rebus omnibus anteire canit?
question_en: What does Alcumena in Plautus' Amphitruo sing is the best reward and surpasses all things?
derivation: Alcumena's celebrated canticum in praise of virtus — one of the most quoted moral tags in Plautus ('virtus praemium est optimum'). Anchored to Alcumena + the play; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Per supremi regis regnum iuro et matrem familias Iunonem, quam me vereri et metuere est par maxume, ut mi extra unum te mortalis nemo corpus corpore contigit, quo me impudicam faceret.
question: Per quam deam Alcumena in Amphitruone Plauti pudicitiam suam iurat?
question_en: By what goddess does Alcumena in Plautus' Amphitruo swear to her chastity?
derivation: The matron's oath by Juno, the married woman's own goddess, styled 'mater familias' — Roman matronal religion evidenced verbatim. Anchored to Alcumena; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: Bacchae bacchanti si velis advorsarier, ex insana insaniorem facies, feriet saepius; si obsequare, una resolvas plaga.
question: Quid fieri Sosia apud Plautum dicit, si quis Bacchae bacchanti advorsari velit?
question_en: What does Sosia in Plautus say happens if one tries to oppose a raving Bacchant?
derivation: Proverbial wisdom with a checkable point, built on the shared image of the frenzied Bacchant (Bacchic rites as ambient cultural knowledge). Short answer stated verbatim (ex insana insaniorem facies).

author: Plautus
source_text: sed, mulier, postquam experrecta es, te prodigiali Iovi aut mola salsa hodie aut ture comprecatam oportuit.
question: Quibus rebus oblatis somnia prodigialia Iovi expiari oportebat, ut Sosia in Amphitruone Plauti monet?
question_en: With what offerings ought portentous dreams to be expiated before Jupiter, as Sosia advises in Plautus' Amphitruo?
answer_en: With salted meal (mola salsa) or with incense.
derivation: Genuine Roman rite through the Greek mask: prodigies and ominous dreams expiated by prayer to Iuppiter prodigialis with mola salsa or incense — the mola salsa being the quintessential Roman offering. Two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nonne hac noctu nostra navis huc ex portu Persico venit, quae me advexit?
question: Ex quo portu navis, quae Sosiam Thebas revexit, in Amphitruone Plauti advenit?
question_en: From what harbor did the ship that brought Sosia back to Thebes arrive, in Plautus' Amphitruo?
derivation: The named harbor of the play — the portus Persicus where Amphitruo's ship lay (also 'cenavi in navi in portu Persico'). A checkable place-name detail of the canonical comedy; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Non ego illam mihi dotem duco esse, quae dos dicitur, sed pudicitiam et pudorem et sedatum cupidinem, deum metum, parentum amorem et cognatum concordiam, tibi morigera atque ut munifica sim bonis, prosim probis.
question: Quam rem Alcumena in Amphitruone Plauti pro vera dote sua maxime ducit, non pecuniam?
question_en: What does Alcumena in Plautus' Amphitruo count as her true dowry, rather than money?
derivation: Alcumena's famous 'my dowry is my virtue' speech — pudicitia heads her list (with pudor, fear of the gods, love of parents). A celebrated statement of Roman matronal ideals framed against the money-dowry (dos). Anchored to Alcumena; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: valeas, tibi habeas res tuas, reddas meas.
question: Quibus verbis sollemnibus Alcumena in Amphitruone Plauti matrimonium renuntiat?
answer: Valeas, tibi habeas res tuas, reddas meas.
question_en: With what formulaic words does Alcumena in Plautus' Amphitruo renounce her marriage?
answer_en: 'Farewell; keep your things for yourself, and give back mine.'
derivation: The Roman divorce formula ('tuas res tibi habeto', known from the jurists) placed in the Theban matron's mouth — Roman law through the Greek mask. A saying quoted verbatim per the proverb rule; anchored to Alcumena + the play.

author: Plautus
source_text: Iube vero vasa pura adornari mihi, ut quae apud legionem vota vovi, si domum rediissem salvos, ea ego exsolvam omnia.
question: Qualia vasa sibi adornari iubet Iuppiter, Amphitruonis forma indutus, ut vota apud legionem suscepta exsolvat?
question_en: What kind of vessels does Jupiter, in Amphitruo's form, order prepared so that he may discharge the vows he made with the legion?
derivation: Roman votive religion evidenced verbatim: vows made on campaign, conditional on safe return, discharged at home with sacrifice using the ritually 'pure' vessels (vasa pura, a technical term of Roman cult). Short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: gubernatorem qui in mea navi fuit Blepharonem arcessat, qui nobiscum prandeat.
question: Quo munere Blepharo in Amphitruone Plauti fungitur?
question_en: What role does Blepharo fill in Plautus' Amphitruo?
answer_en: That of the pilot (helmsman) of Amphitruo's ship.
derivation: Named character fact of the canonical play: Blepharo is the gubernator of Amphitruo's ship (so also the personae list), invited to lunch and later made arbiter. One-office answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Blepharo captus arbiter Vter sit non quit Amphitruo decernere.
question: Quis in Amphitruone Plauti arbiter captus uter verus Amphitruo esset decernere non potuit?
question_en: Who in Plautus' Amphitruo, taken as arbiter, could not decide which was the real Amphitruo?
derivation: The famous judgment scene: Blepharo, called in as arbiter between Jupiter and Amphitruo, cannot tell them apart and walks off ('qui utri sim advocatus nescio'). Anchored to the named play; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam mihi quidem hercle qui minus liceat deo minitarier populo, ni decedat mihi, quam servolo in comoediis? ille navem salvam nuntiat aut irati adventum senis
question: Quae duo nuntiare solet servolus currens in comoediis, ut Mercurius in Amphitruone Plauti ait?
answer: Navem salvam aut irati senis adventum.
question_en: What two things does the running slave in comedies usually announce, as Mercury says in Plautus' Amphitruo?
answer_en: That the ship is safe, or that the angry old man is coming.
derivation: Meta-theatrical fact: the stock 'servus currens' convention of Roman comedy, described by Mercury himself — theater conventions are criterion 8's home turf. Two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: capiam coronam mi in caput, adsimulabo me esse ebrium
question: Quo capitis ornatu Mercurius in Amphitruone Plauti se ebrium esse simulat?
question_en: With what head-adornment does Mercury in Plautus' Amphitruo pretend to be drunk?
answer_en: With a garland put on his head.
derivation: Banquet custom: the corona (garland) worn on the head was the recognized sign of the drinker fresh from a party — Mercury dons one precisely to play drunk. Short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: At ego te cruce et cruciatu mactabo, mastigia.
question: Quo supplicio Amphitruo apud Plautum ei minatur, quem servum suum Sosiam esse credit?
question_en: With what punishment does Amphitruo in Plautus threaten the man he believes to be his slave Sosia?
derivation: The crux as the servile punishment par excellence — the stock slave-threat of Roman comedy, hurled here at the false Sosia. Roman penal realia through the Greek mask; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ego pol illum ulciscar hodie Thessalum veneficum, qui pervorse perturbavit familiae mentem meae.
question: Vnde oriundum esse veneficum Amphitruo apud Plautum suspicatur eum, qui familiae suae mentem perturbavit?
question_en: From where does Amphitruo in Plautus suspect the sorcerer who has deranged his household comes?
derivation: Thessaly as the proverbial homeland of witches and poisoners — a shared ancient commonplace, evidenced by 'Thessalum veneficum'. Anchored to Amphitruo; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Puer ambo angues enicat.
question: Quid fecit puer, quem Alcumena Iovi peperit, cum angues ad cunas eius venissent, in Amphitruone Plauti?
question_en: What did the boy whom Alcumena bore to Jupiter do when the serpents came to his cradle, in Plautus' Amphitruo?
