derivation: The canonical infant-Hercules deed: the newborn leaps from the cradle and strangles the two snakes (the play never names Hercules, but every reader carries the story). Anchored to Jupiter's son + the cradle; brief answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: postquam in cunas conditust, devolant angues iubati deorsum in impluvium duo maximi: continuo extollunt ambo capita.
question: In quam partem aedium duo angues iubati in Amphitruone Plauti devolaverunt?
question_en: Into what part of the house did the two crested serpents fly down in Plautus' Amphitruo?
answer_en: Into the impluvium (the rain-basin of the atrium).
derivation: Roman realia through the Greek mask: the snakes descend into the impluvium — the rain-catching basin of the Roman atrium house, anachronistically placed in 'Thebes'. Also fixes the number (duo) and epithet (iubati). One-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: is se dixit cum Alcumena clam consuetum cubitibus, eumque filium suom esse qui illos angues vicerit; alterum tuom esse dixit puerum.
question: Vter geminorum ab Alcumena editorum Iovis filius erat, ut ipse Iuppiter in Amphitruone Plauti declaravit?
question_en: Which of the twins borne by Alcumena was Jupiter's son, as Jupiter himself declared in Plautus' Amphitruo?
answer_en: The one who overcame the serpents.
derivation: Jupiter's own identification of his child (the future Hercules) by the snake-victory, the other twin being Amphitruo's. Anchored to Jupiter + Alcumena's twins; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ego Teresiam coniectorem advocabo et consulam quid faciundum censeat
question: Quem coniectorem Amphitruo de prodigiis domus suae consulere constituit apud Plautum?
question_en: Which seer did Amphitruo decide to consult about the prodigies in his house, in Plautus?
derivation: The canonical Theban seer Tiresias, summoned to interpret the portents — then dismissed when Jupiter himself explains ('missum facio Teresiam senem'). Anchored to Amphitruo + the named seer; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: donec cum tonitru voce missa ex aethere adulterum se Iuppiter confessus est.
question: Quis deus in fine Amphitruonis Plauti, voce ex aethere missa, se adulterum esse confessus est?
question_en: Which god at the end of Plautus' Amphitruo, with a voice sent from the sky, confessed himself the adulterer?
derivation: The deus-ex-machina ending: Jupiter appears amid thunder, confesses the deed and reconciles the couple ('ego in caelum migro'). Anchored to the named play; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: invocat deos immortales, ut sibi auxilium ferant, manibus puris, capite operto.
question: Quo corporis habitu Alcumena parturiens deos immortales invocavit, ut Bromia in Amphitruone Plauti narrat?
question_en: In what bodily attitude did Alcumena in labor call upon the immortal gods, as Bromia relates in Plautus' Amphitruo?
answer_en: With clean hands and covered head.
derivation: Roman prayer ritual evidenced verbatim: praying capite operto (with veiled head) and with pure hands — the characteristically Roman posture of worship, worn here by a Theban matron. Short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ne quis miretur qui sim, paucis eloquar. ego Lar sum familiaris ex hac familia unde exeuntem me aspexistis.
question: Quis deus prologum Aululariae Plauti agit?
question_en: What god speaks the prologue of Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: Canonical literary fact: the Aulularia's prologue is spoken by the household Lar — Roman domestic religion stepping through the Greek mask to open the play. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed mi avos huius obsecrans concredidit thensaurum auri clam omnis: in medio foco defodit, venerans me ut id servarem sibi.
question: Quo loco avus Euclionis thensaurum auri defoderat, ut Lar in Aululariae prologo narrat?
question_en: Where had Euclio's grandfather buried the treasure of gold, as the Lar tells in the prologue of the Aulularia?
answer_en: In the middle of the hearth.
derivation: The treasure entrusted to the Lar and buried in the hearth — the focus being precisely the Lar's seat in the Roman house. Anchored to Euclio's grandfather + the Lar; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: huic filia una est. ea mihi cottidie aut ture aut vino aut aliqui semper supplicat, dat mihi coronas.
question: Quibus donis filia Euclionis Larem familiarem cottidie colit, ut ipse Lar apud Plautum narrat?
question_en: With what gifts does Euclio's daughter honor the household Lar every day, as the Lar himself tells in Plautus?
derivation: Roman household cult in daily practice: incense, wine, and garlands offered to the Lar — the standard domestic offerings. Anchored to Euclio's daughter + the Lar; three-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: eius honoris gratia feci, thensaurum ut hic reperiret Euclio, quo illam facilius nuptum, si vellet, daret.
question: Cuius honoris gratia Lar familiaris effecit, ut Euclio thensaurum reperiret?
answer: Filiae Euclionis, quae eum cottidie colebat.
question_en: For whose sake did the household Lar bring it about that Euclio found the treasure?
answer_en: For Euclio's daughter, who worshipped him daily.
derivation: The Lar's stated motive: he reveals the treasure to reward the pious daughter and provide her a dowry — the theology of the household cult (honor repaid) driving the plot. Anchored to the Lar + Euclio; short answer verbatim in substance.

author: Plautus
source_text: is adulescentis illius est avonculus, qui illam stupravit noctu, Cereris vigiliis.
question: Quo festo tempore filia Euclionis in Aulularia Plauti vitiata est?
question_en: At what festival time was Euclio's daughter violated in Plautus' Aulularia?
answer_en: At night, during the vigil of Ceres.
derivation: Named rite anchoring the plot: the nocturnal vigil of Ceres, at which Lyconides assaulted the girl. Festival knowledge (criterion 8) with a one-phrase answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Aulam repertam auri plenam Euclio Vi summa servat, miseris adfectus modis.
question: Quam rem Euclio senex avarus in Aulularia Plauti summa vi servat?
question_en: What does the miserly old man Euclio guard with all his might in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: The title-fact of the play: Euclio the miser and his aula (pot) of gold, from which the Aulularia is named — the canonical literature-fact every Latin reader carries. Short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam noster nostrae qui est magister curiae dividere argenti dixit nummos in viros
question: Quis, ut Euclio in Aulularia Plauti refert, nummos argenti in viros dividere dixerat?
question_en: Who, as Euclio reports in Plautus' Aulularia, had announced a distribution of silver coins per man?
derivation: Roman civic institution through the Greek mask: the curia and its magister distributing a money dole man by man — the errand that forces Euclio from home. One-office answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Post mediam aetatem qui media ducit uxorem domum, si eam senex anum praegnatem fortuito fecerit, quid dubitas, quin sit paratum nomen puero Postumus?
question: Quod nomen puero paratum esse Megadorus in Aulularia iocatur, quem senex ex anu uxore genuerit?
question_en: What name does Megadorus in the Aulularia joke is ready-made for a boy begotten by an old man on an aged wife?
derivation: Roman naming custom: Postumus, the cognomen for the late-born (or after-born) child, deployed as the punchline of Megadorus' joke about old men marrying. Anchored to Megadorus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: istas magnas factiones, animos, dotes dapsiles, clamores, imperia, eburata vehicla, pallas, purpuram, nil moror quae in servitutem sumptibus redigunt viros.
question: Quo uxores magnis cum dotibus viros suos redigere Megadorus apud Plautum dicit?
question_en: To what condition does Megadorus in Plautus say wives with great dowries reduce their husbands?
derivation: Megadorus' famous tirade on dowered wives — their retinues, ivory carriages, mantles and purple enslave the husband. A mores locus classicus on the Roman dowry debate; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: hoc magnum est periclum, ab asinis ad boves transcendere.
question: Quid Euclio in Aulularia Plauti magnum periculum esse dicit, cum de nuptiis cum divite loquitur?
question_en: What does Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia say is a great danger, speaking of marriage with a rich man?
answer_en: To climb over from the asses to the oxen.
derivation: Proverbial saying the play made famous: the poor man 'crossing from asses to oxen' (marrying above his station) courts ruin. Quoted verbatim per the proverb rule; anchored to Euclio.

author: Plautus
source_text: altera manu fert lapidem, panem ostentat altera.
question: Quid altera manu fert, qui panem altera ostentat, secundum proverbium apud Plautum in Aulularia?
question_en: What does he carry in one hand who shows bread with the other, according to the proverb in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: The proverb of the two-faced benefactor — bread on show, stone in hand — coined of the rich man flattering the poor. Quoted point is checkable; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ego istos novi polypos, qui ubi quidquid tetigerunt tenent.
question: Quibus animalibus Euclio in Aulularia Plauti divites comparat, qui quidquid tetigerunt tenent?
question_en: To what animals does Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia compare the rich, who hold whatever they have touched?
derivation: Proverbial image: the grasping man as a polypus that never lets go of what it touches. Anchored to Euclio + the rich; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Mirum quin tua me causa faciat Iuppiter Philippum regem aut Dareum, trivenefica.
question: Quos duos reges Euclio in Aulularia Plauti ut exempla summarum divitiarum nominat?
question_en: Which two kings does Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia name as bywords for the greatest wealth?
derivation: Philip of Macedon and Darius of Persia as proverbially rich kings — the shared byword for fabulous wealth (cf. the Philippei nummi). Two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: cultrum, securim, pistillum, mortarium, quae utenda vasa semper vicini rogant, fures venisse atque abstulisse dicito.
question: Quae quattuor vasa vicinos semper utenda rogare Euclio in Aulularia Plauti dicit?
question_en: What four utensils does Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia say the neighbors are always asking to borrow?
answer_en: The knife, the axe, the pestle, and the mortar.
derivation: Daily-life custom: the standing neighborly loan of kitchen implements (vasa utenda), the four named items being the stock list. Anchored to Euclio + the neighbors; four-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: interea senex Megadorus a sorore suasus ducere uxorem avari gnatam deposcit sibi.
question: A qua persuasus Megadorus senex uxorem ducere in Aulularia Plauti statuit?
question_en: By whom was the old man Megadorus persuaded to take a wife in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: Named relation of the plot: Megadorus moves to marry at his sister's urging (Eunomia in the play). Anchored to Megadorus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quid nunc? etiam mihi despondes filiam? Illis legibus, cum illa dote quam tibi dixi. Sponden ergo? Spondeo.
question: Quo verbo sollemni Euclio filiam suam Megadoro in Aulularia Plauti despondet?
question_en: With what solemn word does Euclio betroth his daughter to Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: The Roman betrothal by sponsio — the formal question-and-answer 'sponden? / spondeo' — enacted on stage. Roman law of engagement through the Greek mask; one-word answer verbatim. Speaker tags stripped per normalization.

author: Plautus
source_text: At nihil est dotis quod dem. Ne duas. dum modo morata recte veniat, dotata est satis.
question: Qua re satis dotatam esse virginem Megadorus in Aulularia Plauti dicit, etiam sine pecunia?
question_en: With what does Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia say a girl is sufficiently dowered, even without money?
derivation: The famous sententia on dowries: 'dum modo morata recte veniat, dotata est satis' — character as dowry, the moral counterpart to Megadorus' anti-dowry tirade. Short answer supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Tun, trium litterarum homo, me vituperas? fur.
question: Quis appellatur 'trium litterarum homo' apud Plautum in Aulularia?
question_en: Who is called 'a man of three letters' in Plautus' Aulularia?
answer_en: A thief (fur — spelled with three letters).
derivation: The celebrated 'trium litterarum homo' joke: the three letters are f-u-r, 'thief' — a proverbial tag the play made famous, hurled by one cook at the other. Kept per instructions as a famous checkable saying; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Cocus ille nundinalest, in nonum diem solet ire coctum.
question: Quoto quoque die cocus 'nundinalis' coctum ire solet, ut Anthrax in Aulularia Plauti iocatur?
question_en: Every how many days does the 'market-day cook' go out to cook, as Anthrax jokes in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: The Roman nundinae — the ninth-day market cycle — underlie the joke of the cook hired only once a market-week. Calendar realia through the Greek mask; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Postquam obsonavit erus et conduxit coquos tibicinasque hasce apud forum, edixit mihi ut dispertirem obsonium hic bifariam.
question: Vbi Megadorus coquos tibicinasque in nuptias conduxit, ut in Aulularia Plauti narratur?
question_en: Where did Megadorus hire the cooks and the flute-girls for the wedding, as told in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: Roman wedding logistics: cooks and tibicinae hired in the forum, with the provisions (obsonium), for a nuptial feast — daily-life custom evidenced verbatim. One-place answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: Vicini huius Euclionis senis e proximo. ei adeo obsoni hinc iussit dimidium dari, cocum alterum itidemque alteram tibicinam.
question: Quantam obsonii partem Megadorus ad Euclionem in nuptias mitti iussit apud Plautum?
answer: Dimidium, cum altero coco et altera tibicina.
question_en: How large a share of the provisions did Megadorus order sent to Euclio for the wedding, in Plautus?
answer_en: Half, with one of the two cooks and one of the two flute-girls.
derivation: The rich groom underwrites the poor father-in-law's share of the feast, split 'bifariam' — wedding custom and the play's plot engine. Short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: i sane cum illo, Phrugia. tu autem, Eleusium, huc intro abi ad nos.
question: Quibus nominibus duae tibicinae in Aulularia Plauti appellantur?
question_en: By what names are the two flute-girls in Plautus' Aulularia called?
derivation: The named tibicinae of the wedding — the hired flute-girl being a fixture of Roman festivity (and of the comic stage). Anchored to the play; two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Tu, Congrio, quem illic reliquit agnum, eum sume atque abi intro illuc
question: Vter coquorum in Aulularia Plauti ad aedes Euclionis coquere missus est?
question_en: Which of the two cooks in Plautus' Aulularia was sent to cook at Euclio's house?
derivation: The canonical cook Congrio (named for the conger eel) drawn by lot to the miser's house, where Euclio cudgels him — a scene every reader of the play carries. One-name answer verbatim; editorial brackets stripped.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quia ad tris viros iam ego deferam nomen tuom. Quam ob rem? Quia cultrum habes.
question: Ad quos magistratus Euclio nomen Congrionis coqui deferre minatur, quia cultrum habet?
question_en: To which magistrates does Euclio threaten to report the cook Congrio's name, because he carries a knife?
answer_en: To the tresviri (the Roman police board of three).
derivation: Roman policing through the Greek mask: carrying a blade gets you denounced to the tresviri capitales — the same anachronistic board Sosia fears in the Amphitruo. One-office answer verbatim; speaker tags stripped.

author: Plautus
source_text: pulmentum pridem ei eripuit milvos: homo ad praetorem plorabundus devenit; infit ibi postulare plorans, eiulans, ut sibi liceret milvom vadarier.
question: Ad quem magistratum Euclio plorabundus devenit, cum milvus ei pulmentum eripuisset, ut in Aulularia iocose narratur?
question_en: To which magistrate did Euclio come weeping when a kite had snatched his food, as jokingly told in the Aulularia?
derivation: Roman legal anachronism in Greek dress: the miser asks the praetor for leave to summon the kite to court (vadari — the formal vadimonium). Anchored to Euclio + the praetor; one-office answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ita me bene amet Laverna, uti te iam, nisi reddi mihi vasa iubes, pipulo hic differam ante aedis.
question: Quam deam Congrio cocus in Aulularia Plauti iurans invocat?
question_en: Which goddess does the cook Congrio invoke in his oath in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: Laverna, the Roman goddess of thieves, sworn by — aptly — a cook, the proverbially light-fingered trade. Roman popular religion evidenced verbatim; one-name answer. Editorial brackets stripped.

author: Plautus
source_text: Cererin, Pythodice, has sunt facturi nuptias? Qui? Quia temeti nihil allatum intellego.
question: Cui deae nuptias parari Staphyla in Aulularia iocatur, quia nihil temeti allatum est?
question_en: For which goddess does Staphyla in the Aulularia joke the wedding is being prepared, since no wine has been brought?
derivation: Rite-specific joke: a 'wedding for Ceres' would be wineless, since Ceres' rites excluded wine (temetum, the archaic word for it) — Roman sacral knowledge evidenced by the joke's own logic. One-name answer verbatim; speaker tags stripped.

author: Plautus
source_text: festo die si quid prodegeris, profesto egere liceat, nisi peperceris.
question: Quid ei licebit profesto die, qui festo die prodegerit, secundum proverbium apud Plautum in Aulularia?
question_en: What will he be free to do on the working day who has squandered on the feast day, according to the proverb in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: Proverb of thrift built on the Roman calendar division of dies festi and profesti: waste on the holiday, want on the workday. Point checkable, quoted verbatim; one-word answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc tusculum emi hoc et coronas floreas: haec imponentur in foco nostro Lari, ut fortunatas faciat gnatae nuptias.
question: Cui deo Euclio tusculum et coronas floreas in foco imposuit, ut gnatae nuptias fortunaret?
question_en: To which god did Euclio offer a bit of incense and flower garlands on the hearth, to bless his daughter's wedding?
derivation: Wedding-day domestic rite: incense and garlands laid on the hearth for the Lar to prosper the marriage — the household cult at the heart of the play. Anchored to Euclio + the Lar; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Apollo, quaeso, subveni mi atque adiuva, confige sagittis fures thensaurarios
question: Quem deum Euclio invocat, ut fures thensaurarios sagittis configat, apud Plautum?
question_en: Which god does Euclio invoke to pierce the treasure-thieves with arrows, in Plautus?
derivation: Apollo the archer — his canonical attribute, the arrows — invoked against thieves. Shared divine iconography evidenced verbatim; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: condigne etiam meus med intus gallus gallinacius, qui erat anu peculiaris, perdidit paenissume. ubi erat haec defossa, occepit ibi scalpurrire ungulis cirum circa. quid opust verbis? ita mihi pectus peracuit: capio fustem, obtrunco gallum, furem manufestarium.
question: Quod animal Euclio in Aulularia Plauti fuste obtruncavit, quia ibi ubi aurum defossum erat scalpurribat?
question_en: What animal did Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia strike dead with a club, because it was scratching where the gold was buried?
derivation: The famous comic scene: the old woman's rooster scratches over the hiding place and Euclio kills it as a 'thief caught in the act' — a set piece every reader of the play carries. Short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: neque ego umquam nisi hodie ad Bacchas veni in Bacchanal coquinatum, ita me miserum et meos discipulos fustibus male contuderunt.
question: Quo se coquinatum venisse Congrio cocus queritur, cum ab Euclione fustibus contusus fugit?
question_en: Where does the cook Congrio complain he has come to cook, as he flees cudgelled by Euclio?
answer_en: To the Bacchants, into a Bacchic shrine.
derivation: The Bacchanal as shared byword for violent frenzy — Congrio can only compare the miser's house to cooking among raving Bacchae. Bacchic rites as ambient cultural knowledge; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam meo quidem animo si idem faciant ceteri opulentiores, pauperiorum filias ut indotatas ducant uxores domum, et multo fiat civitas concordior
question: Qualis fieret civitas, si opulentiores pauperum filias indotatas ducerent, secundum Megadorum apud Plautum?
question_en: What would the state become if the wealthier married poor men's daughters without dowries, according to Megadorus in Plautus?
derivation: Megadorus' civic argument for dowry-less marriage — the mores speech the run instructions flag as a goldmine on Roman dowry debate. One-word comparative answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ego faxim muli, pretio qui superant equos, sint viliores Gallicis cantheriis.
question: Quae iumenta pretio equos superare Megadorus in Aulularia Plauti dicit?
question_en: Which beasts of burden does Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia say exceed horses in price?
derivation: Roman market realia: mules — the carriage animals of wealthy matrons — actually outpriced horses, which is the premise of Megadorus' threat to cheapen them below Gallic geldings. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Dromo, desquama piscis. tu, Machaerio, congrum, murenam exdorsua quantum potest.
question: Quos duos pisces Machaerio exdorsuare iubetur in cena nuptiali apud Plautum in Aulularia?
question_en: Which two fish is Machaerio ordered to fillet for the wedding dinner in Plautus' Aulularia?
answer_en: The conger eel and the moray.
derivation: Named dishes of the Roman festive table: conger and murena, the prestige fish (the murena a Roman delicacy), being dressed for the wedding feast. Two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam quae indotata est, ea in potestate est viri; dotatae mactant et malo et damno viros.
question: In cuius potestate esse uxorem indotatam Megadorus in Aulularia Plauti dicit?
question_en: In whose power does Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia say the undowered wife is?
derivation: The point of the whole dowry debate stated as a maxim: the undowered wife is in the husband's power, the dowered wife ruins him. Roman marriage mores (potestas/manus language) verbatim; short answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: qui mi intro misti in aedis quingentos coquos, cum senis manibus, genere Geryonaceo
question: Cuius monstri generi Euclio coquos senis manibus praeditos adsimulat apud Plautum?
question_en: To what monster's breed does Euclio liken the cooks endowed with six hands apiece, in Plautus?
derivation: Geryon the triple-bodied giant (hence six hands) — canonical myth-figure invoked in Euclio's hyperbole about the thieving cooks. Anchored to Euclio + Geryon; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quos si Argus servet, qui oculeus totus fuit, quem quondam Ioni Iuno custodem addidit, is numquam servet.
question: Quem custodem Iuno quondam Ioni addidit, ut in Aulularia Plauti memoratur?
question_en: What guardian did Juno once set over Io, as recalled in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: Canonical myth as shared story: Argus the all-eyed watcher whom Juno appointed to guard Io — cited casually as ambient knowledge. Names and attribute all verbatim; short answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: praeterea tibicinam, quae mi interbibere sola, si vino scatat, Corinthiensem fontem Pirenam potest.
question: Cuius urbis fons erat Pirena, ut apud Plautum in Aulularia dicitur?
question_en: Of what city was Pirene the spring, as said in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: The famous spring Pirene at Corinth — shared Greek-Roman geography, the standard of the joke that the flute-girl could drink it dry. One-place answer verbatim (Corinthiensem fontem Pirenam).

author: Plautus
source_text: quin exta inspicere in sole ei vivo licet: ita is pellucet quasi lanterna Punica.
question: Cui rei Euclio agnum macrum pellucentem in Aulularia Plauti comparat?
question_en: To what does Euclio in Plautus' Aulularia compare the scrawny lamb you can see through?
answer_en: To a Punic lantern (of translucent horn).
derivation: Realia of trade: the 'Punic lantern' of thin translucent horn, proverbially see-through — a Carthaginian import familiar enough to carry the joke. Short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ego, nisi quid me vis, eo lavatum, ut sacruficem.
question: Quid Megadorus in Aulularia Plauti prius facit, quam sacrificet?
question_en: What does Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia do before he sacrifices?
derivation: Ritual purity before sacrifice: one washes first (so too Euclio, 'nunc lavabo, ut rem divinam faciam'). Roman sacral custom evidenced verbatim; short answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc hoc mihi factu est optumum, ut ted auferam, aula, in Fidei fanum: ibi abstrudam probe.
question: In cuius deae fanum Euclio aulam auri e domo sublatam primum abstrusit?
question_en: In which goddess's shrine did Euclio first hide the pot of gold taken from his house?
derivation: The cult of Fides with her fanum — Roman deified abstraction — chosen by the miser with the running pun on fides/trust ('fretus tua, Fides, fiducia'). Anchored to Euclio + the aula; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc hoc ubi abstrudam cogito solum locum. Silvani lucus extra murum est avius, crebro salicto oppletus. ibi sumam locum. certumst, Silvano potius credam quam Fide.
question: Quo Euclio aulam auri, e fano Fidei ablatam, deinde abstrusit apud Plautum?
question_en: Where did Euclio then hide the pot of gold he had removed from the shrine of Fides, in Plautus?
answer_en: In the grove of Silvanus outside the wall.
derivation: Silvanus the extra-urban woodland god, his lonely grove outside the wall — Roman religion's topography, and the site of the fateful theft. Anchored to Euclio + Fides/Silvanus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Non temere est quod corvos cantat mihi nunc ab laeva manu; semul radebat pedibus terram et voce croccibat sua
question: A qua parte corvus Euclioni cecinit, quod omen ille non temere esse putavit?
question_en: On which side did the raven croak at Euclio, an omen he thought not without meaning?
derivation: Roman bird-omen lore: the raven's cry on the left as a significant sign (Euclio later credits it with saving him: 'ni subvenisset corvos'). Augural realia verbatim; short answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed si repperero, o Fides, mulsi congialem plenam faciam tibi fideliam. id adeo tibi faciam; verum ego mihi bibam, ubi id fecero.
question: Quid Strobilus deae Fidei se daturum vovet, si aurum reppererit, apud Plautum?
question_en: What does Strobilus vow to give the goddess Fides if he finds the gold, in Plautus?
answer_en: A gallon-jar (congius-sized pot) full of honey-wine (mulsum).
derivation: A comic votum with real furniture: mulsum (honey-wine) as offering, the congius measure, the fidelia jar — and the punchline that he'll drink it himself. Vow-practice realia; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Perii, mea nutrix. obsecro te, uterum dolet. Iuno Lucina, tuam fidem!
question: Quam deam filia Euclionis parturiens in Aulularia Plauti invocat?
question_en: Which goddess does Euclio's daughter call upon in labor in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: Juno Lucina, the Roman goddess of childbirth, invoked in the canonical birth-cry of comedy — shared religious knowledge evidenced verbatim. One-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quid vis fieri? factum est illud: fieri infectum non potest.
question: Quid de re facta fieri non posse Lyconides in Aulularia Plauti dicit?
question_en: What does Lyconides in Plautus' Aulularia say cannot happen to a thing once done?
derivation: The proverb 'factum fieri infectum non potest' — what is done cannot be undone — a saying this scene helped make canonical (echoed by Terence). Quoted verbatim per the proverb rule.

author: Plautus
source_text: ibo intro, ubi de capite meo sunt comitia.
question: Quid de capite suo intus haberi Lyconides in Aulularia Plauti iocatur, dum mater cum avunculo agit?
question_en: What does Lyconides in Plautus' Aulularia joke is being held indoors concerning his life, while his mother deals with his uncle?
answer_en: The comitia (the Roman voting assembly, as a capital court).
derivation: Roman institutional anachronism: the comitia that voted 'de capite' (on a citizen's life) transplanted into Greek Athens as a metaphor for the family council. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: hic mihi est Megadorus avonculus, meus pater fuit Antimachus, ego vocor Lyconides, mater est Eunomia.
question: Quo patre et qua matre natus est Lyconides adulescens in Aulularia Plauti?
question_en: Of what father and mother was the young Lyconides born, in Plautus' Aulularia?
answer_en: Of Antimachus as father and Eunomia as mother.
derivation: Lyconides' formal self-identification gives the family tree in one line: father Antimachus, mother Eunomia. Named-relation fact of the canonical play; two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: hic mihi est Megadorus avonculus
question: Quis erat Lyconidi avunculus in Aulularia Plauti?
question_en: Who was Lyconides' maternal uncle in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: The kinship on which the plot turns: Megadorus, the girl's aged suitor, is the young lover's avunculus (mother's brother), and yields the bride to him. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quis me Athenis nunc magis quisquam est homo cui di sint propitii?
question: In qua urbe fabula Plauti quae Aulularia inscribitur agitur?
question_en: In what city is Plautus' play called the Aulularia set?
derivation: The nominal setting of the comedy, evidenced by Strobilus counting himself the most god-favored man 'at Athens' — the Greek frame through which the Roman realia poke. One-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quadrilibrem aulam auro onustam habeo. quis me est ditior?
question: Quanti ponderis erat aula auro onusta Euclionis, ut Strobilus in Aulularia gloriatur?
question_en: Of what weight was Euclio's pot laden with gold, as Strobilus boasts in the Aulularia?
derivation: The one number attached to the famous pot: a four-pounder of gold ('quadrilibrem... aulam', repeated at 821-822). Measure fact of the canonical play; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Is me nunc renuntiare repudium iussit tibi.
question: Quid Megadorus per Lyconidem Euclioni renuntiavit, nuptiis iam exornatis?
question_en: What did Megadorus have Lyconides announce to Euclio, though the wedding was already prepared?
answer_en: The repudium (formal breaking-off of the betrothal).
derivation: Roman legal institution: repudium, the formal renunciation of a sponsio-betrothal, duly 'renuntiatum' by messenger. Anchored to Megadorus + Euclio; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ut mi ignoscas eamque uxorem mihi des, ut leges iubent.
question: Quid fieri leges iubent, cum adulescens virginem vitiavit, ut Lyconides in Aulularia adfirmat?
question_en: What do the laws command to be done when a young man has violated a maiden, as Lyconides asserts in the Aulularia?
answer_en: That she be given to him as wife.
derivation: The comic-law commonplace (from Attic law, naturalized in the palliata): the seducer must marry the girl — 'ut leges iubent'. Anchored to Lyconides + Euclio's daughter; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam tua gnata peperit, decumo mense post: numerum cape
question: Quoto mense post Cereris vigilias filia Euclionis peperit, ut Lyconides apud Plautum computat?
question_en: In what month after the vigil of Ceres did Euclio's daughter give birth, as Lyconides reckons in Plautus?
derivation: The Roman ten-month reckoning of pregnancy ('decumo mense post: numerum cape'), tying the birth to the Ceres-vigil assault. Number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: In arca apud me. nunc volo me emitti manu.
question: Quod praemium Strobilus servus, aula auri inventa, ab ero suo petit in Aulularia Plauti?
question_en: What reward does the slave Strobilus, having found the pot of gold, ask of his master in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: Manumissio — freedom bought with a windfall — the standing dream of the comic slave and a real Roman institution ('emitti manu'). Anchored to Strobilus + the aula; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Re omni inspecta compressoris servolus Id surpit.
question: Cuius servus aulam auri Euclionis e luco Silvani surripuit in Aulularia Plauti?
question_en: Whose slave stole Euclio's pot of gold from the grove of Silvanus in Plautus' Aulularia?
answer_en: Lyconides' — the man who had violated the girl.
derivation: The theft that breaks the miser: the ravisher's slave (Strobilus in the play) spies out the hiding place and lifts the pot. Anchored via the argumentum's 'compressoris servolus'; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: per dolum mox Euclio cum perdidisset aulam, insperato invenit laetusque natam conlocat Lyconidi.
question: Cui Euclio, aula insperato recuperata, filiam suam tandem in matrimonium conlocavit?
question_en: To whom did Euclio, having unexpectedly recovered the pot, finally give his daughter in marriage?
derivation: The resolution of the play as the ancient argumentum preserves it — the play's own final scenes are lost (the text breaks off in Act V), so the transmitted summary is the evidence; nothing invented. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nec noctu nec diu quietus umquam servabam eam: nunc dormiam.
question: Quid Euclio, cura auri tandem liberatus, se facturum esse dicit in fragmento Aululariae?
question_en: What does Euclio, freed at last from worry over the gold, say he will do, in a fragment of the Aulularia?
derivation: The celebrated fragment of the lost ending: the miser who watched night and day can say 'nunc dormiam' once the gold is out of his hands — the moral of the play in one word. Short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: qui mi holera cruda ponunt, hallec adduint.
question: Quod condimentum holeribus crudis addendum esse dicit fragmentum Aululariae Plauti?
question_en: What condiment does a fragment of Plautus' Aulularia say should be supplied with raw vegetables?
derivation: Staple table realia: hallec/allec, the sediment of garum, as the dressing owed to a dish of raw greens — the fish-sauce family the guidelines flag as core food culture. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: pro illis corcotis, strophiis, sumptu uxorio
question: Quae duo vestimenta muliebria fragmentum Aululariae inter sumptum uxorium numerat?
question_en: Which two articles of women's wear does a fragment of the Aulularia count among a wife's expenses?
derivation: Dress realia from the dowry-tirade tradition: the crocota (saffron robe) and strophium as typical items of wifely luxury. Two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quod si tacuisset, tamen ego eram dicturus, deus, qui poteram planius. nam mihi Auxilio est nomen. nunc operam date, ut ego argumentum hoc vobis plane perputem.
question: Quis deus in Cistellaria Plauti argumentum fabulae spectatoribus eloquitur?
question_en: Which god recounts the plot of the play to the spectators in Plautus' Cistellaria?
derivation: The play's theatrical curiosity: a personified god named Auxilium delivers a delayed prologue (only after the opening scenes, grumbling that the tipsy old woman has already told half the story). Canonical literature-fact of the named play; one-name answer verbatim (mihi Auxilio est nomen).

author: Plautus
source_text: bene valete et vincite virtute vera, quod fecistis antidhac; servate vostros socios, veteres et novos, augete auxilia vostra iustis legibus, perdite perduelles, parite laudem et lauream, ut vobis victi Poeni poenas sufferant.
question: Quos hostes victos poenas Romanis daturos esse Auxilium deus in fine prologi Cistellariae Plauti optat?
question_en: Which conquered enemies does the god Auxilium at the end of the prologue of Plautus' Cistellaria pray will pay the penalty to the Romans?
derivation: The famous patriotic aside that dates the play: the prologue-god urges the audience to destroy the foe 'that the vanquished Poeni may suffer punishment' — composed while the Second Punic War was still being fought. Historical fact embedded in the named play; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus

author: Plautus
source_text: eaque extemplo ubi vino has conspersi fores, de odore adesse me scit, aperit ilico.
question: Qua re Phaedromus fores lenonis conspergere solebat, ut Leaena anus odore adesse eum sciret et aperiret?
question_en: With what did Phaedromus sprinkle the pimp's door, so that the old woman Leaena would smell that he was there and open it?
derivation: The celebrated device of the opening: the door sprinkled with wine as bait for the wine-sniffing old ianitrix. Wine realia carrying the serenade scene; anchored to both names; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quasi tu lagoenam dicas, ubi vinum Chium solet esse.
question: Quod vinum in lagoena esse solere Palinurus dicit, cum Leaenam anum lagoenae comparat?
question_en: What wine does Palinurus say is usually kept in a flagon, when he compares the old woman Leaena to one?
derivation: A named luxury wine: Chium, the celebrated Greek wine of Chios, as the flagon's typical content. Wine realia of the Roman table; anchored to the named characters; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Sitit haec anus. Pal. Quantillum sitit? Phaed. Modica est, capit quadrantal.
question: Quantum vini Leaenam anum capere Phaedromus iocatur?
question_en: How much wine does Phaedromus joke that the old woman Leaena can hold?
answer_en: A quadrantal (a full amphora, some 26 liters).
derivation: The joke turns on the Roman liquid measure: the quadrantal, the amphora-measure of about 26 liters — the 'moderate' old woman holds one. Measure realia; anchored to Leaena; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Semper tu scito, flamma fumo est proxima; fumo comburi nil potest, flamma potest.
question: Cui rei flammam proximam esse Palinurus in Curculione Plauti proverbialiter dicit?
question_en: To what does Palinurus in Plautus' Curculio proverbially say flame is next?
derivation: The proverb 'flame is next to smoke' — smoke burns nothing, flame does — the Latin ancestor of 'where there's smoke, there's fire', said of kisses leading further. Checkable proverbial point; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: qui e nuce nuculeum esse volt, frangit nucem.
question: Quid frangit, ut in Curculione Plauti proverbialiter dicitur, qui e nuce nuculeum esse volt?
question_en: What does he crack, as the proverb in Plautus' Curculio has it, who wants to eat the kernel from the nut?
derivation: The nut proverb: who wants the kernel must crack the nut — effort before enjoyment. A quotable Latin proverb with a checkable point; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nemo ire quemquam publica prohibet via; dum ne per fundum saeptum facias semitam.
question: Qua via ire neminem prohiberi Palinurus in Curculione proverbialiter ait, dum ne per fundum saeptum semita fiat?
question_en: On what road does Palinurus in the Curculio proverbially say no one is forbidden to travel, so long as one cuts no path through fenced land?
derivation: The public-road maxim applied to love: the common way (venal love) is open to all; only trespass on enclosed property (respectable women) is barred. Proverbial image with legal color (via publica vs fundus saeptus); short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: dum ted abstineas nupta, vidua, virgine, iuventute et pueris liberis, ama quid lubet.
question: Quibus personis abstinere debet amator, ut Palinurus in Curculione praecipit, si vult amare quod lubet?
answer: Nupta, vidua, virgine, iuventute et pueris liberis.
question_en: From what persons must a lover keep away, as Palinurus lays down in the Curculio, if he would love whatever he pleases?
answer_en: A married woman, a widow, a maiden, freeborn youths and boys.
derivation: The classic Roman statement of licensed love: everything is permitted except the protected classes — married women, widows, virgins, and the freeborn young. A celebrated mores rule of the palliata; the enumerated answer is verbatim and brief.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quo Venus Cupidoque imperat, suadet Amor: si media nox est sive est prima vespera, si status condictus cum hoste intercedit dies, tamen est eundum quo imperant ingratiis.
question: Quo eundum esse Phaedromus ait, etiamsi status condictus cum hoste intercedat dies?
question_en: Where does Phaedromus say one must go, even if a court-day formally appointed with a foreigner intervenes?
derivation: Love outranks even the archaic legal duty: the status condictus cum hoste dies — the appointed court-day with a foreigner, in the old XII-Tables sense of hostis — must yield to Venus and Cupid. Legal-formula realia carried by a short verbatim answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: Venus, de paulo paululum hoc tibi dabo haud lubenter. nam tibi amantes propitiantes vinum potantes danunt omnes, mihi haud saepe evenunt tales hereditates.
question: Cui deae amantes, cum vinum potant, propitiantes de eo dare solent, ut Leaena anus apud Plautum ait?
question_en: To which goddess do lovers, when they drink wine, customarily give a propitiating share, as the old woman Leaena says in Plautus?
derivation: Cult custom of lovers: a libation-share of the wine to Venus to win her favor — Leaena grudges the goddess even a drop. Religio of everyday love-cult, with the altar of Venus standing before the leno's door; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Hac nocte in somnis visus sum viderier procul sedere longe a me Aesculapium, neque eum ad me adire neque me magni pendere visumst.
question: Quem deum Cappadox leno in somnis procul a se sedere neque ad se adire vidit, cum in fano incubaret?
question_en: What god did the pimp Cappadox see in his dream sitting far off and refusing to approach him, while he slept in the shrine?
derivation: The mechanics of incubation: the healing god appears (or pointedly does not) in the incubant's dream — Aesculapius sits aloof, showing the leno is past cure. Religio realia of the healing cult; anchored to Cappadox; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Flos veteris vini meis naribus obiectust, eius amor cupidam me huc prolicit per tenebras. ubi ubi est, prope me est. euax, habeo. salve, anime mi, Liberi lepos. ut veteris vetus tui cupida sum. nam omnium unguentum odor prae tuo nautea est.
question: Quid esse odorem omnium unguentorum prae vino vetere Leaena anus exclamat?
question_en: What does the old woman Leaena exclaim the scent of every perfume is, compared with old wine?
derivation: The bibulous hymn to old wine ('the charm of Liber'): beside its bouquet every unguent — stacte, cinnamon, rose, saffron, casia, telinum — is mere bilge-water (nautea). Wine-and-perfume realia in a famous monologue; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Lien enecat, renes dolent, pulmones distrahuntur, cruciatur iecur, radices cordis pereunt, hirae omnes dolent.
question: Quae pars corporis Cappadocem lenonem enecare in primis dicitur, cum in fano Aesculapi medicinam quaereret?
question_en: What organ is said first and foremost to be killing the pimp Cappadox, when he sought healing in the shrine of Aesculapius?
derivation: The leno's canonical ailment: the monstrous spleen — he walks 'girdled with his spleen like a belt' and seems to carry twins in his belly. The disease that motivates the incubation plot; anchored to Cappadox; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Siquidem incubare velint qui periuraverint, locus non praeberi potis est in Capitolio.
question: Quo in loco locum non praeberi posse Cappadox iocatur, si omnes qui periuraverint incubare velint?
question_en: In what place does Cappadox joke there could be no room, if all who have perjured themselves wished to sleep there for a cure?
derivation: Perjurers swear by Jupiter, so they would have to incubate at his temple — and the Capitol could not hold them all. A Roman-frame joke naming the Capitolium inside the Greek play; anchored to Cappadox; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: tum isti Graeci palliati, capite operto qui ambulant, qui incedunt suffarcinati cum libris, cum sportulis, constant, conferunt sermones inter se drapetae, obstant, obsistunt, incedunt cum suis sententiis, quos semper videas bibentes esse in thermipolio.
question: Quo in loco Graecos palliatos, libris suffarcinatos, bibentes semper videri Curculio queritur?
question_en: In what establishment does Curculio complain the cloaked Greeks, stuffed with their books, are always to be seen drinking?
derivation: The running-parasite's tirade satirizes Greek philosopher-types drinking calidum (the hot spiced drink) in the thermopolium — Roman street-and-tavern realia. Anchored to the named speech; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ibi me interrogat, ecquem in Epidauro Lyconem tarpezitam noverim. dico me novisse. 'quid? lenonem Cappadocem?'
question: In qua urbe Graeca fabula Plauti quae Curculio inscribitur agitur, ubi Lyco trapezita et Cappadox leno habitabant?
question_en: In what Greek city is Plautus' play called Curculio set, where the banker Lyco and the pimp Cappadox lived?
derivation: The setting of the play: Epidaurus, seat of the great sanctuary of Aesculapius where the leno incubates. Anchored to the named play and characters; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: 'Miles Lyconi in Epidauro hospiti suo Therapontigonus Platagidorus plurimam salutem dicit.'
question: Quod nomen erat militi qui Planesium virginem a Cappadoce lenone emerat?
question_en: What was the name of the soldier who had bought the maiden Planesium from the pimp Cappadox?
derivation: The braggart soldier of the play, named in full in the letter's salutation. A fixed cast-name; anchored to the purchase plot; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: 'immo apud trapezitam situm est illum quem dixi Lyconem, atque ei mandavi, qui anulo meo tabellas obsignatas attulisset, ut daret operam, ut mulierem a lenone cum auro et veste abduceret.'
question: Apud quem miles Therapontigonus argentum pro virgine empta depositum reliquit?
question_en: With whom did the soldier Therapontigonus leave on deposit the money for the girl he had bought?
derivation: Banking realia of the trapezita/argentarius: money on deposit, to be released to whoever brings tablets sealed with the depositor's ring — the very mechanism Curculio's stolen ring and forged letter exploit. Anchored to both names; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: cape, signum nosce. nostin? Lyc. Quidni noverim? clupeatus elephantum ubi machaera dissicit.
question: Quid in signo anuli Therapontigoni militis insculptum erat?
question_en: What was engraved on the seal of the soldier Therapontigonus' ring?
answer_en: A shield-bearing warrior cleaving an elephant with his sword.
derivation: Signet culture: the seal-device authenticates the letter, and the banker knows it at sight — a braggart's blazon of elephant-slaying. Anchored to the named soldier's ring; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: propino magnum poclum: ille ebibit, caput deponit, condormiscit. ego ei subduco anulum, deduco pedes de lecto clam, ne miles sentiat.
question: Quid Curculio militi Therapontigono, vino sopito, clam subduxit?
question_en: What did Curculio secretly slip off the soldier Therapontigonus as he lay sunk in wine?
derivation: The theft that drives the plot: after dinner and dice Curculio pledges the soldier a great cup, and when he passes out steals the signet ring used to seal the forged letter. Anchored to both names; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: iacit volturios quattuor. talos arripio, invoco almam meam nutricem Herculem, iacto basilicum.
question: Quem iactum talorum Curculio iecit, cum miles volturios quattuor iecisset?
question_en: What throw of the knucklebones did Curculio cast, after the soldier had thrown four 'vultures'?
derivation: Named dice-throws of Roman gaming: the volturii ('vultures'), a losing cast, against the basilicus ('king'), a winning one — realia of play at tali over the wine. Anchored to the dice scene in Caria; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: talos arripio, invoco almam meam nutricem Herculem, iacto basilicum.
question: Quem deum Curculio, talos arripiens, almam nutricem suam invocavit?
question_en: What god did Curculio invoke as his 'kindly nurse' as he snatched up the knucklebones?
derivation: Gamblers' religio: Hercules invoked at the dice-throw for luck — the parasite comically calls the hero his foster-nurse. Anchored to Curculio + the dice scene; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Vnocule, salve. Cvrc. Quaeso, deridesne me? Lyc. De Coclitum prosapia te esse arbitror, nam ei sunt unoculi.
question: De cuius prosapia esse Lyco trapezita Curculionem, unoculum simulantem, iocatur?
question_en: From what clan does the banker Lyco joke that Curculio, posing as a one-eyed man, must come?
answer_en: From the clan of the Coclites (the 'one-eyed').
derivation: The joke presumes shared Roman knowledge that Cocles means one-eyed — the family of Horatius Cocles, 'for the Coclites are one-eyed'. Roman allusion inside the Greek frame; anchored to both names; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quis tu homo es? Cvrc. Libertus illius, quem omnes Summanum vocant. Lyc. Summane, salve. qui Summanu's? fac sciam. Cvrc. Quia vestimenta, ubi obdormivi ebrius, summano, ob eam rem me omnes Summanum vocant.
question: Quo nomine ficto Curculio se libertum militis Therapontigoni esse apud Lyconem simulavit?
question_en: Under what false name did Curculio pass himself off to Lyco as the freedman of the soldier Therapontigonus?
derivation: The alias of the disguised parasite: Summanus — the name of the Roman god of night thunder, comically derived here from wetting (summanare) his clothes when drunk. Anchored to Curculio + Lyco; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Catapulta hoc ictum est mihi apud Sicyonem.
question: Vbi oculum suum catapulta ictum esse Curculio, unoculum simulans, mentitus est?
question_en: Where did Curculio, feigning to be one-eyed, claim his eye had been struck by a catapult?
derivation: The cover-story of the eye-patch disguise: a catapult wound at Sicyon, worn 'for the republic's sake'. Anchored to Curculio's disguise; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quia enim Persas, Paphlagones, Sinopes, Arabes, Cares, Cretanos, Syros, Rhodiam atque Lyciam, Perediam et Perbibesiam, Centauromachiam et Classiam Vnomammiam, Libyamque oram omnem Conterebromniam, dimidiam partem nationum usque omnium subegit solus intra viginti dies.
question: Intra quot dies dimidiam partem nationum omnium Therapontigonum solum subegisse Curculio mentitur?
question_en: Within how many days does Curculio pretend that Therapontigonus single-handedly subdued half of all the nations?
derivation: The braggart-soldier boast catalogue, complete with joke-nations (Peredia 'Gluttonland', Perbibesia 'Drinkland', Unomammia 'One-breast-land' of Amazons): half of all peoples conquered alone in twenty days. Single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ibi nunc statuam volt dare auream solidam faciundam ex auro Philippo, quae siet septempedalis, factis monumentum suis.
question: Quantam statuam auream ex auro Philippo sibi faciundam Therapontigonus miles volebat, ut Curculio narrat?
question_en: How large a golden statue of Philippic gold did the soldier Therapontigonus want made of himself, as Curculio tells it?
derivation: The vanity monument: a solid gold statue, seven feet tall, of Philippic gold, 'a memorial of his deeds'. Number-and-coinage realia in the boast; anchored to the named soldier; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: habent hunc morem plerique argentarii, ut alius alium poscant, reddant nemini, pugnis rem solvant, si quis poscat clarius.
question: Quem morem plerosque argentarios habere Lyco trapezita ipse fatetur?
answer: Vt alius alium poscant, reddant nemini.
question_en: What habit does the banker Lyco himself confess most bankers have?
answer_en: They dun one another but repay nobody.
derivation: Banker satire from a banker's own mouth: the argentarii demand payment of each other, pay no one back, and settle with fists if dunned too loudly. Roman financial mores; anchored to Lyco; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: item genus est lenonium inter homines meo quidem animo ut muscae, culices, cimices pedesque pulicesque.
question: Quibus bestiolis genus lenonium inter homines simile esse Curculio pronuntiat?
question_en: To what vermin does Curculio declare the tribe of pimps among mankind is like?
answer_en: To flies, gnats, bedbugs, lice, and fleas.
derivation: The canonical anti-leno invective: pimps are the vermin of humanity — a pest, of use to no one, with whom no honest man dares stand in the forum. Quotable simile with a checkable list, verbatim and brief.

author: Plautus
source_text: Edepol nugatorem lepidum lepide hunc nactust Phaedromus. halapantam an sycophantam magis esse dicam nescio. ornamenta quae locavi metuo ut possim recipere.
question: Quis in Curculione Plauti, sua persona loquens, ornamenta se Phaedromo locavisse ait?
question_en: Who in Plautus' Curculio, speaking in his own person, says he has rented out the costumes to Phaedromus?
derivation: A celebrated rupture of the dramatic frame: the choragus, the man who rents the production its costumes and properties, steps forward worrying about his ornamenta — theater-business realia of the Roman stage. One-word answer from the speaker heading and his own words.

author: Plautus
source_text: qui periurum convenire volt hominem ito in comitium.
question: Quo ire debet, ut Choragus in Curculione Plauti docet, qui hominem periurum convenire volt?
question_en: Where should one go, as the Choragus in Plautus' Curculio instructs, to meet a perjurer?
derivation: First stop of the Choragus' famous tour of the Roman Forum — a topography of low life dropped into the Greek play: perjurers at the Comitium, the old assembly-place where courts met. One-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: qui mendacem et gloriosum, apud Cloacinae sacrum.
question: Apud cuius deae sacrum mendaces et gloriosi inveniuntur, ut Choragus in Curculione docet?
question_en: At whose goddess's shrine are liars and braggarts to be found, as the Choragus instructs in the Curculio?
derivation: Second stop of the Forum tour: liars and boasters at the sacrum Cloacinae, the little shrine of Venus Cloacina in the Forum. Real Roman topography; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ditis damnosos maritos sub basilica quaerito. ibidem erunt scorta exoleta quique stipulari solent.
question: Vbi divites damnososque maritos quaerendos esse Choragus in Curculione praecipit?
question_en: Where does the Choragus in the Curculio direct one to look for rich, spendthrift husbands?
derivation: The Forum tour continues: rich wastrel husbands (with worn-out prostitutes and professional deal-makers) under the basilica — among the earliest literary mentions of a basilica at Rome. One-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: symbolarum collatores apud forum piscarium.
question: Vbi symbolarum collatores inveniri Choragus in Curculione dicit?
question_en: Where does the Choragus in the Curculio say the contributors to dinner-clubs are to be found?
derivation: The Forum tour: the symbolarum collatores — men who club together paying shares (symbolae) for common dinners — haunt the fish-market. Dining-club mores mapped onto real Roman topography; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: in foro infimo boni homines atque dites ambulant.
question: Qua in parte fori boni homines atque dites ambulare dicuntur apud Choragum Plauti?
question_en: In what part of the Forum are good and wealthy men said to stroll, according to Plautus' Choragus?
derivation: The tour's one respectable address: solid, rich citizens walk the lower end of the Forum. Topography of social sorting in the Roman Forum; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: in medio propter canalem, ibi ostentatores meri.
question: Qui homines in medio foro propter canalem stare dicuntur, ut Choragus in Curculione docet?
question_en: What sort of men are said to stand in the middle of the Forum by the drainage channel, as the Choragus explains in the Curculio?
derivation: The Forum tour: by the canalis, the open drain crossing the middle Forum, stand the sheer self-advertisers. A checkable place-to-type mapping; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: confidentes garrulique et malevoli supera lacum, qui alteri de nihilo audacter dicunt contumeliam.
question: Vbi confidentes garrulique et malevoli versari dicuntur in Choragi de foro Romano oratione?
question_en: Where are the brazen, the chatterers, and the malicious said to hang about in the Choragus' speech on the Roman Forum?
derivation: The Forum tour: slanderers who insult others without cause loiter 'above the lake' — the Lacus Curtius in the middle of the Forum. Real topography; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sub veteribus, ibi sunt qui dant quique accipiunt faenore.
question: Vbi sunt, ut Choragus in Curculione docet, qui faenore dant quique accipiunt?
question_en: Where, as the Choragus instructs in the Curculio, are those who lend and borrow at interest?
answer_en: Under the Old Shops (the tabernae veteres).
derivation: The Forum tour: moneylending under the tabernae veteres, the Old Shops on the south side of the Forum where the bankers did business. Financial topography of Rome; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: pone aedem Castoris, ibi sunt subito quibus credas male.
question: Pone cuius dei aedem sunt ii quibus male credas, ut Choragus in Curculione monet?
question_en: Behind whose temple are the men you would be ill-advised to trust, as the Choragus warns in the Curculio?
derivation: The Forum tour: behind the aedes Castoris — the temple of Castor at the Forum's south-east corner — lurk the quick men not to be trusted. Real Roman monument in the low-life map; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: in Tusco vico, ibi sunt homines qui ipsi sese venditant, vel qui ipsi vorsant vel qui aliis ubi vorsentur praebeant.
question: Quo in vico homines qui ipsi sese venditant esse Choragus in Curculione dicit?
question_en: In what street does the Choragus in the Curculio say the people are who sell their own bodies?
answer_en: In the Vicus Tuscus (the Etruscan quarter).
derivation: The tour's last stop: the Vicus Tuscus, the street running from the Forum past the temple of Castor, notorious for prostitution — 'men who sell themselves'. Real street of Rome; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam illam minis olim decem puellam parvolam emi, sed eum qui mi illam vendidit numquam postilla vidi.
question: Quot minis Cappadox leno Planesium puellam parvolam olim emerat?
question_en: For how many minae had the pimp Cappadox once bought Planesium as a little girl?
derivation: The leno's own account of the purchase: ten minae for the stolen child, whose seller he never saw again — against the thirty minae he later charged the soldier. Slave-trade money realia; anchored to both names; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Memento promisisse te, si quisquam hanc liberali causa manu assereret, mihi omne argentum redditum iri, minas triginta.
question: Quid Cappadox leno repromisit facturum, si quisquam Planesium liberali causa manu assereret?
question_en: What did the pimp Cappadox guarantee to do if anyone should formally claim Planesium as freeborn?
answer_en: To repay all the money, the thirty minae.
derivation: Roman legal procedure inside the sale: the manus assertio liberali causa — the formal claim of a person's free status — triggers the leno's warranty to refund the price. Ius realia that resolves the plot; anchored to the named parties; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Antiquom poetam audivi scripsisse in tragoedia, mulieres duas peiores esse quam unam. res itast.
question: Quid antiquum poetam in tragoedia scripsisse Curculio audivisse ait?
answer: Mulieres duas peiores esse quam unam.
question_en: What does Curculio say he has heard an old poet wrote in a tragedy?
answer_en: That two women are worse than one.
derivation: A quoted sententia with a literary pedigree: the 'old poet's' tragic line that two women are worse than one, endorsed by the parasite. Checkable proverbial point; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: pater meus habuit Periplanes Planesium is prius quam moritur mihi dedit tamquam suo, ut aequom fuerat, filio.
question: Quod nomen erat patri Therapontigoni militis, qui ei moriens anulum reliquit?
question_en: What was the name of the soldier Therapontigonus' father, who left him the ring at his death?
derivation: The recognition genealogy: the ring descends from the father Periplanes to his son — and so identifies Planesium, who is revealed as the same father's daughter. Anchored to Therapontigonus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: cedo, si vera memoras, quae fuit mater tua? Plan. Cleobula. Ther. Nutrix quae fuit? Plan. Archestrata.
question: Quod nomen fuisse matri suae Planesium respondit, cum frater eam recognoscens interrogaret?
question_en: What did Planesium answer was her mother's name, when her brother questioned her in the recognition scene?
derivation: The recognition quiz: the brother tests the claimed sister on family names, and she answers her mother was Cleobula. A fixed name of the play's anagnorisis; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Nutrix quae fuit? Plan. Archestrata. ea me spectatum tulerat per Dionysia.
question: Quae nutrix Planesium parvolam spectatum per Dionysia tulerat?
question_en: Which nurse had taken little Planesium to watch the shows at the Dionysia?
derivation: The second answer of the recognition quiz: the nurse Archestrata, who carried the child to the Dionysia where she was lost. Anchored to Planesium; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ea me spectatum tulerat per Dionysia. postquam illo ventum est, iam, ut me collocaverat, exoritur ventus turbo, spectacla ibi ruont, ego pertimesco: tum ibi me nescio quis arripit timidam atque pavidam.
question: Quo festo Planesium parvola, cum spectatum ducta esset, in tumultu surrepta est?
question_en: At what festival was little Planesium stolen in the panic, when she had been taken to watch the shows?
derivation: The canonical loss story: at the Dionysia a whirlwind rose, the spectators' stands collapsed, and in the terror an unknown man snatched the child. Festival-and-theater realia (temporary spectacula that could fall); anchored to Planesium; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Cedo, ut inspiciam. Cvrc. Sanan es, quae isti committas? Plan. Sine modo. Ther. Pro Iuppiter, hic est quem ego tibi misi natali die. tam facile novi quam me. salve, mea soror.
question: Quo die Therapontigonus anulum, quo postea soror agnita est, parvolae Planesio miserat?
question_en: On what day had Therapontigonus sent little Planesium the ring by which the sister was later recognized?
derivation: The recognition token: the ring she kept through her captivity was her brother's birthday gift — natalicium gift-custom realia sealing the anagnorisis. Anchored to both names; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Pro Iuppiter, hic est quem ego tibi misi natali die. tam facile novi quam me. salve, mea soror. Plan. Frater mi, salve.
question: Cuius militis soror esse Planesium anulo inspecto cognita est?
question_en: Of which soldier was Planesium, once the ring was examined, recognized to be the sister?
derivation: The play's anagnorisis: the very soldier who bought the girl proves to be her brother, the ring giving the proof — she is freeborn and the sale is void. The canonical resolution of the Curculio; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Vt mihi hanc despondeas. Cvrc. Quid cessas, miles, hanc huic uxorem dare? T. Si haec volt. Pl. Mi frater, cupio. T. Fiat. C. Bene facis. Phaed. Spondesne, miles, mi hanc uxorem? Ther. Spondeo.
question: Quis Planesium Phaedromo uxorem sollemni verbo spopondit?
question_en: Who formally betrothed Planesium as wife to Phaedromus with the solemn word of pledge?
derivation: Betrothal realia: the Roman sponsalia formula — Spondesne? Spondeo — spoken by the woman's nearest male kin, here the newfound brother (with her consent asked: si haec volt). Anchored to all three names; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: tu istanc desponde huic, miles. ego dotem dabo. Ther. Quid dotis? Cvrc. Egone? ut semper, dum vivat, me alat.
question: Quam dotem Curculio parasitus se daturum dixit, cum Planesium Phaedromo desponderetur?
answer: Vt Phaedromus semper, dum vivat, se alat.
question_en: What dowry did the parasite Curculio say he would give when Planesium was betrothed to Phaedromus?
answer_en: That Phaedromus feed him for as long as he lives.
derivation: The parasite's economy crowned as the play closes: his 'dowry' is a lifetime place at Phaedromus' table. The flattery-for-food contract stated openly; anchored to the named betrothal; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: tu ut hodie adveniens cenam des sororiam, hic nuptialem cras dabit. promittimus.
question: Quam cenam Therapontigonus, sorore reperta, hodie dare iussus est, cum Phaedromus cras nuptialem daturus esset?
question_en: What dinner was Therapontigonus, his sister found, told to give that day, while Phaedromus would give the wedding dinner on the morrow?
derivation: Named feast realia: the cena sororia to celebrate the recovered sister, paired with the cena nuptialis of the wedding — two named dinner-occasions demanded, of course, by the parasite. Anchored to both hosts; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Qui scis mercari furtivas atque ingenuas virgines, ambula in ius. Ther. Non eo. Phaed. Licet te antestari? Ther. Non licet.
question: Quo Phaedromus Therapontigonum ambulare iussit, quod furtivas atque ingenuas virgines mercari sciret?
question_en: Where did Phaedromus order Therapontigonus to march, for knowingly buying stolen freeborn girls?
derivation: Roman civil procedure verbatim in the Greek play: the in ius vocatio ('ambula in ius') followed by the antestatio ('licet te antestari?'), the formal calling of a witness to the summons from the Twelve Tables' procedure. Anchored to both names; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quoi homini di sunt propitii, lucrum ei profecto obiciunt.
question: Quid dei ei homini cui propitii sunt obicere dicuntur, ut Cappadox in Curculione sententiose ait?
question_en: What are the gods said to throw in the way of a man they favor, as Cappadox says sententiously in the Curculio?
derivation: A proverb-shaped sententia of Roman commercial piety: whom the gods favor, they toss profit to — the leno's creed as he goes to sacrifice. Checkable point; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Vbi nunc Curculionem inveniam? Capp. In tritico facillume, vel quingentos curculiones pro uno faxo reperias.
question: Vbi Curculionem facillime inveniri posse Cappadox iocatur, quod eo nomine bestiolae frumentariae vocentur?
question_en: Where does Cappadox joke that Curculio can most easily be found, since the little grain-pests bear that name?
derivation: The play's own gloss on its title: curculio is the grain-weevil — look in the wheat and you will find five hundred weevils for one. The name-fact of the title parasite, delivered verbatim; one-place answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: At ita me volsellae, pecten, speculum, calamistrum meum bene me amassint meaque axitia linteumque extersui.
question: Per quae cultus sui instrumenta Cappadox leno iuravit, cum miles per machaeram et clupeum iurasset?
question_en: By what implements of his toilette did the pimp Cappadox swear, after the soldier had sworn by his sword and shield?
answer_en: By his tweezers, comb, mirror, and curling-iron.
derivation: A parody oath that maps each man's world: the soldier swears by machaera and clupeus, the primped leno by tweezers, comb, mirror, and curling-iron. Grooming realia in a checkable list, verbatim and brief.

author: Plautus
source_text: Atque hoc poetae faciunt in comoediis: omnis res gestas esse Athenis autumant, quo illud vobis graecum videatur magis; ego nusquam dicam nisi ubi factum dicitur.
question: In qua urbe poetae comici omnes res gestas esse autumant, ut prologus Menaechmorum Plauti ait?
question_en: In what city do comic poets claim all their plots take place, as the prologue of Plautus' Menaechmi says?
derivation: The prologue states the standing convention of the fabula palliata: comic poets set everything at Athens to make the play seem more Greek. A theatrical-convention fact of Roman comedy; anchored to the Menaechmi prologue; one-place answer verbatim (Athenis).

author: Plautus
source_text: atque adeo hoc argumentum graecissat, tamen non atticissat, verum sicilicissitat.
question: Cuius terrae esse argumentum Menaechmorum prologus Plauti profitetur, cum id non atticissare sed sicilicissitare dicat?
question_en: Of what land does the prologue of Plautus' Menaechmi declare the plot to be, saying it does not 'Atticize' but 'Sicilicizes'?
derivation: The prologue's famous coinage sicilicissitat marks the story as Sicilian (the twins are Syracusans), not Attic. The underlying fact — the plot is Sicilian — survives translation even though the coined verbs carry the joke. Anchored to the Menaechmi prologue.

author: Plautus
source_text: Mercator quidam fuit Syracusis senex, ei sunt nati filii gemini duo
question: In qua urbe habitabat mercator senex, pater geminorum Menaechmorum, apud Plautum?
question_en: In what city lived the old merchant, father of the twin Menaechmi, in Plautus?
derivation: The canonical setup of the play: the twins are sons of a Syracusan merchant. Anchored to the father of the Menaechmi; one-place answer verbatim (Syracusis).

author: Plautus
source_text: ita forma simili pueri, ut mater sua non internosse posset quae mammam dabat, neque adeo mater ipsa quae illos pepererat
question: Quis, ut prologus Menaechmorum Plauti ait, geminos pueros prae nimia similitudine internoscere non poterat?
answer: Ne mater quidem ipsa quae eos pepererat.
question_en: Who, as the prologue of Plautus' Menaechmi says, could not tell the twin boys apart because of their extreme likeness?
answer_en: Not even their own mother who bore them.
derivation: The comic premise of perfect twin likeness, stated in the prologue: neither the nurse nor the very mother who bore them could tell them apart. Canonical play-fact; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: postquam iam pueri septuennes sunt, pater oneravit navem magnam multis mercibus; imponit geminum alterum in navem pater, Tarentum avexit secum ad mercatum simul, illum reliquit alterum apud matrem domi.
question: Quot annos nati erant gemini Menaechmi, cum pater alterum secum Tarentum ad mercatum avexit?
question_en: How old were the twin Menaechmi when their father carried one of them with him to Tarentum to market?
derivation: Number fact from the prologue: the boys were septuennes (seven years old) at the fateful voyage to the market at Tarentum. Anchored to the twins + Tarentum; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Tarenti ludi forte erant, cum illuc venit. mortales multi, ut ad ludos, convenerant: puer aberravit inter homines a patre.
question: Qua occasione puer Menaechmus Tarenti a patre aberravit, ut prologus Plauti narrat?
answer: Inter turbam hominum qui ad ludos convenerant.
question_en: On what occasion did the boy Menaechmus stray from his father at Tarentum, as the prologue of Plautus tells?
answer_en: In the crowd of people who had gathered for the games.
derivation: The canonical loss of the twin: games (ludi) were being held at Tarentum, and the boy wandered from his father in the festival crowd. Roman spectacle realia (the games as mass gathering) carrying the plot; anchored to Tarentum + the boy Menaechmus.

author: Plautus
source_text: Epidamniensis quidam ibi mercator fuit, is puerum tollit avehitque Epidamnium.
question: In quam urbem mercator ille, qui puerum Menaechmum Tarenti sustulit, eum avexit?
question_en: To what city did the merchant who picked up the boy Menaechmus at Tarentum carry him off?
derivation: Geography of the canonical plot: the stolen twin was carried from Tarentum to Epidamnus (on the Adriatic), where the play is set. Anchored to the boy Menaechmus + Tarentum; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: pater eius autem postquam puerum perdidit, animum despondit, eaque is aegritudine paucis diebus post Tarenti emortuost.
question: Quid patri geminorum Menaechmorum accidit, postquam alterum puerum Tarenti perdidit?
answer: Prae aegritudine paucis post diebus Tarenti mortuus est.
question_en: What happened to the father of the twin Menaechmi after he lost one of the boys at Tarentum?
answer_en: He died of grief at Tarentum a few days later.
derivation: Prologue fact: the father lost heart and died of grief within a few days at Tarentum. Anchored to the father of the twins + Tarentum; short verifiable answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Nomen surrepticii illi indit qui domist Avos paternus, facit Maenaechmum e Sosicle.
question: Quod nomen puero Sosicli avus paternus apud Plautum indidit, postquam frater eius geminus surreptus est?
question_en: What name did the paternal grandfather give the boy Sosicles in Plautus, after his twin brother was stolen?
derivation: The renaming that gives both twins the same name Menaechmus — the engine of the whole comedy of errors (facit Maenaechmum e Sosicle). Anchored to Sosicles + the paternal grandfather; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: adoptat illum puerum surrupticium sibi filium eique uxorem dotatam dedit, eumque heredem fecit, quom ipse obiit diem.
question: Quid mercator Epidamniensis, qui liberos non habebat, de puero Menaechmo surrepto fecit?
answer: Adoptavit eum sibi filium heredemque fecit.
question_en: What did the childless merchant of Epidamnus do with the stolen boy Menaechmus?
answer_en: He adopted him as his son and made him his heir.
derivation: Roman legal-family color through the Greek plot: adoption, a dowered wife (uxorem dotatam), and inheritance. The childless kidnapper adopts the boy and leaves him heir. Anchored to the Epidamnian merchant + Menaechmus.

author: Plautus
source_text: haec urbs Epidamnus est, dum haec agitur fabula: quando alia agetur, aliud fiet oppidum
question: In qua urbe fabula Plauti quae Menaechmi inscribitur agitur?
question_en: In what city is Plautus' play called Menaechmi set?
derivation: The setting of the play, declared by the prologue. Anchored to the named play; one-place answer verbatim (haec urbs Epidamnus est).

author: Plautus
source_text: haec urbs Epidamnus est, dum haec agitur fabula: quando alia agetur, aliud fiet oppidum; sicut familiae quoque solent mutarier
question: Quid de oppido scaenico prologus Menaechmorum Plauti futurum esse dicit, quando alia fabula agetur?
question_en: What does the prologue of Plautus' Menaechmi say will become of the stage town when another play is performed?
derivation: A theatrical-convention fact stated outright: the same stage set serves as a different city for each play, just as the troupe changes roles. Roman theater practice; anchored to the Menaechmi prologue; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Iuventus nomen fecit Peniculo mihi, ideo quia mensam, quando edo, detergeo.
question: Quam ob rem iuventus parasito in Menaechmis Plauti nomen Peniculo fecit?
question_en: Why did the young men give the parasite in Plautus' Menaechmi the name Peniculus ('the little brush')?
answer_en: Because he wipes the table clean when he eats.
derivation: The parasite's name-joke is stated in the text itself: Peniculus, 'the little brush/sponge,' because he sweeps the table clean. A canonical character-fact of the play tied to the parasite stock figure; the reason translates. Anchored to Peniculus + Menaechmi.

author: Plautus
source_text: quem tu adservare recte, ne aufugiat, voles, esca atque potione vinciri decet. apud mensam plenam homini rostrum deliges;
question: Quibus vinculis, ut Peniculus parasitus apud Plautum censet, homo vinciendus est quem ne aufugiat adservare velis?
question_en: With what chains, in the view of the parasite Peniculus in Plautus, should a man be bound whom you wish to keep from running away?
derivation: The parasite's proverbial doctrine: food and drink are the surest chains — the softer they are, the tighter they bind (lenta vincla escaria). A quotable saying with a checkable point; anchored to Peniculus.

author: Plautus
source_text: hanc modo uxori intus pallam surrupui, ad scortum fero.
question: Quod vestimentum Menaechmus Epidamniensis uxori suae intus surripuit, ut amicae meretrici ferret?
question_en: What garment did Menaechmus of Epidamnus steal from his wife indoors, to carry to his mistress?
derivation: The stolen palla — the woman's mantle that drives the entire plot of the Menaechmi (the mistress is Erotium, named shortly after at v. 173). Roman dress realia (the palla as the matron's outer garment) plus the canonical plot object; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Dic mi, enumquam tu vidisti tabulam pictam in pariete, ubi aquila Catameitum raperet aut ubi Venus Adoneum?
question: Quem puerum aquila rapuisse in tabulis pictis in pariete dicitur, quas Menaechmus apud Plautum memorat?
question_en: Which boy is shown being carried off by the eagle in the wall-paintings that Menaechmus mentions in Plautus?
derivation: Canonical myth as shared story: Jupiter's eagle carrying off Ganymede (Latin Catamitus), paired in the text with Venus and her beloved Adonis (Adoneus). Also evidence that such myth scenes were stock wall-painting subjects. Anchored to the eagle + the paintings Menaechmus cites; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: meo quidem animo ab Hippolyta subcingulum Hercules haud aeque magno umquam abstulit periculo.
question: A qua regina Hercules subcingulum magno periculo abstulit, ut Menaechmus apud Plautum memorat?
