question_en: From which queen did Hercules carry off the girdle at great peril, as Menaechmus recalls in Plautus?
derivation: Canonical labor of Hercules — the girdle taken from Hippolyta the Amazon — invoked as a comic comparison for stealing the palla. Myth as shared story; anchored to Hercules + Hippolyta; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quattuor minis ego emi istanc anno uxori meae. PEN. Quattuor minae perierunt plane, ut ratio redditur.
question: Quanti Menaechmus Epidamniensis pallam, quam uxori emerat et Erotio dedit, se emisse dicit?
question_en: For how much does Menaechmus of Epidamnus say he bought the palla that he had bought for his wife and gave to Erotium?
derivation: Price fact in Greek currency (minae): the plot-driving palla cost four minae. 'istanc' refers to the palla just handed over (salta sic cum palla, v. 197). Money realia through the Greek dress; anchored to Menaechmus + the palla; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ego et Menaechmus et parasitus eius. CYL. Iam isti sunt decem; nam parasitus octo hominum munus facile fungitur.
question: Quot hominum munus parasitum in edendo facile fungi Cylindrus coquos in Menaechmis Plauti dicit?
question_en: The office of how many men does the cook Cylindrus in Plautus' Menaechmi say a parasite easily performs at table?
derivation: The cook's joke quantifies the parasite stock figure of Roman comedy: one parasite eats for eight. Anchored to Cylindrus the cook + the parasite; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: MEN. Fratrem quaesitum geminum germanum meum. MESS. Nam quid modi futurum est illum quaerere? hic annus sextust postquam ei rei operam damus.
question: Quotus annus agebatur quaerenti fratrem geminum Menaechmo Sosicli, cum Epidamnum venit, ut Messenio servus ait?
question_en: What year of the search was running for Menaechmus Sosicles seeking his twin brother when he came to Epidamnus, as the slave Messenio says?
derivation: The famous length of the search: it is the sixth year (hic annus sextust) of hunting the twin over every coast. Anchored to Menaechmus Sosicles + Messenio + Epidamnus; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: propterea huic urbi nomen Epidamno inditumst, quia nemo ferme huc sine damno devortitur.
question: Quam ob causam urbi Epidamno nomen inditum esse Messenio servus apud Plautum iocatur?
answer: Quia nemo ferme eo sine damno devortitur.
question_en: For what reason does the slave Messenio in Plautus joke that the city of Epidamnus received its name?
answer_en: Because almost no one lodges there without loss (damnum).
derivation: The famous name-omen joke of the play: Epidamnus explained from damnum, the city of 'loss,' full of pleasure-lovers, drinkers, swindlers, and the most seductive courtesans (vv. 258-262). The point — no one leaves without loss — survives translation with the name glossed. Anchored to Messenio + Epidamnus; stated verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Responde mihi, adulescens: quibus hic pretiis porci veneunt sacres sinceri? CYL. Nummis. MEN. Nummum a me accipe: iube te piari de mea pecunia. nam equidem insanum esse te certo scio
question: Cuius animalis hostia insani expiari solebant, ut Menaechmus Sosicles apud Plautum, nummum ad piaculum dans, innuit?
question_en: With the sacrifice of what animal were the mad customarily purified, as Menaechmus Sosicles hints in Plautus when he offers a coin for the expiation?
derivation: Religious realia: purification (piari) of a madman required a porcus sacer sincerus, an unblemished sacrificial pig — Menaechmus asks the price of such pigs and pays a nummus for Cylindrus to 'get himself purified,' i.e. calls him insane. Ambient Roman expiation rite; anchored to Menaechmus Sosicles + Cylindrus.

author: Plautus
source_text: morem hunc meretrices habent: ad portum mittunt servolos, ancillulas; si quae peregrina navis in portum advenit, rogitant cuiatis sit, quid ei nomen siet, postilla extemplo se applicant, agglutinant: si pellexerunt, perditum amittunt domum.
question: Quo meretrices servolos ancillulasque mittere solent, ut advenientium peregrinorum nomina patriamque sciscitentur, ut Messenio apud Plautum docet?
question_en: Where do courtesans customarily send their slave-boys and little maids to find out the names and homeland of arriving strangers, as Messenio explains in Plautus?
derivation: A custom stated as such by the text (morem hunc meretrices habent): harbor scouts greet every foreign ship, learn the stranger's name and origin, then the courtesan fastens on and sends him home ruined. Mores of the demimonde, generalized by the speaker; anchored to Messenio; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sternite lectos, incendite odores; munditia inlecebra animost amantium.
question: Quid, ut Erotium meretrix apud Plautum pronuntiat, inlecebra animi amantium est?
question_en: What, as the courtesan Erotium declares in Plautus, is the lure of lovers' hearts?
derivation: Erotium's sententia while ordering the couches spread and perfumes burned: munditia — refined elegance — is what lures lovers. Quotable saying with a one-word point; the line also evidences banquet preparation (couches, burning scents). Anchored to Erotium; answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Non ego te novi Menaechmum, Moscho prognatum patre, qui Syracusis perhibere natus esse in Sicilia
question: Quo patre prognatus erat Menaechmus Syracusanus, ut Erotium apud Plautum refert?
question_en: Of what father was Menaechmus of Syracuse born, as Erotium relates in Plautus?
derivation: The twins' father — the Syracusan merchant of the prologue — is here named: Moschus. Genealogical play-fact; anchored to Menaechmus + Syracuse; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: qui Syracusis perhibere natus esse in Sicilia, ubi rex Agathocles regnator fuit et iterum Phintia, tertium Liparo, qui in morte regnum Hieroni tradidit, nunc Hiero est?
question: Quos quattuor Siciliae regnatores deinceps Erotium in Menaechmis Plauti enumerat?
question_en: Which four rulers of Sicily in succession does Erotium list in Plautus' Menaechmi?
derivation: The famous Sicilian king-list of the Menaechmi: Agathocles, then Phintias, third Liparo, who dying handed the kingdom to Hiero (Hiero II), the reigning king. A historical enumeration embedded in the play, much discussed for its chronology; four-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Pallam illam, quam dudum dederas, ad phrygionem ut deferas, ut reconcinnetur atque ut opera addantur quae volo.
question: Ad quem artificem Erotium pallam sibi datam deferri voluit, ut reconcinnaretur?
question_en: To what craftsman did Erotium want the palla given to her taken, to be refurbished?
derivation: Craft realia: the phrygio, the embroiderer (named from Phrygian gold-thread work), the tradesman to whom garments went for refashioning — a plot hinge for the palla. Anchored to Erotium + the palla; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: numquam quicquam facinus feci peius neque scelestius, quam hodie, quom in contionem mediam me immersi miser. ubi ego dum hieto, Menaechmus se subterduxit mihi atque abiit ad amicam, credo, neque me voluit ducere.
question: Quo in conventu civium Peniculus parasitus detentus est, dum Menaechmus ei se subducit atque ad amicam abit?
question_en: In what gathering of the citizens was the parasite Peniculus caught while Menaechmus slipped away from him and went off to his mistress?
derivation: Roman civic realia through the Greek dress: the contio — and Peniculus goes on to demand that only idle men be assigned to attend the contio and the comitia (v. 458). Anchored to Peniculus + Menaechmus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Menaechme, amare ait te multum Erotium, ut hoc una opera sibi ad aurificem deferas, atque huc ut addas auri pondo unciam iubeasque spinter novom reconcinnarier.
question: Quantum auri Erotium spinteri addi voluit, cum id ad aurificem reconcinnandum mitteret?
question_en: How much gold did Erotium want added to the bracelet when she sent it to the goldsmith to be refashioned?
derivation: Weight-and-craft realia: an uncia of gold to be added, and the aurifex as the jewelry craftsman. Anchored to Erotium + the spinter (armband); one-measure answer verbatim (auri pondo unciam).

author: Plautus
source_text: Hoc est quod olim clanculum ex armario te surrupuisse aiebas uxori tuae.
question: Unde Menaechmus Epidamniensis spinter, quod Erotio dedit, uxori clanculum surripuisse dicebatur?
question_en: From where was Menaechmus of Epidamnus said to have secretly stolen from his wife the bracelet he gave to Erotium?
derivation: The second stolen ornament of the plot: the spinter, filched from the wife's armarium — household realia (the armarium as the cupboard for clothes and valuables), parallel to the stolen palla. Anchored to Menaechmus + Erotium + the spinter.

author: Plautus
source_text: quando ego tibi ancillas, penum, lanam, aurum, vestem, purpuram bene praebeo nec quicquam eges, malo cavebis si sapis, virum observare desines.
question: Quae uxori suae se bene praebere Menaechmus Epidamniensis apud Plautum enumerat, ne quicquam egeat?
answer: Ancillas, penum, lanam, aurum, vestem, purpuram.
question_en: What things does Menaechmus of Epidamnus in Plautus list as amply providing for his wife, so that she lacks nothing?
answer_en: Maids, provisions, wool, gold, clothing, and purple.
derivation: The canonical catalogue of a matron's maintenance — what a well-kept Roman wife could expect from her husband (maids, the larder, wool to work, gold, dress, purple). Mores of marriage stated verbatim as a six-item list; anchored to Menaechmus + his wife.

author: Plautus
source_text: MEN. Fiat. cedo aurum, ego manupretium dabo. ANC. Da sodes abs te: ego post reddidero tibi.
question: Quid Menaechmus se daturum dixit, cum aurum ad inaures faciendas sibi dari ab ancilla Erotii posceret?
question_en: What did Menaechmus say he would pay, while demanding that Erotium's maid supply the gold for having the earrings made?
answer_en: The manupretium (the fee for the workmanship).
derivation: Jewelry-trade realia: the material (gold) was furnished separately from the craftsman's making-fee, the manupretium. The maid has just asked for drop-earrings (stalagmia) of two nummi weight. Anchored to Menaechmus + Erotium's ancilla; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: clientes sibi omnes volunt esse multos: bonine an mali sint, id haud quaeritant; res magis quaeritur quam clientum fides cuius modi clueat.
question: Quid in clientibus magis quam fidem quaeri Menaechmus Epidamniensis apud Plautum queritur?
question_en: What, more than good faith, does Menaechmus of Epidamnus in Plautus complain is sought in clients?
derivation: The patronage canticum: all men want many clients and ask after the client's wealth, not whether he is good or honest. Roman patronus-cliens mores stated as a general custom; anchored to Menaechmus' complaint; short answer verbatim (res magis quaeritur quam fides).

author: Plautus
source_text: eis ubi dicitur dies, simul patronis dicitur. quippe qui pro illis loquimur quae male fecerunt: aut ad populum aut in iure aut apud aedilem res est.
question: Quibus, ubi clienti dies dicta est, eodem tempore dictam esse Menaechmus apud Plautum ait?
question_en: For whom, when a court day is appointed for a client, is it appointed at the same time, as Menaechmus says in Plautus?
derivation: Patronus-cliens legal realia: when the client is summoned, the patron is in effect summoned too, since he must speak for his client's misdeeds — before the people, in iure, or before the aedile. Roman institution through the Greek dress; anchored to Menaechmus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: apud aediles pro eius factis plurumisque pessumisque dixi causam, condiciones tetuli tortas, confragosas
question: Apud quos magistratus Menaechmus Epidamniensis pro cliente suo causam dixisse se ait?
question_en: Before which magistrates does Menaechmus of Epidamnus say he pleaded the case for his client?
derivation: Roman magistracy realia poking through the Greek setting: the aediles' court, where the patron pleads for his client. Anchored to Menaechmus + his cliens; one-office answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: non ego te modo hic ante aedis cum corona florea vidi astare? quom negabas mi esse sanum sinciput
question: Qua corona ornatum Peniculus parasitus Menaechmum, e prandio egressum, ante aedis Erotii vidisse ait?
question_en: Wearing what garland does the parasite Peniculus say he saw Menaechmus, come out from the lunch, standing before Erotium's house?
derivation: Banquet realia: the corona florea, the flower garland worn by banqueters over their wine — here the telltale sign that the lunch was eaten without Peniculus. Anchored to Peniculus + Menaechmus; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Equidem ecastor tuam nec chlamydem do foras nec pallium cuiquam utendum. mulierem aequom est vestimentum muliebre dare foras, virum virile.
question: Quae duo vestimenta virilia matrona in Menaechmis Plauti nominat, quae se numquam cuiquam utenda dare dicat?
question_en: Which two men's garments does the matron in Plautus' Menaechmi name, saying she never lends them out to anyone?
derivation: Dress realia: chlamys and pallium as men's outer garments, opposed to the woman's palla — with the matron's maxim that a woman should lend only women's clothing, a man men's. Anchored to the matrona + the play; two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Non tu scis, mulier, Hecubam quapropter canem Graii esse praedicabant? MAT. Non equidem scio. MEN. Quia idem faciebat Hecuba quod tu nunc facis: omnia mala ingerebat, quemquem aspexerat. itaque adeo iure coepta appellari est canes.
question: Quam Troianam reginam Graii canem praedicabant, ut Menaechmus Sosicles apud Plautum memorat?
question_en: Which Trojan queen did the Greeks call 'the dog,' as Menaechmus Sosicles recalls in Plautus?
derivation: Canonical myth as shared story: Hecuba called canis by the Greeks (the tradition of her transformation into a dog after Troy's fall), with the aetiology given — she heaped abuse on everyone she saw. Anchored to Hecuba + the Greeks; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ita istaec solent, quae viros subservire sibi postulant, dote fretae, feroces.
question: Qua re fretae uxores, ut senex in Menaechmis Plauti ait, feroces fiunt virosque sibi subservire postulant?
question_en: Relying on what, as the old man in Plautus' Menaechmi says, do wives become fierce and demand that their husbands serve them?
derivation: The uxor dotata — the dowered wife emboldened by her dowry — a central fact of Roman marriage economics and a stock theme of the palliata, stated as a general rule (ita istaec solent). Anchored to the senex's dictum; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: serviren tibi postulas viros? dare una opera pensum postules, inter ancillas sedere iubeas, lanam carere.
question: Quod opus inter ancillas sedens facere iuberetur vir, si uxori serviret, ut senex apud Plautum in Menaechmis iocatur?
question_en: What work would a husband be ordered to do sitting among the slave-girls, if he served his wife, as the old man jokes in Plautus' Menaechmi?
answer_en: To do the daily wool allotment and card wool.
derivation: Household realia: the pensum, the weighed daily portion of wool assigned to the ancillae, and wool-carding as proverbial women's slave work — invoked as the absurd extreme of a husband's servitude. Anchored to the senex + the matrona; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quid mihi meliust, quam quando illi me insanire praedicant, ego med adsimulem insanire, ut illos a me absterream?
question: Quid consilii Menaechmus Sosicles apud Plautum cepit, cum matrona et senex eum insanire praedicarent?
answer: Vt se insanire adsimularet, ut eos absterreret.
question_en: What plan did Menaechmus Sosicles adopt in Plautus when the matron and the old man kept declaring him insane?
answer_en: To pretend to be mad himself, in order to scare them away.
derivation: The celebrated feigned-madness scene of the Menaechmi: the Syracusan twin, harassed as a madman, decides to play mad in earnest. A canonical scene-fact of the play; anchored to Menaechmus Sosicles + the matrona and senex; supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Euhoe Bacche, Bromie, quo me in silvam venatum vocas?
question: Quem deum, et quo cognomine, Menaechmus Sosicles insaniam simulans primum invocat apud Plautum?
question_en: Which god, and by what epithet, does Menaechmus Sosicles first invoke while feigning madness in Plautus?
derivation: The feigned madman opens with the Bacchic cry (Euhoe Bacche, Bromie): Bacchic possession as the very type of frenzy, and Bromius ('the Roarer') as the god's cult epithet. Religious realia through the mad scene; anchored to Menaechmus Sosicles; answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ecce, Apollo mi ex oraclo imperat, ut ego illi oculos exuram lampadibus ardentibus.
question: Cuius dei oraculum sibi imperare Menaechmus Sosicles, insaniam simulans, fingebat?
question_en: Which god's oracle did Menaechmus Sosicles, feigning madness, pretend was giving him commands?
derivation: In the feigned-madness scene the commands come from Apollo's oracle — Apollo as the oracular god whose voice the frenzied hear. Anchored to Menaechmus Sosicles; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ait se obligasse crus fractum Aesculapio, Apollini autem brachium. nunc cogito, utrum me dicam ducere medicum an fabrum.
question: Quibus deis medicus in Menaechmis Plauti crus fractum et brachium obligavisse se iactabat?
question_en: For which gods did the doctor in Plautus' Menaechmi boast he had bound up a broken leg and an arm?
answer_en: A leg for Aesculapius, an arm for Apollo.
derivation: The medicus' absurd boast, reported by the senex: he has treated Aesculapius — the god of healing himself — and Apollo, making the old man wonder whether he is fetching a doctor or a carpenter. Canonical satire of the braggart doctor; two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: num laruatust aut cerritus? fac sciam. num eum veternus aut aqua intercus tenet?
question: Quos duos morbos medicus in Menaechmis quaerit num aegrotum teneant, cum primum de Menaechmo percontatur?
question_en: Which two diseases does the doctor in the Menaechmi ask whether they grip the sick man, when he first inquires about Menaechmus?
derivation: Medical realia: the doctor's stock diagnostic questions — is the man laruatus (ghost-possessed) or cerritus (frenzied), sunk in veternus (lethargy), or held by aqua intercus (dropsy, 'water under the skin')? Named ailments of ancient medicine; anchored to the medicus of the play.

author: Plautus
source_text: Dic mihi hoc quod te rogo: album an atrum vinum potas?
question: Quid de vino medicus in Menaechmis Plauti Menaechmum interrogavit?
question_en: What did the doctor in Plautus' Menaechmi ask Menaechmus about wine?
answer_en: Whether he drank white or dark wine.
derivation: The famous diagnostic question — white wine or dark? — which provokes Menaechmus' retort about purple bread and feathered fish. Wine was classed album/atrum in daily speech; anchored to the medicus + Menaechmus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: MED. Elleborum potabis faxo aliquos viginti dies.
question: Quod medicamentum medicus in Menaechmis Menaechmo, pro insano habito, per viginti fere dies potandum minatur?
question_en: What drug does the doctor in the Menaechmi threaten that Menaechmus, taken for a madman, will drink for some twenty days?
derivation: Hellebore, the proverbial cure for madness in antiquity, here prescribed for some twenty days. Ambient medical culture (elleborum as the madman's drink); anchored to the medicus + Menaechmus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: At ego te sacram coronam surrupuisse Iovi scio, et ob eam rem in carcerem ted esse compactum scio
question: Quid senem surripuisse Iovi Menaechmus Sosicles, male dicta rependens, criminatur, ob quod in carcerem compactus sit?
question_en: What does Menaechmus Sosicles, paying back insult with insult, charge the old man with having stolen from Jupiter, for which he was thrown into prison?
derivation: Roman penal color through the mock-charges: temple theft — the sacred crown of Jupiter — punished with the carcer. Anchored to Menaechmus Sosicles + the senex + Jupiter; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: et postquam es emissus, caesum virgis sub furca scio; tum patrem occidisse et matrem vendidisse etiam scio.
question: Quo supplicio senem, e carcere emissum, adfectum esse Menaechmus Sosicles per convicium ait?
question_en: With what punishment does Menaechmus Sosicles abusively claim the old man was visited after being let out of prison?
answer_en: Beaten with rods under the furca (the yoke-fork).
derivation: Roman punishment realia: flogging with rods while bound under the furca, the fork-shaped yoke of slaves and criminals — part of the celebrated mock-madness slanging match. Anchored to the senex; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: recordetur id, qui nihili sunt, quid eis preti detur ab suis eris, ignavis, improbis viris: verbera compedes molae, magna lassitudo fames frigus durum, haec pretia sunt ignaviae.
question: Quae pretia ignaviae servis improbis ab eris dari Messenio servus apud Plautum enumerat?
answer: Verbera, compedes, molae, lassitudo, fames, frigus.
question_en: What wages of laziness does the slave Messenio in Plautus list as given by masters to worthless slaves?
answer_en: Beatings, fetters, the mill, weariness, hunger, and hard cold.
derivation: The canonical catalogue of slave punishments — above all the mill (molae, the pistrinum dreaded by every comic slave) — recited by the model slave Messenio in his good-slave monologue. Slave-culture mores; anchored to Messenio; list answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam ego hominem hominis similiorem numquam vidi alterum. neque aqua aquae nec lacte est lactis, crede mi, usquam similius, quam hic tui est, tuque huius autem
question: Quibus rerum similitudinibus Messenio geminorum Menaechmorum similitudinem apud Plautum comparat?
answer: Aquae ad aquam et lactis ad lac.
question_en: To what likenesses does Messenio compare the resemblance of the twin Menaechmi in Plautus?
answer_en: Of water to water and of milk to milk.
derivation: The proverbial comparison for perfect likeness — 'not water to water nor milk to milk is more alike' — the ancestor of 'as like as two drops of water.' A quotable saying with a checkable point; anchored to Messenio + the twins; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quot eras annos gnatus, quom te pater a patria avehit? MEN. Septuennis: nam tunc dentes mihi cadebant primulum.
question: Quo corporis signo Menaechmus se septuennem fuisse probat, cum pater eum a patria avexit?
question_en: By what bodily sign does Menaechmus establish that he was seven years old when his father carried him from his homeland?
answer_en: His teeth were then just beginning to fall out.
derivation: Childhood realia: the shedding of the milk teeth around age seven, used as the memory-proof in the recognition catechism. Ambient shared knowledge of the life course; anchored to Menaechmus + the recognition scene; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: MEN. Quid erat nomen nostrae matri? SOS. Teuximarchae. MEN. Convenit.
question: Quod nomen erat matri geminorum Menaechmorum, ut in agnitione fabulae Plautinae convenit?
question_en: What was the name of the mother of the twin Menaechmi, as agreed in the recognition scene of Plautus' play?
derivation: The clinching recognition token: the twins' mother was named Teuximarcha. One-name genealogical play-fact; anchored to the twin Menaechmi; answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: MESS. Numquid me morare quin ego liber, ut iusti, siem? MEN. Optimum atque aequissimum orat, frater: fac causa mea. SOS. Liber esto.
question: Quo praemio Messenio servus in fine Menaechmorum donatus est, quod erum e raptoribus servaverat?
question_en: With what reward was the slave Messenio presented at the end of the Menaechmi, because he had saved his master from the kidnappers?
derivation: Manumission realia: the master's bare declaration 'liber esto' frees the slave on the spot — Messenio's reward for the rescue, first asked for with 'med emittas manu' (v. 1023). Roman institution through the Greek dress; anchored to Messenio + the twins.

author: Plautus
source_text: in patriam redeamus ambo. MEN. Frater, faciam, ut tu voles. auctionem hic faciam et vendam quidquid est.
question: Quid Menaechmus Epidamniensis in fine fabulae facere constituit, priusquam cum fratre Syracusas rediret?
question_en: What did Menaechmus of Epidamnus decide to hold at the end of the play, before returning with his brother to Syracuse?
answer_en: An auction, to sell everything he had.
derivation: The famous auction ending: everything — slaves, furniture, farms, house — to be sold, on the seventh day, for ready cash (praesenti pecunia), so the brothers can go home to Syracuse. Canonical close of the play; anchored to Menaechmus + Syracuse; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: MES. Praeconium mi ut detis. M. Dabitur. MES. Ergo nunciam vis conclamari auctionem fore? MEN. Equidem die septimi.
question: Quod munus Messenio sibi dari rogavit, cum auctio Menaechmi indiceretur?
question_en: What office did Messenio ask to be given when Menaechmus' auction was announced?
derivation: Auction realia: the praeco cries the sale — the newly freed Messenio asks for the job and at once proclaims the auction, set for the seventh day. Anchored to Messenio + the auction; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: venibunt servi, supellex, fundi, aedes, omnia. venibunt quiqui licebunt, praesenti pecunia. venibit uxor quoque etiam, si quis emptor venerit.
question: Quis in auctione Menaechmi venibit, si quis emptor venerit, ut Messenio in extrema fabula Plauti proclamat?
question_en: Who too will be sold at Menaechmus' auction, if any buyer turns up, as Messenio proclaims at the very end of Plautus' play?
derivation: The play's closing joke: at the auction of slaves, furniture, farms, and house — all for ready cash — 'the wife too will be sold, if a buyer comes.' Canonical ending of the Menaechmi; anchored to Messenio's proclamation; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Alazon Graece huic nomen est comoediae, id nos Latine gloriosum dicimus.
question: Quod nomen Graecum fuisse comoediae quae Latine Miles Gloriosus dicitur Plautus per Palaestrionem tradit?
question_en: What Greek name does Plautus, through Palaestrio, report the comedy called in Latin Miles Gloriosus to have had?
derivation: The delayed prologue names the Greek original of the play: Alazon ('the Braggart'), rendered in Latin as gloriosus. A canonical literary-history fact of the fabula palliata (the play's own statement of its Greek model); anchored to the named play; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: hoc oppidum Ephesust; illest miles meus erus, qui hinc ad forum abiit, gloriosus, impudens, stercoreus, plenus periuri atque adulteri.
question: In quo oppido fabula Plauti quae Miles Gloriosus inscribitur agitur?
question_en: In what town is Plautus' play called Miles Gloriosus set?
derivation: The setting of the play, declared by Palaestrio's delayed prologue (hoc oppidum Ephesust). Anchored to the named play; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed ubi Artotrogus hic est? Art. Stat propter virum fortem atque fortunatum et forma regia; tum bellatorem—Mars haud ausit dicere neque aequiperare suas virtutes ad tuas.
question: Quis parasitus in Milite Glorioso Plauti Pyrgopolynici militi adsentatur eiusque facinora ficta in caelum fert?
question_en: Which parasite in Plautus' Miles Gloriosus flatters the soldier Pyrgopolynices and puffs his invented exploits to the sky?
derivation: The canonical pairing of the play's opening: the parasite Artotrogus feeding the braggart Pyrgopolynices' vanity (even Mars would not dare match his virtues). Anchored to both named characters; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: venter creat omnis hasce aerumnas: auribus peraurienda sunt, ne dentes dentiant, et adsentandumst quidquid hic mentibitur.
question: Quae res, ut ipse clam fatetur, Artotrogum parasitum cogit ut omnibus militis gloriosi mendaciis adsentetur?
question_en: What, as he himself confesses aside, compels the parasite Artotrogus to assent to all the braggart soldier's lies?
derivation: The flattery-for-food economy of the Roman comic parasite, stated openly: the belly creates these woes, the ears must endure so the teeth have something to chew. Emblematic statement of the parasitus role; anchored to Artotrogus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nisi unum, epityrum estur insanum bene.
question: Quod edulium unum apud militem Pyrgopolynicem 'insanum bene' edi Artotrogus parasitus concedit?
question_en: What one dish does the parasite Artotrogus concede is eaten 'insanely well' at the soldier Pyrgopolynices' house?
derivation: In his aside Artotrogus grants the liar one true excellence: the epityrum, the Italian olive relish (the dish Cato also gives a recipe for). Named food realia; anchored to Artotrogus + Pyrgopolynices; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: edepol vel elephanto in India, quo pacto ei pugno praefregisti bracchium.
question: In qua terra Pyrgopolynices elephanto pugno bracchium praefregisse ab Artotrogo fertur?
question_en: In what land is Pyrgopolynices said by Artotrogus to have broken an elephant's foreleg with his fist?
derivation: The most famous of Artotrogus' inflations: the soldier smashed an elephant's 'bracchium' with a bare fist in India. Canonical scene of the play; anchored to both names; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Memini: centum in Cilicia et quinquaginta, centum in Scytholatronia, triginta Sardos, sexaginta Macedones sunt homines quos tu occidisti uno die. Pyrg. Quanta istaec hominum summast? Art. Septem milia.
question: Quot hominum summam uno die a Pyrgopolynice occisorum Artotrogus parasitus computat?
question_en: What total of men slain by Pyrgopolynices in a single day does the parasite Artotrogus reckon up?
derivation: The absurd arithmetic of flattery: an itemized list (Cilicia, Scytholatronia, Sardinians, Macedonians) summed to 'seven thousand' killed in one day, which the soldier approves. Canonical number of the play's opening scene; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quid in Cappadocia, ubi tu quingentos simul, ni hebes machaera foret, uno ictu occideras?
question: Quot homines Pyrgopolynices in Cappadocia uno ictu occidisset, nisi machaera hebes fuisset, ut Artotrogus adulatur?
question_en: How many men would Pyrgopolynices have killed with a single stroke in Cappadocia, had his blade not been dull, as Artotrogus flatters?
derivation: Another item of the flattery catalogue: five hundred at one blow in Cappadocia, foiled only by a dull sword. Anchored to Pyrgopolynices + Cappadocia; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Rogitabant: 'hicine Achilles est?' inquit mihi. 'immo eius frater' inquam 'est'.
question: Quem heroem esse Pyrgopolynicem mulieres rogitabant, ut Artotrogus militi narrat?
question_en: Which hero did the women keep asking whether Pyrgopolynices was, as Artotrogus tells the soldier?
derivation: Artotrogus' tale that women mistook the soldier for Achilles (he answered 'no — his brother'). The comparison to the handsomest of Greek heroes is the point of the flattery; anchored to both names; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam rex Seleucus me opere oravit maxumo, ut sibi latrones cogerem et conscriberem.
question: Cui regi Pyrgopolynices in Milite Glorioso latrones, id est milites mercennarios, conscribendos curat?
question_en: For which king does Pyrgopolynices in the Miles Gloriosus undertake to muster and enroll latrones, that is, mercenary soldiers?
derivation: The Hellenistic frame of the play: the braggart recruits hired soldiers for King Seleucus (latro here in its old sense of mercenary). Anchored to Pyrgopolynices + Seleucus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Curate ut splendor meo sit clupeo clarior quam solis radii esse olim quom sudumst solent, ut, ubi usus veniat, contra conserta manu praestringat oculorum aciem in acie hostibus.
question: Quid Pyrgopolynices primis verbis Militis Gloriosi splendidius quam solis radios fieri iubet?
question_en: What does Pyrgopolynices, in the opening words of the Miles Gloriosus, order to be made brighter than the rays of the sun?
derivation: The celebrated opening of the play: the braggart orders his shield polished brighter than sunbeams so it may dazzle enemies in battle. Anchored to Pyrgopolynices + the play's opening; short answer verbatim (clupeo clarior).

author: Plautus
source_text: interibi hic miles forte Athenas advenit, insinuat sese ad illam amicam eri occepit eius matri suppalparier vino, ornamentis opiparisque obsoniis, itaque intimum ibi se miles apud lenam facit. ubi primum evenit militi huic occasio, sublinit os illi lenae, matri mulieris, quam erus meus amabat; nam is illius filiam conicit in navem miles clam matrem suam, eamque huc invitam mulierem in Ephesum advehit.
question: Ex qua urbe miles gloriosus Philocomasium, amicam adulescentis Atheniensis, clam matre invitam in Ephesum avexit?
question_en: From what city did the braggart soldier carry off Philocomasium, the Athenian young man's sweetheart, to Ephesus against her will and without her mother's knowledge?
derivation: The plot's founding fact from the delayed prologue: the soldier wormed his way in at Athens, tricked the girl's mother, and shipped the girl off to Ephesus. Anchored to Philocomasium + Ephesus; one-place answer supported verbatim (Athenas advenit ... in Ephesum advehit).

author: Plautus
source_text: is publice legatus Naupactum fuit magnai rei publicai gratia.
question: Quo missus erat publice legatus adulescens Atheniensis, amator Philocomasii, cum miles eam Athenis abstulit?
question_en: To what place had the young Athenian, Philocomasium's lover, been sent as a public envoy when the soldier stole her from Athens?
derivation: Why the lover was absent: he was away as an official envoy at Naupactus on great state business. Anchored to the Athenian lover of Philocomasium; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ubi sumus provecti in altum, fit quod di volunt, capiunt praedones navem illam ubi vectus fui: prius perii quam ad erum veni, quo ire occeperam. ille qui me cepit dat me huic dono militi.
question: A quibus captus est Palaestrio servus, cum Naupactum ad erum suum navigaret?
question_en: By whom was the slave Palaestrio captured while sailing to Naupactus to his master?
derivation: How the clever slave came into the braggart's household: pirates took his ship on the high sea and his captor gave him as a gift to the soldier. Anchored to Palaestrio + Naupactus; short answer verbatim (capiunt praedones navem).

author: Plautus
source_text: nam unum conclave, concubinae quod dedit miles, quo nemo nisi eapse inferret pedem, in eo conclavi ego perfodi parietem, qua commeatus clam esset hinc huc mulieri.
question: Quid Palaestrio in conclavi concubinae militis perfodit, ut Philocomasium clam in vicini aedes commeare posset?
question_en: What did Palaestrio dig through in the room of the soldier's concubine, so that Philocomasium could pass secretly into the neighbor's house?
derivation: The play's famous stage device: a hole cut through the party wall between the soldier's and the neighbor's houses, giving the girl a secret passage. Anchored to Palaestrio + Philocomasium; one-word answer verbatim (perfodi parietem).

author: Plautus
source_text: ut Philocomasio huc sororem geminam germanam alteram dicam Athenis advenisse cum amatore aliquo suo, tam similem, quam lacte lactist.
question: Quam personam fictam Philocomasium in Milite Glorioso agit, ut custos qui eam osculantem viderat falleretur?
question_en: What invented character does Philocomasium play in the Miles Gloriosus, to fool the guard who had seen her kissing?
derivation: The geminae fiction, engine of the play's middle acts: Palaestrio invents a twin sister 'as like as milk to milk' arrived from Athens, and Philocomasium plays both women through the pierced wall. Anchored to Philocomasium; short answer verbatim (sororem geminam germanam).

author: Plautus
source_text: atque adeo ut ne legi fraudem faciant aleariae, adcuratote ut sine talis domi agitent convivium.
question: Cui legi ne fraus fiat, Periplectomenus senex apud Plautum servos militis sine talis convivium agitare iubet?
question_en: To keep which law from being cheated does the old man Periplectomenus in Plautus order the soldier's slaves to hold their party without knucklebones?
derivation: Direct comic evidence for a Roman lex alearia restricting dice-play: the joke (break their ankle-bones so they feast 'without tali') presumes the audience knows gambling with tali was legally curbed. Roman legal realia breaking the Greek frame; anchored to Periplectomenus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam mulier holitori numquam supplicat, si quast mala: domi habet hortum et condimenta ad omnis mores maleficos.
question: Cui mulier mala numquam supplicat, ut Palaestrio in Milite Glorioso proverbii loco dicit, quia domi hortum habet?
question_en: To whom does a wicked woman never have to beg, as Palaestrio says proverbially in the Miles Gloriosus, because she has a garden at home?
derivation: A proverb-shaped sententia: the bad woman never begs the holitor — she keeps at home her own garden and seasonings for every mischief. Checkable point (who is never petitioned) with the reason verbatim; anchored to the play and speaker.

author: Plautus
source_text: simiam hodie sum sectatus nostram in horum tegulis.
question: Quod animal Sceledrus servus in tegulis sectabatur, cum Philocomasium osculantem in proxumo conspexit?
question_en: What animal was the slave Sceledrus chasing on the roof-tiles when he caught sight of Philocomasium kissing next door?
derivation: The famous premise of the guard's discovery: chasing the household monkey over the tiles, Sceledrus looked down and saw the kiss. Canonical scene of the play; anchored to Sceledrus + Philocomasium; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Forte fortuna per impluvium huc despexi in proxumum, atque ego illi aspicio osculantem Philocomasium cum altero nescio quo adulescente.
question: Per quam aedium partem Sceledrus, in tegulis stans, in vicini domum despexit et Philocomasium osculantem vidit?
question_en: Through what part of the house did Sceledrus, standing on the roof-tiles, look down into the neighbor's home and see Philocomasium kissing?
answer_en: Through the impluvium (the open roof-basin of the atrium).
derivation: Roman domestic architecture carrying the plot: from the roof one could see into a house through the impluvium, the atrium's roof opening. Realia of the Roman house; anchored to Sceledrus + Philocomasium; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: scio crucem futuram mihi sepulcrum; ibi mei sunt maiores siti, pater, avos, proavos, abavos.
question: Quem locum Sceledrus servus in Milite Glorioso sepulcrum suum futurum ait, ubi pater, avus, proavus siti sint?
question_en: What place does the slave Sceledrus in the Miles Gloriosus say will be his tomb, where his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather lie?
derivation: The grim slave joke that the cross is the family sepulcher of slaves, generation after generation — a memorable statement of crucifixion as the servile punishment. Culturally salient realia of Roman servitude; anchored to Sceledrus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quis igitur vocare? Phil. Diceae nomen est.
question: Quod nomen sibi esse dixit Philocomasium, cum apud Plautum sororem geminam Athenis advectam se esse simularet?
question_en: What name did Philocomasium claim as her own when, in Plautus, she pretended to be the twin sister arrived from Athens?
derivation: The assumed name of the fictitious twin: Dicea ('the Just one'). A fixed onomastic fact of the play's central deception; anchored to Philocomasium + the twin fiction; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Inde ignem in aram, ut Ephesiae Dianae laeta laudes gratesque agam eique ut Arabico fumificem odore amoene, quom me in locis Neptuniis templisque turbulentis servavit, saevis fluctibus ubi sum adflictata multum.
question: Cui deae Philocomasium, sororem geminam simulans, laudes gratesque agere vult, quod se e saevis fluctibus maris servaverit?
question_en: To which goddess does Philocomasium, playing the twin sister, wish to give praise and thanks for saving her from the savage waves of the sea?
derivation: Religio in the Ephesian setting: thanksgiving at an altar to Diana of Ephesus (the city's great goddess) for rescue at sea. Anchored to Philocomasium + Ephesus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ut Ephesiae Dianae laeta laudes gratesque agam eique ut Arabico fumificem odore amoene.
question: Quo odore Philocomasium Dianae Ephesiae in ara fumificare constituit?
question_en: With what scent does Philocomasium decide to make fumigation on the altar for Ephesian Diana?
derivation: Cult realia: the offering of Arabian incense (the standard luxury import for Roman altars) in a thanksgiving rite. Anchored to Diana of Ephesus + the named worshipper; short answer verbatim (Arabico ... odore).

author: Plautus
source_text: Ergo, si sapis, mussitabis: plus oportet scire servom quam loqui.
question: Quem, ut Palaestrio in Milite Glorioso sententiose monet, plus scire oportet quam loqui?
question_en: Who, as Palaestrio warns in a maxim in the Miles Gloriosus, ought to know more than he says?
derivation: A proverb of servile prudence: a slave should know more than he speaks. Checkable point (of whom the maxim is said), short answer verbatim; anchored to speaker and play.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam ex uno puteo similior numquam potis aqua aquai sumi quam haec est atque ista hospita.
question: Cui rei Sceledrus similitudinem Philocomasii et fictae sororis geminae proverbialiter comparat?
question_en: To what does Sceledrus proverbially compare the likeness of Philocomasium and the invented twin sister?
answer_en: To water drawn from the same well.
derivation: The Latin likeness-proverb 'as like as water to water from one well' (companion to the play's 'as like as milk to milk'). Proverbial simile with a checkable point; anchored to Sceledrus + the twins; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam equidem haud sum natus annos praeter quinquaginta et quattuor, clare oculis video, pernix sum manibus, pedibus mobilis.
question: Quot annos natum se esse Periplectomenus senex in Milite Glorioso profitetur?
question_en: How many years old does the old man Periplectomenus in the Miles Gloriosus declare himself to be?
derivation: The sprightly senex's self-portrait: only fifty-four, sharp-eyed, quick of hand and foot. A fixed number fact of the play's celebrated praise-of-the-bachelor scene; anchored to Periplectomenus; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam mihi, deum virtute dicam, propter divitias meas licuit uxorem dotatam genere summo ducere; sed nolo mi oblatratricem in aedis intro mittere.
question: Quid Periplectomenus senex, quamquam propter divitias suas liceret, domum ducere recusat?
question_en: What does the old man Periplectomenus refuse to bring home, although his wealth would have allowed it?
derivation: The heart of Periplectomenus' famous praise of the single life: rich enough for a high-born dowered wife, he will not admit a 'barker' into his house. Mores of marriage and the uxor dotata (the tyrannical dowered wife of Roman comedy); anchored to the named senex; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: mea bona in morte cognatis didam, inter eos partiam.
question: Quibus Periplectomenus, senex caelebs et sine liberis, bona sua post mortem se divisurum esse dicit?
question_en: Among whom does Periplectomenus, the unmarried and childless old man, say he will divide his goods at his death?
derivation: The childless bachelor's economy: his relatives feast him, send gifts, and court him because they gape after his estate — the legacy-hunting (captatio) theme — and he will parcel his goods among the cognati. Mores of inheritance; anchored to Periplectomenus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: dicat 'da, mi vir, kalendis meam qui matrem munerem'.
question: Quo die uxor apud Plautum a viro pecuniam poscit qua matrem suam muneret?
question_en: On what day does the wife in Plautus demand money from her husband with which to send her mother a present?
derivation: Roman calendar realia inside the Greek play: the Kalends (the matrons' gift-day, the Matronalia of March 1) heads the imagined wife's list of demands in Periplectomenus' tirade. Anchored to the Miles' bachelor speech; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: da quod dem quinquatribus praecantrici, coniectrici, hariolae atque haruspicae; flagitiumst, si nil mittetur quae supercilio spicit.
question: Quo festo die uxor apud Plautum poscit quod praecantrici, coniectrici, hariolae atque haruspicae donet?
question_en: On what festival does the wife in Plautus demand something to give to the charm-singer, the dream-reader, the soothsayer, and the entrail-reading woman?
derivation: A named Roman festival (the Quinquatrus, Minerva's March feast) breaking the Greek frame, as the day for tipping the four female ritual specialists — praecantrix, coniectrix, hariola, haruspica. Festival and divination realia; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: post Ephesi sum natus, non enim in Apulis; non sum Animulas.
question: In qua urbe se natum esse Periplectomenus gloriatur, negans se in Apulia natum?
question_en: In what city does Periplectomenus boast he was born, denying that he comes from Apulia?
derivation: The urbane senex claims Ephesian birth and mocks Apulian Animula as the home of boors — an Italian-geography jab rupturing the Greek setting. Anchored to Periplectomenus; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam hospes nullus tam in amici hospitium devorti potest, quin, ubi triduom continuom fuerit, iam odiosus siet.
question: Post quot dies continuos hospes etiam apud amicum odiosus fieri dicitur, ut in Milite Glorioso Plauti legitur?
question_en: After how many days running is even a guest at a friend's house said to become tiresome, as one reads in Plautus' Miles Gloriosus?
derivation: The classic guest proverb: no guest can stay three days straight without becoming a burden. Checkable proverbial point (the number of days); anchored to the play; single-number answer verbatim (triduom).

author: Plautus
source_text: verum ubi dies decem continuos sit, east odiorum Ilias.
question: Quid fieri dicitur hospitium decem dierum continuorum, ut Pleusicles apud Plautum in Milite Glorioso ait?
question_en: What is a guest-stay of ten days running said to become, as Pleusicles puts it in Plautus' Miles Gloriosus?
derivation: The famous coinage 'odiorum Ilias' — a ten-day guest breeds an epic of grudges. Proverbial phrase with a checkable point, resting on the shared Homeric touchstone; anchored to speaker and play; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: At ego mi anulum dari istunc tuom volo. Per. Quam ad rem usui est? Pal. Quando habebo, igitur rationem mearum fabricarum dabo. Per. Vtere, accipe.
question: Quid Palaestrio a Periplectomeno mutuum accepit, quo Pyrgopolynicem sycophantia caperet?
question_en: What did Palaestrio borrow from Periplectomenus in order to snare Pyrgopolynices with his trick?
derivation: The signet ring borrowed from the old man becomes the token of the seduction-trap, passed off as a love-gift from the 'wife' next door. Anulus culture (the ring as personal token) carrying the intrigue; anchored to both names; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Isque Alexandri praestare praedicat formae suam, itaque omnis se ultro sectari in Epheso memorat mulieres.
question: Cuius formae suam formam praestare Pyrgopolynices praedicat, ut Palaestrio in Milite Glorioso narrat?
question_en: Whose beauty does Pyrgopolynices boast that his own surpasses, as Palaestrio tells it in the Miles Gloriosus?
derivation: The braggart rates his looks above Alexander — the Greek name of Paris, the proverbial beauty — and claims all the women of Ephesus chase him unbidden. Mythic touchstone anchoring the soldier's vanity; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Rem omnem tibi, Acroteleutium, tibique una, Milphidippa, domi demonstravi in ordine. hanc fabricam fallaciasque minus si tenetis, denuo volo percipiatis plane.
question: Quae meretrix, Periplectomeni clienta, in Milite Glorioso uxorem eius esse se simulavit, ut Pyrgopolynices caperetur?
question_en: Which courtesan, a client of Periplectomenus, pretended in the Miles Gloriosus to be his wife so that Pyrgopolynices might be snared?
derivation: The old man drills Acroteleutium and her maid in the fabrica; Palaestrio then has her play his neighbor's wife (huius uxorem volo te esse adsimulare, 908). The named agent of the famous seduction-trap; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Rem omnem tibi, Acroteleutium, tibique una, Milphidippa, domi demonstravi in ordine.
question: Quod nomen erat ancillae quae in Milite Glorioso internuntia inter fictam amatricem et Pyrgopolynicem fuit?
question_en: What was the name of the maid who in the Miles Gloriosus acted as go-between for the pretended lover and Pyrgopolynices?
derivation: Milphidippa, Acroteleutium's clever ancilla, carries the ring and the love-messages to the soldier. A fixed name of the play's cast; anchored to the trap plot; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed quis east? Pal. Senis huius uxor Periplectomeni ex proxumo; ea demoritur te atque ab illo cupit abire: odit senem.
question: Cuius viri uxor esse fingebatur mulier quae Pyrgopolynicem deperire simulabat?
question_en: Whose wife was the woman pretended to be who feigned to be dying of love for Pyrgopolynices?
derivation: The core of the trap: the soldier is told his new admirer is the next-door wife of old Periplectomenus, longing to leave her husband — the bait that makes him a would-be adulterer. Anchored to both names; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Postriduo natus sum ego, mulier, quam Iuppiter ex Ope natust.
question: Quanto post Iovem ex Ope natum se ipsum natum esse Pyrgopolynices iactat?
question_en: How soon after Jupiter's birth from Ops does Pyrgopolynices boast that he himself was born?
derivation: The crowning boast of the braggart: born one day after Jupiter, son of Ops (the Roman equation Ops = Rhea, mother of Jupiter, is assumed as shared myth). Palaestrio caps it: a day earlier and he would hold the kingdom of heaven. Anchored to Pyrgopolynices + Jupiter/Ops; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Meri bellatores gignuntur, quas hic praegnatis fecit, et pueri annos octingentos vivont. Milph. Vae tibi, nugator. Pyrg. Quin mille annorum perpetuo vivont, ab saeclo ad saeclum.
question: Quot annos vivere pueros a se genitos Pyrgopolynices ipse gloriatur?
question_en: How many years does Pyrgopolynices himself boast that boys begotten by him live?
derivation: The boast catalogue: Palaestrio credits the soldier's sons with eight hundred years, and the soldier corrects him upward — a full thousand, age to age. Canonical comic hyperbole of the play; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Talentum Philippi huic opus auri est; minus ab nemine accipiet.
question: Quantum auri Palaestrio pro Pyrgopolynicis amore poscendum esse Milphidippae dictitat?
question_en: How much gold does Palaestrio tell Milphidippa must be paid for Pyrgopolynices' love?
derivation: Money realia of the palliata: the talent of 'Philippi' — gold philippics, the coinage of the Macedonian kings — as the standard extravagant price. Anchored to the named characters; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Non mihi avaritia umquam innatast: satis habeo divitiarum, plus mi auri mille est modiorum Philippi.
question: Quot modios auri Philippi se habere Pyrgopolynices gloriatur?
question_en: How many bushels of Philippic gold does Pyrgopolynices boast that he owns?
derivation: Wealth measured by the bushel: over a thousand modii of gold philippics, 'not counting the treasures' and mountains of silver higher than Aetna. The braggart's canonical riches-boast; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Cedo signum, si harunc Baccharum es. Pal. Amat mulier quaedam quendam.
question: Quarum sodalium quasi signum Milphidippa a Palaestrione poscit, priusquam consilia ei aperiat?
question_en: Of what sisterhood does Milphidippa demand the pass-sign from Palaestrio before she will open the plans to him?
derivation: The joke assumes shared knowledge that Bacchic initiates recognized one another by a secret signum — the cult-realia behind the Bacchanalia affair. Anchored to the named characters; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: aurum atque vestem muliebrem omnem habeat sibi, quae illi instruxisti: sumat, habeat, auferat; dicasque tempus maxume esse, ut eat domum.
question: Quae dona Pyrgopolynices Philocomasio abeunti habere concessit, ut placide a se abiret?
question_en: What gifts did Pyrgopolynices allow the departing Philocomasium to keep, so that she would leave him quietly?
answer_en: The gold and the women's clothing.
derivation: How the girl leaves with the loot: on Palaestrio's advice the soldier lets her carry off all the gold and finery he had furnished her. Canonical resolution device of the play; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Mil. Pulcher, salve. Pyrg. Meum cognomentum commemoravit.
question: Quod cognomentum suum esse Pyrgopolynices adfirmat, cum a Milphidippa 'pulcher' salutatur?
question_en: What does Pyrgopolynices claim as his cognomen when Milphidippa greets him as 'handsome one'?
derivation: The vanity joke turns on Roman cognomen culture: greeted as pulcher, the soldier takes it for his own cognomen Pulcher (a real Roman cognomen). Anchored to both names; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam in mala uxore atque inimico si quid sumas, sumptus est, in bono hospite atque amico quaestus est quod sumitur et quod in divinis rebus sumptumst, sapienti lucrumst.
question: Quod genus sumptus sapienti lucrum esse Periplectomenus apud Plautum sententiose docet?
question_en: What kind of expense does Periplectomenus in Plautus declare, as a maxim, to be gain for a wise man?
answer_en: What is spent on religious rites.
derivation: The senex's three-part maxim on spending: on a bad wife or an enemy it is loss, on a good guest it is profit, and outlay on divine things is the wise man's gain. Checkable proverbial point tying piety to profit; anchored to Periplectomenus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ibi tu ilico facito uti venias ornatu huc ad nos nauclerico; causeam habeas ferrugineam, et scutulam ob oculos laneam, palliolum habeas ferrugineum (nam is colos thalassicust).
question: Quo ornatu Pleusicles, Philocomasii amator, ad militem venit, ut eam quasi ad navem matris arcesseret?
question_en: In what costume did Pleusicles, Philocomasium's lover, come to the soldier, to summon her as if to her mother's ship?
derivation: The final device: the lover disguised as a nauclerus — broad hat, eye-patch, seaman's cloak — 'fetches' the girl to the harbor. Canonical disguise of the play, anchored to Pleusicles; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: causeam habeas ferrugineam, et scutulam ob oculos laneam, palliolum habeas ferrugineum (nam is colos thalassicust).
question: Cuius coloris palliolum Palaestrio Pleusicli nauclerum simulaturo praescribit, quod is colos thalassicus sit?
question_en: What color cloak does Palaestrio prescribe for Pleusicles when he is to play the shipmaster, because that is the 'sea' color?
derivation: Dress realia: ferrugineus — the dark rust/sea hue — is named as the seaman's color (colos thalassicus), with the broad causea hat completing the outfit. A checkable costume-color fact; anchored to the named disguise; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam ille qui lanam ob oculum habebat laevom, nauta non erat. Pyrg. Quis erat igitur? Ser. Philocomasio amator.
question: Quid Pleusicles, nautam simulans, ob oculum laevom gestabat?
question_en: What did Pleusicles, playing the sailor, wear over his left eye?
derivation: The wool patch over the left eye is the disguise's telltale detail: by it the slave reveals at the end that the 'sailor' was really Philocomasium's lover. Anchored to the disguised lover; one-word answer verbatim (lanam ob oculum).

author: Plautus
source_text: Non tu scis, quom ex alto puteo sursum ad summum escenderis, maxumum periclum inde esse ab summo ne rusum cadas?
question: Vbi maximum periculum esse Palaestrio proverbialiter dicit ei qui ex alto puteo sursum escendit?
question_en: Where does Palaestrio proverbially say the greatest danger lies for one who has climbed up out of a deep well?
answer_en: At the top — of falling back down.
derivation: The well proverb: the peril is greatest at the brink, just before success — said of the intrigue at its critical point. Proverbial image with a checkable point; anchored to Palaestrio; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam nulli mortali scio obtigisse hoc, nisi duobus, tibi et Phaoni Lesbio, tam mulier se ut amaret.
question: Cui uni mortali praeter Pyrgopolynicem hoc obtigisse Palaestrio ait, ut mulier eum tam perdite amaret?
question_en: To what one mortal besides Pyrgopolynices does Palaestrio say it has ever befallen to be so desperately loved by a woman?
derivation: Phaon of Lesbos, the proverbially irresistible beloved (famed from the Sappho legend), is the mythic yardstick of being loved — flattery that assumes the audience knows the story. Anchored to both names; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Nescio, tu ex me hoc audiveris an non: nepos sum Veneris.
question: Cuius deae nepotem se esse Pyrgopolynices gloriatur?
question_en: Of what goddess does Pyrgopolynices boast that he is the grandson?
derivation: The braggart claims descent from Venus — echoed mockingly at the finale, where he is spared as a 'little grandson of Venus' (Venerium nepotulum). Anchored to Pyrgopolynices; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: salve, vir lepidissime, cumulate commoditate, praeter ceteros duo di quem curant. Pyrg. Qui duo? Pver. Mars et Venus.
question: Qui duo di Pyrgopolynicem prae ceteris hominibus curare dicuntur, ut puer adulans ait?
question_en: Which two gods are said to care for Pyrgopolynices above other men, as the flattering slave-boy puts it?
derivation: The soldier's two patron deities — war and love, the twin poles of his vanity — named as he is lured into the trap. Anchored to Pyrgopolynices; two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nisi modo unum hoc: hasce esse aedis dicas dotalis tuas, hinc senem aps te abiisse, postquam feceris divortium: ne ille mox vereatur intro ire in alienam domum.
question: Quales aedes suas esse Acroteleutium dicere iussa est, ne Pyrgopolynices in alienam domum intro ire vereretur?
question_en: What kind of house was Acroteleutium instructed to say was hers, so that Pyrgopolynices would not be afraid to enter another man's home?
derivation: Roman dowry law dressing the trap: the house is claimed as the wife's dotal property, the husband gone after a divorce — so the adulterer enters no other man's house. Ius realia (aedes dotales, divortium) inside the Greek plot; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quod volui ut volui impetravi, per amicitiam et gratiam, a Philocomasio. Pal. Quid tam intus fuisse te dicam diu? Pyrg. Numquam ego me tam sensi amari quam nunc ab illa muliere. Pal. Quid iam? Pyrg. Vt multa verba feci, ut lenta materies fuit. verum postremo impetravi ut volui: donavi dedi quae voluit, quae postulavit; te quoque ei dono dedi.
question: Cui Pyrgopolynices ipsum Palaestrionem servum dono dedit, cum eam dimitteret?
question_en: To whom did Pyrgopolynices give the slave Palaestrio himself as a parting gift?
derivation: The resolution's neat stroke: besides the gold and clothing, the soldier hands over Palaestrio himself as a gift to the departing Philocomasium — so the schemer sails off with the lovers. Anchored to all three names; one-name answer supported verbatim (a Philocomasio ... te quoque ei dono dedi).

author: Plautus
source_text: Etiam nunc saluto te, Lar familiaris, prius quam eo.
question: Quem deum domesticum Palaestrio, ex aedibus militis abiturus, salutat?
question_en: What household god does Palaestrio salute as he is about to leave the soldier's house?
derivation: Domestic religio: on quitting a house one salutes its Lar familiaris, the household's guardian god — a Roman rite performed inside the Greek play. Anchored to Palaestrio's departure; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Per. Immo etiam prius verberetur fustibus. Car. Multum quidem. Per. Cur es ausus subigitare alienam uxorem, impudens? Pyrg. Ita me di ament, ultro ventumst ad me. Per. Mentitur, feri.
question: Quo supplicio Pyrgopolynices, quasi moechus in aliena uxore deprehensus, apud Periplectomenum adfectus est?
question_en: What punishment was inflicted on Pyrgopolynices at Periplectomenus' house as an adulterer caught with another man's wife?
derivation: The moechus treatment that ends the play: the would-be adulterer is seized and cudgeled (with worse threatened) for daring another man's wife. The customary self-help punishment of the adulterer — mores realia; anchored to both names; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: vide ut istic tibi sit acutus, Cario, culter probe. Cario Quin iamdudum gestit moecho hoc abdomen adimere, ut ea iam quasi puero in collo pendeant crepundia.
question: Quod nomen erat servo Periplectomeni qui cultrum acutum in Pyrgopolynicem moechum parabat?
question_en: What was the name of Periplectomenus' slave who was readying a sharp knife against the adulterer Pyrgopolynices?
derivation: Cario (the cook, by his stock name) itches to geld the moechus with his knife — the traditional mutilation threatened against caught adulterers. Anchored to Periplectomenus' household + the named slave; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ergo des minam auri nobis. Pyrg. Quam ob rem? Car. Salvis testibus ut te hodie hinc amittamus Venerium nepotulum.
question: Quantum auri Pyrgopolynices dare iussus est, ut salvus atque integer dimitteretur?
question_en: How much gold was Pyrgopolynices ordered to pay in order to be let go safe and intact?
derivation: The caught adulterer buys himself off: a gold mina as ransom to be released 'with witnesses intact'. Money realia (the mina) in the punishment scene; anchored to Pyrgopolynices; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Iuro per Iovem et Mavortem, me nociturum nemini, quod ego hic hodie vapularim, iureque id factum arbitror.
question: Per quos deos Pyrgopolynices iuravit se nemini ob verbera accepta nociturum esse?
question_en: By which gods did Pyrgopolynices swear that he would harm no one on account of the beating he had received?
derivation: Oath realia: the extorted oath of the beaten soldier, sworn by Jupiter and Mavors (the old Latin name of Mars), even conceding the beating was just. Anchored to Pyrgopolynices; two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Tu urbanus vero scurra, deliciae popli, rus mihi tu obiectas? sane hoc, credo, Tranio, quod te in pistrinum scis actutum tradier.
question: Quem servum urbanum Grumio bubulcus in prima scaena Mostellariae Plauti 'urbanum scurram, delicias populi' appellat?
question_en: Which city slave does the ox-herd Grumio in the first scene of Plautus' Mostellaria call 'a city buffoon, the people's darling'?
derivation: The opening country-versus-city slave quarrel: Grumio the rusticus up from the farm confronts Tranio the urbanus — the mores contrast that frames the play, with the pistrinum (the mill) as the city slave's promised punishment. Anchored to Grumio + Tranio; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc, dum tibi lubet licetque, pota, perde rem, corrumpe erilem adulescentem optumum; dies noctesque bibite, pergraecamini, amicas emite liberate, pascite parasitos, obsonate pollucibiliter.
question: Quo uno verbo Grumio in Mostellaria Plauti dies noctesque potare et luxuriose Graecorum more vivere complectitur?
question_en: With what single word does Grumio in Plautus' Mostellaria sum up drinking day and night and living luxuriously in the Greek manner?
derivation: The Roman cultural verb pergraecari — to carouse in Greek fashion — the Roman habit of labeling round-the-clock debauchery as 'living Greek,' hurled by the country slave at the city household. A named-custom fact that survives translation; anchored to Grumio + the Mostellaria; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: O carnuficium cribrum, quod credo fore, ita te forabunt patibulatum per vias stimulis carnufices, si huc reveniat senex.
question: Quo supplicii instrumento oneratum Tranionem per vias agitatum iri Grumio minatur, si senex redierit?
question_en: Loaded with what instrument of punishment does Grumio threaten that Tranio will be driven through the streets, if the old man comes back?
derivation: Roman penal realia through the Greek dress: the condemned slave paraded patibulatus — carrying the cross-beam — through the streets while the carnufices (executioners) prod him full of holes like 'a hangman's sieve.' Anchored to Grumio + Tranio; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Tace atque abi rus. ego ire in Piraeum volo, in vesperum parare piscatum mihi.
question: Quem in portum Tranio in Mostellaria piscatum ad vesperum paraturus se ire dicit?
question_en: To what harbor does Tranio in the Mostellaria say he is going, to lay in fish for the evening?
derivation: Geography of the setting: the Piraeus, the harbor of Athens (the play's city), where Tranio goes to buy the evening's fish — fish as the delicacy of the carousing table. Anchored to Tranio + the Piraeus; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: facite, huc ut redeat noster quam primum senex, triennium qui iam hinc abest, prius quam omnia periere, et aedis et ager
question: Quot annos Theopropides senex peregre iam afuerat, cum Grumio deos precatur ut quam primum redeat?
question_en: For how many years had the old man Theopropides already been away abroad, when Grumio prays the gods for his speedy return?
derivation: The canonical time-frame of the Mostellaria: the father three years abroad while the son devours house and land. Anchored to Theopropides (the absent senex) + Grumio's prayer; one-word number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: novarum aedium esse arbitror similem ego hominem, quando natus est.
question: Cui rei Philolaches in celebri cantico Mostellariae hominem, quando natus est, similem esse arbitratur?
question_en: To what does Philolaches, in the famous canticum of the Mostellaria, judge a man to be similar when he is born?
derivation: The celebrated building-simile canticum of the play: a man is like a newly built house — the parents are the builders, and the storm of idleness and the rain of love rot the timbers. Canonical literary fact; anchored to Philolaches; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: expoliunt: docent litteras, iura leges, sumptu suo et labore nituntur, ut alii sibi esse illorum similis expetant.
question: Quas artes parentes liberos suo sumptu docere Philolaches in Mostellaria enumerat, dum eos quasi fabri expoliunt?
question_en: What subjects does Philolaches in the Mostellaria list that parents have their children taught at their own expense, polishing them like builders?
derivation: Education realia inside the building-simile: the freeborn son's curriculum — letters, rights, laws — paid for with the parents' own money and labor. Anchored to Philolaches' canticum; three-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ad legionem cum ita paratos mittunt, adminiclum eis danunt tum iam, aliquem cognatum suom.
question: Quem adminiculi loco parentes filio ad legionem misso dare solent, ut Philolaches in Mostellaria ait?
question_en: Whom do parents customarily give as a support to a son sent off to the legion, as Philolaches says in the Mostellaria?
derivation: Military-social realia: the young recruit sent to the legion under the wing of a kinsman; after one campaign served (emeritum stipendium, v. 131) the quality of the 'building' shows. Anchored to Philolaches; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quo neque industrior de iuventute erat quisquam nec clarior arte gymnastica: disco, hastis, pila, cursu, armis, equo victitabam volup
question: Quibus exercitationibus gymnasticis Philolaches adulescens, priusquam amori se dedit, victitasse se dicit?
answer: Disco, hastis, pila, cursu, armis, equo.
question_en: In what gymnastic exercises does the young Philolaches say he used to pass his life, before he gave himself to love?
answer_en: The discus, javelins, ball-play, running, arms, and horsemanship.
derivation: The catalogue of a model youth's training — discus, javelin, ball, running, arms drill, riding — the shared ideal of gymnastic education for the young. Anchored to Philolaches; six-item list verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Manu misit emptos suos amores Philolaches Omnemque absente rem suo absumit patre.
question: Quid Philolaches adulescens de Philematio meretrice, amoribus suis emptis, fecit apud Plautum in Mostellaria?
question_en: What did the young Philolaches do with the courtesan Philematium, his purchased love, in Plautus' Mostellaria?
answer_en: He manumitted her (bought her and set her free).
derivation: The premise of the play, stated in the argumentum: Philolaches bought his beloved and freed her — 'Solam ille me soli sibi suo sumptu liberavit' (v. 204) — the spending that drives the whole plot. Manumission realia; anchored to Philolaches + Philematium.

author: Plautus
source_text: non vestem amatores amant mulieris, sed vestis fartim.
question: Quid amatores re vera amare Scapha ancilla in Mostellaria dicit, non vestem mulieris?
question_en: What does the maid Scapha in the Mostellaria say lovers really love, not a woman's dress?
answer_en: The 'stuffing' of the dress (what fills it).
derivation: Scapha's quotable maxim from the dressing scene: lovers love not the dress but its filling. A saying with a checkable one-phrase point; anchored to Scapha + the Mostellaria; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Tu ecastor erras, quae quidem illum expectes unum atque illi morem praecipue sic geras atque alios asperneris. matronae, non meretricium est unum inservire amantem.
question: Cuius mulieris esse Scapha in Mostellaria dicit uni amanti inservire — matronae an meretricis?
question_en: Whose part does Scapha in the Mostellaria say it is to devote oneself to a single lover — the matron's or the courtesan's?
derivation: The mores contrast stated as a rule: serving one lover alone befits the matrona, not the meretrix trade. Ambient social knowledge of the two roles; anchored to Scapha advising Philematium; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Vt fama est homini, exin solet pecuniam invenire. ego si bonam famam mihi servasso, sat ero dives.
question: Qua re servata Philematium in Mostellaria satis divitem se fore dicit?
question_en: By keeping what does Philematium in the Mostellaria say she will be rich enough?
derivation: Philematium's sententia: as a person's reputation is, so comes the money — keep good fame and you are rich enough. A quotable maxim with a one-phrase answer; anchored to Philematium; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Edepol si summo Iovi bovi eo argento sacruficassem, pro illius capite quod dedi, numquam aeque id bene locassem.
question: Quod animal summo Iovi sacrificari solitum Philolaches in Mostellaria memorat, cum argentum pro Philematio datum bene locatum esse gaudet?
question_en: What animal, customarily sacrificed to highest Jupiter, does Philolaches mention in the Mostellaria, rejoicing that the money paid for Philematium was well spent?
derivation: Religious realia: the ox as the victim for supreme Jupiter — Philolaches says even sacrificing an ox to Jove with that silver would not have placed it better. Anchored to Philolaches + Iuppiter; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Cedo mi speculum et cum ornamentis arculam actutum, Scapha, ornata ut sim, quom huc adveniat Philolaches voluptas mea.
question: Quae duo Philematium a Scapha sibi adferri iubet, ut ornata sit cum Philolaches adveniat?
question_en: What two things does Philematium order Scapha to bring her, so that she may be adorned when Philolaches arrives?
answer_en: A mirror and the little casket with her ornaments.
derivation: Toilette realia of the dressing scene: the speculum and the arcula ornamentorum (jewel-casket) — the standard kit of a woman's adornment; Scapha retorts that she who spurns her age needs the mirror. Anchored to Philematium + Scapha; two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Cedo cerussam. SC. Quid cerussa opust nam? PHILEM. Qui malas oblinam. SC. Vna opera ebur atramento candefacere postules. PHILOL. Lepide dictum de atramento atque ebore. euge, plaudo Scaphae. PHILEM. Tum tu igitur cedo purpurissum.
question: Quae duo pigmenta Philematium in ornatu a Scapha poscit, alterum quo malas oblinat, alterum quo eas rubricet?
question_en: What two cosmetics does Philematium demand from Scapha at her toilette, one to whiten her cheeks and one to redden them?
derivation: Cosmetics realia: cerussa (white lead) for whitening the cheeks and purpurissum (purple rouge) — with Scapha's retort that painting the young girl is like whitening ivory with ink. The two staple face-paints of the Roman toilette; anchored to Philematium + Scapha; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Etiamne unguentis unguendam censes? SC. Minime feceris. PHILEM. Quapropter? SC. Quia ecastor mulier recte olet, ubi nihil olet.
question: Quando mulier recte olet, ut Scapha ancilla in Mostellaria Plauti pronuntiat?
question_en: When does a woman smell right, as the maid Scapha declares in Plautus' Mostellaria?
derivation: The famous maxim against perfumes — a woman smells best when she smells of nothing; old women who drench themselves in unguents smell, once the sweat mixes in, like a cook's confusion of sauces. A celebrated quotable saying (echoed by later authors); anchored to Scapha; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: pulchra mulier nuda erit quam purpurata pulchrior
question: Qualis pulchra mulier pulchrior erit quam purpurata, ut Scapha in Mostellaria ait?
question_en: In what state will a beautiful woman be more beautiful than one robed in purple, as Scapha says in the Mostellaria?
derivation: Scapha's dressing-scene maxim: real beauty needs no purple — 'if she is beautiful, she is adorned enough' (v. 292). Quotable saying with a one-word point; anchored to Scapha; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Etiam nunc decem minae apud te sunt; vel rationem puta. triginta minas pro capite tuo dedi.
question: Quantum argenti Philolaches pro capite Philematii liberando dedisse se dicit?
question_en: How much money does Philolaches say he paid for Philematium's freedom?
derivation: The price of the beloved's head: thirty minae — the sum borrowed at interest from the danista, the debt that drives the play's second intrigue. Money realia in Greek currency; anchored to Philolaches + Philematium; number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Age accumbe igitur. cedo aquam manibus, puere, appone hic mensulam. vide, tali ubi sint. vin unguenta?
question: Quos ad lusum Philematium, convivio cum Philolache parato, ubi sint videri iubet?
question_en: What gaming pieces does Philematium, as the little banquet with Philolaches is laid, order to be looked out?
derivation: Banquet realia in one line: water for the hands, the little serving table, and the tali — knucklebone dice, the standard game over wine. Anchored to Philematium + the banquet; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc comissatum ibo ad Philolachetem, ubi nos hilari ingenio et lepide accipient.
question: Ad quem se comissatum ire Callidamates ebrius in Mostellaria dicit?
question_en: To whose house does the drunken Callidamates in the Mostellaria say he is going to carry the revel (comissatum)?
derivation: The comissatio custom: quitting one party to descend, drunk and merry, on a friend's house to keep drinking — Callidamates arrives propped up by his girl Delphium. Mores of the banquet; anchored to Callidamates + Philolaches; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ego dabo ei talentum, primus qui in crucem excucurrerit; sed ea lege, ut offigantur bis pedes, bis bracchia.
question: Quod praemium Tranio ei se daturum ait, qui primus pro se in crucem excucurrerit, ea lege ut bis pedes bisque bracchia offigantur?
question_en: What reward does Tranio say he will give the man who first runs to the cross in his place, on condition that his feet and arms be nailed twice over?
derivation: Crucifixion realia — a rare explicit testimony to the nailing of feet and arms on the crux — in the comic slave's gallows humor, with a talent as the fee. Anchored to Tranio; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ubi sunt isti plagipatidae, ferritribaces viri, vel isti qui hosticas trium nummum causa subeunt sub falas, ubi quinis aut denis hastis corpus transfigi solet?
question: Quanti mercedis causa homines perditos sub falas hosticas subire Tranio in Mostellaria dicit?
question_en: For how small a fee does Tranio in the Mostellaria say desperate men go in under the enemy's siege-towers?
derivation: Military realia: hired men taking three nummi to serve beneath the falae (siege towers), where a body is commonly run through with five or ten spears — with the comic coinages plagipatidae ('sons of stripes') and ferritribaces ('iron-wearers'). Anchored to Tranio; price answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Clavem mi harunc aedium Laconicam iam iube efferri intus: hasce ego aedis occludam hinc foris.
question: Cuius generis clavem Tranio sibi efferri iubet, ut aedes forinsecus occludat?
question_en: What kind of key does Tranio order brought out to him, so that he can lock the house from the outside?
derivation: Household realia: the clavis Laconica, the key type that locked a door from the outside — the very instrument of the haunted-house trick, sealing the house as if long abandoned. Anchored to Tranio + the aedes; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Habeo, Neptune, gratiam magnam tibi, quom med amisisti abs te vix vivom domum.
