question: Cui deo Theopropides, domum advectus, gratias agit, quod se vix vivum e mari amiserit?
question_en: To which god does Theopropides, arrived home, give thanks for letting him back from the sea barely alive?
derivation: Neptune as lord of the sea, thanked with comic resentment by the merchant home from his voyage — he swears never to set foot on a wave again. Religious realia of seafaring; anchored to Theopropides + Neptune; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Triennio post Aegypto advenio domum; credo exspectatus veniam familiaribus.
question: Vnde Theopropides senex post triennium domum advenit?
question_en: From where does the old man Theopropides come home after three years?
derivation: Geography of the plot: the father's three-year trading absence was in Egypt — the great commercial destination of the age. Anchored to Theopropides; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quia septem menses sunt, quom in hasce aedis pedem nemo intro tetulit, semel ut emigravimus.
question: Quot menses iam neminem pedem in aedes intulisse Tranio Theopropidi mentitur, postquam semel emigraverint?
question_en: For how many months does Tranio lie to Theopropides that no one has set foot in the house, since they once moved out?
derivation: A fixed number of the haunted-house fiction: seven months since anyone entered the 'accursed' house. Anchored to Tranio + Theopropides; number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Hospes necavit hospitem captum manu; iste, ut ego opinor, qui has tibi aedis vendidit. TH. Necavit? TR. Aurumque ei ademit hospiti eumque hic defodit hospitem ibidem in aedibus.
question: Quod scelus in aedibus olim commissum esse Tranio Theopropidi fingit, ut eum ab aedibus absterreat?
answer: Hospitem ab hospite auri causa necatum ibidemque defossum esse.
question_en: What crime does Tranio invent for Theopropides as committed long ago in the house, to frighten him away from it?
answer_en: That a guest was murdered by his host for his gold and buried on the spot in the house.
derivation: The haunted-house tale that gives the play its name: the man who sold the house murdered his guest, took his gold, and buried him there — the violation of hospitium making the house scelestae aedes. Canonical plot-fact; anchored to Tranio + Theopropides; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Mirum quin vigilanti diceret, qui abhinc sexaginta annos occisus foret.
question: Quot abhinc annos hospitem illum in aedibus occisum esse Tranio in fabula ficta Mostellariae dicit?
question_en: How many years before does Tranio, in the invented tale of the Mostellaria, say that the guest was killed in the house?
derivation: Another fixed number of the ghost story: the murder happened sixty years ago — which is why, Tranio quips, the dead man appears in dreams rather than waking. Anchored to Tranio's tale; number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ego transmarinus hospes sum Diapontius. hic habito, haec mihi dedita est habitatio.
question: Quod nomen sibi esse umbra hospitis transmarini in somnio ficto Mostellariae profitetur?
question_en: What name does the ghost of the overseas guest give itself in the invented dream of the Mostellaria?
derivation: The ghost's name in Tranio's tale: Diapontius, 'the man from over the sea' — the transmarine guest who claims the house as his dwelling. Canonical name-fact of the play (the name's meaning is glossed by transmarinus in the text itself); verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam me Acheruntem recipere Orcus noluit, quia praemature vita careo.
question: Quam ob causam Orcus umbram Diapontii Acheruntem recipere noluit, ut ipsa umbra in Mostellaria queritur?
question_en: For what reason did Orcus refuse to receive the shade of Diapontius into Acheron, as the ghost itself complains in the Mostellaria?
answer_en: Because he lost his life before his time.
derivation: The shared afterlife belief behind the ghost story: the untimely dead (and unburied — defodit insepultum, v. 502) are refused entry to Acheron by Orcus and must haunt the living. Myth as shared story; anchored to Orcus + Diapontius; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: tu, ut occepisti, tantum quantum quis fuge, atque Herculem invoca. TH. Hercules, ted invoco.
question: Quem deum Tranio Theopropidem, ab aedibus sceleratis fugientem, invocare iubet?
question_en: Which god does Tranio order the fleeing Theopropides to invoke against the accursed house?
derivation: Religious custom: Hercules invoked in sudden terror as the averter of evils — the old man obeys on the spot (Hercules, ted invoco). Anchored to Tranio + Theopropides; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: scelestae hae sunt aedes, impia est habitatio. quae hic monstra fiunt, anno vix possum eloqui.
question: A quibus rebus, quas in aedibus fieri Tranio finxit, fabula Plauti quae Mostellaria inscribitur nomen traxit?
question_en: From what things, which Tranio pretended were happening in the house, does Plautus' play entitled Mostellaria take its name?
answer_en: From the monstra — the 'little ghosts' (mostella) of the haunting.
derivation: The title-fact: Mostellaria, 'the ghost play,' from mostellum, diminutive of monstrum — the apparitions Tranio claims fill the house (quae hic monstra fiunt). Canonical literary fact anchored in the text's own word monstra; short answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: Scelestiorem ego annum argento faenori numquam ullum vidi quam hic mihi annus optigit. a mani ad noctem usque in foro dego diem, locare argenti nemini nummum queo.
question: Vbi danista in Mostellaria a mane ad noctem diem degere se dicit, dum argentum faenori locare conatur?
question_en: Where does the moneylender in the Mostellaria say he spends his day from morning to night, trying to place his silver at interest?
derivation: Faenus culture realia: the moneylender's working day in the forum, the marketplace of credit — he complains he cannot place a single nummus at interest all year. Anchored to the danista of the play; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: occidit Spes nostra, nusquam stabulum est Confidentiae, nec Salus nobis saluti iam esse, si cupiat, potest
question: Quae dea ne cupiens quidem saluti esse posse dicitur perditis, ut Tranio in Mostellaria lamentatur?
question_en: Which goddess, even if she wished, is said to be unable to save the ruined, as Tranio laments in the Mostellaria?
derivation: Salus as a Roman cult goddess, named beside personified Spes — the proverbial turn 'not even Salus could save us now,' a joke Plautus uses more than once. Religious realia; anchored to Tranio; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: salvere iubeo te, Misargyrides, bene. DAN. Salve et tu. quid de argentost?
question: Quod nomen erat danistae in Mostellaria Plauti, qui faenus sortemque a Philolachete flagitabat?
question_en: What was the name of the moneylender in Plautus' Mostellaria, who kept demanding interest and principal from Philolaches?
derivation: The moneylender's speaking name — Misargyrides — a canonical character-fact of the play (the danista of the argumentum, 'lucripeta faenerator'). Anchored to the Mostellaria + the loan plot; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: TR. Sortem accipe. DAN. Immo faenus, id primum volo.
question: Vtrum prius sibi reddi Misargyrides danista in Mostellaria postulat, sortem an faenus?
question_en: Which does the moneylender Misargyrides in the Mostellaria demand be paid him first — the principal or the interest?
derivation: Faenus culture: sors (principal) versus faenus (interest) — offered the principal, the lender refuses and demands his interest first, chanting 'cedo faenus, redde faenus' through the scene. Anchored to Misargyrides + Tranio; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: TR. Quattuor quadraginta illi debentur minae, et sors et faenus. DAN. Tantumst, nihilo plus peto.
question: Quantum omnino Misargyridi danistae a Philolachete debebatur, et sorte et faenore computatis?
question_en: How much in all was owed to the moneylender Misargyrides by Philolaches, principal and interest together?
derivation: The debt total of the plot: forty minae of principal plus four of interest — forty-four minae, confirmed by the lender himself. Money realia; anchored to Misargyrides + Philolaches; number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed arraboni has dedit quadraginta minas; hinc sumpsit quas ei dedimus. satin intellegis?
question: Cuius rei nomine Philolaches quadraginta minas pro aedibus dedisse dicebatur, ut Tranio Theopropidi finxit?
question_en: Under what name was Philolaches said to have paid the forty minae toward the 'purchased' house, in Tranio's fiction to Theopropides?
answer_en: As arrabo — earnest-money, the binding deposit.
derivation: Commercial-legal realia: the arrabo, the earnest-money that binds a purchase — Tranio converts the borrowed forty minae into a deposit on the neighbor's house. Anchored to Tranio's tale + Theopropides; term verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nullum edepol hodie genus est hominum taetrius nec minus bono cum iure, quam danisticum.
question: Quod genus hominum nullo taetrius minusque bono cum iure esse Tranio in Mostellaria pronuntiat?
question_en: What class of men does Tranio in the Mostellaria declare none is fouler or less within its rights than?
derivation: The verdict on the faenus trade — no breed fouler than the danisticum genus — voicing the shared Roman resentment of faeneratores. Anchored to Tranio + the moneylender scene; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: calidum hercle esse audivi optimum mendacium. quidquid dei dicunt, id decretumst dicere.
question: Quale mendacium optimum esse Tranio in Mostellaria audivisse se ait?
question_en: What kind of lie does Tranio in the Mostellaria say he has heard is best?
answer_en: A hot one (freshly made on the spot).
derivation: Tranio's proverbial rule of improvisation: the best lie is a hot one, served fresh — so he will say whatever the gods put in his mouth. Quotable saying with a one-word point; anchored to Tranio; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed senex gynaeceum aedificare volt hic in suis et balineas et ambulacrum et porticum.
question: Quas quattuor aedium partes Theopropides in suis aedificare velle dicebatur, cum aedes Simonis exemplo inspicere cuperet?
question_en: What four parts of a house was Theopropides said to want to build on his own property, when he wished to inspect Simo's house as a model?
answer_en: A women's wing (gynaeceum), baths, a promenade, and a portico.
derivation: Domestic architecture realia: the amenities of a fine house — the gynaeceum (women's quarters, meant for the son's intended bride, vv. 758-759), balineae, ambulacrum, porticus — the pretext for the house tour. Anchored to Theopropides + Simo; four-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nec mi umbra hic usquamst, nisi si in puteo quaepiamst. TR. Quid, Sarsinatis ecqua est, si Vmbram non habes?
question: Ex qua Italiae regione oritur mulier Sarsinatis, quam Tranio, de umbra iocatus, in Mostellaria memorat?
question_en: From what region of Italy does a woman of Sarsina come, whom Tranio, punning on 'shade' (umbra/Umbrian), mentions in the Mostellaria?
derivation: The geographic fact carried by the pun: Sarsina is an Umbrian town — treasured too as Plautus' own traditional birthplace, which makes the aside a signature in-joke. The town-in-region fact itself survives translation; anchored to Sarsina + Umbria.

author: Plautus
source_text: Alexandrum magnum atque Agathoclem aiunt maximas duo res gessisse: quid mihi fiet tertio, qui solus facio facinora immortalia?
question: Quos duos viros maximas res gessisse aiunt, quibus Tranio in Mostellaria se tertium gloriabundus adiungit?
question_en: Which two men are said to have done the greatest deeds, to whom Tranio in the Mostellaria boastfully adds himself as a third?
derivation: The canonical pairing of the age's world-beaters — Alexander of Macedon and Agathocles of Syracuse — invoked by the triumphant slave. Shared historical knowledge; anchored to Tranio; two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Heus tu, si voles verbum hoc cogitare, simul flare sorbereque haud factu facilest.
question: Quae duo simul facere haud facile esse Tranio proverbio in Mostellaria dicit?
question_en: What two things does Tranio in the Mostellaria say, proverbially, it is not easy to do at once?
derivation: The proverb simul flare sorbereque haud facile — you cannot blow and swallow at the same time, i.e., cannot be in two places or do two things at once (Tranio's excuse for his delay). Anchored to Tranio; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sibi quisque ruri metit. si male emptae forent, nobis istas redhibere haud liceret. lucri quidquid est, id domum trahere oportet.
question: Vbi sibi quisque metit, ut Theopropides proverbio in Mostellaria utitur?
question_en: Where does each man reap for himself, in the proverb Theopropides uses in the Mostellaria?
answer_en: In his own field (each reaps for himself).
derivation: The proverb sibi quisque ruri metit — every man harvests for himself, look to your own gain — capped by the maxim that whatever the profit, haul it home; with the legal color of redhibere (returning a defective purchase). Anchored to Theopropides; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Pol mihi eo pretio empti fuerant olim. TR. Audin 'fuerant' dicere? vix videtur continere lacrimas. TH. Quanti hosce emeras? SI. Tris minas pro istis duobus praeter vecturam dedi.
question: Quanti Simo duos postes aedium suarum emisse se dicit, praeter vecturam?
question_en: For how much does Simo say he bought the two doorposts of his house, not counting the haulage?
derivation: Building-trade realia from the house tour: three minae for the pair of doorposts, with the vectura (cartage) extra — the postes admired for their strength and thickness. Anchored to Simo + the house tour; price answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: atque etiam nunc satis boni sunt, si sunt inducti pice; non enim haec pultiphagus opifex opera fecit barbarus.
question: A quo cibo Tranio in Mostellaria opificem 'barbarum' (Italicum) pultiphagum appellat?
question_en: From what food does Tranio in the Mostellaria call the 'barbarian' (Italian) workman a 'pultiphagus'?
derivation: Criterion-8 gold: puls, the grain porridge that was the proverbial staple of early Italy — Plautus, speaking from the Greek stage, calls the Italian workman pultiphagus barbarus, 'the porridge-eating foreigner.' Ambient food culture; anchored to Tranio's remark; the word is glossed by its food.

author: Plautus
source_text: Viden pictum, ubi ludificat cornix una volturios duos? TH. Non edepol video. TR. At ego video. nam inter volturios duos cornix astat, ea volturios duo vicissim vellicat.
question: Quae avis in pictura illa, quam Tranio Theopropidi frustra monstrat, duos volturios ludificatur?
question_en: What bird, in the 'painting' that Tranio vainly points out to Theopropides, is making fools of two vultures?
derivation: The celebrated visual joke of the house tour: the (nonexistent) picture of one crow plucking two vultures in turn — Tranio's emblem of himself gulling the two old men. Canonical scene-fact of the Mostellaria; anchored to Tranio + Theopropides; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Servi qui, quom culpa carent, tamen malum metuont, ei solent esse eris utibiles.
question: Quales servi eris utibiles esse solent, ut Phaniscus in Mostellaria pronuntiat?
answer: Qui, quamquam culpa carent, tamen malum metuont.
question_en: What sort of slaves are usually serviceable to their masters, as Phaniscus declares in the Mostellaria?
answer_en: Those who, though free of fault, still fear punishment.
derivation: The good-slave maxim of Phaniscus' monologue (a doublet of Messenio's in the Menaechmi): fear keeps even the blameless slave useful — the slave-culture doctrine of the palliata. Anchored to Phaniscus; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Tace sis, faber, qui cudere soles plumbeos nummos.
question: Ex quo metallo nummos cudere solere Pinacium Phaniscum per convicium in Mostellaria dicit?
question_en: Out of what metal does Pinacium abusively say in the Mostellaria that Phaniscus is wont to strike coins?
derivation: Counterfeiting realia: plumbei nummi, lead coins as the proverbial false money — 'a smith who strikes lead coins' as an insult for a cheat. Currency culture; anchored to Pinacium + Phaniscus; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Triduom unum est haud intermissum hic esse et bibi, scorta duci, pergraecari, fidicinas tibicinas ducere.
question: Quae musicae mulieres ad convivia Philolachis duci solebant, ut Phaniscus in Mostellaria refert?
question_en: What music-girls used to be brought in for Philolaches' parties, as Phaniscus reports in the Mostellaria?
derivation: Banquet-entertainment realia: fidicinae (string-players) and tibicinae (pipe-girls) hired for the revels — listed beside the drinking, the wenching, and pergraecari, never three days interrupted. Anchored to Phaniscus' report + Philolaches; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: TH. Servavisti omnem ratem. nempe octoginta debentur huic minae? TR. Hau nummo amplius. TH. Hodie accipiat.
question: Quot minas Simoni vicino pro aedibus reliquas deberi Theopropides credebat, arrabone quadraginta minarum iam dato?
question_en: How many minae did Theopropides believe were still owed to his neighbor Simo for the house, the deposit of forty minae already paid?
derivation: The arithmetic of Tranio's fiction: the 'house' cost two great talents (v. 644), forty minae paid as arrabo, eighty outstanding — which the duped father undertakes to pay that very day. Money realia; anchored to Theopropides + Simo; number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Qui homo timidus erit in rebus dubiis, nauci non erit; atque equidem quid id esse dicam verbum nauci, nescio.
question: Quanti erit homo timidus in rebus dubiis, ut Tranio in Mostellaria pronuntiat?
question_en: What will a timid man be worth in a tight spot, as Tranio declares in the Mostellaria?
derivation: The idiom non nauci esse — worth not a naucum, a husk, a trifle — in a quotable maxim on boldness, capped by Tranio's own joke that he has no idea what naucum means. Anchored to Tranio; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ego interim hanc aram occupabo. TH. Quid ita? TR. Nullam rem sapis. ne enim illi huc confugere possint, quaestioni quos dabit. hic ego tibi praesidebo, ne interbitat quaestio.
question: Quo Tranio, dolis iam patefactis, in extrema Mostellaria confugit, ne a Theopropide comprehenderetur?
question_en: Where does Tranio take refuge at the end of the Mostellaria, his tricks now exposed, so that Theopropides cannot seize him?
answer_en: At the altar (he took possession of the altar).
derivation: The stage altar as sanctuary — the suppliant seated on the altar may not be dragged off — the canonical last refuge of the cornered comic slave, which Tranio 'occupies' with the cheeky excuse of guarding it; he adds that counsels are firmer from holy places (v. 1104). Cultural fact of religio and the theater; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: TH. Dixi ego istuc idem illi. TR. Quid ait? TH. Servos pollicitust dare suos mihi omnes quaestioni.
question: Cui rei Simo omnes servos suos se daturum pollicitus est, ut Theopropides in Mostellaria refert?
question_en: For what did Simo promise to hand over all his slaves, as Theopropides reports in the Mostellaria?
answer_en: For the quaestio — examination under torture.
derivation: Legal realia: to clear himself of the false sale, the householder offers his slaves for the quaestio, the interrogation of slaves by torture that made their evidence admissible. Roman legal color through the Greek plot; anchored to Simo + Theopropides; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Iam iubebo ignem et sarmenta, carnifex, circumdari. TR. Ne faxis, nam elixus esse quam assus soleo suavior.
question: Quid Theopropides Tranioni, in ara supplici sedenti, circumdari iubere minatur?
question_en: What does Theopropides threaten to have piled around Tranio as he sits as a suppliant on the altar?
derivation: The counter-move to altar asylum: the suppliant cannot be dragged off, so he is threatened with being burned off — met by Tranio's gallows joke that he is tastier boiled than roasted (elixus quam assus). Anchored to Theopropides + Tranio at the altar; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Si amicus Diphilo aut Philemoni es, dicito eis, quo pacto tuos te servos ludificaverit: optumas frustrationes dederis in comoediis.
question: Quos duos poetas comicos Tranio in Mostellaria nominat, quibus Theopropides ludificationes suas pro argumento comoediarum narrare possit?
question_en: Which two comic poets does Tranio name in the Mostellaria, to whom Theopropides could tell his gullings as material for comedies?
derivation: Canonical literary fact: the Greek New Comedy poets Diphilus and Philemon named on the Roman stage — the more pointed since Philemon's Phasma is held to be the Greek original of the Mostellaria itself. Anchored to Tranio; two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: faenus, sortem sumptumque omnem, qui amica empta est, omnia nos dabimus, nos conferemus, nostro sumptu, non tuo.
question: Quis Theopropidi promisit sodales Philolachis faenus sortemque et omnem sumptum collaturos esse, ut filio ignosceretur?
question_en: Who promised Theopropides that Philolaches' companions would contribute the interest, the principal, and all the expense, so that the son might be forgiven?
derivation: The resolution of the play: Callidamates, the son's sodalis and chosen spokesman of the club (de sodalitate solus orator datus, v. 1152), pledges that the friends will repay principal, interest, and the cost of the amica — and wins the father's pardon. Anchored to Callidamates + Theopropides; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: TH. Quanti? PHAN. Triginta. TH. Talentis? PHAN. Ma ton Apollo, sed minis.
question: Quem deum Phaniscus, Graeca voce iurans, testatur, cum Philematium triginta minis, non talentis, liberatam esse affirmat?
question_en: By which god does Phaniscus swear, in Greek, when he affirms that Philematium was freed for thirty minae, not talents?
derivation: The Greek oath ma ton Apollo dropped into the Latin line — the code-switching of comedy's Greek world, with Apollo as the oath-god; the exchange also reconfirms the thirty-minae price of Philematium's freedom. Anchored to Phaniscus + Philematium; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: CALL. Sine te exorem. TH. Age abi, abi impune. em huic habeto gratiam. spectatores, fabula haec est acta, vos plausum date.
question: Quo exitu Tranio servus in fine Mostellariae e poena evasit?
question_en: With what outcome did the slave Tranio escape punishment at the end of the Mostellaria?
answer_en: He was let off scot-free, at Callidamates' intercession.
derivation: The amnesty ending: the master, worn down by the intercessor, dismisses Tranio unpunished (abi impune) — Tranio having quipped that he will earn a fresh offense tomorrow to be punished for both at once. Canonical close of the play; anchored to Tranio + Callidamates; verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Leno me peregre militi Macedonio minis viginti vendidit, voluptas mea.
question: Quanti leno Ballio Phoenicium militi Macedonio apud Plautum in Pseudolo vendidit?
question_en: For how much did the pimp Ballio sell Phoenicium to the Macedonian soldier in Plautus' Pseudolus?
derivation: The price that drives the whole plot, stated in Phoenicium's letter: the leno sold her abroad to a Macedonian soldier for twenty minae. Anchored to the named play, girl, and buyer; single-number answer verbatim (minis viginti).

author: Plautus
source_text: et prius quam hinc abiit, quindecim miles minas dederat; nunc unae quinque remorantur minae.
question: Quot minas miles Macedonius, qui Phoenicium viginti minis emerat, lenoni in Pseudolo Plauti adhuc debebat?
question_en: How many minae did the Macedonian soldier, who had bought Phoenicium for twenty minae, still owe the pimp in Plautus' Pseudolus?
derivation: The down-payment arithmetic of the plot: fifteen minae paid, five outstanding — the five minae Pseudolus will intercept. Anchored to soldier + Phoenicium + leno; single-number answer verbatim (unae quinque... minae).

author: Plautus
source_text: ea causa miles hic reliquit symbolum, expressam in cera ex anulo suam imaginem, ut qui huc adferret eius similem symbolum, cum eo simul me mitteret.
question: Quod symbolum miles Macedonius apud lenonem in Pseudolo Plauti reliquit, ut qui simile attulisset Phoenicium abduceret?
answer: Imaginem suam ex anulo in cera expressam.
question_en: What token did the Macedonian soldier leave with the pimp in Plautus' Pseudolus, so that whoever brought its match might take Phoenicium away?
answer_en: His own likeness stamped in wax from his signet ring.
derivation: The seal-token (symbolus) mechanism of the play, and a clean piece of realia: identity verified by matching a wax impression of a signet ring. Anchored to the soldier + Phoenicium; short answer verbatim (expressam in cera ex anulo suam imaginem).

author: Plautus
source_text: ei rei dies haec praestituta est, proxuma Dionysia.
question: Quo die praestituto Phoenicium militi Macedonio a lenone tradenda erat apud Plautum in Pseudolo?
question_en: On what appointed day was Phoenicium to be handed over by the pimp to the Macedonian soldier in Plautus' Pseudolus?
derivation: The festival frame of the plot: the deadline for the transaction is the Dionysia, the Greek festival of Dionysus — the Greek-calendar setting of the palliata. Anchored to Phoenicium + soldier + leno; one-festival answer verbatim (proxuma Dionysia).

author: Plautus
source_text: Phoenicium Calidoro amatori suo per ceram et lignum litterasque interpretes salutem mittit et salutem abs te expetit.
question: Quae meretrix apud Plautum in Pseudolo Calidoro amatori suo per ceram et lignum salutem mittit?
question_en: Which courtesan in Plautus' Pseudolus sends greetings to her lover Calidorus 'through wax and wood'?
derivation: The tear-stained wax-tablet letter that opens the play, with its salutation naming both lovers — and the realia of the tabellae ('wax and wood and letters as go-betweens'). Anchored to Calidorus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc, ne quis dictum sibi neget, dico omnibus pube praesenti in contione: omni poplo, omnibus amicis notisque edico meis, in hunc diem a me ut caveant, ne credant mihi.
question: Quid Pseudolus servus in Pseudolo Plauti omni poplo amicisque suis palam edicit?
answer: Vt in eum diem ab se caveant.
question_en: What does the slave Pseudolus openly proclaim to the whole people and his friends in Plautus' Pseudolus?
answer_en: That for that day they should beware of him.
derivation: The arch clever-slave's signature gesture: a mock public edict warning everyone that he is going to cheat someone today. A celebrated set-piece of the play; anchored to Pseudolus; short answer supported verbatim (a me ut caveant, ne credant mihi). [Answer trimmed to the core warning during validation.]

author: Plautus
source_text: atque hoc, ne dictum tibi neges, dico prius: si neminem alium potero, tuom tangam patrem.
question: Quem Pseudolus servus, si neminem alium possit, argenti causa se tacturum esse Calidoro praedicit?
question_en: Whom does the slave Pseudolus forewarn Calidorus he will fleece for the money, if he can manage no one else?
derivation: The clever slave announces in advance that his victim will be his master's father (Simo) — the classic servus callidus versus senex configuration. Anchored to Pseudolus + Calidorus; short answer verbatim (tuom tangam patrem).

author: Plautus
source_text: nam mi hodie natalis dies est, decet eum omnis vos concelebrare.
question: Quo die fabula Plauti Pseudolus agitur, ut Ballio leno ipse declarat?
question_en: On what day does Plautus' play Pseudolus take place, as the pimp Ballio himself declares?
derivation: The play's one-day action falls on Ballio's birthday, declared in his entrance monologue — the reason for the feast, the cook, and the presents demanded of his women. A canonical frame-fact of the play; anchored to Ballio; short answer verbatim (mi hodie natalis dies est).

author: Plautus
source_text: pernam callum glandium sumen facito in aqua iaceant. satin audis?
question: Quae obsonia Ballio leno die natali suo in aqua iacere famulos apud Plautum iubet?
question_en: What pork delicacies does the pimp Ballio order his servants to lay in water (to soak) for his birthday in Plautus?
answer_en: Ham, pork rind, neck-glands, and sow's udder.
derivation: Roman festive food realia in Ballio's household orders: the four salted pork delicacies (perna, callum, glandium, sumen — sow's udder the classic luxury) put to soak before cooking. Anchored to Ballio + his birthday; list answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ego eo in macellum, ut piscium quidquid ibist pretio praestinem.
question: Quo Ballio leno, ut pisces pretio praestinet, die natali suo se iturum esse dicit?
question_en: Where does the pimp Ballio say he will go on his birthday to buy up whatever fish are there?
answer_en: To the macellum, the provision market.
derivation: Daily-life realia: fish for a feast is bought at the macellum, the food market. Anchored to Ballio + his birthday preparations; one-word answer verbatim (in macellum).

author: Plautus
source_text: cras te quasi Dircam olim, ut memorant, duo gnati Iovis devinxere ad taurum, item ego te distringam ad carnarium.
question: Quam mulierem duo gnati Iovis, ut apud Plautum in Pseudolo memoratur, olim ad taurum devinxerunt?
question_en: Which woman did the two sons of Jupiter, as recalled in Plautus' Pseudolus, once bind to a bull?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Ballio's threat assumes the audience knows that Amphion and Zethus, the twin sons of Jupiter, punished Dirce by tying her to a bull. Anchored to Dirce + the sons of Jupiter; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ita ego vestra latera loris faciam ut valide varia sint, ut ne peristromata quidem aeque picta sint Campanica neque Alexandrina beluata tonsilia tappetia.
question: Quibus e regionibus peristromata picta et tappetia beluata Ballio leno apud Plautum in Pseudolo nominat?
question_en: From which regions do the embroidered coverlets and beast-figured tapestries come that the pimp Ballio names in Plautus' Pseudolus?
derivation: Luxury-textile realia embedded in the whip-threat: Campanian coverlets (peristromata Campanica) and Alexandrian tapestries figured with animals (Alexandrina beluata tappetia) as bywords for variegated color. Anchored to Ballio; two-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: tu qui urnam habes aquam ingere, face plenum ahenum sit coco.
question: Quod vas servus aquarius in familia Ballionis lenonis coco plenum facere iubetur?
question_en: What vessel is the water-carrying slave in the pimp Ballio's household ordered to fill for the cook?
derivation: Household-organization realia from Ballio's task-drill: the slave with the urna must carry water and fill the bronze cooking-cauldron for the cook. Anchored to Ballio's household + the cook; one-word answer verbatim (plenum ahenum sit coco).

author: Plautus
source_text: tu esto lectisterniator. tu argentum eluito, idem exstruito.
question: Quo nomine servus qui lectos convivio sternit in Ballionis familia apud Plautum appellatur?
question_en: By what title is the slave who spreads the couches for the banquet called in Ballio's household in Plautus?
derivation: A named household office from Ballio's job-assignments: the lectisterniator who makes up the dining couches (beside the slave who washes and sets out the silver). Job-title realia of the Roman banquet; anchored to Ballio's household; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: principio, Hedytium, tecum ago, quae amica es frumentariis, quibus cunctis montes maxumi acervi frumenti sunt domi: fac sis sit delatum huc mihi frumentum, hunc annum quod satis.
question: Quae e mulieribus Ballionis lenonis, frumentariorum amica, frumentum in annum satis deferendum curare iubetur?
question_en: Which of the pimp Ballio's women, the mistress of the grain-dealers, is ordered to see that grain enough for a year is delivered?
derivation: The set-piece roll-call of Ballio's courtesans by their lovers' trades: Hedytium serves the frumentarii and must levy a year's grain as a birthday gift. Anchored to Ballio + the named woman + the trade; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Aeschrodora, tu quae amicos tibi habes lenonum aemulos lanios, qui, item ut nos iurando, iure malo male quaerunt rem, audi: nisi carnaria tria gravida tegoribus onere uberi hodie mihi erunt, cras te quasi Dircam olim, ut memorant, duo gnati Iovis devinxere ad taurum, item ego te distringam ad carnarium.
question: Quot carnaria tegoribus gravida Ballio leno ab Aeschrodora, quae lanios amicos habet, die natali suo exigit?
question_en: How many meat-racks laden with sides of meat does the pimp Ballio demand on his birthday from Aeschrodora, whose lovers are butchers?
derivation: Second entry of the roll-call: Aeschrodora's butcher lovers (lanii, jokingly 'the pimps' rivals') must fill three carnaria with meat. Anchored to Ballio + Aeschrodora + the butchers; single-number answer verbatim (carnaria tria).

author: Plautus
source_text: Xystilis, fac ut animum advortas, quoius amatores olivi denamin domi habent maxumam. si mihi non iam huc culleis oleum deportatum erit, te ipsam culleo ego cras faciam ut deportere—in pergulam.
question: Quam mercem amatores Xystilidis, mulieris Ballionis lenonis, culleis deportare apud Plautum iubentur?
question_en: What commodity are the lovers of Xystilis, one of the pimp Ballio's women, ordered to deliver in leather sacks in Plautus?
derivation: Third entry of the roll-call: Xystilis' lovers are oil-magnates and must send oil by the culleus (the great leather sack, the standard bulk container). Trade-realia of the oil business; anchored to Ballio + Xystilis; one-word answer verbatim (oleum).

author: Plautus
source_text: atque adeo ut frumento afluam, ut civitas nomen mihi commutet meque ut praedicet lenone ex Ballione regem Iasonem.
question: Quem regem se pro Ballione lenone civitatem praedicaturam esse Ballio iactat, si frumento affluat?
question_en: What king does Ballio boast the city will proclaim him in place of 'Ballio the pimp,' if he overflows with grain?
derivation: Ballio's boast turns on Jason (the fabulously rich tyrant of Pherae, for the audience a byword for wealth): with enough grain the city would rename the leno 'King Jason.' Anchored to Ballio + the named king; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam si sacruficem summo Iovi atque in manibus exta teneam, ut poriciam, interea loci si lucri quid detur, potius rem divinam deseram.
question: Quid Ballio leno apud Plautum se deserturum esse profitetur, si inter exta porricienda lucri quid detur?
question_en: What does the pimp Ballio in Plautus profess he would abandon, if any profit were offered while he was presenting the entrails?
derivation: The defining creed of the model pimp of Latin literature: he would drop a sacrifice to Jupiter, entrails already in hand, for profit. Anchored to Ballio + Jupiter; short answer verbatim (rem divinam deseram).

author: Plautus
source_text: Eme die caeca hercle olivom, id vendito oculata die: iam hercle vel ducentae fieri possunt praesentes minae.
question: Qua 'die' emere et qua vendere olivom Ballio leno proverbialiter suadet, ut ducentae minae praesentes fiant?
answer: Caeca die emere, oculata die vendere.
question_en: On what 'day' does the pimp Ballio proverbially advise buying olive oil, and on what 'day' selling it, to make two hundred minae in ready cash?
answer_en: Buy on the 'blind day' (on credit), sell on the 'seeing day' (for cash down).
derivation: The proverbial merchant's formula caeca die emere, oculata die vendere — buy on credit (the day that does not see the money), sell for cash. Commercial proverb verbatim in the text; anchored to Ballio's advice.

author: Plautus
source_text: Perii, annorum lex me perdit quinavicenaria. metuont credere omnes.
question: Quae lex, ut Calidorus adulescens apud Plautum in Pseudolo queritur, efficit ut omnes ei pecuniam credere metuant?
question_en: Which law, as the young Calidorus complains in Plautus' Pseudolus, makes everyone afraid to lend him money?
answer_en: The 'twenty-five-year law' (the law protecting minors under twenty-five).
derivation: A famous piece of legal realia: the lex quinavicenaria — the law on minors under twenty-five (the lex Plaetoria), which made loans to young men unrecoverable, so no one would lend. Anchored to Calidorus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam istuc quod nunc lamentare, non esse argentum tibi, apud novercam querere.
question: Apud quam personam frustra queri aliquem proverbio apud Plautum in Pseudolo dicitur?
question_en: Before what figure is one proverbially said, in Plautus' Pseudolus, to be complaining in vain?
derivation: The proverb apud novercam queri — to complain where no pity is to be had, resting on the stepmother's proverbial hard-heartedness. Spoken by Ballio to Calidorus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quia pol qua opera credam tibi, una opera alligem fugitivam canem agninis lactibus.
question: Cui rei Ballio leno fidem Pseudolo servo habere apud Plautum comparat?
question_en: To what does the pimp Ballio compare putting trust in the slave Pseudolus in Plautus?
answer_en: Tying up a runaway dog with a leash of lamb's guts.
derivation: Proverbial comparison for a futile precaution: a runaway dog leashed with lamb's intestines (which it will eat). Anchored to Ballio + Pseudolus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: iuravistin te illam nulli venditurum nisi mihi? BAL. Fateor. CAL. Nempe conceptis verbis? BAL. Etiam consutis quoque.
question: Cui soli Ballio leno Phoenicium se venditurum esse conceptis verbis iuraverat, ut in Pseudolo Plauti fatetur?
question_en: To whom alone had the pimp Ballio sworn in due form of words that he would sell Phoenicium, as he admits in Plautus' Pseudolus?
derivation: The broken oath that brands Ballio periuri caput: he had sworn conceptis verbis (in the formal wording of an oath) to sell Phoenicium to no one but Calidorus, then sold her to the soldier. Anchored to all three parties; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: numquam ad praetorem aeque cursim curram, ut emittar manu.
question: Ad quem magistratum servus manu emittendus, ut Pseudolus apud Plautum significat, currere solet?
question_en: To which magistrate, as Pseudolus indicates in Plautus, does a slave about to be freed run?
derivation: Roman legal realia dropped into the Greek setting: manumission (emitti manu) is performed before the praetor, and no slave ever ran to him as fast as Pseudolus will run to abuse Ballio. Anchored to Pseudolus + the office; one-office answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: In pertusum ingerimus dicta dolium, operam ludimus.
question: In quale vas dicta frustra ingeri Pseudolus proverbialiter ait, cum Ballio maledictis nihil moveatur?
question_en: Into what kind of vessel does Pseudolus proverbially say their words are being poured to no purpose, since Ballio is unmoved by all the insults?
answer_en: Into a jar full of holes (a leaky jar).
derivation: The proverb of wasted effort — pouring into the perforated dolium (the image of the Danaids' jar) — capping the famous insult-litany that Ballio cheerfully absorbs. Anchored to Pseudolus + Ballio; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed quasi poeta, tabulas cum cepit sibi, quaerit quod nusquamst gentium, reperit tamen, facit illud veri simile, quod mendacium est, nunc ego poeta fiam: viginti minas, quae nusquam nunc sunt gentium, inveniam tamen.
question: Cui artifici Pseudolus servus se ipse comparat, cum viginti minas quae nusquam gentium sint inventurus sit?
question_en: To what maker does the slave Pseudolus compare himself, when he must find twenty minae that exist nowhere on earth?
derivation: The celebrated metatheatrical monologue: the clever slave 'will become a poet' — one who seeks what exists nowhere, finds it, and makes the lie plausible. A canonical fame-fact of the play; anchored to Pseudolus + the twenty minae; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: bonus animus in mala re dimidiumst mali.
question: Quid in mala re dimidium mali esse apud Plautum in Pseudolo proverbio dicitur?
question_en: What, according to the proverb in Plautus' Pseudolus, is 'half the evil' in a bad situation (i.e. halves the trouble)?
derivation: A quotable Plautine sententia spoken by Callipho: courage in adversity halves the adversity. Proverb verbatim; short answer (bonus animus).

author: Plautus
source_text: SIM. Ecquas viginti minas per sycophantiam atque per doctos dolos paritas ut auferas a me? PS. Abs te ego auferam? SIM. Ita, quas meo gnato des, qui amicam liberet?
question: Quot minas Pseudolus servus per sycophantiam a Simone ero suo auferre parat, quas Calidoro det ad amicam liberandam?
question_en: How many minae does the slave Pseudolus set out to take by trickery from his master Simo, to give Calidorus for freeing his sweetheart?
derivation: The famous stake of the play: the twenty minae Pseudolus openly announces he will trick out of Simo — the sum Simo in the end must pay. Anchored to Pseudolus + Simo + Calidorus; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Siquidem istaec opera, ut praedicas, perfeceris, virtute regi Agathocli antecesseris.
question: Cui regi Pseudolum virtute antecessurum esse Simo senex ait, si quae praedicat perfecerit?
question_en: Which king does old Simo say Pseudolus will have surpassed in prowess, if he accomplishes what he proclaims?
derivation: Agathocles of Syracuse as the proverbial self-made king of great exploits: Simo says success would rank the slave above him. Anchored to Simo + Pseudolus + the named king; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed si non faxis, numquid causaest, ilico quin te in pistrinum condam?
question: Quo Simo senex Pseudolum se conditurum esse minatur, nisi quae promisit perfecerit?
question_en: Where does old Simo threaten to shut Pseudolus up, if he does not accomplish what he has promised?
derivation: The penalty side of the wager, and standing Roman realia: the pistrinum, the grinding-mill, as the standard punishment for a slave. Anchored to Simo + Pseudolus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam qui in scaenam provenit, novo modo novom aliquid inventum adferre addecet; si id facere nequeat, det locum illi qui queat.
question: Quid eum qui in scaenam provenit adferre addecere Pseudolus apud Plautum pronuntiat?
question_en: What does Pseudolus in Plautus declare it befits the man who comes on stage to bring?
answer_en: Something newly invented, in a new way.
derivation: A celebrated statement of the comic poet's creed, put in the slave's mouth: whoever takes the stage owes the audience novelty, or should yield to one who can supply it. Theater-convention fact; anchored to Pseudolus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: tibicen vos interibi hic delectaverit.
question: Quis spectatores fabulae Plautinae interea delectat, dum Pseudolus intro abiit, ut ipse abiens promittit?
question_en: Who entertains the spectators of the Plautine play in the meantime, while Pseudolus has gone inside, as he himself promises on leaving?
derivation: A rare explicit attestation of Roman stage practice: during a pause in the action the tibicen plays for the audience. Anchored to the play + Pseudolus' announcement; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: HARP. Tune es Ballio? PS. Immo vero ego eius sum Subballio. HARP. Quid istuc verbist? PS. Condus promus sum, procurator peni.
question: Quod munus domesticum Pseudolus, cum Subballionem se nominat, se gerere Harpaci mentitur?
question_en: What household office does Pseudolus, styling himself 'Subballio,' falsely claim to Harpax that he holds?
answer_en: Storeroom-keeper and dispenser, manager of the provisions.
derivation: Household-staff realia: the condus promus, the slave who stores and issues the provisions (penus), ranking even above the atriensis in Pseudolus' boast. Anchored to Pseudolus + Harpax; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed quid est tibi nomen? HARP. Harpax. PS. Apage te, Harpax, hau places; huc quidem hercle haud ibis intro, ne quid harpax feceris. HARP. Hostis vivos rapere soleo ex acie: eo hoc nomen mihi est.
question: Cur cacula militis Macedonii in Pseudolo Plauti Harpax nominari se ipse explicat?
answer: Quia hostis vivos ex acie rapere solet.
question_en: Why does the Macedonian soldier's orderly in Plautus' Pseudolus explain that he himself is called Harpax?
answer_en: Because he is wont to snatch enemies alive out of the battle line.
derivation: The canonical name-fact of the play: Harpax 'the Snatcher' explains his own name by his battlefield snatching. The explanation is given in the text itself, so it survives translation. Anchored to the named character; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ego devortor extra portam huc in tabernam tertiam, apud anum illam doliarem, claudam crassam, Chrysidem.
question: Apud quam anum cauponam Harpax extra portam in taberna tertia devorti se dicit?
question_en: With which old hostess does Harpax say he is lodging, at the third inn outside the gate?
derivation: Traveler's realia: lodging at a taberna outside the city gate, kept by a named old innkeeper (Chrysis 'shaped like a storage-jar, lame and fat') — where Harpax waits to be summoned, letting the impersonation proceed. Anchored to Harpax + the named hostess; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: centum doctum hominum consilia sola haec devincit dea, Fortuna.
question: Quae dea una centum doctorum hominum consilia devincere apud Plautum in Pseudolo dicitur?
question_en: Which goddess alone is said in Plautus' Pseudolus to defeat the plans of a hundred learned men?
derivation: A quotable Plautine sententia from Pseudolus' mock-philosophical monologue: Fortune beats the schemes of a hundred wise men. Anchored to the named goddess; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc ego hac epistula tris deludam, erum et lenonem et qui hanc dedit mi epistulam.
question: Quot homines Pseudolus una epistula intercepta se delusurum esse gloriatur?
question_en: How many men does Pseudolus boast he will dupe with the one intercepted letter?
answer_en: Three (his master, the pimp, and the man who handed him the letter).
derivation: The economy of the central trick, counted by Pseudolus himself: one letter, three dupes — Simo, Ballio, Harpax. Anchored to Pseudolus + the letter; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: etiam opust chlamyde et machaera et petaso. CHAR. Possum a me dare.
question: Quibus tribus ornamentis ad militis caculam mentiendum opus esse Pseudolus Charino dicit?
question_en: What three pieces of gear does Pseudolus tell Charinus are needed to impersonate the soldier's orderly?
answer_en: A military cloak, a sword, and a traveling hat (chlamys, machaera, petasus).
derivation: The stage-soldier's costume kit, itemized: the Greek chlamys, the machaera, and the broad petasus mark the military traveler. Dress realia of the palliata; anchored to Pseudolus + Charinus + the impersonation plot; three-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quid, si opus sit ut dulce promat indidem, ecquid habet? CH. Rogas? murrinam, passum, defrutum, mellam, mel quoivismodi.
question: Quae dulcia Charinus apud Plautum in Pseudolo enumerat, cum servum suum ex pectore ea promere posse iactat?
question_en: What sweet things does Charinus list in Plautus' Pseudolus, when he boasts his slave can dispense them from his breast?
answer_en: Spiced myrrh-wine, raisin wine, boiled-down must, honey-wine, and honey of every kind.
derivation: A catalogue of the standard Roman sweet drinks — murrina, passum, defrutum, mella — capped by 'honey of every sort,' the stock of a whole pantopolium. Food-and-drink realia; anchored to Charinus + the play; list answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quid cum manifesto tenetur? CHAR. Anguillast, elabitur.
question: Cui animali homo lubricus, qui cum manifesto tenetur elabitur, apud Plautum in Pseudolo comparatur?
question_en: To what animal is the slippery fellow who, even when caught red-handed, slips away compared in Plautus' Pseudolus?
derivation: The proverbial eel: the character who escapes even when caught in the act 'is an eel — he slips away.' Proverbial comparison verbatim; anchored via Charinus' praise of the trickster-slave.

author: Plautus
source_text: omnes ordine sub signis ducam legiones meas, avi sinistra, auspicio liquido atque ex mea sententia.
question: Qua avi, dextra an sinistra, auspicium prosperum esse Pseudolus, legiones suas ducturus, significat?
question_en: With the bird on which side, right or left, does Pseudolus, about to lead out his 'legions,' indicate that the auspices are favorable?
answer_en: With the bird on the left.
derivation: Roman augural realia in the slave's mock-triumphal language: in Roman practice the bird on the left (avis sinistra) is the favorable sign, paired here with auspicio liquido, 'a clear auspice.' Anchored to Pseudolus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Forum coquinum qui vocant, stulte vocant, nam non coquinum est, verum furinum est forum.
question: Quo in foro coqui apud Plautum in Pseudolo conduci solent?
question_en: In what market are cooks customarily hired in Plautus' Pseudolus?
answer_en: In the forum coquinum, the cooks' market.
derivation: The cook-market realia: cooks were hired for the day at a dedicated market, the forum coquinum — which Ballio, returning with his hire, jokes should rather be called furinum, 'the thieves' market.' Anchored to Ballio + the named institution; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: hoc ego fui hodie solus obsessor fori. illi drachmissent miseri: me nemo potest minoris quisquam nummo ut surgam subigere.
question: Quo pretio coqui vulgares in foro coquino, ut coquos a Ballione conductus narrat, se locare solebant?
question_en: At what price did the common cooks in the cooks' market hire themselves out, as the cook Ballio hired relates?
derivation: The wage realia of the cook-market: the ordinary cooks 'would go for a drachma' (drachmissent), while this self-styled master will not stand up for less than a nummus (a two-drachma piece). Anchored to the forum-coquinum scene + Ballio's cook; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: indunt coriandrum, feniculum, alium, atrum holus, apponunt rumicem, brassicam, betam, blitum, eo laserpici libram pondo diluont.
question: Quantum laserpici coqui alii, ut eos coquos Ballionis vituperat, in patinas diluere solent?
question_en: How much silphium-juice do the other cooks dissolve into their dishes, as Ballio's cook derides them?
derivation: The seasoning satire of the cook scene: rival cooks serve 'seasoned meadows' — coriander, fennel, garlic, herbs — and melt in a full pound of laserpicium (silphium), the celebrated and costly condiment. Anchored to the cook's tirade; measure answer verbatim (libram pondo).

author: Plautus
source_text: nam vel ducenos annos poterunt vivere meas qui essitabunt escas quas condivero.
question: Quot annos vivere poterunt qui escas coqui a Ballione conducti essitabunt, ut ipse coquos gloriatur?
question_en: How many years will those be able to live who eat the dishes of the cook Ballio hired, as the cook himself boasts?
derivation: The gloriosus-cook's boast, satirizing gourmet quackery: his divine seasonings prolong life to two hundred years. Anchored to Ballio's cook; single-number answer verbatim (vel ducenos annos).

author: Plautus
source_text: haec ad Neptuni pecudes condimenta sunt: terrestris pecudes cicimalindro condio, hapalocopide aut cataractria.
question: Quae animalia coquos gloriosus apud Plautum in Pseudolo 'Neptuni pecudes' vocat?
question_en: What creatures does the boastful cook in Plautus' Pseudolus call 'Neptune's flocks'?
derivation: The kenning Neptuni pecudes for seafood, set explicitly against terrestres pecudes (land animals) in the cook's list of invented condiments. Anchored to the cook scene + Neptune; one-word answer supported by the verbatim contrast.

author: Plautus
source_text: eum odorem cenat Iuppiter cottidie. BAL. Si nusquam is coctum, quidnam cenat Iuppiter? COC. It incenatus cubitum.
question: Quid Iuppiter cottidie cenare dicitur, ut coquos a Ballione conductus gloriatur?
question_en: What is Jupiter said to dine on every day, according to the boast of the cook Ballio hired?
derivation: The famous punchline of the cook scene: Jupiter dines daily on the smell of his cooking — and goes to bed dinnerless when the cook is not hired. Anchored to the cook + Jupiter; short answer verbatim (eum odorem cenat Iuppiter).

author: Plautus
source_text: An tu invenire postulas quemquam coquom nisi miluinis aut aquilinis ungulis?
question: Quibus unguibus omnem coquom praeditum esse apud Plautum in Pseudolo dicitur?
question_en: With what kind of talons is every cook said to come equipped, in Plautus' Pseudolus?
derivation: The thieving-cook topos stated as a rule by the cook himself: no cook exists without the claws of the raptor birds. A proverbial-style characterization of the trade; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quia sorbitione faciam ego hodie te mea, item ut Medea Peliam concoxit senem, quem medicamento et suis venenis dicitur fecisse rursus ex sene adulescentulum, item ego te faciam.
question: Quem senem Medea medicamento et venenis suis ex sene adulescentulum rursus fecisse apud Plautum dicitur?
question_en: What old man is Medea said, in Plautus, to have made young again from an old man by her drugs and potions?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Medea 'boiled down' old Pelias — the rejuvenation-cauldron tale, cited by the cook as the model for his life-giving broth. Anchored to Medea + Pelias; one-name answer verbatim; dicitur keeps the as-the-story-goes frame.

author: Plautus
source_text: Minus malum hunc hominem esse opinor quam esse censebam coquom, nam nihil etiam dum harpagavit praeter cyathum et cantharum.
question: Quae duo vasa coquos conductus Ballioni lenoni, ut ipse leno ait, iam harpagaverat?
question_en: Which two vessels had the hired cook already pilfered from the pimp Ballio, by the pimp's own account?
derivation: The thieving-cook joke made concrete with named drinking-ware: the cyathus (dipper for serving wine) and cantharus (large cup) are the first things to vanish. Anchored to Ballio + his cook; two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Oh, Polymachaeroplagides purus putus est ipsus. novi. heus, Polymachaeroplagides nomen est.
question: Quod nomen erat militi Macedonio qui Phoenicium a Ballione lenone viginti minis emerat?
question_en: What was the name of the Macedonian soldier who had bought Phoenicium from the pimp Ballio for twenty minae?
derivation: The soldier's grandiose comic name ('son of many-sword-blows'), revealed when Ballio reads the seal on the letter. A canonical name-fact of the play; anchored to Ballio + Phoenicium; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ita militaris disciplinast, Ballio: manu salutem mittunt benevolentibus; eadem malam rem mittunt malevolentibus.
question: Qua re milites, ut militaris disciplina apud Plautum in Pseudolo fertur, salutem benevolentibus mittunt?
question_en: By what means do soldiers send their greeting to well-wishers, according to 'military discipline' as reported in Plautus' Pseudolus?
derivation: The mock-explanation for the letter's missing salutation: soldiers greet friends — and punish enemies — with the hand, not with written compliments. A crisp military-mores quip anchored to the letter scene; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Si de damnosis aut si de amatoribus dictator fiat nunc Athenis Atticis, nemo anteveniat filio, credo, meo.
question: In qua urbe fabula Plauti quae Pseudolus inscribitur agitur?
question_en: In what city is Plautus' play entitled Pseudolus set?
derivation: The setting of the play: Simo speaks of 'now at Attic Athens,' and the characters repeatedly name Athens as the here of the action. Anchored to the named play; one-place answer verbatim (Athenis Atticis).

author: Plautus
source_text: Pauci istuc faciunt homines quod tu praedicas, nam in foro vix decumus quisque est qui ipsus sese noverit.
question: Quotus quisque in foro, ut Simia apud Plautum in Pseudolo philosophatur, ipse sese novit?
question_en: How many a man in the forum, as Simia philosophizes in Plautus' Pseudolus, actually knows himself?
derivation: A Plautine sententia playing on the Delphic 'know thyself': hardly every tenth man in the forum knows himself. Quotable maxim; anchored to Simia + the play; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: SIMIA Ne plora, nescis ut res sit, Phoenicium, verum haud multo post faxo scibis accubans. non ego te ad illum duco dentatum virum Macedoniensem, qui te nunc flentem facit: cuiam esse te vis maxime, ad eum ducere: Calidorum haud multo post faxo amplexabere.
question: Quis servus, subditicius Harpax a Pseudolo exornatus, Phoenicium a Ballione abductam ad Calidorum duxit?
question_en: Which slave, dressed up by Pseudolus as a counterfeit Harpax, led Phoenicium away from Ballio and brought her to Calidorus?
derivation: The central impersonation of the play: Simia ('the Monkey'), the sharp slave borrowed from Charinus, plays the fake Harpax, delivers the token and five minae, and walks off with Phoenicium for Calidorus. Anchored to all named parties; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: quin hinc metimur gradibus militariis? PS. Atque edepol, quamquam nequam homo es, recte mones. ite hac triumphi ad cantharum recta via.
question: Quo Pseudolus, muliere e manibus lenonis erepta, triumphi recta via ire iubet?
question_en: Where does Pseudolus, once the woman has been snatched from the pimp's hands, order the march to go 'in triumph, straight ahead'?
derivation: The slave's mock-triumph: victory over Ballio is celebrated in Roman triumphal language — military paces, then 'this way in triumph' — with the cantharus as the goal. Anchored to Pseudolus + the victory; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Viso quid rerum meus Vlixes egerit, iamne habeat signum ex arce Ballionia.
question: Cui heroi Simo senex Pseudolum comparat, cum visit iamne signum ex arce Ballionia habeat?
question_en: To which hero does old Simo compare Pseudolus, when he goes to see whether he yet has the 'statue from the Ballionian citadel'?
derivation: Simo casts Pseudolus as 'my Ulysses' and the trick as the theft of the signum (the Palladium) from the citadel — the shared myth of Ulysses stealing Troy's talisman, transferred to 'the citadel of Ballio.' Anchored to Simo + Pseudolus + the hero; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Roga me viginti minas, si ille hodie illa sit potitus muliere sive eam tuo gnato hodie, ut promisit, dabit, roga opsecro hercle, gestio promittere. omnibus modis tibi esse rem ut salvam scias; atque etiam habeto mulierem dono tibi.
question: Quid Ballio leno Simoni ultro spopondit, si Pseudolus illo die muliere potitus esset?
question_en: What did the pimp Ballio of his own accord pledge to Simo, should Pseudolus get possession of the woman that day?
answer_en: Twenty minae — and the woman as a gift besides.
derivation: Ballio's rash counter-wager, sworn when he thinks the woman already safely handed to the soldier's man: twenty minae plus Phoenicium gratis if Pseudolus wins — exactly what he must then forfeit. Anchored to Ballio + Simo + Pseudolus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quanti te emit? HAR. Suarum in pugna virium victoria. nam ego eram domi imperator summus in patria mea.
question: Quo pacto miles Polymachaeroplagides Harpacem servom sibi comparavit, ut ipse Harpax respondet?
question_en: How did the soldier Polymachaeroplagides acquire Harpax as his slave, as Harpax himself answers?
answer_en: By the victory of his strength in battle (Harpax was a war captive).
derivation: Slavery realia: Harpax was not bought but captured in war — he claims he was supreme commander in his own country. War captivity as the source of slaves; anchored to both named men; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quotumo die ex Sicyone huc pervenisti? HAR. Altero ad meridie.
question: Quotumo die Harpax ex Sicyone Athenas se pervenisse Ballioni dicit?
question_en: On which day after setting out does Harpax tell Ballio he arrived from Sicyon to Athens?
answer_en: On the second day, by noon.
derivation: A travel-time fact fixing the geography: the soldier waits at Sicyon, a day and a half's journey from the Athens of the play. Anchored to Harpax + Sicyon; short answer verbatim (altero ad meridie).

author: Plautus
source_text: Rufus quidam, ventriosus, crassis suris, subniger, magno capite, acutis oculis, ore rubicundo, admodum magnis pedibus.
question: Quo colore capilli Pseudolus servus ab Harpace apud Ballionem describitur?
question_en: With what color of hair is the slave Pseudolus described by Harpax before Ballio?
derivation: The famous portrait of Pseudolus: red-haired, pot-bellied, thick-calved, swarthy, big-headed, sharp-eyed, ruddy-faced, enormous feet — the description by which Ballio recognizes who duped him ('you finished me when you said the feet'). The red hair of the comic slave; anchored to Pseudolus; one-word answer verbatim (rufus).

author: Plautus
source_text: Pseudolus mihi centuriata habuit capitis comitia.
question: Quae comitia de capite suo Pseudolum habuisse Ballio leno queritur?
question_en: What assembly does the pimp Ballio complain that Pseudolus has held over his life?
answer_en: A comitia centuriata (the Roman centuriate assembly).
derivation: Roman constitutional realia in a Greek costume: judgment on a citizen's caput belonged to the comitia centuriata, so the ruined Ballio says Pseudolus has held one over him. Anchored to Ballio + Pseudolus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc mihi certum est alio pacto Pseudolo insidias dare, quam in aliis comoediis fit, ubi cum stimulis aut flagris insidiantur.
question: Quibus rebus servis dolosis in aliis comoediis insidiari solitum esse Simo apud Plautum dicit?
question_en: With what implements does Simo in Plautus say people usually lie in wait for tricky slaves in other comedies?
derivation: A metatheatrical convention-fact: the stock comic ambush of the clever slave is with goads and whips — which Simo pointedly declines, bringing the twenty minae instead. Anchored to Simo + Pseudolus + the genre; two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: superavit dolum Troianum atque Vlixem Pseudolus.
question: Quem dolum atque quem heroem Pseudolus superavisse a Simone senex praedicatur?
question_en: What stratagem and what hero is Pseudolus declared by old Simo to have outdone?
answer_en: The Trojan trick (the wooden horse) and Ulysses.
derivation: The fame-line of the play: the slave's ruse tops the dolus Troianus — the horse — and its contriver Ulysses. Anchored to Pseudolus + the named myth; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: magnum hoc vitium vino est: pedes captat primum, luctator dolosust.
question: Quid vinum, quasi luctator dolosus, primum captare Pseudolus ebrius apud Plautum dicit?
question_en: What does wine, like a crafty wrestler, seize first, as the drunken Pseudolus says in Plautus?
derivation: A quotable Plautine sententia on drink: wine is a tricky wrestler — it goes for the feet first. Spoken by the staggering Pseudolus; anchored to him; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: unguenta atque odores, lemniscos, corollas dari dapsiles, non enim parce promi.
question: Quae deliciae in convivio, ubi Pseudolus victor acceptus est, dapsiles dari solitae esse memorantur?
question_en: What luxuries are recalled as lavishly handed round at the banquet where the victorious Pseudolus was entertained?
derivation: Banquet realia itemized: scented oils, perfumes, lemnisci (the ribbons hung from garlands), and the garlands themselves, given out unsparingly. Anchored to Pseudolus' victory-party narration; list answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nimis ex discipulina, quippe ego qui probe Ionica perdidici.
question: Quod genus saltandi Pseudolus se probe perdidicisse in convivio gloriatur?
question_en: What style of dancing does Pseudolus boast he has thoroughly mastered at the drinking-party?
derivation: Leisure-culture realia: the Ionica, the soft Ionic dance of the Greek symposium, which the drunk slave performs (and falls doing). Anchored to Pseudolus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: PS. Cum corona ebrium Pseudolum tuom.
question: Quo habitu Pseudolus victor in extrema fabula coram Simone ero apparet?
question_en: In what state does the victorious Pseudolus appear before his master Simo at the end of the play?
derivation: The canonical closing image of the play: the triumphant slave reels in from the party garlanded and drunk, belching in his master's face, to collect the wager. The corona is the banqueter's festal garland; anchored to Pseudolus + Simo; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Credo equidem potesse te, scelus, Massici montis uberrumos quattuor fructus ebibere in hora una. PS. Hiberna addito.
question: Cuius montis quattuor uberrumos fructus una hora Pseudolum ebibere posse Simo credit?
question_en: Of what mountain does Simo believe Pseudolus could drink down four most abundant vintages in a single hour?
derivation: Wine realia: Massic wine from Mons Massicus in Campania, one of the celebrated Italian crus, used as the measure of the slave's drinking (with his retort 'make them winter hours'). Anchored to Simo + Pseudolus + the named mountain; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: satin ultro et argentum aufert et me inridet? PS. Vae victis.
question: Quibus verbis proverbialibus Pseudolus Simonem victum, argentum umero ferentem, inridet?
question_en: With what proverbial words does Pseudolus mock the defeated Simo as he shoulders the money?
derivation: The famous Gallic taunt (the cry of Brennus over conquered Rome) flung by the slave at his own beaten master — proverb quoted verbatim in the text. Anchored to Pseudolus + Simo; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: verum si voltis adplaudere atque adprobare hunc gregem et fabulam, in crastinum vos vocabo.
question: Quo die Pseudolus spectatores, si gregem et fabulam adprobaverint, se vocaturum esse in fine fabulae promittit?
question_en: For what day does Pseudolus, at the end of the play, promise to invite the spectators, if they applaud the troupe and the play?
derivation: Theater-closing convention: the actor asks for applause for the grex (the acting company) and invites the audience back 'tomorrow.' Anchored to the play's epilogue; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: M. IUNIO. M. FIL. PR. URB. AC. M.
question: Quo praetore urbano fabulam Pseudolum Plauti actam esse didascalia tradit?
question_en: Under which urban praetor does the production notice say Plautus' Pseudolus was staged?
answer_en: Under Marcus Junius, son of Marcus.
derivation: The transmitted didascalia dates the premiere by the urban praetor M. Iunius M. fil. (191 BC, the year the Megalensian games dedicated the Magna Mater's temple) — a canonical literary-history fact of the play. Abbreviations of the notice kept verbatim; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: ita sum, ut videtis, splendens stella candida, signum quod semper tempore exoritur suo hic atque in caelo: nomen Arcturo est mihi.
question: Quod sidus in Rudente Plauti prologum loquitur?
question_en: Which star speaks the prologue in Plautus' Rudens?
derivation: The famous theatrical curiosity of the Rudens: the prologue-god is a constellation, the star Arcturus, who names himself (nomen Arcturo est mihi). Canonical literature-fact of the fabula palliata; anchored to the named play; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: qui est imperator divom atque hominum Iuppiter, is nos per gentis alium alia disparat, qui facta hominum, mores, pietatem et fidem noscamus, ut quemque adiuvet opulentia.
question: Quam ob causam Iuppiter stellas inter gentes hominum disparat, ut Arcturus in prologo Rudentis Plauti narrat?
answer: Vt facta hominum, mores, pietatem et fidem noscant.
question_en: For what purpose does Jupiter distribute the stars among the nations of men, as Arcturus recounts in the prologue of Plautus' Rudens?
answer_en: So that they may learn men's deeds, characters, piety, and good faith.
derivation: The moral bookkeeping of heaven: Jupiter stations stars among mortals as observers of human conduct. The celebrated theological conceit of the Rudens prologue; anchored to Jupiter + Arcturus + the play; answer is a brief purpose clause taken directly from the source.

author: Plautus
source_text: Qui falsas litis falsis testimoniis petunt quique in iure abiurant pecuniam, eorum referimus nomina exscripta ad Iovem;
question: Ad quem deum Arcturus in Rudente Plauti nomina periurorum exscripta referri dicit?
question_en: To which god does Arcturus in Plautus' Rudens say the written-out names of perjurers are reported?
derivation: The stars keep written lists of litigious perjurers and deliver them to Jupiter — the prologue's heavenly ledger. Anchored to Arcturus + the play; one-name answer verbatim (ad Iovem).

author: Plautus
source_text: primumdum huic esse nomen urbi Diphilus Cyrenas voluit.
question: Ex quo poeta Graeco Plautus fabulam Rudentem sumpsit, ut prologus ipse testatur?
question_en: From which Greek poet did Plautus take the play Rudens, as the prologue itself attests?
derivation: The prologue names Diphilus as the poet who set the play's city at Cyrene — the play's own statement of its Greek original. Canonical literary-history fact; anchored to the named play; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: primumdum huic esse nomen urbi Diphilus Cyrenas voluit. illic habitat Daemones in agro atque villa proxima propter mare,
question: Apud quam urbem fabula Plauti quae Rudens inscribitur agitur?
question_en: Near what city is Plautus' play called Rudens set?
derivation: The setting of the Rudens: the shore near Cyrene in North Africa, declared by the prologue. Anchored to the named play; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: illic habitat Daemones in agro atque villa proxima propter mare, senex, qui huc Athenis exul venit, hau malus;
question: Ex qua urbe Daemones senex, qui in Rudente Plauti prope mare Cyrenaeum villam habitat, exul venit?
question_en: From what city did the old man Daemones, who in Plautus' Rudens lives in a villa by the Cyrenean shore, come as an exile?
derivation: Daemones' backstory: an honest Athenian exile living by the sea at Cyrene, who lost his fortune through generosity. Anchored to the named character + play; one-place answer verbatim (Athenis exul venit).

author: Plautus
source_text: adulescens quidam civis huius Atticus eam vidit ire e ludo fidicinio domum, amare occepit: ad lenonem devenit, minis triginta sibi puellam destinat datque arrabonem et iure iurando alligat.
question: Quot minis Plesidippus adulescens Palaestram puellam a lenone in Rudente Plauti sibi destinavit?
question_en: For how many minae did the young man Plesidippus contract to buy the girl Palaestra from the pimp in Plautus' Rudens?
derivation: The purchase price at the root of the plot: thirty minae, agreed with earnest money and an oath. A clean number fact; anchored to the named characters + play; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: minis triginta sibi puellam destinat datque arrabonem et iure iurando alligat.
question: Quo pignore Plesidippus emptionem Palaestrae apud lenonem Labracem in Rudente Plauti firmavit?
question_en: With what pledge did Plesidippus secure his purchase of Palaestra from the pimp Labrax in Plautus' Rudens?
derivation: The arrabo — the earnest money binding a sale, a standard institution of ancient commercial practice — plus an oath. Cultural-legal realia of buying and selling; anchored to the named characters; one-phrase answer verbatim (datque arrabonem).

author: Plautus
source_text: ei erat hospes par sui, Siculus senex scelestus, Agrigentinus, urbis proditor;
question: Ex qua urbe Sicula Charmides, hospes Labracis lenonis in Rudente Plauti, oriundus erat?
question_en: From what Sicilian city did Charmides, the guest-friend of the pimp Labrax in Plautus' Rudens, come?
derivation: The leno's rascally guest is a Sicilian of Agrigentum, 'betrayer of his city.' Anchored to the named characters + play; one-place answer verbatim (Agrigentinus).

author: Plautus
source_text: infit lenoni suadere, ut secum simul eat in Siciliam: ibi esse homines voluptarios dicit, potesse ibi eum fieri divitem.
question: Quo Charmides Labraci lenoni in Rudente Plauti persuasit ut meretrices navi aveheret?
question_en: To where did Charmides persuade the pimp Labrax in Plautus' Rudens to carry off his courtesans by ship?
derivation: The voyage that causes the shipwreck: Charmides talks Labrax into sailing for Sicily, where men are pleasure-loving and a pimp can grow rich. Anchored to the named characters; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ego quoniam video virginem asportarier, tetuli ei auxilium et lenoni exitium simul: increpui hibernum et fluctus movi maritimos.
question: Quod sidus in Rudente Plauti tempestatem movisse qua navis Labracis lenonis fracta est narrat?
question_en: Which star in Plautus' Rudens recounts that it raised the storm by which the pimp Labrax's ship was wrecked?
derivation: The divine machinery of the plot: Arcturus himself raised the winter storm to save the girl and destroy the pimp. Canonical fact of the play's design; anchored to the named star, pimp, and play; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam Arcturus signum sum omnium acerrimum: vehemens sum exoriens, cum occido vehementior.
question: Vtrum oriens an occidens Arcturus sidus vehementius esse apud Plautum in Rudente dicitur?
question_en: Is the star Arcturus said in Plautus' Rudens to be more violent at its rising or at its setting?
derivation: Ancient weather-lore: Arcturus was the proverbial storm-star (cf. Vergil's and Pliny's stormy Arcturus), and the prologue states the doctrine — fierce rising, fiercer setting. Shared star-calendar knowledge; anchored to Arcturus; one-word comparative answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: detexit ventus villam — quid verbis opust? non ventus fuit, verum Alcumena Euripidi, ita omnis de tecto deturbavit tegulas;
question: Cuius poetae tragoediam fuisse ventum qui villam Daemonis detexit Sceparnio servus in Rudente Plauti iocatur?
question_en: Which poet's tragedy does the slave Sceparnio in Plautus' Rudens joke the wind that unroofed Daemones' villa really was?
derivation: A celebrated literary allusion (and a testimonium for Euripides' lost Alcmene, evidently famous for its storm scene): the gale 'was no wind but Euripides' Alcumena.' Anchored to Sceparnio + the play; short two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Cererem te meliust quam Venerem sectarier: amori haec curat; tritico curat Ceres.
question: Cui rei Ceres dea curat, ut Sceparnio in Rudente Plauti ait, cum Venus amori curet?
question_en: What does the goddess Ceres look after, as Sceparnio says in Plautus' Rudens, while Venus looks after love?
derivation: The canonical division of divine provinces — Venus over love, Ceres over grain — stated as folk wisdom (the same pairing behind 'sine Cerere et Libero friget Venus'). Shared religious knowledge; anchored to the two named goddesses; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed, o Palaemon, sancte Neptuni comes, qui Herculis socius esse diceris,
question: Cuius dei sanctus comes Palaemon apud Plautum in Rudente invocatur?
question_en: Of which god is Palaemon invoked as holy companion in Plautus' Rudens?
derivation: Mythological attribute: Palaemon (the deified Melicertes) as sea-god in Neptune's train, invoked by Sceparnio watching the shipwrecked women. Shared myth knowledge; anchored to Palaemon + the play; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: AMP. Veneris fanum, obsecro, hoc est? PTOL. Fateor. ego huius fani sacerdos clueo.
question: Quo nomine sacerdos Veneris appellatur quae in Rudente Plauti Palaestram et Ampeliscam naufragas hospitio recipit?
question_en: What is the name of the priestess of Venus who in Plautus' Rudens takes in the shipwrecked Palaestra and Ampelisca?
derivation: The kindly priestess of the Venus shrine at Cyrene, named in the scene heading and addressed by name at v. 481 (heus exi, Ptolemocratia); she shelters the castaways. Canonical character of the play; anchored to Venus' shrine + the two girls; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ergo aequius vos erat candidatas venire hostiatasque. ad hoc fanum ad istunc modum non veniri solet.
question: Quo cultu supplices ad fanum Veneris venire solere Ptolemocratia sacerdos in Rudente Plauti docet?
question_en: In what guise does the priestess Ptolemocratia in Plautus' Rudens teach that suppliants customarily come to the shrine of Venus?
answer_en: Dressed in white and bringing sacrificial victims.
derivation: Cult realia: the proper approach to a temple is in white garments and with victims for sacrifice — the priestess states the norm while excusing the castaways. Shared religious custom; anchored to the named priestess and shrine; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nos iam de ornatu propemodum ut locupletes simus scitis: hisce hami atque haec harundines sunt nobis quaestu et cultu.
question: Quibus instrumentis piscatores pauperes in Rudente Plauti quaestum et cultum sibi esse canunt?
question_en: With what implements do the poor fishermen in Plautus' Rudens sing that they get their living and keep?
derivation: The fishermen's chorus on the hard sea-livelihood of the poor: hook and rod are their whole trade and sustenance; if nothing is caught they go home to bed unsupped. Mores of working poverty; anchored to the fishermen of the named play; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Estne hic Trachalio, quem conspicor, calator Plesidippi?
question: Cuius adulescentis servus erat Trachalio in Rudente Plauti?
question_en: Whose young master did the slave Trachalio serve in Plautus' Rudens?
derivation: The master-slave pairing of the play: Trachalio is Plesidippus' attendant (calator), later the engine of the rescue and the arbitration. Anchored to both named characters + play; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Novi, Neptunus ita solet, quamvis fastidiosus aedilis est: si quae improbae sunt merces, iactat omnis.
question: Cui magistratui Neptunum similem esse Trachalio in Rudente Plauti iocatur, quod merces improbas omnes iactet?
