question_en: To which magistrate does Trachalio in Plautus' Rudens jokingly compare Neptune, because he throws out all defective merchandise?
derivation: The joke presumes the aedile's real duty of inspecting market wares and condemning the bad — institutional realia carried by every Roman playgoer. Anchored to Neptune + Trachalio + the play; one-word office answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quia leno ademit cistulam ei, quam habebat ubique habebat qui suos parentis noscere posset: eam veretur ne perierit. TRACH. Vbinam ea fuit cistellula? AMP. Ibidem in navi. conclusit ipse in vidulum, ne copia esset eius, qui suos parentes nosceret.
question: Qua in re condita erant ea quibus Palaestra in Rudente Plauti parentes suos noscere posset?
question_en: In what container were the things kept by which Palaestra in Plautus' Rudens could recognize her parents?
derivation: The recognition-token casket that drives the plot: Palaestra's cistula holds the proofs of her parentage, and the leno locked it in his trunk (vidulus) on the ship. The exposure-and-recognition apparatus is core cultural knowledge of New Comedy; anchored to Palaestra + the play; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: etiam qui it lavatum in balineas, cum ibi sedulo sua vestimenta servat, tamen surripiuntur, quippe qui quem illorum observet falsust; fur facile qui observat videt: custos qui fur sit nescit.
question: Quid hominibus qui lavatum eunt in balineis surripi solere Trachalio in Rudente Plauti commemorat?
question_en: What does Trachalio in Plautus' Rudens remark is habitually stolen from men who go to bathe at the baths?
derivation: Clothes-theft at the public baths — the notorious fur balnearius of ancient daily life (a standing theme from comedy to the jurists). Mores realia; anchored to Trachalio + the play; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ergo animus aequos optimum est aerumnae condimentum.
question: Quid optimum aerumnae condimentum esse apud Plautum in Rudente dicitur?
question_en: What is said in Plautus' Rudens to be the best seasoning for hardship?
derivation: A proverb verbatim: equanimity is the best condiment of trouble — one of the Rudens' quotable sententiae. Checkable point (what is the condimentum?); anchored to the play; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sacram urnam Veneris? mi exhibeat negotium. metuo hercle ne illa mulier mi insidias locet, ut comprehendar cum sacra urna Veneria. nempe optimo me iure in vinclis enicet magistratus si quis me hanc habere viderit. nam haec litteratast, eapse cantat cuia sit.
question: Quo indicio urna sacra Veneris in Rudente Plauti ipsa cuia esset cantabat?
question_en: By what token did the sacred urn of Venus in Plautus' Rudens itself proclaim whose it was?
answer_en: By the letters inscribed on it.
derivation: Realia of temple property: sacred vessels were inscribed with the owner-deity's name (haec litteratast, eapse cantat cuia sit), so possession of one incriminated the holder before a magistrate. Anchored to Venus' urn + the play; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Scelestiorem cenam cenavi tuam, quam quae Thyestae quondam aut posita est Tereo.
question: Quibus duobus fabularum heroibus cenae scelestae adpositae esse in Rudente Plauti memorantur?
question_en: For which two heroes of legend are accursed dinners recalled as having been served in Plautus' Rudens?
derivation: Myth as shared story: the cannibal feasts of Thyestes (served his sons by Atreus) and Tereus (served Itys by Procne) are the paradigm of the scelesta cena, casually cited by Charmides. Anchored to the two named figures; two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ad hirundininum nidum visa est simia ascensionem ut faceret admolirier neque eas eripere quibat inde. postibi videtur ad me simia adgredirier, rogare scalas ut darem utendas sibi.
question: Quod animal in somnio Daemonis in Rudente Plauti hirundines e nido eripere conabatur?
question_en: What animal in Daemones' dream in Plautus' Rudens was trying to snatch the swallows from their nest?
derivation: The prophetic dream of the play: a monkey assaults a swallows' nest and asks Daemones for a ladder — later decoded by Daemones himself as the leno attacking the girls (haec illast simia, 771-773). A celebrated set piece of the Rudens; anchored to Daemones + the play; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ego ad hoc exemplum simiae respondeo, natas ex Philomela atque ex Progne esse hirundines. ago cum illa, ne quid noceat meis popularibus.
question: Ex quibus duabus sororibus natas esse hirundines Daemones in Rudente Plauti simiae respondet?
question_en: From which two sisters does Daemones in Plautus' Rudens reply to the monkey that swallows are descended?
derivation: Myth as shared story: the Athenian sisters Philomela and Procne, transformed into birds, are the ancestresses of the swallows — which is why Daemones the Athenian calls the swallows his 'countrywomen' (popularibus). Anchored to the named heroines; two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Teque oro et quaeso, si speras tibi hoc anno multum futurum sirpe et laserpicium eamque eventuram exagogam Capuam salvam et sospitem,
question: Quae merx nobilissima in agro Cyrenensi provenire ex Rudente Plauti apparet, ubi Trachalio Daemoni multam eam hoc anno futuram optat?
question_en: What most famous product is shown by Plautus' Rudens to grow in the territory of Cyrene, where Trachalio wishes Daemones a plentiful crop of it this year?
derivation: Cyrene's legendary export: silphium (sirpe) and laserpicium, here with an export run to Capua (exagogam Capuam). The identification of Cyrene with silphium was ambient Mediterranean knowledge (it stamped Cyrene's coins). Anchored to Cyrene + the named characters; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: TRACH. Ne, inquam, timete; adsidite hic in ara. ... PAL. Tibi auscultamus et, Venus alma, ambae te obsecramus, aram amplexantes hanc tuam lacrumantes, genibus nixae, in custodelam nos tuam ut recipias et tutere;
question: Quo Palaestra et Ampelisca in Rudente Plauti, vim lenonis Labracis fugientes, supplices confugerunt?
question_en: Where did Palaestra and Ampelisca in Plautus' Rudens flee as suppliants, escaping the violence of the pimp Labrax?
derivation: The great asylum scene: the girls sit on Venus' altar and embrace it as suppliants, and the altar's protection is treated as inviolable (aram habete hanc vobis pro castris). Altar-asylum is core religious realia; anchored to the named girls, pimp, and goddess; one-phrase answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: te ex concha natam esse autumant, cave tu harum conchas spernas.
question: Ex qua re Venerem natam esse homines autumant, ut Trachalio in Rudente Plauti deam ipsam admonet?
question_en: From what do people assert that Venus was born, as Trachalio in Plautus' Rudens reminds the goddess herself?
derivation: Canonical myth: Venus born from the sea in a shell — Trachalio puns that she should therefore not spurn these girls' 'shells.' Shared iconographic knowledge (the Anadyomene type); anchored to Venus + the play; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Atque eras tuas quidem hercle, atque ex germana Graecia; nam altera haec est nata Athenis ingenuis parentibus.
question: In qua urbe Palaestra, quam Labrax leno in Rudente Plauti ancillam suam vindicabat, ingenuis parentibus nata erat?
question_en: In what city was Palaestra, whom the pimp Labrax in Plautus' Rudens claimed as his slave-girl, born of freeborn parents?
derivation: The crux of the recognition plot: Palaestra is freeborn and Athenian — which makes her Daemones' fellow-citizen and, it emerges, his daughter. Anchored to the named girl and pimp; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: O filia mea, quom hanc video, mearum me absens miseriarum commones; trima quae periit mihi, iam tanta esset, si vivit, scio.
question: Quot annos nata erat filiola Daemonis cum ei periit, ut ipse in Rudente Plauti memorat?
question_en: How old was Daemones' little daughter when he lost her, as he himself recalls in Plautus' Rudens?
derivation: A clean number fact of the recognition plot: the daughter was lost as a three-year-old (trima), stolen and sold to the pimp. Anchored to Daemones + the play; one-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: DAEM. Quid facies? LABR. Volcanum adducam, is Venerist adversarius.
question: Quem deum Labrax leno in Rudente Plauti Veneri adversarium esse dicit, cum ignem petiturus minatur?
question_en: Which god does the pimp Labrax in Plautus' Rudens call Venus' adversary, when he threatens to fetch fire?
derivation: Mythological pairing played for a joke: Vulcan (fire, and Venus' ill-matched husband) as the adversary of Venus — Labrax will burn the suppliants off her altar. Shared myth knowledge; anchored to the named god, goddess, and pimp; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Heu hercle, ne istic fana mutantur cito: iam hoc Herculi est, Veneris fanum quod fuit, ita duo destituit signa hic cum clavis senex.
question: Cuius dei factum esse fanum Veneris Labrax in Rudente Plauti iocatur, postquam Daemones duos servos cum clavis ibi statuit?
question_en: Whose god's shrine does Labrax in Plautus' Rudens joke the shrine of Venus has become, after Daemones posts two slaves with clubs there?
derivation: The joke turns on Hercules' canonical attribute, the club (clava): two club-bearing 'statues' convert Venus' shrine into Hercules'. Shared iconography; anchored to the named gods and characters; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: LORARIVS Nullum habemus ignem, ficis victitamus aridis.
question: Quo cibo se victitare, cum ignem nullum haberent, servus Daemonis in Rudente Plauti respondet?
question_en: On what food does Daemones' slave in Plautus' Rudens reply that they live, since they have no fire?
derivation: Food realia of the poor rustic household: dried figs, eaten without cooking — the slave's deadpan excuse for having no fire to lend. Anchored to Daemones' household + the play; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quasi vinis Graecis Neptunus nobis suffudit mare, itaque alvom prodi speravit nobis salsis poculis;
question: Quibus vinis Charmides naufragus in Rudente Plauti mare a Neptuno sibi infusum comparat?
question_en: To what wines does the shipwrecked Charmides in Plautus' Rudens compare the sea Neptune poured into him?
derivation: The joke rests on real oenological practice: Greek wines were treated with seawater (salted), so a bellyful of brine is 'Greek wine' from Neptune's cellar. Food-and-drink realia every Roman drinker knew; anchored to Charmides + Neptune; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Dominus huic, ne frustra sis, nisi ego nemo natust, hunc qui cepi in venatu meo.
question: Quis piscator in Rudente Plauti vidulum lenonis Labracis e mari extraxit?
question_en: Which fisherman in Plautus' Rudens hauled the pimp Labrax's trunk out of the sea?
derivation: The pivotal catch of the play: Gripus, Daemones' slave-fisherman, nets the vidulus containing the recognition tokens and claims it as his 'hunt.' Canonical plot fact; anchored to the named fisherman, pimp, and play; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: Heus, mane. GRIP. Quid maneam? TRACH. Dum hanc tibi, quam trahis, rudentem complico.
question: Qua re retenta Trachalio Gripum piscatorem vidulum trahentem moratur, unde comoediae Plautinae nomen Rudens inditum est?
question_en: By holding onto what does Trachalio delay the fisherman Gripus as he drags the trunk — the thing from which the Plautine comedy takes its name Rudens?
derivation: The title-fact: the rudens is the rope of Gripus' net, which Trachalio seizes (and later: mitte rudentem, sceleste, 1015), turning the tug-of-war over the trunk into the play's name. Literary-history fact of the named play; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Neptuno has ago gratias meo patrono, qui salsis locis incolit pisculentis,
question: Quem deum Gripus piscator in Rudente Plauti patronum suum vocat?
question_en: Which god does the fisherman Gripus in Plautus' Rudens call his patron?
derivation: Religious realia of the trade: the fisherman thanks Neptune, dweller of the fishy salt places, as his patronus — the sea-god as patron of fishermen. Anchored to Gripus + the play; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: oppidum magnum communibo, ei ego urbi Gripo indam nomen, monimentum meae famae et factis, ibi qui regnum magnum instituam.
question: Quod nomen urbi quam se conditurum somniat Gripus piscator in Rudente Plauti se inditurum ait?
question_en: What name does the fisherman Gripus in Plautus' Rudens say he will give the city he dreams of founding?
derivation: The slave's daydream of wealth ends in eponymous city-founding — 'I will name the city Gripus, a monument to my fame.' A parody of the royal founder-eponym custom; anchored to the named character; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: post animi causa mihi navem faciam atque imitabor Stratonicum, oppida circumvectabor.
question: Quem virum clarum se imitaturum Gripus in Rudente Plauti dicit, cum navi animi causa oppida circumvectabitur?
question_en: What famous man does Gripus in Plautus' Rudens say he will imitate, sailing around from town to town for pleasure?
derivation: A cultural name-drop: Stratonicus, the celebrated Greek citharode famous for touring the cities, is the daydreaming slave's model of the rich travelling celebrity. Anchored to the named figure + character; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sed hic rex cum aceto pransurust et sale, sine bono pulmento.
question: Quo prandio Gripus, qui se regem futurum modo somniaverat, in Rudente Plauti contentum se fore ait?
question_en: On what lunch does Gripus, who had just been dreaming of becoming a king, say in Plautus' Rudens he will have to make do?
derivation: Food realia of poverty: the poor man's meal is vinegar and salt with no proper relish (pulmentum) — the comic deflation of Gripus' royal daydream. Anchored to the named character; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: mare quidem commune certost omnibus.
question: Quid omnibus commune esse Gripus piscator apud Plautum in Rudente pronuntiat?
question_en: What does the fisherman Gripus declare in Plautus' Rudens to be common to all?
derivation: The famous maxim of the arbitration scene — 'the sea is certainly common to all' — a proverbial statement of the sea's common status (later a tag of natural-law doctrine). Verbatim proverb with a checkable point; anchored to Gripus + the play; one-word answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: In manu non est mea: ubi demisi rete atque hamum, quidquid haesit extraho. meum quod rete atque hami nancti sunt, meum potissimumst.
question: Quo iure Gripus piscator in Rudente Plauti vidulum e mari extractum suum esse contendit?
answer: Quod rete atque hami sui nancti sunt, id suum potissimum esse.
question_en: By what right does the fisherman Gripus in Plautus' Rudens maintain that the trunk pulled from the sea is his?
answer_en: That whatever his net and hooks have caught is emphatically his.
derivation: The fisherman's salvage principle stated as a rule: what my net and hook take is mine — the maritime-law flavor of the great arbitration over the trunk (against Trachalio's retort that a trunk is no fish). Anchored to Gripus + the vidulus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Non probare pernegando mihi potes, nisi pars datur aut ad arbitrum reditur aut sequestro ponitur.
question: Quas duas vias litis de vidulo componendae Trachalio Gripo in Rudente Plauti proponit, nisi pars praedae detur?
answer: Vt ad arbitrum eatur aut res sequestro ponatur.
question_en: What two ways of settling the dispute over the trunk does Trachalio propose to Gripus in Plautus' Rudens, unless a share of the haul is given?
answer_en: To go before an arbiter, or to deposit the thing with a sequester (neutral stakeholder).
derivation: Legal-procedure realia: a disputed chattel goes to an arbiter or into sequestration (sequestro ponitur) — the everyday institutions of private dispute-settlement, staged in the tug-of-war. Anchored to the named characters + the vidulus; short two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Eo tacent, quia tacitast melior mulier semper quam loquens.
question: Vtra mulier melior semper esse apud Plautum in Rudente dicitur, tacita an loquens?
question_en: Which woman is said in Plautus' Rudens always to be better — the silent one or the talking one?
derivation: A proverb verbatim from the arbitration scene: a silent woman is always better than a speaking one — quotable comic misogyny with a single checkable point. Anchored to the play; one-word answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: una istinc cistella excepta est modo cum crepundiis, quibuscum hodie filiam inveni meam.
question: Quibus signis Daemones in Rudente Plauti Palaestram filiam suam esse cognovit?
question_en: By what tokens did Daemones in Plautus' Rudens recognize Palaestra as his daughter?
answer_en: By the childhood tokens (crepundia) that were in the little casket.
derivation: The recognition fact of the play, in Daemones' own words: the cistella with the crepundia is how he found his daughter. The crepundia — the tokens exposed or lost children carried — are the standard recognition apparatus of New Comedy; anchored to the named father and daughter; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: PAL. Ensiculust aureolus primum litteratus. DAEM. Dice dum, in eo ensiculo litterarum quid est? PAL. Mei nomen patris. ... dic, in ensiculo quid nomen est paternum? PAL. Daemones.
question: Quod nomen in ensiculo aureolo, primo inter crepundia Palaestrae, inscriptum erat?
question_en: What name was inscribed on the little golden sword, first among Palaestra's childhood tokens?
derivation: The first named crepundium: a lettered gold toy sword bearing the father's name Daemones — the very word that triggers the recognition. Anchored to Palaestra + the tokens; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: post altrinsecust securicula ancipes, itidem aurea litterata: ibi matris nomen in securiculast. ... DAEM. Loquere matris nomen hic quid in securicula siet. PAL. Daedalis.
question: Quod nomen matris in securicula aurea inter crepundia Palaestrae in Rudente Plauti inscriptum erat?
question_en: What mother's name was inscribed on the little golden axe among Palaestra's tokens in Plautus' Rudens?
derivation: The second named crepundium: a two-edged gold toy axe lettered with the mother's name Daedalis — thereby also fixing the name of Daemones' wife. Anchored to the named tokens and family; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: PAL. Post sicilicula argenteola et duae conexae maniculae et sucula.
question: Ex quo metallo sicilicula inter crepundia Palaestrae in Rudente Plauti facta erat?
question_en: Of what metal was the little sickle among Palaestra's tokens in Plautus' Rudens made?
derivation: The token inventory continues: a little silver sickle (sicilicula argenteola), two linked little hands, and a little windlass. The named crepundia are the play's celebrated recognition props; anchored to Palaestra + the tokens; one-word answer verbatim (argenteola).

author: Plautus
source_text: Et bulla aurea est, pater quam dedit mi natali die.
question: Quod ornamentum aureum pater Palaestrae natali die ei dedisse in Rudente Plauti inter crepundia memoratur?
question_en: What golden ornament is recorded among the tokens in Plautus' Rudens as given to Palaestra by her father on her birthday?
derivation: The last crepundium: the golden bulla, the amulet of the freeborn child, given by the father at birth — core Roman childhood realia, and proof of Palaestra's free birth. Anchored to Palaestra + her father; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: atque adorna, ut rem divinam faciam, cum intro advenero, Laribus familiaribus, cum auxerunt nostram familiam. sunt domi agni et porci sacres.
question: Quibus dis Daemones in Rudente Plauti rem divinam facere paravit, quod familiam eius auxissent?
question_en: To which gods did Daemones in Plautus' Rudens prepare to sacrifice, because they had increased his household?
derivation: Domestic religion: the recovered daughter is an increase of the familia, owed to the Lares familiares, who receive a thanksgiving sacrifice. Core Roman household cult; anchored to Daemones + the occasion; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: sunt domi agni et porci sacres.
question: Quas victimas domi se habere Daemones in Rudente Plauti dicit, cum Laribus familiaribus sacrificare vellet?
question_en: What sacrificial victims does Daemones in Plautus' Rudens say he has at home, when he wishes to sacrifice to the household Lares?
derivation: Sacrificial realia: lambs and porci sacres (pigs set apart for sacrifice) kept ready on the farm — the pig being the classic victim of household cult. Anchored to Daemones + the Lares; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: et eam de genere summo adulescenti dabo ingenuo, Atheniensi et cognato meo.
question: Cui adulescenti Daemones in Rudente Plauti filiam Palaestram repertam uxorem se daturum dixit?
question_en: To which young man did Daemones in Plautus' Rudens say he would give his recovered daughter Palaestra as wife?
derivation: The betrothal ending: the daughter goes to the young Athenian lover Plesidippus, who — the recognition's bonus — turns out to be Daemones' own kinsman (cognato meo). Anchored to the named characters; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: TRACH. Atque ut mi Ampelisca nubat, ubi ego sim liber. DAEM. Licet.
question: Quam mulierem Trachalio servus in Rudente Plauti, ubi liber esset, uxorem petivit?
question_en: What woman did the slave Trachalio in Plautus' Rudens ask to marry once he should be free?
derivation: The secondary match of the finale: Trachalio bargains his reward — manumission and marriage to Ampelisca — in the famous 'licet' exchange. Anchored to both named characters; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quis me est mortalis miserior qui vivat alter hodie, quem ad recuperatores modo damnavit Plesidippus?
question: Apud quos iudices Plesidippus Labracem lenonem in Rudente Plauti damnavit?
question_en: Before which panel of judges did Plesidippus get the pimp Labrax condemned in Plautus' Rudens?
derivation: Legal realia: the leno is condemned before recuperatores, the Roman board of judges for swift restitution suits — a distinctly Roman institution planted in the Greek setting. Anchored to the named litigants; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Nummi octingenti aurei in marsuppio infuerunt, praeterea centum minaria Philippa in pasceolo sorsus.
question: Quot nummos aureos in marsuppio suo, qui in vidulo erat, fuisse Labrax leno in Rudente Plauti recenset?
question_en: How many gold coins does the pimp Labrax in Plautus' Rudens reckon were in his purse inside the trunk?
derivation: The itemized treasure of the vidulus: 800 gold coins in the purse, plus a hundred Philippics in a separate pouch — the 'signa' by which Labrax proves the trunk is his. Clean number fact; anchored to Labrax + the vidulus; one-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: GRIP. Venus Cyrenensis, testem te testor mihi, si vidulum illum, quem ego in navi perdidi, cum auro atque argento salvom investigavero isque in potestatem meam pervenerit, tum ego huic Gripo, inquito, et me tangito— LABR. Tum ego huic Gripo— dico, Venus, ut tu audias— talentum argenti magnum continuo dabo.
question: Quantum argenti Labrax leno, aram Veneris tangens, Gripo se daturum in Rudente Plauti iuravit, si vidulum recepisset?
question_en: How much silver did the pimp Labrax, touching the altar of Venus, swear in Plautus' Rudens to give Gripus if he got his trunk back?
derivation: The oath scene: Gripus dictates and Labrax swears by Venus Cyrenensis, hand on her altar, to pay a talentum magnum for the trunk's recovery. Oath-at-altar realia plus a clean sum; anchored to the named characters and goddess; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ius iurandum rei servandae, non perdendae conditum est.
question: Cui rei ius iurandum conditum esse Labrax leno periurus apud Plautum in Rudente pronuntiat?
question_en: For what purpose does the perjured pimp Labrax in Plautus' Rudens declare that the oath was invented?
answer_en: For keeping one's property, not losing it.
derivation: The pimp's cynical maxim verbatim — oaths exist to save your goods, not to lose them — the quotable creed of the periurus leno. Proverb with a checkable point; anchored to Labrax + the play; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Cedo quicum habeam iudicem, ni dolo malo instipulatus sis nive etiamdum haud siem quinque et viginti annos natus.
question: Quot annos natum se nondum esse Labrax leno in Rudente Plauti causatur, ut sponsio cum Gripo facta irrita fiat?
question_en: How many years old does the pimp Labrax in Plautus' Rudens plead he is not yet, so that his bargain with Gripus may be voided?
derivation: A joke resting on real law: contracts extracted from those under twenty-five could be undone (the protection later associated with the lex Plaetoria) — the grizzled pimp absurdly claims minority. Legal realia every Roman would catch; anchored to Labrax + Gripus; one-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Dic mihi, quanti illam emisti tuam alteram mulierculam, Ampeliscam? LABR. Mille nummum denumeravi.
question: Quanti Labrax leno Ampeliscam emisse se in Rudente Plauti dicit?
question_en: For how much does the pimp Labrax in Plautus' Rudens say he bought Ampelisca?
derivation: The stated purchase price of the second girl, the basis for Daemones' settlement. Clean number fact of the slave trade; anchored to Labrax + Ampelisca; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: D. Dividuom talentum faciam. L. Bene facis. D. Pro illa altera, libera ut sit, dimidium tibi sume, dimidium huc cedo. LABR. Maxime. DAEM. Pro illo dimidio ego Gripum emittam manu, quem propter tu vidulum et ego gnatam inveni.
question: In quas duas res talentum a Labrace iuratum Daemones in fine Rudentis Plauti dividit?
answer: In libertatem Ampeliscae et in manumissionem Gripi.
question_en: To what two ends does Daemones in the finale of Plautus' Rudens divide the talent Labrax had sworn?
answer_en: To the freedom of Ampelisca and the manumission of Gripus.
derivation: The famous half-talent settlement: Daemones splits the sworn talent — half buys Ampelisca's liberty from the leno, and with the other half he manumits Gripus, finder of the trunk. Anchored to all named parties; short two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: DAEM. Hic hodie cenato, leno. LABR. Fiat, condicio placet. ... vos hic hodie cenatote ambo. LABR. Fiat. DAEM. Plausum date.
question: Quem lenonem Daemones in fine Rudentis Plauti, contra morem comicum, ad cenam vocat?
question_en: Which pimp does Daemones at the end of Plautus' Rudens, against comic custom, invite to dinner?
derivation: The Rudens' famously mild ending: instead of the usual thrashing, the punished leno is asked to dinner along with Gripus (cenatote ambo). A canonical literature-fact about the play's close; anchored to both named characters; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: spectatores, vos quoque ad cenam vocem, ni daturus nil sim neque sit quicquam pollucti domi, nive adeo vocatos credam vos esse ad cenam foras. verum si voletis plausum fabulae huic clarum dare, comissatum omnes venitote ad me ad annos sedecim.
question: Ad quot annos spectatores comissatum ad se venire Daemones in extremo Rudente Plauti invitat?
question_en: In how many years does Daemones at the very end of Plautus' Rudens invite the spectators to come revel at his house?
derivation: The closing joke to the audience: applaud, and you are all invited to a party — sixteen years from now. A quotable epilogue-fact of the play's last lines; anchored to the play + speaker; one-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: GRAECA ADELPHOE MENANDRU
question: Quae fabula Graeca, ut didascalia tradit, Sticho Plauti exemplo fuit?
question_en: What Greek play, according to the production notice, was the model for Plautus' Stichus?
derivation: The transmitted didascalia of the Stichus — the most complete for any Plautine play — names the Greek original: Menander's Adelphoe (the earlier play of that name, not Terence's model). Canonical literary-history fact; anchored to the named play; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ACTA LUDIS PLEBEIS CN. BAEBIO C. TERENTIO AED. PL.
question: Quibus ludis fabula Stichus Plauti primum acta est, ut didascalia tradit?
question_en: At which games was Plautus' Stichus first performed, according to the production notice?
derivation: The didascalia records the festival of the premiere: the Ludi Plebeii, given by the plebeian aediles Cn. Baebius and C. Terentius (November, 200 BC). Festival-and-theater fact; anchored to the named play; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: T. PUBLILIUS PELLIO
question: Quis fabulam Stichum Plauti egit, ut didascalia tradit?
question_en: Who acted (produced) Plautus' Stichus, according to the production notice?
derivation: The didascalia names the actor-manager: Pellio, Plautus' famous leading actor (mocked by name in the Bacchides). Theater-history fact; anchored to the play; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: TIBIIS SARRANIS TOTAM
question: Quibus tibiis tota fabula Stichus Plauti cantata est, ut didascalia tradit?
question_en: On what kind of pipes was the whole of Plautus' Stichus accompanied, according to the production notice?
derivation: The didascalia specifies the music: the whole play accompanied on the tibiae Sarranae (the matched pair of pipes named from Sarra/Tyre); the notice also preserves the musician's name, Marcipor, slave of Oppius. Stage-music realia; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: C. SULPICIO C. AURELIO COS.
question: Quibus consulibus fabula Stichus Plauti acta est, ut didascalia tradit?
answer: C. Sulpicio et C. Aurelio consulibus.
question_en: In the consulship of which men was Plautus' Stichus performed, according to the production notice?
answer_en: In the consulship of C. Sulpicius and C. Aurelius (200 BC).
derivation: The consular date of the premiere preserved in the didascalia: C. Sulpicius Galba and C. Aurelius Cotta, consuls of 200 BC. Anchored to the named play; two-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Credo ego miseram fuisse Penelopam, soror, suo ex animo, quae tam diu vidua viro suo caruit; nam nos eius animum de nostris factis noscimus, quarum viri hinc apsunt.
question: Cui heroinae fideli Panegyris se sororemque suam, quarum viri peregre aberant, primis Stichi Plautini versibus comparat?
question_en: To which faithful heroine does Panegyris, in the opening lines of Plautus' Stichus, compare herself and her sister, whose husbands were away abroad?
derivation: The celebrated opening of the play: the loyal wives measure their own longing by Penelope's, the canonical wife who endured her husband's long absence. Myth as shared story; anchored to Panegyris + the play's opening; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam viri nostri domo ut abierunt, hic tertius annus.
question: Quotus annus agebatur, ex quo viri duarum sororum in Sticho Plauti domo abierant?
question_en: The how-many-eth year was running since the husbands of the two sisters in Plautus' Stichus had left home?
derivation: The time-frame of the plot: the husbands have been trading abroad into the third year (the argumentum's per triennium). Anchored to the sisters + the play; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: neque ille sibi mereat Persarum montis, qui esse aurei perhibentur, ut istuc faciat quod tu metuis.
question: Cuius gentis montes aurei esse perhibentur, ut proverbialiter apud Plautum in Sticho dicitur?
question_en: Whose mountains are proverbially said to be of gold, as the saying goes in Plautus' Stichus?
derivation: The proverbial 'golden mountains of the Persians' as the image of limitless wealth (montes auri polliceri became the standard idiom). Anchored to the named people; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: vos meministis quot kalendis petere demensum cibum: qui minus meministis quod opus sit facto facere in aedibus?
question: Quo mensis die servi demensum cibum petere meminerunt, ut Antipho senex in Sticho Plauti exprobrat?
question_en: On what day of the month do slaves remember to ask for their rationed food, as old Antipho complains in Plautus' Stichus?
derivation: Household realia: the demensum, the slave's measured monthly ration, drawn on the kalends — the one duty Antipho says his slaves never forget. Anchored to Antipho + the institution; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Placet ille meus mihi mendicus: suos rex reginae placet.
question: Quis reginae placere proverbio apud Plautum in Sticho dicitur?
question_en: Who is proverbially said in Plautus' Stichus to please the queen?
derivation: The sister's proverb defending her beggared husband: 'my beggar suits me — her own king suits the queen,' i.e. every woman is content with her own man. Proverb verbatim; short answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: Stultitiast, pater, venatum ducere invitas canes.
question: Quales canes venatum ducere stultitia esse proverbio apud Plautum in Sticho dicitur?
question_en: What sort of dogs is it proverbially foolish to take hunting, according to the saying in Plautus' Stichus?
derivation: The proverb with which the daughter answers her father's remarriage plan: taking unwilling hounds to the hunt is folly. Proverb verbatim; anchored to the Stichus scene; one-word answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: hostis est uxor, invita quae viro nuptum datur.
question: Qualis uxor viro hostis esse apud Plautum in Sticho dicitur?
question_en: What kind of wife is said in Plautus' Stichus to be an enemy to her husband?
answer_en: One given in marriage to the man against her will.
derivation: The companion maxim to the hunting-dogs proverb: a wife married unwilling is an enemy, not a wife. A quotable sententia on Roman marriage; verbatim; short answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: adeunt, perquirunt quid sit causae ilico: alienum aes cogat an pararit praedium, uxorin sit reddenda dos divortio.
question: Quid uxori divortio facto reddendum esse apud Plautum in Sticho memoratur?
question_en: What is mentioned in Plautus' Stichus as having to be given back to a wife when a divorce takes place?
derivation: Legal realia embedded in Gelasimus' list of stock reasons for holding an auction: debts to be paid, an estate bought, or a dowry to be returned upon divorce — the actio rei uxoriae in everyday form. Anchored to the auction scene; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Famem ego fuisse suspicor matrem mihi, nam postquam natus sum, satur numquam fui.
question: Quam matrem sibi fuisse Gelasimus parasitus in Sticho Plauti suspicatur?
question_en: Whom does the parasite Gelasimus in Plautus' Stichus suspect to have been his mother?
derivation: The parasite's signature self-definition opening his monologue: Hunger personified must be his mother, since he has never once been full. Anchored to the named parasite; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: nam illa me in alvo menses gestavit decem, at ego illam in alvo gesto plus annos decem.
question: Quot menses mater Gelasimum in alvo gestavit, ut ipse parasitus computat?
question_en: For how many months did his mother carry Gelasimus in her womb, as the parasite himself reckons?
derivation: The Roman reckoning of pregnancy as ten (lunar) months, the standard ancient count — against which Gelasimus has carried his 'mother' Hunger more than ten years. Anchored to Gelasimus; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: atque auditavi saepe hoc volgo dicier, solere elephantum gravidam perpetuos decem esse annos.
question: Quot annos elephantum gravidam esse solere volgo dicitur, ut Gelasimus in Sticho refert?
question_en: For how many years is a she-elephant commonly said to be pregnant, as Gelasimus reports in Plautus' Stichus?
derivation: A piece of shared ancient nature-lore, marked in the text as a common saying (volgo dicier): the elephant's ten-year pregnancy (the belief Pliny also records). Anchored to the elephant + the common report; number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Gelasimo nomen mi indidit parvo pater, quia inde iam a pausillo puero ridiculus fui.
question: Quam ob rem Gelasimo parasito id nomen a patre parvo inditum est, ut ipse narrat?
answer: Quia iam a puero ridiculus fuit.
question_en: Why was the parasite Gelasimus given that name by his father when small, as he himself tells?
answer_en: Because he was 'laughable' (ridiculus) from early boyhood.
derivation: The name-fact of the parasite: Gelasimus, from Greek gelasimos 'laughable,' explained in the text by his lifelong role of ridiculus — the jester who earns dinners by being laughed at. The etymology is glossed in the Latin itself, so it survives translation; anchored to the named character.

author: Plautus
source_text: eo quia paupertas fecit ridiculus forem; nam illa artis omnis perdocet, ubi quem attigit.
question: Quae res artis omnis perdocet, ubi quem attigit, ut Gelasimus apud Plautum in Sticho ait?
question_en: What thing teaches a man all the arts once it has touched him, as Gelasimus says in Plautus' Stichus?
derivation: The famous maxim: poverty is the teacher of all arts — here explaining how want made the parasite funny. Proverb verbatim; one-word answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: Nunc auctionem facere decretumst mihi: foras necessumst quidquid habeo vendere. adeste sultis, praeda erit praesentium. logos ridiculos vendo. age licemini.
question: Quas merces Gelasimus parasitus, auctione facta, in Sticho Plauti venditat?
question_en: What wares does the parasite Gelasimus put up for sale at his auction in Plautus' Stichus?
answer_en: His jokes (logi ridiculi, his stock of witticisms).
derivation: The set-piece of the play: the starving parasite auctions his working capital — his funny stories (logi), priced at a lunch or a dinner. Canonical scene of parasite-culture; anchored to Gelasimus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: robiginosam strigilem, ampullam rubidam, parasitum inanem quo recondas reliquias.
question: Quae duo instrumenta balnearia Gelasimus parasitus inter bona sua auctione vendenda enumerat?
question_en: What two pieces of bath-gear does the parasite Gelasimus list among his goods for auction?
answer_en: A rusty strigil and a reddish oil-flask.
derivation: Bath-culture realia: the strigil (scraper) and ampulla (oil-flask), the standard personal kit a man carried to the baths — here rusted and shabby, the parasite's whole estate. Anchored to Gelasimus' auction; two-item answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Fuit disertim, verum id usu perdidi: nunc Miccotrogus nomine e vero vocor.
question: Quo nomine 'e vero' se nunc vocari Gelasimus parasitus fame confectus iocatur?
question_en: By what name does the starved parasite Gelasimus joke that he is now 'truly' called?
derivation: The parasite's second name-joke: having lost the use of the name Gelasimus, he goes by the 'true' name Miccotrogus, Greek for one who nibbles crumbs. Name stated in the text; anchored to Gelasimus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quid igitur me volt? CROC. Tritici modios decem rogare, opinor te volt. GEL. Mene, ut ab sese petam? CROC. Immo ut a vobis mutuom nobis dares.
question: Quot modios tritici Panegyris a Gelasimo parasito mutuos rogari iussit?
question_en: How many measures of wheat did Panegyris have asked of the parasite Gelasimus as a loan?
derivation: Household-economy realia: grain borrowed by the modius between houses — ten modii of wheat, the request that panics the penniless parasite. Anchored to Panegyris + Gelasimus; single-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Mercurius, Iovis qui nuntius perhibetur, numquam aeque patri suo nuntium lepidum attulit quam ego nunc meae erae nuntiabo.
question: Cuius dei nuntius Mercurius esse perhibetur, ut apud Plautum in Sticho dicitur?
question_en: Of which god is Mercury reputed to be the messenger, as stated in Plautus' Stichus?
derivation: Myth as shared knowledge, stated outright: Mercury is Jupiter's messenger — and his son (patri suo) — the standard against which the slave-boy measures his own good news. Anchored to Mercury + Jupiter; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: secundas fortunas decent superbiae.
question: Quid secundas fortunas decere Pinacium puer apud Plautum in Sticho pronuntiat?
question_en: What does the boy Pinacium in Plautus' Stichus declare befits good fortune?
derivation: A quotable Plautine sententia from the boy's mock-grand monologue: prosperity licenses pride. Maxim verbatim; short answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: contundam facta Talthubi contemnamque omnis nuntios.
question: Cuius nuntii veteris facta se contusurum esse Pinacium, laetum nuntium ferens, gloriatur?
question_en: Whose deeds — of what famous messenger of old — does Pinacium, bearing his glad news, boast he will eclipse?
derivation: Talthybius, the herald of Agamemnon and the Greeks at Troy, as the proverbial messenger whom the slave-boy claims to outdo. Myth-figure named verbatim; anchored to Pinacium; one-name answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: simulque ad cursuram meditabor me ad ludos Olympios.
question: Ad quos ludos cursuram se meditari Pinacium puer citus iocatur?
question_en: For what games does the swift boy Pinacium joke that he is training himself in running?
derivation: The Olympic games and their footrace as shared Greek athletic culture, invoked by the running slave-boy. Anchored to Pinacium; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ecquis huc effert nassiternam cum aqua? GEL. Sine suffragio populi tamen aedilitatem hic quidem gerit.
question: Quem magistratum Pinacium sine suffragio populi gerere Gelasimus iocatur, cum munditias vias spargendo fieri iubet?
question_en: What magistracy does Gelasimus joke that Pinacium is exercising without the people's vote, as he orders the cleaning and sprinkling?
derivation: Institutional realia in a joke: street-cleaning and sprinkling belonged to the aediles, magistrates elected suffragio populi — so the bossy slave-boy 'holds the aedileship without an election.' Anchored to both named characters; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: dum percontor portitores, ecquae navis venerit ex Asia, negant venisse, conspicatus sum interim cercurum, quo ego me maiorem non vidisse censeo. in portum vento secundo, velo passo pervenit. alius alium percontamur: quoiast navis? quid vehit? interibi Epignomum conspicio tuom virum et servom Stichum.
question: Ex qua terra Epignomus, Panegyris vir, cum servo Sticho divitiis onustus navi rediit?
question_en: From what land did Epignomus, Panegyris' husband, return by ship with his slave Stichus, laden with riches?
derivation: The core plot-fact of the play: the impoverished husbands went trading and return rich from Asia — the boy questions the harbor customs-men (portitores) for a ship from Asia and spots Epignomus and Stichus. Anchored to the named husband + slave; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: conspicatus sum interim cercurum, quo ego me maiorem non vidisse censeo. in portum vento secundo, velo passo pervenit.
question: Quo genere navis Epignomus in portum vento secundo, velo passo, pervenit?
question_en: On what type of ship did Epignomus reach harbor with a fair wind and full sail?
answer_en: On a cercurus (a light merchant galley).
derivation: Seafaring realia: the cercurus, the swift Cypriot-style merchant vessel — the biggest one the boy claims ever to have seen — brings the trader home. Anchored to Epignomus' arrival; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Tum Babylonica et peristroma tonsilia et tappetia advexit, nimium bonae rei.
question: Qualia stragula pretiosa Epignomus ex Asia secum advexisse a Pinacio nuntiatur?
question_en: What costly coverings is Epignomus reported by Pinacium to have brought back with him from Asia?
derivation: Luxury-trade realia in the cargo catalogue: Babylonica — the famed figured coverlets of Babylon — with shorn peristromata and tapetia, alongside gold, silver, purple and ivoried couches. Anchored to Epignomus' cargo; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Poste, ut occepi narrare, fidicinas, tibicinas, sambucas advexit secum forma eximia.
question: Quas artifices feminas forma eximia Epignomus secum ex Asia advexit?
question_en: What women performers of striking beauty did Epignomus bring back with him from Asia?
derivation: Entertainment realia of the rich man's household: the imported music-girls — fidicinae (lyre), tibicinae (pipes), sambucae (the triangular harp) — part of the Asian cargo; one of the fidicinae becomes the slaves' party companion. List answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Poste autem advexit parasitos secum. GEL. Ei, perii miser. PIN. Ridiculissumos.
question: Quos homines ridiculissimos Epignomum secum ex Asia advexisse Pinacium nuntiat, quo nuntio Gelasimus perit?
question_en: What 'most amusing' men does Pinacium report Epignomus has brought back from Asia — the news that undoes Gelasimus?
derivation: The joke that ruins the resident parasite: the master returns with his own imported parasites, funnier than Gelasimus — who instantly takes his jokes off the market. Anchored to Epignomus + Gelasimus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quom bene re gesta salvos convortor domum, Neptuno grates habeo et Tempestatibus; simul Mercurio, qui me in mercimoniis iuvit lucrisque quadruplicavit rem meam.
question: Quibus dis Epignomus, mari salvos domum reversus, grates habere se dicit?
question_en: To which gods does Epignomus, returned home safe by sea, say he gives thanks?
answer_en: To Neptune, the Storm-goddesses (Tempestates), and Mercury.
derivation: The merchant-sailor's thanksgiving triad: Neptune and the Tempestates (who had a real cult at Rome) for the safe voyage, Mercury for the profits of trade. Rite-and-cult realia; anchored to Epignomus; three-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: simul Mercurio, qui me in mercimoniis iuvit lucrisque quadruplicavit rem meam.
question: Quantum rem suam lucris auctam esse Epignomus, Mercurio iuvante, praedicat?
question_en: By how much does Epignomus declare his fortune increased in profits, with Mercury's help?
derivation: The scale of the trading windfall, credited to Mercury, god of commerce: his estate multiplied fourfold. Anchored to Epignomus + Mercury; single-word number answer verbatim (quadruplicavit).

author: Plautus
source_text: nunc hunc diem unum ex illis multis miseriis volo me eleutheria capere advenientem domum. EPIG. Et ius et aequom postulas: sumas, Stiche.
question: Quid Stichus servus, domum cum ero reversus, unum diem sibi capere ab Epignomo postulat?
question_en: What does the slave Stichus, back home with his master, ask of Epignomus to take for one day?
answer_en: A 'freedom-festival' (eleutheria) — a day of holiday license.
derivation: The slaves'-holiday frame of the finale: after the shared hardships Stichus claims one day of eleutheria (Greek 'freedom-feast'), and the master grants it as fair. The licensed day off behind the closing party; anchored to Stichus + Epignomus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: cadum tibi veteris vini propino.
question: Quod donum Epignomus Sticho servo in diem festum eius propinat?
question_en: What gift does Epignomus pledge to the slave Stichus for his holiday?
derivation: The master's contribution to the slaves' party: a cadus of vintage wine — old wine being the prized kind — which becomes the one amphora shared at the finale. Anchored to Epignomus + Stichus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: amicam ego habeo Stephanium hinc ex proxumo, tui fratris ancillam: eo condixi in symbolam ad cenam, ad eius conservom Sangarinum Syrum. eademst amica ambobus, rivales sumus.
question: Quae ancilla et Sticho et Sangarino servis amica erat, ita ut rivales essent?
question_en: Which slave-girl was sweetheart to both the slaves Stichus and Sangarinus, making them rivals?
derivation: The famous arrangement of the finale: one girlfriend, Stephanium, shared amicably by the two slaves — 'she is sweetheart to both; we are rivals.' Anchored to all three named slaves; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: eo condixi in symbolam ad cenam, ad eius conservom Sangarinum Syrum.
question: Quo more Stichus cenam apud Sangarinum conservom condixit?
question_en: On what arrangement did Stichus engage for dinner at his fellow-slave Sangarinus' place?
answer_en: By contribution — each paying his share (symbola).
derivation: Dining realia: the symbola, the Greek-style club dinner to which each guest contributes his share — the basis of the slaves' pot-luck party. Anchored to Stichus + Sangarinus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: atque id ne vos miremini, hominis servolos potare, amare atque ad cenam condicere: licet haec Athenis nobis.
question: Vbi servolis potare, amare atque ad cenam condicere licere Stichus spectatores monet?
question_en: Where does Stichus remind the spectators that it is permitted for slaves to drink, make love, and arrange dinner parties?
derivation: The celebrated aside on the Greek license of the palliata: do not marvel at slaves partying — 'this is allowed us at Athens' (not at Rome). A theater-convention fact about the genre itself; anchored to Stichus' address; one-place answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: est etiam hic ostium aliud posticum nostrarum harunc aedium: posticam partem magis utuntur aedium. ea ibo opsonatum, eadem referam opsonium: per hortum utroque commeatus continet.
question: Quo ostio aedium Stichus, ne invidiam inveniat, opsonatum ire et opsonium referre constituit?
question_en: Through which door of the house does Stichus decide to go marketing and bring back the provisions, to avoid ill-will?
answer_en: Through the back door, by way of the garden.
derivation: Domestic-architecture realia: the posticum, the back door opening on the garden, giving passage between the two houses — used to keep the slaves' shopping out of sight. Anchored to Stichus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ut cuique homini res paratast, perinde amicis utitur: si res firma, item firmi amici sunt; sin res laxe labat, itidem amici conlabascunt: res amicos invenit.
question: Quid amicos invenire proverbio apud Plautum in Sticho dicitur?
question_en: What is proverbially said in Plautus' Stichus to find a man his friends?
derivation: The quotable maxim capping Antipho's reflection: friends stand firm as one's fortune stands — res amicos invenit, 'money finds friends.' Proverb verbatim; one-word answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: 'Ego tibi meam filiam, bene quicum cubitares, dedi: nunc mihi reddi ego aequom esse abs te quicum cubitem censeo.'
question: Quid Antipho senex viduos, qui filias generis dederat, sibi vicissim reddi aequom esse per apologum significat?
question_en: What does the widowed old Antipho, who gave his daughters to his sons-in-law, hint through his fable that it is fair he get back in turn?
answer_en: Someone to sleep with — a concubine (one of the imported music-girls).
derivation: The famous apologus scene: the old man tells a thinly-veiled fable ('a certain old man, just like me...') to extract one of the music-girls as his bedmate, arguing he gave dowries with his daughters; Epignomus grants him the girl. Anchored to Antipho + his sons-in-law; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: atque eccum tibi lupum in sermone: praesens esuriens adest.
question: Quod animal 'in sermone' adesse proverbialiter apud Plautum in Sticho dicitur, cum is de quo loquuntur ipse supervenit?
question_en: What animal is proverbially said to be 'in the talk' in Plautus' Stichus, when the man being spoken of turns up himself?
derivation: The proverb lupus in sermone (the familiar lupus in fabula): speak of the wolf and he appears — here the starving Gelasimus arriving as the brothers discuss him. Proverb verbatim; one-word answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: Salvete, Athenae, quae nutrices Graeciae, sperata erilis patria, te video libens.
question: Quo praeconio Sangarinus servus, cum ero peregre reversus, Athenas salutat?
question_en: With what title of honor does the slave Sangarinus, back from abroad with his master, greet Athens?
derivation: The celebrated salute fixing the play's setting: Athens hailed as the nurse of Greece, the master's longed-for homeland. Anchored to Sangarinus + Athens; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: fero convivam Dionysum mihique et tibi.
question: Quem 'convivam' Stichus, cadum vini adportans, se sibi et Sangarino ferre dicit?
question_en: What 'dinner-guest' does Stichus, carrying in the jar of wine, say he brings for himself and Sangarinus?
answer_en: Dionysus (the wine itself, by the god's name).
derivation: The shared metonymy of the wine-god: the jar of wine is 'the guest Dionysus.' Myth-as-culture, anchored to Stichus + Sangarinus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Hoc conviviumst pro opibus nostris satis commodule nucibus, fabulis, ficulis, oleae interiplio, lupillo, comminuto crustulo.
question: Quibus cibis convivium servorum Stichi et Sangarini pro opibus eorum instructum erat?
answer: Nucibus, fabulis, ficulis, olea, lupillo, crustulo comminuto.
question_en: With what foods was the slaves' banquet of Stichus and Sangarinus furnished, as their means allowed?
answer_en: Nuts, little beans, little figs, olives, lupine seeds, and crumbled pastry.
derivation: The poor man's dessert-board itemized: the cheap nibbles (bellaria) of the slaves' party — nuts, beans, figs, olives, lupines, broken cake. Food realia; anchored to the two named slaves; list answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: quibus divitiae domi sunt, scaphiis cantharis batiocis bibunt, at nos nostro Samiolo poterio.
question: Quali poterio Stichus et Sangarinus servi, cum divites scaphiis cantharis batiocis bibant, vinum bibunt?
question_en: From what sort of cup do the slaves Stichus and Sangarinus drink their wine, while the rich drink from bowls, tankards, and goblets?
answer_en: From a little Samian (cheap earthenware) cup.
derivation: Tableware realia along the social scale: the rich drink from scaphia, canthari, batiocae; the slaves from the humble Samian-ware cup — Samian pottery as the byword for cheap crockery. Anchored to the named slaves; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Age dice uter utrubi accumbamus. STICH. Abi tu sane superior.
question: Quem locum accumbendi Stichus Sangarino, cum uter utrubi accumbat quaeritur, concedit?
question_en: Which dining place does Stichus yield to Sangarinus, when the question is who reclines where?
derivation: Dining-etiquette realia: even the slaves' two-man party observes the ranked places of the couch, and 'who lies where' (uter utrubi accumbamus) must be settled first — Stichus gives up the locus superior. Anchored to both slaves; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quid istuc est provinciai? STICH. Vtrum Fontine an Libero imperium te inhibere mavis? SANG. Nimio liquido Libero.
question: Vtri deo Sangarinus imperium inhibere mavolt, Fontine an Libero?
question_en: Over which god does Sangarinus prefer to exercise command — Fons or Liber?
answer_en: Over Liber (the wine rather than the water).
derivation: The banquet 'provinces' divided by their gods: Fons, god of springs, stands for the water, Liber for the wine, and Sangarinus chooses the wine-command. Cult-name realia of the mixing of wine; anchored to both slaves + both gods; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: strategum te facio huic convivio.
question: Quem magistratum convivii sui Sangarinus Sticho mandat?
question_en: What office over their banquet does Sangarinus confer on Stichus?
answer_en: That of 'general' (strategus) — master of the drinking.
derivation: Banquet-custom realia: the party elects a master of ceremonies (the Greek strategos here, the Roman magister or rex bibendi) to command the drinking. Anchored to the two slaves; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: vide, quot cyathos bibimus. STICH. Tot quot digiti tibi sunt in manu. cantio Graecast: e pevt e tria pin e me tettara.
question: Quot cyathos bibi Stichus, cantionem Graecam secutus, respondet?
answer: Tot quot digiti sunt in manu: quinque.
question_en: How many ladles (cyathi) does Stichus answer they are drinking, following the Greek catch?
answer_en: As many as the fingers on the hand: five.
derivation: Drinking-rule realia: wine is measured out by the cyathus, and the Greek catch quoted in the text prescribes 'drink five or three, not four' — so Stichus counts five, the fingers of the hand. Anchored to the named slave + the drinking scene; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Tibi propino. decumam a fonte tibi tute inde, si sapis. bene vos, bene nos, bene te, bene me, bene nostram etiam Stephanium.
question: Quibus verbis sollemnibus Sangarinus, poculum propinans, convivis salutem precatur?
answer: Bene vos, bene nos, bene te, bene me.
question_en: With what set words does Sangarinus, pledging the cup, drink the health of the company?
answer_en: 'Health to you, to us, to thee, to me' — the bene te toast.
derivation: The Roman toast-formula verbatim: bene te ('your health'), run round the whole company and extended to 'our Stephanium too.' Convivial-custom realia; anchored to Sangarinus' pledge; formula answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Stiche, uter demutassit, poculo multabitur. STICH. Bonum ius dicis. impetrare oportet qui aequom postulat. SANG. Age ergo observa. si pecassis, multam hic retinebo ilico.
question: Qua multa, uter in ludo demutasset, apud Stichum et Sangarinum multandus erat?
question_en: With what fine was whichever of Stichus and Sangarinus changed the step in their game to be punished?
derivation: Party-game realia: the forfeit of the symposium — whoever slips in the dance-and-mimicry game is fined a cup, the fine exacted on the spot. Anchored to the two named slaves; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: haec facetiast, amare inter se rivalis duos, uno cantharo potare, unum scortum ducere.
question: Quot cantharis duo rivales Stichus et Sangarinus in fine fabulae potant, et quot amicas ducunt?
question_en: From how many tankards do the two rivals Stichus and Sangarinus drink at the play's end, and how many girls do they take?
answer_en: One tankard — and one girl between them.
derivation: The emblem of the finale, stated by Stichus himself as the joke of the piece: two rivals who love each other, drink from a single cantharus, and share a single girl, neither begrudging the other. Anchored to both named slaves; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Vapulat peculium, actum est. SANG. Fugit hoc libertas caput.
question: Quid vapulare Stichus ait, cum Stephanium ambos amare se dicit?
question_en: What does Stichus say is 'taking a beating' when Stephanium declares she loves them both?
derivation: Slave-economy realia: the peculium, the slave's own hoard (his hope of buying freedom), will be spent on the shared girlfriend — as Sangarinus caps it, 'liberty flees this head.' Anchored to the named slaves + Stephanium; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: satis esse nobis non magis potis quam fungo imber.
question: Cui rei imbrem numquam nimium esse posse proverbio apud Plautum in Sticho dicitur?
question_en: For what thing can rain never be too much, according to the proverbial comparison in Plautus' Stichus?
derivation: Proverbial comparison closing the dance-off: the revelers can no more have their fill than a mushroom can have too much rain. Proverb verbatim; one-word answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: vos, spectatores, plaudite atque ite ad vos comissatum.
question: Quid spectatores in extremo Sticho Plauti, praeter plausum, facere iubentur?
question_en: What are the spectators told to do at the very end of Plautus' Stichus, besides applauding?
answer_en: To go home and hold a revel of their own.
derivation: The closing formula of the play: the plaudite plus an invitation to the audience to carry the comissatio (drinking-revel) home — fitting the slaves'-party finale. Theater-convention fact; short answer verbatim.

author: Pliny the Younger

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Pyrenaei montes Hispanias Galliasque disterminant promunturiis in duo diversa maria proiectis.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: praefari necessarium est auctorem nos Divum Augustum secuturos discriptionemque ab eo factam Italiae totius in regiones XI.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Est ergo folio maxime querno adsimulata, multo proceritate amplior quam latitudine.

derivation: Pliny's well-known simile for the shape of Italy (an oak leaf). Subject (Italia) is the running topic; the question supplies it, making it decontextualizable. Short answer supported verbatim by folio querno adsimulata. Indirect statement governed by scribit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: conplexa montes septem. ipsa dividitur in regiones XIIII, compita Larum CCLXV.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Tiberis, ante Thyberis appellatus et prius Albula, e media fere longitudine Appennini finibus Arretinorum profluit.

question_en: By what name does Pliny say the river Tiber was called in earliest times?
derivation: The Tiber's oldest name. The text gives prius Albula (earlier than both Tiberis and Thyberis), so Albula is the earliest. Entity-anchored to the Tiber, single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: a recurring antiquarian fact in Latin literature.

author: Pliny the Elder

author: Pliny the Elder

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Padus, e gremio Vesuli montis celsissimum in cacumen Alpium elati finibus Ligurum Bagiennorum visendo fonte profluens condensque se cuniculo et in Forovibiensium agro iterum exoriens, nullo amnium claritate inferior, Graecis dictus Eridanus ac poena Phaethontis inlustratus.

author: Pliny the Elder

author: Pliny the Elder

author: Senatus Romanus

author: Senatus Romanus

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: Haice utei in coventionid exdeicatis ne minus trinum noundinum, senatuosque sententiam utei scientes esetis.

answer_en: For a trinum nundinum — not less than three successive market-days.

Supported verbatim; the nundinum is a Roman institution, so the fact is culturally salient and translatable as a span of market-days.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: Sei ques esent, quei arvorsum ead fecisent, quam suprad scriptum est, eeis rem caputalem faciendam censuere.
question: Quae poena constituta est eis, qui contra senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus fecissent?
question_en: What penalty was laid down for those who acted contrary to the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus?
answer_en: A capital charge (it was made a capital offense).
derivation: The sanction clause: 'eeis rem caputalem faciendam censuere' — proceedings against violators are to be capital. Answer 'res capitalis' is the archaic caputalem normalized; supported verbatim. With the mass executions Livy 39.18 reports, the capital penalty is the decree's most notorious feature.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: atque utei hoce in tabolam ahenam inceideretis, ita senatus aiquom censuit, uteique eam figier ioubeatis, ubei facilumed gnoscier potisit.
question: In quam tabulam senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus incidi senatus aequum censuit?
question_en: Onto what kind of tablet did the senate deem it right that the decree about the Bacchanalia be engraved?
derivation: The engraving order: 'in tabolam ahenam inceideretis' — cut this onto a bronze tablet. Answer supported verbatim (archaic tabolam ahenam = tabulam aeneam); the surviving Tiriolo bronze is that very object, which is precisely why the document is famous.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: atque utei hoce in tabolam ahenam inceideretis, ita senatus aiquom censuit, uteique eam figier ioubeatis, ubei facilumed gnoscier potisit.
question: Ubi tabulam aeneam senatus consulti de Bacchanalibus figi oportuit?
question_en: Where was the bronze tablet of the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus to be posted?
answer_en: Where it could most easily be known (read).
derivation: The posting order: 'uteique eam figier ioubeatis, ubei facilumed gnoscier potisit' — fasten it up where it can most easily be known. The brief purpose-phrase is the answer, normalized from one of the most-quoted archaic phrases of the inscription; supported verbatim.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: Atque utei ea Bacanalia, sei qua sunt, exstrad quam sei quid ibei sacri est, ita utei suprad scriptum est, in diebus X, quibus vobeis tabelai datai erunt, faciatis utei dismota sient.
question: Intra quot dies, postquam tabellae datae essent, Bacchanalia ex senatus consulto dimovenda erant?
question_en: Within how many days after the tablets were delivered were the Bacchanalia to be dismantled under the senatus consultum?
derivation: The demolition clause: existing Bacchanalia (shrines) are to be dismantled 'in diebus X, quibus vobeis tabelai datai erunt' — within ten days of the tablets' delivery. Single number answer supported verbatim; the ten-day deadline is a standard quoted detail of the decree.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: Atque utei ea Bacanalia, sei qua sunt, exstrad quam sei quid ibei sacri est, ita utei suprad scriptum est, in diebus X, quibus vobeis tabelai datai erunt, faciatis utei dismota sient.
question: Quid unum excipiebatur, cum Bacchanalia ex senatus consulto dimoveri iuberentur?
question_en: What one thing was excepted when the Bacchanalia were ordered dismantled under the senatus consultum?
answer_en: Anything sacred that was there (sacred objects were exempt from the demolition).
derivation: The exception to demolition: 'exstrad quam sei quid ibei sacri est' — except insofar as anything sacred is there. Brief answer supported verbatim; the scrupulous exemption of consecrated objects even while destroying the shrines is a noted, characteristically Roman feature of the decree.

author: Senatus Romanus
source_text: In agro Teurano.
question: Ad quem agrum pertinet exemplum aeneum senatus consulti de Bacchanalibus, quod adhuc exstat?
question_en: To which territory does the still-extant bronze copy of the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus pertain?
answer_en: To the ager Teuranus (in Bruttium; the bronze was found at modern Tiriolo).
derivation: The subscription 'In agro Teurano' localizes this copy to the ager Teuranus in Bruttium, where the bronze was found (Tiriolo, 1640). Named-place answer supported verbatim; the findspot is part of the document's fame as one of the oldest surviving Latin inscriptions.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Natus est Augustus M. Tullio Cicerone C. Antonio conss. XIIII. Kal. Octob., paulo ante solis exortum, regione Palati, ad Capita bubulo, ubi nunc sacrarium habet, aliquanto post quam excessit constitutum.
question: Quibus consulibus natum esse Augustum Suetonius tradit?
answer: M. Tullio Cicerone et C. Antonio.
question_en: In whose consulship does Suetonius say Augustus was born?
answer_en: When Marcus Tullius Cicero and Gaius Antonius were consuls.

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

derivation: Atia was daughter of Iulia, sister of C. Caesar, making Augustus the dictator's great-nephew (and adopted heir). Supported by 'Iulia, sorore C. Caesaris.' Entity-anchored, single answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: superstitibus liberis Octavia maiore, quam ex Ancharia, et Octavia minore item Augusto, quos ex Atia tulerat.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Infanti cognomen Thurino inditum est, in memoriam maiorum originis.

derivation: His original childhood cognomen, before 'Augustus'. Indirect statement (inditum esse) under tradit; supported by 'cognomen Thurino inditum est.' Closed-book naming fact.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Postea Gai Caesaris et deinde Augusti cognomen assumpsit, alterum testamento maioris avunculi, alterum Munati Planci sententia, cum, quibusdam censentibus Romulum appellari oportere quasi et ipsum conditorem urbis, praevaluisset, ut Augustus potius vocaretur.

answer_en: On the motion of Munatius Plancus.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Bella civilia quinque gessit: Mutinense, Philippense, Perusinum, Siculum, Actiacum.

derivation: Source enumerates five named civil wars. Indirect statement (gessisse) under scribit; single number answer, entity-anchored.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Atque ab eo tempore exercitibus comparatis primum cum M. Antonio M. que Lepido deinde tantum cum Antonio per duodecim fere annos, novissime per quattuor et quadraginta solus rem publicam tenuit.

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

derivation: Supported by 'Liviam Drusillam matrimonio Tiberi Neronis ... abduxit.' Entity-anchored (Augustus, Livia, her first husband), single answer.

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius
source_text: Habuit in matrimonio Agrippinam, M. Agrippae et Iuliae filiam, et ex ea nouem liberos tulit.

derivation: Subject is Germanicus (from the preceding chapters). His wife and Caligula's mother is Agrippina the Elder, daughter of M. Agrippa and Iulia (Augustus's daughter). Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Germanicus/Caligula; single named answer with parentage; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Habuit in matrimonio Agrippinam, M. Agrippae et Iuliae filiam, et ex ea nouem liberos tulit.

derivation: Number fact, supported verbatim by 'ex ea nouem liberos tulit.' Entity-anchored to Germanicus and Agrippina; single-number answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Caligulae cognomen castrensi ioco traxit, quia manipulario habitu inter milites educabatur.

answer: Quia manipulario habitu inter milites educabatur.
question_en: Why did Gaius Caesar receive the nickname 'Caligula,' according to Suetonius?
answer_en: Because he was brought up among the soldiers dressed as a common soldier.
derivation: Origin of the famous nickname: a camp joke, because as a boy he was reared among the troops in a private soldier's outfit (the caligae, soldier's boots, give the name 'Caligula', little boot). Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Caligula; closed-book (the etymology is the best-known fact about him); brief causal answer matching the source.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Ego in actis Anti editum inuenio.

derivation: Suetonius, weighing conflicting traditions about Caligula's birthplace, settles on Antium on the authority of the public records (acta). Indirect statement (natum esse Gaium) under tradit; the attribution frame fits a claim Suetonius argues for. Place answer in the locative (Antii); entity-anchored, single answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: At in memoriam patris Septembrem mensem Germanicum appellauit.

derivation: He renamed September 'Germanicus' after his father. Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Caligula and Germanicus; single-month answer; closed-book, parallel to Augustus renaming Sextilis.

author: Suetonius
source_text: patruum Claudium, equitem R. ad id tempus, collegam sibi in consulatu assumpsit.

author: Suetonius

derivation: Number fact, supported verbatim by 'Consulatus quattuor gessit.' Entity-anchored to Caligula; single-number answer; closed-book.

derivation: Place fact: he entered his third consulship alone at Lugdunum. Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Caligula and the third consulship; single place answer in the locative (Luguduni).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Nam Baiarum medium interuallum ad Puteolanas moles, trium milium et sescentorum fere passuum spatium, ponte coniunxit contractis undique onerariis nauibus et ordine duplici ad anchoras conlocatis superiectoque terreno ac derecto in Appiae uiae formam.

answer_en: Between Baiae and the moles of Puteoli.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Incitato equo, cuius causa pridie circenses, ne inquietaretur, uiciniae silentium per milites indicere solebat, praeter equile marmoreum et praesaepe eburneum praeterque purpurea tegumenta ac monilia e gemmis domum etiam et familiam et supellectilem dedit, quo lautius nomine eius inuitati acciperentur; consulatum quoque traditur destinasse.

author: Suetonius

author: Suetonius

answer_en: On the ninth day before the Kalends of February (24 January).
derivation: Date of the assassination: a.d. IX Kal. Feb. (= 24 January). Supported verbatim ('VIIII. Kal. Febr.'), the day on which, leaving for lunch, he was cut down. Entity-anchored to Caligula; single date answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius

derivation: Age-at-death fact, supported verbatim by 'Vixit annis uiginti nouem.' Entity-anchored to Caligula; single-number answer; closed-book.

answer_en: Three years, ten months, and eight days.
derivation: Reign-length fact, supported verbatim by 'imperauit triennio et decem mensibus diebusque octo.' Answer kept in the ablative of duration as in the source. Entity-anchored to Caligula; precise span; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Ex Antonia minore complures quidem liberos tulit, verum tres omnino reliquit: Germanicum, Livillam, Claudium.
question: Quis fuit frater maior Claudii imperatoris?
question_en: Who was the elder brother of the emperor Claudius?
derivation: Of Drusus and Antonia's three surviving children (Germanicus, Livilla, Claudius), Germanicus was the eldest; ch. 2 confirms 'fratre maiore.' Anchored to Claudius, single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Claudius natus est Iullo Antonio Fabio Africano conss. Kal. Aug. Luguduni eo ipso die quo primum ara ibi Augusto dedicata est, appellatusque Tiberius Claudius Drusus.
question: In quo oppido natus est Claudius?
question_en: In what town was Claudius born?
derivation: Birthplace fact, supported by 'natus est ... Luguduni.' Single place-name answer, entity-anchored to Claudius; closed-book (he was the only emperor born in Gaul).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Claudius natus est Iullo Antonio Fabio Africano conss. Kal. Aug. Luguduni eo ipso die quo primum ara ibi Augusto dedicata est, appellatusque Tiberius Claudius Drusus.
question: Quibus consulibus natum esse Claudium Suetonius tradit?
question_en: In whose consulship does Suetonius say Claudius was born?
answer_en: When Iullus Antonius and Fabius Africanus were consuls.
derivation: Birth-year fact (10 BC). Indirect statement (natum esse) under tradit; answer in the ablative matching 'Iullo Antonio Fabio Africano conss.' Entity-anchored, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Aviae Liviae diuinos honores et circensi pompa currum elephantorum Augustino similem decernenda curavit.
question: Cui aviae suae Claudius divinos honores decernendos curavit?
question_en: For which grandmother of his did Claudius see to it that divine honors were decreed?
derivation: Claudius consecrated his grandmother Livia (Augustus's wife), supported by 'Aviae Liviae diuinos honores ... decernenda curavit.' Names the grandmother plus a checkable act; entity-anchored, single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Per haec ac talia maxima aetatis parte transacta quinquagesimo anno imperium cepit quantumuis mirabili casu.
question: Quoto aetatis anno Claudius imperium cepit, ut Suetonius tradit?
question_en: In which year of his age did Claudius take power, according to Suetonius?
derivation: Age-at-accession fact, supported by 'quinquagesimo anno imperium cepit.' Ordinal answer, entity-anchored to Claudius, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Verum postero die et senatu segniore in exeqvendis conatibus per taedium ac dissensionem diversa censentium et multitudine, quae circumstabat, unum rectorem iam et nominatim exposcente, armatos pro contione iurare in nomen suum passus est promisitque singulis quina dena sestertia, primus Caesarum fidem militis etiam praemio pigneratus.
question: Quantum praemium Claudius singulis militibus promisit, primus Caesarum fidem militis praemio pigneratus?
question_en: What bounty did Claudius promise to each soldier, being the first of the Caesars to secure the soldiers' loyalty even with a reward?
derivation: The accession donative to the praetorians who made him emperor; supported by 'promisitque singulis quina dena sestertia, primus Caesarum fidem militis etiam praemio pigneratus.' Number fact, entity-anchored to Claudius; closed-book (the famous first imperial accession donative).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Cum decretis sibi a senatu ornamentis triumphalibus leviorem maiestati principali titulum arbitraretur velletque iusti triumphi decus, unde adquireret Britanniam potissimum elegit, neque temptatam ulli post Diuum Iulium et tunc tumultuantem ob non redditos transfugas.
question: Quam insulam Claudius, post Diuum Iulium a nullo temptatam, expeditione sua in deditionem recepit?
question_en: Which island, untried by anyone since the deified Julius, did Claudius receive in surrender by his expedition?
derivation: Claudius's annexation of Britain, his sole military expedition, supported by 'unde adquireret Britanniam potissimum elegit, neque temptatam ulli post Diuum Iulium.' Place answer, anchored to Claudius and Julius Caesar; iconic closed-book fact.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Fucinum adgressus est non minus conpendii spe quam gloriae, cum quidam privato sumptu emissuros se repromitterent, si sibi siccati agri concederentur. Per tria autem passuum milia partim effosso monte partim exciso canalem absoluit aegre et post undecim annos, quamuis continuis XXX hominum milibus sine intermissione operantibus.
question: Quot hominum milia Claudius in emissario Fucini lacus per undecim annos perficiendo adhibuit?
question_en: How many thousands of men did Claudius employ over eleven years to complete the outlet of the Fucine Lake?
derivation: The draining of Lake Fucinus, supported by 'post undecim annos, quamuis continuis XXX hominum milibus ... operantibus.' Number fact, entity-anchored to the Fucine project; closed-book engineering work.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Iudaeos impulsore Chresto assidue tumultuantis Roma expulit.
question: Quam gentem Claudius, impulsore Chresto assidue tumultuantem, Roma expulit?
question_en: Which people, continually rioting at the instigation of Chrestus, did Claudius expel from Rome?
derivation: The expulsion of the Jews from Rome (cf. Acts 18:2), supported verbatim. Entity-anchored (Claudius + 'impulsore Chresto'), single-noun answer, closed-book famous.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Verum inlecebris Agrippinae, Germanici fratris sui filiae, per ius osculi et blanditiarum occasiones pellectus in amorem, subornavit proximo senatu qui censerent, cogendum se ad ducendum eam uxorem, quasi rei p. maxime interesset, dandamque ceteris veniam talium coniugiorum, quae ad id tempus incesta habebantur.
question: Quam feminam, Germanici fratris sui filiam, Claudius novissimam uxorem duxit?
