derivation: Anchored to the freedman Atilius + the amphitheatre disaster; single place, supported verbatim by 'coepto apud Fidenam amphitheatro Atilius quidam libertini generis'. Closed-book: the collapse of the amphitheatre at Fidenae is a famous disaster of Tiberius's reign.

author: Tacitus
source_text: quinquaginta hominum milia eo casu debilitata vel obtrita sunt; cautumque in posterum senatus consulto ne quis gladiatorium munus ederet cui minor quadringentorum milium res neve amphitheatrum imponeretur nisi solo firmitatis spectatae.
question: Quot hominum milia ruina amphitheatri Fidenatis debilitata vel obtrita esse Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many thousands of people does Tacitus say were maimed or crushed by the collapse of the amphitheatre at Fidenae?
derivation: The famous toll of the Fidenae amphitheatre disaster. Anchored to the Fidenae collapse; single number, supported verbatim by 'quinquaginta hominum milia eo casu debilitata vel obtrita sunt'. Closed-book number fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: perosus tamen municipia et colonias omniaque in continenti sita Capreas se in insulam abdidit trium milium freto ab extremis Surrentini promunturii diiunctam.
question: In quam insulam Tiberius, relictis municipiis et continenti, se abdidit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: To what island did Tiberius withdraw, leaving the towns and the mainland, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius; single named place, supported verbatim by 'Capreas se in insulam abdidit'. Closed-book: Tiberius's retirement to Capri is among the best-known facts of his reign.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Ceterum Tiberius neptem Agrippinam Germanico ortam cum coram Cn. Domitio tradidisset, in urbe celebrari nuptias iussit.
question: Cui Tiberius Agrippinam, Germanico ortam, in matrimonium tradidit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: To whom did Tiberius give Agrippina, daughter of Germanicus, in marriage, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + Agrippina the Younger, daughter of Germanicus; single named person, supported verbatim by 'neptem Agrippinam Germanico ortam cum coram Cn. Domitio tradidisset'. Closed-book: the marriage of Agrippina the Younger to Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus, the future parents of the emperor Nero, is a stock genealogical fact; this is the closing sentence of book 4.

author: Tacitus
source_text: differtur per manipulos, Tacfarinatem omnes notum tot proeliis consectentur: non nisi duce interfecto requiem belli fore. at ille deiectis circum stipatoribus vinctoque iam filio et effusis undique Romanis ruendo in tela captivitatem haud inulta morte effugit; isque finis armis impositus.
question: Cuius ducis interitu diuturnum bellum Africanum sub Tiberio confectum esse Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By the death of what leader does Tacitus say the long African war under Tiberius was brought to an end?
derivation: Anchored to Tacfarinas + the African war; single named person, supported by 'non nisi duce interfecto requiem belli fore' and 'isque finis armis impositus' (Tacfarinas fell rushing into the Roman weapons rather than be captured). Closed-book: Tacfarinas, the Numidian leader of the long revolt in Africa, is a recurring figure whose death ended the war in this year.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Post quos Sex. Marius Hispaniarum ditissimus defertur incestasse filiam et saxo Tarpeio deicitur.
question: Quis, Hispaniarum ditissimus, sub Tiberio incesti accusatus saxo Tarpeio deiectus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Who, the richest man of the Spanish provinces, was accused of incest under Tiberius and thrown from the Tarpeian Rock, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Sextus Marius + the Spanish provinces + the Tarpeian Rock; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Sex. Marius Hispaniarum ditissimus ... saxo Tarpeio deicitur'. Closed-book: Sextus Marius, the richest man in Spain whose gold/copper mines Tiberius then confiscated, is a memorable Tacitean vignette of the terror.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Non omiserim praesagium Tiberii de Servio Galba tum consule; quem accitum et diversis sermonibus pertemptatum postremo Graecis verbis in hanc sententiam adlocutus 'et tu, Galba, quandoque degustabis imperium,' seram ac brevem potentiam significans
question: De quo viro, tum consule, Tiberius praedixit eum quandoque imperium degustaturum esse, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Concerning what man, then consul, did Tiberius foretell that he would one day taste of empire, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + Servius Galba; single named person, supported verbatim by 'praesagium Tiberii de Servio Galba ... et tu, Galba, quandoque degustabis imperium'. Closed-book: Tiberius's prophecy of Galba's brief future reign (Galba did become emperor in 68-69) is a famous anecdote.

author: Tacitus
source_text: scientia Chaldaeorum artis, cuius apiscendae otium apud Rhodum, magistrum Thrasullum habuit
question: Quem magistrum artis Chaldaeorum Tiberius apud Rhodum habuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Whom did Tiberius have as his teacher of the Chaldaean (astrological) art at Rhodes, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + Rhodes + the Chaldaean art; single named person, supported verbatim by 'apud Rhodum, magistrum Thrasullum habuit' (text spells it 'Thrasullum'). Closed-book: Thrasyllus, the astrologer who taught Tiberius on Rhodes, is a stock figure of the reign.

author: Tacitus
source_text: cum de Agrippina auditum, quam interfecto Seiano spe sustentatam provixisse reor, et postquam nihil de saevitia remittebatur, voluntate extinctam, nisi si negatis alimentis adsimulatus est finis qui videretur sponte sumptus.
question: Quo mortis genere Agrippina, Germanici uxor et Tiberii nurus, vitam finivit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By what kind of death did Agrippina, wife of Germanicus and daughter-in-law of Tiberius, end her life, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Agrippina the Elder (wife of Germanicus, Tiberius's daughter-in-law) to distinguish her from the younger Agrippina; the death by starvation is supported by 'voluntate extinctam' and 'negatis alimentis ... sponte sumptus'. Closed-book: the elder Agrippina's death by self-starvation under Tiberius is a stock fact of the reign.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Paulo Fabio L. Vitellio consulibus post longum saeculorum ambitum avis phoenix in Aegyptum venit praebuitque materiem doctissimis indigenarum et Graecorum multa super eo miraculo disserendi.
question: In quam terram avem phoenicem post longum saeculorum ambitum advenisse Tacitus refert?
question_en: Into what land does Tacitus report that the phoenix bird came after a long cycle of ages?
derivation: Anchored to the phoenix + Egypt; single place, supported verbatim by 'avis phoenix in Aegyptum venit'. Closed-book: the appearance of the phoenix in Egypt is the famous core of Tacitus's ethnographic phoenix excursus. One crisp fact kept from the digression.

author: Tacitus
source_text: neque enim multo post supremi Tiberio consules, Cn. Acerronius C. Pontius, magistratum occepere
question: Qui consules sub Tiberio supremi magistratum inierunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which consuls were the last to enter office under Tiberius, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + the consulship; two named persons, supported verbatim by 'supremi Tiberio consules, Cn. Acerronius C. Pontius, magistratum occepere'. Closed-book, verifiable: these were the ordinary consuls of AD 37, the last under Tiberius.

author: Tacitus
source_text: mutatisque saepius locis tandem apud promunturium Miseni consedit in villa cui L. Lucullus quondam dominus.
question: Apud quod promunturium Tiberius, in villa quondam L. Luculli, vitam finivit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: At what promontory did Tiberius end his life, in the villa that had once belonged to Lucius Lucullus, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + the villa of Lucullus; single place, supported verbatim by 'apud promunturium Miseni consedit in villa cui L. Lucullus quondam dominus'. Closed-book: Tiberius's death at Misenum, in the former villa of Lucullus, is among the best-known facts of his end.

author: Tacitus
source_text: sic Tiberius finivit octavo et septuagesimo aetatis anno.
question: Quoto aetatis anno Tiberius vitam finivit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: In what year of his age did Tiberius end his life, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius; single number, supported verbatim by 'finivit octavo et septuagesimo aetatis anno'. Closed-book number fact: Tiberius died in his 78th year (AD 37).

author: Tacitus
source_text: septimum decimum kal. Aprilis interclusa anima creditus est mortalitatem explevisse
question: Quo die Tiberius, interclusa anima, mortalitatem explevisse creditus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: On what day was Tiberius, his breath cut off, believed to have died, per Tacitus?
answer_en: On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April (16 March).
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + a date; single date, supported verbatim by 'septimum decimum kal. Aprilis interclusa anima creditus est mortalitatem explevisse'. Closed-book: the date of Tiberius's death (a.d. XVII Kal. Apr. = 16 March, AD 37) is a fixed historical fact. Tacitus notes he was only believed dead, then revived ('creditus est').

author: Tacitus
source_text: Macro intrepidus opprimi senem iniectu multae vestis iubet discedique ab limine.
question: Quis senem Tiberium reviviscentem iniectu multae vestis opprimi iussit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Who ordered the old man Tiberius, as he revived, to be smothered by piling on a heap of clothing, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Macro + Tiberius; single named agent, supported verbatim by 'Macro intrepidus opprimi senem iniectu multae vestis iubet'. Closed-book: that Macro the praetorian prefect smothered the reviving Tiberius is a famous detail of the emperor's death.

author: Tacitus
source_text: et multo gratantum concursu ad capienda imperii primordia G. Caesar egrediebatur
question: Quis, Tiberio mortuo, ad capienda imperii primordia egressus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Who came forth to take up the beginnings of empire when Tiberius had died, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius's death + the succession; single named person, supported verbatim by 'ad capienda imperii primordia G. Caesar egrediebatur'. Closed-book: Gaius Caesar (Caligula), grandson of Tiberius and son of Germanicus, succeeded Tiberius in AD 37.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Dein Rhodo regressus vacuos principis penatis duodecim annis, mox rei Romanae arbitrium tribus ferme et viginti obtinuit.
question: Per quot fere annos Tiberius rei Romanae arbitrium obtinuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
answer: Per tres ferme et viginti annos.
question_en: For about how many years did Tiberius hold sway over the Roman state, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius; single number, supported verbatim by 'rei Romanae arbitrium tribus ferme et viginti obtinuit'. Closed-book length-of-reign fact: Tiberius ruled about twenty-three years (AD 14-37).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Germania omnis a Gallis Raetisque et Pannoniis Rheno et Danuvio fluminibus, a Sarmatis Dacisque mutuo metu aut montibus separatur
question: Quibus fluminibus Germaniam a Gallis Raetisque et Pannoniis separari Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By which rivers does Tacitus report that Germania is separated from the Gauls, Raeti, and Pannonii?
answer_en: By the Rhine and the Danube.
derivation: Opening geographical fact. Anchored to Germania + named neighbouring peoples; two named rivers as a single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'Rheno et Danuvio fluminibus ... separatur'. Indirect statement (Germaniam separari) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the Rhine/Danube bounds of Germania are a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Celebrant carminibus antiquis, quod unum apud illos memoriae et annalium genus est, Tuistonem deum terra editum.
question: Quem deum terra editum Germani carminibus antiquis celebrant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which earth-born god do the Germani celebrate in ancient songs, as Tacitus reports?
derivation: The Germanic origin-myth. Anchored to Germani + Tacitus; single named theonym, supported verbatim by 'Tuistonem deum terra editum'. Tuistonem accusative as object of celebrant. Closed-book: Tuisto is the famous earth-born god of Germania.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Ei filium Mannum, originem gentis conditoremque, Manno tris filios adsignant, e quorum nominibus proximi Oceano Ingaevones, medii Herminones, ceteri Istaevones vocentur.
question: Quem filium Tuistonis Germani originem gentis conditoremque appellant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which son of Tuisto do the Germani call the origin and founder of their race, per Tacitus?
derivation: Second link of the origin-myth. Anchored to Tuisto's son; single named answer, supported verbatim by 'Ei filium Mannum, originem gentis conditoremque'. Mannum accusative as object of appellant. Closed-book: Mannus as founder of the Germani is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Deorum maxime Mercurium colunt, cui certis diebus humanis quoque hostiis litare fas habent.
question: Quem deorum Germanos maxime colere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which of the gods does Tacitus report the Germani worship most?
derivation: The chief cult-fact of the Germania. Anchored to Germani + Tacitus; single named god, supported verbatim by 'Deorum maxime Mercurium colunt'. Indirect statement (Germanos colere) governed by tradit; Mercurium accusative.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Vidimus sub divo Vespasiano Veledam diu apud plerosque numinis loco habitam; sed et olim Albrunam et compluris alias venerati sunt, non adulatione nec tamquam facerent deas.
question: Quam feminam sub divo Vespasiano numinis loco habitam esse Tacitus testatur?
question_en: Which woman does Tacitus testify was held in the place of a divinity under the deified Vespasian?
derivation: Named prophetess, dated to a named emperor. Anchored to Vespasian; single named-person answer, supported verbatim by 'Vidimus sub divo Vespasiano Veledam ... numinis loco habitam'. Indirect statement (Veledam habitam esse) governed by testatur.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Rari gladiis aut maioribus lanceis utuntur: hastas vel ipsorum vocabulo frameas gerunt angusto et brevi ferro
question: Quo proprio vocabulo Germani hastas suas appellant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By what native term do the Germani call their spears, per Tacitus?
derivation: Named weapon-custom. Anchored to Germani + Tacitus; single Germanic term, supported verbatim by 'hastas vel ipsorum vocabulo frameas gerunt'. Frameas accusative plural as object of appellant. Closed-book: the framea is Tacitus's well-known native word.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Nec dierum numerum, ut nos, sed noctium computant.
question: Utrum dierum an noctium numerum Germanos computare Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Does Tacitus report that the Germani reckon time by the count of days or of nights?
derivation: Distinctive time-reckoning custom. Anchored to Germani + Tacitus; single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'sed noctium computant'. Indirect statement (Germanos computare) governed by tradit. Famous closed-book fact (origin of 'fortnight'-style night-counting).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Nullas Germanorum populis urbes habitari satis notum est, ne pati quidem inter se iunctas sedes.
question: Quot urbes a Germanorum populis habitari Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many cities does Tacitus report were inhabited by the Germanic peoples?
derivation: The absence of cities. Anchored to Germanic peoples + Tacitus; single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'Nullas Germanorum populis urbes habitari satis notum est'. Closed-book: that the Germani had no cities is a stock ethnographic fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: At Germani Carbone et Cassio et Scauro Aurelio et Servilio Caepione Gnaeoque Mallio fusis vel captis quinque simul consularis exercitus populo Romano, Varum trisque cum eo legiones etiam Caesari abstulerunt
question: Quot legiones Germani una cum Varo Caesari abstulerunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many legions, together with Varus, did the Germani take from Caesar (Augustus), as Tacitus reports?
derivation: The Varus disaster, a famous number fact. Anchored to Varus + the Germani; single number answer, supported verbatim by 'Varum trisque cum eo legiones etiam Caesari abstulerunt'. Closed-book: the loss of three legions in the Teutoburg defeat is among the best-known facts of Roman history.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Sescentesimum et quadragesimum annum urbs nostra agebat, cum primum Cimbrorum audita sunt arma, Caecilio Metello et Papirio Carbone consulibus.
question: Quibus consulibus primum Cimbrorum arma audita esse Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Under which consuls does Tacitus say the arms of the Cimbri were first heard of?
answer_en: Under Caecilius Metellus and Papirius Carbo.
derivation: Dating of the first Cimbric war by named consuls. Anchored to the Cimbri; two named consuls as the verifiable answer, supported verbatim by the ablative absolute 'Caecilio Metello et Papirio Carbone consulibus'. Indirect statement (arma audita esse) governed by tradit.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Insigne gentis obliquare crinem nodoque substringere: sic Suebi a ceteris Germanis, sic Sueborum ingenui a servis separantur.
question: Quod est insigne Sueborum, quo a ceteris Germanis separantur, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: What is the distinctive mark of the Suebi, by which they are set apart from the other Germani, according to Tacitus?
answer_en: To twist the hair sideways and bind it in a knot.
derivation: The Suebian hair-knot. Anchored to the Suebi vs. other Germani; the answer mirrors the source phrase 'obliquare crinem nodoque substringere'. Closed-book: the Suebenknoten is the signature custom of the Suebi in Tacitus.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Fortissimus quisque ferreum insuper anulum (ignominiosum id genti) velut vinculum gestat, donec se caede hostis absolvat.
question: Quid ferreum apud Chattos fortissimus quisque velut vinculum gestat, donec hostem caedat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: What iron object does each bravest Chattus wear like a fetter until he slays an enemy, per Tacitus?
derivation: Named Chattan custom. Anchored to the Chatti; concrete object answer, supported verbatim by 'ferreum ... anulum ... velut vinculum gestat, donec se caede hostis absolvat'. Closed-book: the Chatti's iron ring of dishonour, worn until a first kill, is a distinctive Tacitean detail.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Sed et mare scrutantur, ac soli omnium sucinum, quod ipsi glesum vocant, inter vada atque in ipso litore legunt.
question: Quo nomine Aestii sucinum, quod soli omnium legunt, appellant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By what name do the Aestii call amber (sucinum), which alone of all peoples they gather, per Tacitus?
derivation: The Aestii and amber. Anchored to the Aestii (named in the same chapter as the only amber-gatherers, 'soli omnium'); single native term as answer, supported verbatim by 'sucinum, quod ipsi glesum vocant'. Spelling 'glesum'/'sucinum' kept as in the text. Closed-book: the amber-gathering Aestii are a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Suionibus Sitonum gentes continuantur. Cetera similes uno differunt, quod femina dominatur; in tantum non modo a libertate sed etiam a servitute degenerant.
question: Quo uno Sitones a Suionibus differre Tacitus tradit?
question_en: In what one respect does Tacitus say the Sitones differ from the Suiones?
answer_en: In that a woman rules them.
derivation: The woman-ruled tribe. Anchored to the Sitones vs. the Suiones; single verifiable point of difference, supported verbatim by 'uno differunt, quod femina dominatur'. Sitones accusative (subject of differre) governed by tradit.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Fennis mira feritas, foeda paupertas: non arma, non equi, non penates; victui herba, vestitui pelles, cubile humus: solae in sagittis spes, quas inopia ferri ossibus asperant.
question: Quibus rebus Fenni, ferri inopia, sagittas suas asperant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: With what do the Fenni tip their arrows, for lack of iron, per Tacitus?
derivation: Named custom of the Fenni. Anchored to the Fenni; concrete material answer, supported verbatim by 'solae in sagittis spes, quas inopia ferri ossibus asperant'. Closed-book: bone-tipped arrows of the iron-poor Fenni are a distinctive Tacitean detail.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Reudigni deinde et Aviones et Anglii et Varini et Eudoses et Suardones et Nuithones fluminibus aut silvis muniuntur. Nec quicquam notabile in singulis, nisi quod in commune Nerthum, id est Terram matrem, colunt eamque intervenire rebus hominum, invehi populis arbitrantur.
question: Quam deam, id est Terram matrem, Reudignos ceterasque gentes in commune colere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which goddess, that is Mother Earth, does Tacitus report the Reudigni and the other tribes worship in common?
derivation: Named deity of the Ingaevonic tribes. Anchored to the named group (Reudigni, Aviones, Anglii, etc.); single theonym answer, supported verbatim by 'Nerthum, id est Terram matrem, colunt'. Nerthum accusative; indirect statement governed by tradit. Closed-book: the Nerthus cult is a famous Tacitean datum.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Initium mihi operis Servius Galba iterum Titus Vinius consules erunt.
question: Quibus consulibus initium operis sui Tacitus statuit?
answer: Servio Galba iterum Tito Vinio consulibus.
question_en: In whose consulship does Tacitus set the beginning of his work?
answer_en: In the consulship of Servius Galba (for the second time) and Titus Vinius.
derivation: The famous opening sentence of the Histories. Anchored to Tacitus's opening + the named consuls of AD 69; single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'Servius Galba iterum Titus Vinius consules'. Answer recast as ablative absolute (the standard dating idiom). Closed-book: the dating of the Histories' start to Galba's second consulship and Vinius is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: finis Neronis ut laetus primo gaudentium impetu fuerat, ita varios motus animorum non modo in urbe apud patres aut populum aut urbanum militem, sed omnis legiones ducesque conciverat, evulgato imperii arcano posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri.
question: Quod imperii arcanum, finito Nerone, evulgatum esse Tacitus scribit?
answer: Posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri.
question_en: What secret of empire does Tacitus write was revealed after Nero's death?
answer_en: That an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome.
derivation: Tacitus's celebrated 'arcanum imperii'. Anchored to the end of Nero + the secret of empire; supported verbatim by 'evulgato imperii arcano posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri'. The fact-seeking form ('what secret') yields the famous maxim as a short clause; indirect statement 'arcanum ... evulgatum esse' governed by scribit. Closed-book: among the most-quoted lines of the Histories.

author: Tacitus
source_text: apud frequentem militum contionem imperatoria brevitate adoptari a se Pisonem exemplo divi Augusti et more militari, quo vir virum legeret, pronuntiat.
question: Quem Galba sibi successorem in castris adoptavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Whom did Galba adopt as his successor in the camp, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Galba + his successor; single named person, supported verbatim by 'adoptari a se Pisonem' (subject Galba). His full name 'Piso Licinianus' is fixed at 1.14 ('Pisonem Licinianum accersiri iubet'). Direct question, indicative adoptavit. Closed-book: Galba's adoption of Piso Licinianus is a stock fact of AD 69.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Piso M. Crasso et Scribonia genitus, nobilis utrimque.
question: Quibus parentibus natus erat Piso Licinianus, quem Galba adoptavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Of what parents was Piso Licinianus, whom Galba adopted, born, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Piso Licinianus (Galba's adopted heir); single named relation, supported verbatim by 'Piso M. Crasso et Scribonia genitus'. Ablative of origin matched in the question ('quibus parentibus natus'). Closed-book named-parentage fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: innixus liberto per Tiberianam domum in Velabrum, inde ad miliarium aureum sub aedem Saturni pergit. ibi tres et viginti speculatores consalutatum imperatorem ac paucitate salutantium trepidum et sellae festinanter impositum strictis mucronibus rapiunt.
question: A quot speculatoribus Otho ad miliarium aureum primum imperator consalutatus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By how many speculatores was Otho first hailed as emperor at the golden milestone, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Otho + the golden milestone (the start of his coup); single number, supported verbatim by 'tres et viginti speculatores consalutatum imperatorem ... rapiunt'. Recast as passive (consalutatus est, a + abl.); number kept as 'tres et viginti'. Closed-book: the tiny band of 23 who first hailed Otho is a famous detail.

author: Tacitus
source_text: iuxta Curtii lacum trepidatione ferentium Galba proiectus e sella ac provolutus est.
question: Iuxta quem locum in foro Galba e sella proiectus et interfectus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Beside what place in the forum was Galba thrown from his litter and killed, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Galba's murder; single named place, supported verbatim by 'iuxta Curtii lacum ... Galba proiectus e sella ac provolutus est' (he is dispatched in the lines following). 'iuxta' + accusative. Closed-book: Galba's death by the Lacus Curtius in the forum is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: hunc exitum habuit Servius Galba, tribus et septuaginta annis quinque principes prospera fortuna emensus et alieno imperio felicior quam suo.
question: Quot annos natus Servius Galba mortem obiit, ut Tacitus refert?
question_en: At what age did Servius Galba die, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Galba's death; single number, supported by 'tribus et septuaginta annis ... emensus' (he had traversed 73 years). 'quot annos natus' is the standard age idiom; answer kept as the number 'tres et septuaginta'. Closed-book number fact about Galba.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Proxima legionis primae hiberna erant et promptissimus et legatis Fabius Valens. is die postero coloniam Agrippinensem cum equitibus legionis auxiliariorumque ingressus imperatorem Vitellium consalutavit.
question: Quem Fabius Valens, cum Germaniae legionibus, imperatorem consalutavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Whom did Fabius Valens, with the legions of Germany, hail as emperor, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Fabius Valens + the German legions; single named person, supported verbatim by 'imperatorem Vitellium consalutavit'. Direct question, indicative consalutavit. Closed-book: Vitellius's proclamation by the Rhine armies is the central rival rising of AD 69.

author: Tacitus
source_text: sed profusa cupidine et insigni temeritate legati legionum Alienus Caecina et Fabius Valens.
question: Quibus duobus legatis legionum Vitellius ad imperium nitens praecipue innixus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: On which two legionary legates did Vitellius, striving for power, chiefly rely, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + his two legionary legates; two named persons, supported verbatim by 'legati legionum Alienus Caecina et Fabius Valens', who 'instigare Vitellium' (1.52) and are made his two generals at 1.61 ('duos duces ... destinavit'). innitor + ablative; answer in the ablative. Closed-book: Caecina and Valens are Vitellius's famous commanders.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Syriam et quattuor legiones obtinebat Licinius Mucianus, vir secundis adversisque iuxta famosus.
question: Quot legiones in Syria Licinius Mucianus obtinebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many legions did Licinius Mucianus hold in Syria, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Licinius Mucianus + Syria; single number, supported verbatim by 'Syriam et quattuor legiones obtinebat Licinius Mucianus'. Direct question, indicative obtinebat. Closed-book number fact about the eastern command in AD 69.

author: Tacitus
source_text: bellum Iudaicum Flavius Vespasianus (ducem eum Nero delegerat) tribus legionibus administrabat.
question: Quot legionibus Flavius Vespasianus bellum Iudaicum administrabat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: With how many legions was Flavius Vespasianus conducting the Jewish war, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + the Jewish war; single number, supported verbatim by 'bellum Iudaicum Flavius Vespasianus ... tribus legionibus administrabat'. Ablative of means matched in the question. Closed-book: Vespasian's three-legion command in Judaea is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Aegyptum copiasque, quibus coerceretur, iam inde a divo Augusto equites Romani obtinent loco regum.
question: Inde a quo principe Aegyptum equites Romani loco regum obtinent, ut Tacitus scribit?
question_en: From which emperor onward do Roman knights govern Egypt in place of kings, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Egypt + its equestrian government; single named emperor, supported verbatim by 'iam inde a divo Augusto equites Romani obtinent loco regum'. Direct question, indicative obtinent. Closed-book: the rule that Egypt was governed by equestrian prefects (not senators) since Augustus is a well-known institutional fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: quattuor principes ferro interempti: trina bella civilia, plura externa ac plerumque permixta.
question: Quot principes hoc opere ferro interemptos esse Tacitus initio profitetur?
question_en: How many emperors does Tacitus declare at the outset were slain by the sword in this work?
derivation: Programmatic opening of the Histories. Anchored to Tacitus's preface + the emperors of the period it covers; single number, supported verbatim by 'quattuor principes ferro interempti'. Indirect statement 'principes ... interemptos esse' governed by profitetur. Closed-book: the toll of four emperors slain by the sword (Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Domitian across the Histories) is a salient programmatic fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Valenti inferioris exercitus electi cum aquila quintae legionis et cohortibus alisque, ad quadraginta milia armatorum data; triginta milia Caecina e superiore Germania ducebat, quorum robur legio unaetvicensima fuit.
question: Quot fere milia armatorum Fabio Valenti in Italiam ducenda data sunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: About how many thousand armed men were given to Fabius Valens to lead into Italy, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Fabius Valens + the Vitellian invasion of Italy; single number, supported verbatim by 'ad quadraginta milia armatorum data' (vs. Caecina's 30,000 in the same sentence). 'fere' mirrors the source's approximative 'ad'; passive 'data sunt' + dative Valenti. Closed-book number fact about the strength of Valens's column.

author: Tacitus
source_text: ubi pulsum Caecinam pergere Cremonam accepit, aegre coercitam legionem et pugnandi ardore usque ad seditionem progressam Bedriaci sistit. inter Veronam Cremonamque situs est vicus, duabus iam Romanis cladibus notus infaustusque.
question: Inter quas urbes situs est vicus Bedriacum, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Between which cities is the village of Bedriacum situated, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Bedriacum + its location; single place fact, supported verbatim by 'inter Veronam Cremonamque situs est vicus' (the vicus is Bedriacum, named just before in 'Bedriaci sistit'). 'inter' + accusative. Tacitus's 'duabus iam Romanis cladibus' notes the two battles of Bedriacum in AD 69. Closed-book: Bedriacum, site of the AD 69 battles between Verona and Cremona, is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Et media acie perrupta fugere passim Othoniani, Bedriacum petentes.
question: Utrius partis copiae priore Bedriacensi proelio fusae sunt, Othonis an Vitellii, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Whose forces were routed in the first battle of Bedriacum, Otho's or Vitellius's, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the first battle of Bedriacum + the two contending sides; single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'media acie perrupta fugere passim Othoniani' (Otho's men routed, the Vitellians victorious). A/B framing keeps it decontextualizable. Closed-book: the defeat of Otho's army at the first Bedriacum is the decisive event of his short reign.

author: Tacitus
source_text: vesperascente die sitim haustu gelidae aquae sedavit. tum adlatis pugionibus duobus, cum utrumque pertemptasset, alterum capiti subdidit. et explorato iam profectos amicos, noctem quietam, utque adfirmatur, non insomnem egit: luce prima in ferrum pectore incubuit.
question: Quo modo Otho post cladem Bedriacensem sibi mortem conscivit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: In what manner did Otho take his own life after the defeat at Bedriacum, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Otho + his death after Bedriacum; single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'luce prima in ferrum pectore incubuit'. Answer kept as the source's idiom 'in ferrum incubuit'. Closed-book: Otho's dignified suicide after the defeat is one of the most famous deaths in Roman history.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Othoni sepulchrum extructum est modicum et mansurum. hunc vitae finem habuit septimo et tricensimo aetatis anno.
question: Quoto aetatis anno Otho vitae finem habuit, ut Tacitus refert?
question_en: In what year of his life did Otho meet his end, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Otho's death; single number, supported verbatim by 'hunc vitae finem habuit septimo et tricensimo aetatis anno'. 'quoto aetatis anno' mirrors the ordinal idiom; answer kept as the ordinal 'septimo et tricensimo'. Closed-book number fact about Otho (died in his 37th year, AD 69).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii Alexandriae coeptum, festinante Tiberio Alexandro, qui kalendis Iuliis sacramento eius legiones adegit. isque primus principatus dies in posterum celebratus.
question: Quis primus legiones in verba Vespasiani adegit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Who was the first to swear the legions into allegiance to Vespasian, per Tacitus?
answer_en: Tiberius Alexander, the prefect of Egypt.
derivation: Anchored to Vespasian's proclamation + the man who initiated it; single named person, supported verbatim by 'festinante Tiberio Alexandro, qui ... sacramento eius legiones adegit'. His office, 'praefectus Aegypti ... Alexander', is fixed at 2.74. Closed-book: the prefect of Egypt's leading the swearing-in is the famous opening of the Flavian rising.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii Alexandriae coeptum, festinante Tiberio Alexandro, qui kalendis Iuliis sacramento eius legiones adegit. isque primus principatus dies in posterum celebratus.
question: Quibus Kalendis Tiberius Alexander legiones sacramento Vespasiani adegit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: On which Kalends did Tiberius Alexander swear the legions to Vespasian, per Tacitus?
answer_en: On the Kalends of July (1 July).
derivation: Anchored to Tiberius Alexander + the dated oath to Vespasian; single date, supported verbatim by 'kalendis Iuliis sacramento eius legiones adegit', with 'isque primus principatus dies in posterum celebratus' confirming this became the official first day of his reign. Closed-book: the dating of Vespasian's accession to 1 July AD 69 is a stock dated fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii Alexandriae coeptum, festinante Tiberio Alexandro, qui kalendis Iuliis sacramento eius legiones adegit.
question: In qua urbe initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii coeptum est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: In which city did the bestowal of imperial power on Vespasian begin, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + the start of his elevation to power; single place, supported verbatim by 'Initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii Alexandriae coeptum'. Locative 'Alexandriae'. Closed-book: that the Flavian principate began at Alexandria (under the prefect of Egypt) is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: sed in tanta mole belli plerumque cunctatio; et Vespasianus modo in spem erectus, aliquando adversa reputabat: quis ille dies foret quo sexaginta aetatis annos et duos filios iuvenes bello permitteret?
question: Quot annos natus Vespasianus, cum bellum pro imperio susciperet, fuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many years old was Vespasian when he undertook the war for the throne, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + his age at the Flavian rising; single number, supported verbatim by 'sexaginta aetatis annos ... bello permitteret' (he weighed committing his 60 years to war). 'quot annos natus' is the standard age idiom; answer kept as the number 'sexaginta'. Closed-book: Vespasian's age (about 60 in AD 69) is a stock biographical fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Forte inter Padum viamque patenti campo duae legiones congressae sunt, pro Vitellio unaetvicensima, cui cognomen Rapaci, vetere gloria insignis, e parte Othonis prima Adiutrix, non ante in aciem deducta, sed ferox et novi decoris avida.
question: Quae legio, in Bedriacensi proelio cum prima Adiutrice congressa, cognomen Rapacis ferebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which legion, which engaged the First Adiutrix at Bedriacum, bore the cognomen Rapax, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the legion + its cognomen + its opponent at Bedriacum; single named legion, supported verbatim by 'pro Vitellio unaetvicensima, cui cognomen Rapaci ... e parte Othonis prima Adiutrix'. Direct question, indicative ferebat. Closed-book: Legio XXI Rapax is a well-known named legion.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Titum instare Iudaeae, Vespasianum obtinere claustra Aegypti placuit: sufficere videbantur adversus Vitellium pars copiarum et dux Mucianus et Vespasiani nomen ac nihil arduum fatis.
question: Quem ducem Vespasianus cum parte copiarum adversus Vitellium misit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Whom did Vespasian send as commander, with part of his forces, against Vitellius, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + Vitellius + the Flavian commander; single named person, supported verbatim by 'sufficere videbantur adversus Vitellium pars copiarum et dux Mucianus'. Closed-book: Mucianus's leading the Flavian march on Italy (while Vespasian held Egypt and Titus pressed Judaea) is a stock fact of AD 69.

author: Tacitus
source_text: sic Capitolium ingressus atque ibi matrem complexus Augustae nomine honoravit.
question: Quo nomine Vitellius matrem suam, Capitolium ingressus, honoravit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: With what title did Vitellius honor his mother upon entering the Capitol, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + his mother (Sextilia, 2.64) + the title; single named honor, supported verbatim by 'matrem complexus Augustae nomine honoravit' (subject Vitellius from the sentence's start). Closed-book: Vitellius's bestowal of the title Augusta on his mother on entering Rome is a stock fact of his accession.

author: Tacitus
source_text: est Iudaeam inter Syriamque Carmelus: ita vocant montem deumque. nec simulacrum deo aut templum—sic tradidere maiores—: ara tantum et reverentia. illic sacrificanti Vespasiano, cum spes occultas versaret animo, Basilides sacerdos inspectis identidem extis...
question: In quo monte, inter Iudaeam et Syriam sito, Vespasianus sacrificavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: On which mountain, situated between Judaea and Syria, did Vespasian sacrifice, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + the mountain between Judaea and Syria; single named place, supported verbatim by 'est Iudaeam inter Syriamque Carmelus: ita vocant montem deumque' and 'illic sacrificanti Vespasiano'. Closed-book: Vespasian's sacrifice on Mount Carmel and the priest Basilides's prophecy is a famous omen of his rise.

author: Tacitus
source_text: fuere quattuor legiones, e quibus bina milia praemissa; ipsae modicis intervallis sequebantur, septima a Galba conscripta, veteranae undecima ac tertia decima et praecipui fama quartadecumani, rebellione Britanniae compressa.
question: Quae legio in exercitu Othonis fama praecipua erat, ut quae rebellionem Britanniae compressisset, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which legion was foremost in renown in Otho's army, as having crushed the rebellion in Britain, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Otho's army + the legion that put down the British revolt; single named legion, supported verbatim by 'praecipui fama quartadecumani, rebellione Britanniae compressa'. Closed-book: Legio XIV, which crushed Boudicca's rebellion, is a well-known named legion.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Caecina Padum transgressus, temptata Othonianorum fide per conloquium et promissa, isdem petitus, postquam pax et concordia speciosis et inritis nominibus iactata sunt, consilia curasque in obpugnationem Placentiae magno terrore vertit, gnarus ut initia belli provenissent famam in cetera fore.
question: Quam coloniam, a Spurinna defensam, Caecina frustra obpugnavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which colony, defended by Spurinna, did Caecina besiege in vain, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Caecina (one of Vitellius's invading generals) + Spurinna + the besieged town; single named place, supported verbatim by 'consilia curasque in obpugnationem Placentiae ... vertit'. Spurinna's defense ('defensam Placentiam', 2.23) and Caecina's repulse ('multo suorum cruore pulsus Caecina', 2.21) confirm 'frustra'. Closed-book: Caecina's failed siege of Placentia is a stock episode of the Vitellian invasion of Italy.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Ad ea Antonius Primus (is acerrimus belli concitator) festinationem ipsis utilem, Vitellio exitiosam disseruit.
question: Quis dux partium Flavianarum, quem Tacitus acerrimum belli concitatorem appellat, festinationem belli adversus Vitellium suasit?
question_en: Which leader of the Flavian party, whom Tacitus calls the keenest instigator of the war, argued for haste in the war against Vitellius?
derivation: Anchored to the Flavian party + the man who pressed for speed; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Antonius Primus (is acerrimus belli concitator) festinationem ipsis utilem, Vitellio exitiosam disseruit'. Closed-book: Antonius Primus, the Flavian general who drove the Danubian legions into Italy in AD 69, is a stock figure of the year of the four emperors. The Tacitean tag 'acerrimus belli concitator' is reused as the anchor.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Quaesitum inde quae sedes bello legeretur. Verona potior visa, patentibus circum campis ad pugnam equestrem, qua praevalebant: simul coloniam copiis validam auferre Vitellio in rem famamque videbatur.
question: Quam urbem duces Flaviani sedem bello legerunt, propter campos circum patentis equestri pugnae aptos, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which city did the Flavian leaders choose as the seat of the war, on account of the open plains around it suited to cavalry battle, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the Flavian leaders + their choice of base; single named place, supported verbatim by 'Verona potior visa, patentibus circum campis ad pugnam equestrem'. Mirrors the source's 'sedes bello legeretur'. Closed-book: Verona as the Flavian rallying-point before the advance on Cremona is a fixed point of the AD 69 campaign.

author: Tacitus
source_text: per quadriduum Cremona suffecit. cum omnia sacra profanaque in igne considerent, solum Mefitis templum stetit ante moenia, loco seu numine defensum.
question: Quod unum templum, ceteris omnibus Cremonae igne consumptis, ante moenia incolume stetit, ut Tacitus refert?
question_en: Which single temple, when all the rest of Cremona was consumed by fire, stood unharmed before the walls, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Cremona's burning + the one surviving temple; single named cult site, supported verbatim by 'solum Mefitis templum stetit ante moenia'. Closed-book: that only the temple of Mefitis survived the sack of Cremona is a memorable Tacitean detail. 'quod templum... stetit' indicative direct question.

author: Tacitus
source_text: per quadriduum Cremona suffecit. cum omnia sacra profanaque in igne considerent, solum Mefitis templum stetit ante moenia, loco seu numine defensum.
question: Per quot dies, capta urbe, direptio atque incendium Cremonae duravit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: For how many days did the sack of Cremona last, after the city was taken, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Cremona + the duration of its sack; single number, supported verbatim by 'per quadriduum Cremona suffecit' (Cremona held out / sufficed for the plundering four days). 'per quot dies' mirrors the durative 'per quadriduum'. Closed-book: the four-day sack and burning of Cremona by the victorious Flavian army is a notorious atrocity of AD 69.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Hic exitus Cremonae anno ducentesimo octogesimo sexto a primordio sui.
question: Quoto anno a primordio suo urbs Cremona, a Flavianis direpta atque incensa, deleta est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: In which year from its founding was the city of Cremona, sacked and burned by the Flavians, destroyed, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Cremona + its destruction; single ordinal number, supported verbatim by 'Hic exitus Cremonae anno ducentesimo octogesimo sexto a primordio sui'. Closed-book: Tacitus's dating of Cremona's fall to its 286th year is a stock fact marking the colony's age. 'quoto anno' mirrors the ordinal idiom.

author: Tacitus
source_text: sedem Iovis Optimi Maximi auspicato a maioribus pignus imperii conditam, quam non Porsenna dedita urbe neque Galli capta temerare potuissent, furore principum excindi.
question: Cuius dei aedes in Capitolio, dum Vitelliani et Flaviani Romae armis contendunt, incensa est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: The temple of which god on the Capitol was burned while the Vitellians and Flavians fought in arms at Rome, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the Capitol + the deity whose temple burned; single named god, supported verbatim by 'sedem Iovis Optimi Maximi... furore principum excindi' (confirmed at 3.71 'sic Capitolium... conflagravit' and 3.72 'ea tunc aedes cremabatur'). Closed-book: the burning of the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus during the Flavian assault on Rome in AD 69 is one of the most famous calamities of the civil wars.

author: Tacitus
source_text: voverat Tarquinius Priscus rex bello Sabino, ieceratque fundamenta spe magis futurae magnitudinis quam quo modicae adhuc populi Romani res sufficerent.
question: Quis rex Romanus aedem Iovis Optimi Maximi bello Sabino vovit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which Roman king vowed the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus during the Sabine war, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the temple of Jupiter O.M. + the king who vowed it; single named person, supported verbatim by 'voverat Tarquinius Priscus rex bello Sabino, ieceratque fundamenta' (antecedent: 'sedem Iovis Optimi Maximi' earlier in 3.72). Closed-book: that Tarquinius Priscus vowed and laid the foundations of the Capitoline temple of Jupiter is a stock fact of Roman tradition. 'vovit' + accusative.

author: Tacitus
source_text: At primores civitatis Flavium Sabinum praefectum urbis secretis sermonibus incitabant, victoriae famaeque partem capesseret.
question: Quod munus Romae Flavius Sabinus, Vespasiani frater, eo tempore gerebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which office at Rome did Flavius Sabinus, Vespasian's brother, hold at that time, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Flavius Sabinus + brother of Vespasian + his office; single named magistracy, supported verbatim by 'Flavium Sabinum praefectum urbis'. Closed-book: Flavius Sabinus, the elder brother of Vespasian and prefect of the city, killed in the Flavian struggle for Rome in AD 69, is a fixed figure of the year. 'praefecturam urbis' answers 'quod munus gerebat'.

author: Tacitus
source_text: innocentiam iustitiamque eius non argueres; sermonis nimius erat: id unum septem annis quibus Moesiam, duodecim quibus praefecturam urbis obtinuit, calumniatus est rumor.
question: Per quot annos Flavius Sabinus praefecturam urbis obtinuit, ut Tacitus refert?
question_en: For how many years did Flavius Sabinus hold the prefecture of the city, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Flavius Sabinus + the duration of his city prefecture; single number, supported verbatim by 'duodecim quibus praefecturam urbis obtinuit' (subject Sabinus, 'Hic exitus viri', 3.75). Closed-book number fact about Vespasian's brother's long tenure as praefectus urbi.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Domitianus prima inruptione apud aedituum occultatus, sollertia liberti lineo amictu turbae sacricolarum immixtus ignoratusque, apud Cornelium Primum paternum clientem iuxta Velabrum delituit.
question: Quis filius Vespasiani, capta a Vitellianis Capitolii arce, lineo amictu inter sacricolas occultatus evasit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which son of Vespasian escaped, hidden in a linen garment among the temple-worshippers, when the citadel of the Capitol was taken by the Vitellians, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the son of Vespasian + his escape from the Capitol; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Domitianus... lineo amictu turbae sacricolarum immixtus ignoratusque... delituit'. Closed-book: Domitian's escape in disguise from the burning Capitol, before becoming emperor, is a famous episode of AD 69.

author: Tacitus
source_text: fessusque misero errore et pudenda latebra semet occultans ab Iulio Placido tribuno cohortis protrahitur.
question: Quis tribunus cohortis Vitellium in Palatio latentem protraxit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which cohort tribune dragged Vitellius out as he hid in the Palace, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + the man who hauled him from hiding; single named person, supported verbatim by 'ab Iulio Placido tribuno cohortis protrahitur' (subject Vitellius, from 'in Palatium regreditur' earlier in 3.84). Closed-book: Vitellius's discovery in a wretched hiding place at the fall of Rome is a stock scene of his end.

author: Tacitus
source_text: postremo ad Gemonias, ubi corpus Flavii Sabini iacuerat, propulere. una vox non degeneris animi excepta, cum tribuno insultanti se tamen imperatorem eius fuisse respondit; ac deinde ingestis vulneribus concidit.
question: Quo loco Vitellium milites propulerunt, ubi antea Flavii Sabini corpus iacuerat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: To what place did the soldiers drive Vitellius, where the body of Flavius Sabinus had earlier lain, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + the place of his death + the prior fate of Sabinus's body; single named place, supported verbatim by 'postremo ad Gemonias, ubi corpus Flavii Sabini iacuerat, propulere'. Closed-book: Vitellius killed and his body cast on the Gemoniae, where Sabinus's body had lain, is the famous end of his reign.

author: Tacitus
source_text: septimum et quinquagensimum aetatis annum explebat, consulatum, sacerdotia, nomen locumque inter primores nulla sua industria, sed cuncta patris claritudine adeptus.
question: Quotum aetatis annum Vitellius, cum periit, explebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which year of his life was Vitellius completing when he died, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + his age at death; single ordinal number, supported verbatim by 'septimum et quinquagensimum aetatis annum explebat' (subject Vitellius, just killed in 3.85). 'quotum aetatis annum... explebat' mirrors the source idiom. Closed-book biographical number, parallel to the recorded ages of the other emperors of AD 69.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Isdem diebus Fabius Valens Vrbini in custodia interficitur. caput eius Vitellianis cohortibus ostentatum ne quam ultra spem foverent.
question: In qua urbe Fabius Valens, dux Vitellianus, in custodia interfectus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: In which town was Fabius Valens, the Vitellian general, killed while in custody, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Fabius Valens + the Vitellian command + the place of his death; single named place, supported verbatim by 'Fabius Valens Vrbini in custodia interficitur' (Vrbini = locative of Urbinum). Closed-book: the capture and execution of the Vitellian general Fabius Valens at Urbinum, his severed head shown to his troops, is a key turning point before Rome's fall.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Cartimandua Brigantibus imperitabat, pollens nobilitate; et auxerat potentiam, postquam capto per dolum rege Carataco instruxisse triumphum Claudii Caesaris videbatur.
question: Cui genti Britanniae Cartimandua regina imperabat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which people of Britain did Queen Cartimandua rule, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Queen Cartimandua + the people she ruled; single named people, supported verbatim by 'Cartimandua Brigantibus imperitabat, pollens nobilitate'. 'imperabat' + dative mirrors 'imperitabat'. Closed-book: Cartimandua, queen of the Brigantes who handed over Caratacus, is a stock figure of Roman Britain.

author: Tacitus
source_text: quae ubi relata Civili, incensus ira universam Batavorum gentem in arma rapit; iunguntur Bructeri Tencterique et excita nuntiis Germania ad praedam famamque.
question: Quis universam Batavorum gentem in arma contra Romanos rapuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Who swept the whole Batavian nation into arms against the Romans, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the Batavi + the leader of their revolt against Rome; single named person, supported verbatim by 'incensus ira universam Batavorum gentem in arma rapit' (subject Civilis, from 'relata Civili'). His full name Iulius Civilis is fixed at 4.13. Closed-book: Iulius Civilis as leader of the Batavian revolt of AD 69-70 is the central named fact of the book.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Batavi, donec trans Rhenum agebant, pars Chattorum, seditione domestica pulsi extrema Gallicae orae vacua cultoribus simulque insulam iuxta sitam occupavere, quam mare Oceanus a fronte, Rhenus amnis tergum ac latera circumluit.
question: Cuius gentis pars olim Batavi fuerunt, dum trans Rhenum agebant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Of which people were the Batavi once a part, while they dwelt beyond the Rhine, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the Batavi + their ethnic origin; single named people, supported verbatim by 'Batavi, donec trans Rhenum agebant, pars Chattorum'. Indirect-question frame avoided here (direct relative); 'dum ... agebant' mirrors the source's 'donec ... agebant'. Closed-book: that the Batavi were an offshoot of the Chatti is a stock ethnographic fact of Germania.

author: Tacitus
source_text: ea virgo nationis Bructerae late imperitabat, vetere apud Germanos more, quo plerasque feminarum fatidicas et augescente superstitione arbitrantur deas. tuncque Veledae auctoritas adolevit; nam prosperas Germanis res et excidium legionum praedixerat.
question: Cuius nationis virgo fuit Veleda, quae apud Germanos late imperitabat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Of which people was the maiden Veleda, who ruled widely among the Germans, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the prophetess Veleda + her people; single named nation, supported verbatim by 'ea virgo nationis Bructerae late imperitabat'. Answer kept in the source's form 'nationis Bructerae'. Closed-book: Veleda the Bructeran prophetess, held by the Germans as well-nigh divine, is a famous ethnographic figure of the period.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Munius Lupercus legatus legionis inter dona missus Veledae. ea virgo nationis Bructerae late imperitabat, vetere apud Germanos more, quo plerasque feminarum fatidicas et augescente superstitione arbitrantur deas.
question: Cui Germanae virgini Munius Lupercus, legionis legatus, inter dona missus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: To which German maiden was Munius Lupercus, a legionary legate, sent among the gifts, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the legate Munius Lupercus + the prophetess; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Munius Lupercus legatus legionis inter dona missus Veledae'. Dative 'Veledae' answers 'cui ... virgini'. Closed-book: the dispatch of the captured legate to Veleda as a gift is a signal detail of the revolt (he was killed en route).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Curam restituendi Capitolii in Lucium Vestinum confert, equestris ordinis virum, sed auctoritate famaque inter proceres.
question: Cui viro Vespasianus curam restituendi Capitolii mandavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: To which man did Vespasian entrust the charge of rebuilding the Capitol, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + the rebuilding of the Capitol + the curator; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Curam restituendi Capitolii in Lucium Vestinum confert' (subject Vespasian, who has charge of the rebuilding begun in AD 70). Closed-book: the rebuilding of the burnt Capitol under Vespasian, with the eques Lucius Vestinus as curator, is a stock fact of the early Flavian principate.

author: Tacitus
source_text: XI kalendas Iulias serena luce spatium omne quod templo dicabatur evinctum vittis coronisque; ingressi milites, quis fausta nomina, felicibus ramis; dein virgines Vestales cum pueris puellisque patrimis matrimisque aqua e fontibus amnibusque hausta perluere.
question: Quo die area Capitolii restituendi, sacris rite peractis, consecrata est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: On what day was the site of the Capitol-to-be-rebuilt consecrated, with the rites duly performed, per Tacitus?
answer_en: On the eleventh day before the Kalends of July (21 June).
derivation: Anchored to the rebuilding of the Capitol + the dated inaugural ceremony; single date, supported verbatim by 'XI kalendas Iulias serena luce spatium omne quod templo dicabatur evinctum vittis coronisque'. Answer kept in the source's calendar form. Closed-book/dated fact: the foundation ceremony for the new Capitol on 21 June AD 70.

author: Tacitus
source_text: tum Helvidius Priscus praetor, praeeunte Plautio Aeliano pontifice, lustrata suovetaurilibus area et super caespitem redditis extis, Iovem, Iunonem, Minervam praesidesque imperii deos precatus uti coepta prosperarent sedisque suas pietate hominum inchoatas divina ope attollerent, vittas, quis ligatus lapis innexique funes erant, contigit.
question: Quis praetor aream Capitolii suovetaurilibus lustravit, cum templum sub Vespasiano restitueretur, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which praetor purified the Capitol's site with the suovetaurilia when the temple was being rebuilt under Vespasian, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the rebuilding of the Capitol + the magistrate who performed the rite; single named person with office, supported verbatim by 'tum Helvidius Priscus praetor ... lustrata suovetaurilibus area'. Closed-book: Helvidius Priscus the praetor presiding (under the pontifex Plautius Aelianus) over the Capitol's rededication is a noted episode of AD 70.

author: Tacitus
source_text: interfecto Hordeonio commeavere nuntii inter Civilem Classicumque praefectum alae Trevirorum. Classicus nobilitate opibusque ante alios: regium illi genus et pace belloque clara origo, ipse e maioribus suis hostis populi Romani quam socios iactabat.
question: Cuius gentis alae praefectus erat Iulius Classicus, qui cum Civile contra Romanos coniuravit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Of which people's cavalry wing was Iulius Classicus prefect, who conspired with Civilis against the Romans, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Iulius Classicus (the Treveran ringleader) + his command; single named people, supported verbatim by 'Classicumque praefectum alae Trevirorum'. Closed-book: Iulius Classicus, prefect of the Treveran ala and a leader of the Gallic rising, is a named figure of the revolt.

author: Tacitus
source_text: dein sumptis Romani imperii insignibus in castra venit. nec illi, quamquam ad omne facinus durato, verba ultra suppeditavere quam ut sacramentum recitaret: iuravere qui aderant pro imperio Galliarum.
question: Pro quo imperio iuraverunt milites quos Iulius Classicus, sumptis Romani imperii insignibus, sacramento adegit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: To what empire did the soldiers swear, whom Iulius Classicus, having put on the insignia of Roman power, bound by oath, per Tacitus?
answer_en: To the empire of the Gauls (the Gallic Empire).
derivation: Anchored to Classicus + the oath he imposed; single named institution, supported verbatim by 'iuravere qui aderant pro imperio Galliarum' (the subject who donned the Roman insignia is Classicus, from earlier in 4.59). Closed-book: the proclaimed 'imperium Galliarum' is the defining political fact of the Civilis-Classicus revolt.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Interea Iulius Sabinus proiectis foederis Romani monumentis Caesarem se salutari iubet magnamque et inconditam popularium turbam in Sequanos rapit, conterminam civitatem et nobis fidam.
question: Quem se salutari iussit Iulius Sabinus, cum a populo Romano descivisset, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: As what did Iulius Sabinus order himself to be hailed, when he had revolted from the Roman people, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Iulius Sabinus (the Lingon ringleader) + the title he assumed; single named title, supported verbatim by 'Iulius Sabinus ... Caesarem se salutari iubet'. Predicate accusative 'Caesarem' with 'salutari'. Closed-book: Sabinus's having himself proclaimed Caesar is the memorable mark of the Gallic pretender.

author: Tacitus
source_text: At Romae cuncta in deterius audita Mucianum angebant, ne quamquam egregii duces (iam enim Gallum Annium et Petilium Cerialem delegerat) summam belli parum tolerarent.
question: Quem ducem Mucianus, una cum Annio Gallo, ad bellum Batavicum Gallicumque conficiendum delegit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which commander did Mucianus, together with Annius Gallus, appoint to finish the Batavian and Gallic war, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Mucianus + the generals chosen against the revolt; single named person, supported verbatim by 'iam enim Gallum Annium et Petilium Cerialem delegerat'. Cerialis is the commander who in fact crushes the revolt (4.71-79). Closed-book: Petillius Cerialis as the suppressor of the Batavian/Gallic rising is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: aderant legati regis Vologaesi quadraginta milia Parthorum equitum offerentes. magnificum laetumque tantis sociorum auxiliis ambiri neque indigere: gratiae Vologaeso actae mandatumque ut legatos ad senatum mitteret et pacem esse sciret.
question: Quot milia equitum Parthorum rex Vologaeses Vespasiano in auxilium obtulit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many thousands of Parthian cavalry did King Vologaeses offer Vespasian as aid, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to King Vologaeses + Vespasian + the offer; single number, supported verbatim by 'legati regis Vologaesi quadraginta milia Parthorum equitum offerentes'. Closed-book number fact: the Parthian king's offer of 40,000 horse to Vespasian.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Per eos mensis quibus Vespasianus Alexandriae statos aestivis flatibus dies et certa maris opperiebatur, multa miracula evenere, quis caelestis favor et quaedam in Vespasianum inclinatio numinum ostenderetur. e plebe Alexandrina quidam oculorum tabe notus genua eius advolvitur, remedium caecitatis exposcens gemitu, monitu Serapidis dei, quem dedita superstitionibus gens ante alios colit; precabaturque principem ut genas et oculorum orbis dignaretur respergere oris excremento. alius manum aeger eodem deo auctore ut pede ac vestigio Caesaris calcaretur orabat.
question: In qua urbe Vespasianus caecum quendam et alium manu aegrum, Serapide auctore, sanavisse traditur, ut Tacitus refert?
question_en: In which city is Vespasian said to have healed a blind man and another sick in the hand, at the prompting of Serapis, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + the healing-miracles + the god; single named place, supported by 'Vespasianus Alexandriae ... multa miracula evenere' and the two Alexandrian petitioners (the blind man, the man with the diseased hand) prompted by Serapis. The cure itself ('conversa ad usum manus, ac caeco reluxit dies') follows in the same chapter. Closed-book: Vespasian's healing miracles at Alexandria are among the most famous omens of his reign.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Eiusdem anni principio Caesar Titus, perdomandae Iudaeae delectus a patre et privatis utriusque rebus militia clarus, maiore tum vi famaque agebat, certantibus provinciarum et exercituum studiis.
question: Quis perdomandae Iudaeae a patre delectus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Who was chosen by his father to subdue Judaea, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Opening fact of Book 5: Titus was put in charge of the Jewish war and the siege of Jerusalem. Anchored to Judaea + 'a patre'; single named answer, supported verbatim by 'Caesar Titus, perdomandae Iudaeae delectus a patre'. Closed-book: Titus's capture of Jerusalem (AD 70) is among the best-known facts of Roman history. The father is Vespasian.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Plurimi auctores consentiunt orta per Aegyptum tabe quae corpora foedaret, regem Bocchorim adito Hammonis oraculo remedium petentem purgare regnum et id genus hominum ut invisum deis alias in terras avehere iussum. Sic conquisitum collectumque vulgus, postquam vastis locis relictum sit, ceteris per lacrimas torpentibus, Moysen unum exulum monuisse ne quam deorum hominumve opem expectarent utrisque deserti, sed sibimet duce caelesti crederent, primo cuius auxilio praesentis miserias pepulissent.
question: Quo duce Iudaei ex Aegypto expulsi novas terras petiverunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Under whose leadership did the Jews, after being expelled from Egypt, seek new lands, according to Tacitus?
derivation: In the account Tacitus says most authorities agree on ('plurimi auctores consentiunt', 5.3), a plague in Egypt led king Bocchoris to drive out the Jews, and Moses, one of the exiles, became their leader. Anchored to the Jews + Egypt; single named leader, supported by 'Moysen unum exulum ... sibimet duce caelesti crederent'. Closed-book: Moses leading the Jews out of Egypt is among the most widely known facts across cultures. The rival origin theories (Cretan, Ethiopian, Assyrian, etc.) are dropped as multi-attributed and non-verifiable.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Septimo die otium placuisse ferunt, quia is finem laborum tulerit; dein blandiente inertia septimum quoque annum ignaviae datum.
question: Quoto quoque die Iudaeos otium agere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: On every which day does Tacitus report that the Jews keep rest?
derivation: The Sabbath. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single ordinal-number answer, supported verbatim by 'Septimo die otium placuisse'. Indirect statement (Iudaeos otium agere) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the Jewish seventh-day rest is a stock fact; Tacitus's reported reason ('quia is finem laborum tulerit') is not asked, only the day.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Septimo die otium placuisse ferunt, quia is finem laborum tulerit; dein blandiente inertia septimum quoque annum ignaviae datum.
question: Quotum quemque annum Iudaeos ignaviae dare Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Every which year does Tacitus report the Jews give over to idleness?
derivation: The sabbatical year. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single ordinal answer, supported verbatim by 'septimum quoque annum ignaviae datum'. Indirect statement (Iudaeos dare) governed by tradit. Closed-book ethnographic fact reported by Tacitus, distinct from the seventh-day rest.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Sue abstinent memoria cladis, quod ipsos scabies quondam turpaverat, cui id animal obnoxium.
question: Quo animali Iudaeos abstinere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: From which animal does Tacitus report that the Jews abstain?
derivation: Jewish abstention from pork. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single named animal in the ablative (abstinere + abl.), supported verbatim by 'Sue abstinent'. Closed-book: abstaining from pork is a defining, widely known Jewish custom.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Aegyptii pleraque animalia effigiesque compositas venerantur, Iudaei mente sola unumque numen intellegunt: profanos qui deum imagines mortalibus materiis in species hominum effingant; summum illud et aeternum neque imitabile neque interiturum.
question: Quot numina Iudaeos mente sola intellegere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many deities does Tacitus report the Jews conceive with the mind alone?
derivation: Jewish monotheism. Anchored to the Jews (contrasted with the Egyptians) + Tacitus; single-number answer, supported verbatim by 'Iudaei mente sola unumque numen intellegunt'. Indirect statement (Iudaeos intellegere) governed by tradit. Closed-book: that the Jews worship one God is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Igitur nulla simulacra urbibus suis, nedum templis sistunt; non regibus haec adulatio, non Caesaribus honor.
question: Quot simulacra Iudaei in urbibus suis, nedum templis, statuunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many images do the Jews set up in their cities, let alone their temples, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Jewish aniconism. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single answer 'nulla', supported verbatim by 'nulla simulacra urbibus suis, nedum templis sistunt'. Closed-book ethnographic fact (parallels the Germania 'Nullas ... urbes' structure).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Magna pars Iudaeae vicis dispergitur, habent et oppida; Hierosolyma genti caput. Illic immensae opulentiae templum, et primis munimentis urbs, dein regia, templum intimis clausum.
question: Quae urbs Iudaeae genti caput est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which city is the capital of the Jewish people, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the Jewish people + Tacitus; single named city, supported verbatim by 'Hierosolyma genti caput'. Closed-book: Jerusalem as the Jews' chief city and temple-city is universally known.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Romanorum primus Cn. Pompeius Iudaeos domuit templumque iure victoriae ingressus est: inde vulgatum nulla intus deum effigie vacuam sedem et inania arcana.
question: Quis Romanorum primus Iudaeos domuit et templum Hierosolymorum ingressus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Who was the first of the Romans to subdue the Jews and enter the temple of Jerusalem, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Pompey's capture of Jerusalem (63 BC) and entry into the Temple. Anchored to the Jews/Temple + 'Romanorum primus'; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Romanorum primus Cn. Pompeius Iudaeos domuit templumque ... ingressus est'. Closed-book historical fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Qui ubi fato aut taedio occidit, missu Neronis Vespasianus fortuna famaque et egregiis ministris intra duas aestates cuncta camporum omnisque praeter Hierosolyma urbis victore exercitu tenebat.
question: Cuius missu Vespasianus bellum Iudaicum gessit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By whose dispatch did Vespasian wage the Jewish war, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Nero appointed Vespasian to the Jewish command. Anchored to Vespasian + the Jewish war; single named person in the genitive ('cuius missu' / 'Neronis'), supported verbatim by 'missu Neronis Vespasianus'. Closed-book: Nero's commissioning of Vespasian against the Jews is a stock fact. (Within two summers he held all but Jerusalem.)

author: Tacitus
source_text: Multitudinem obsessorum omnis aetatis, virile ac muliebre secus, sexcenta milia fuisse accepimus: arma cunctis, qui ferre possent, et plures quam pro numero audebant.
question: Quot milia hominum Hierosolymis obsessa fuisse Tacitus accepit?
question_en: How many thousands of people does Tacitus record were besieged at Jerusalem?
derivation: Number of the besieged at Jerusalem. Anchored to the siege of Jerusalem + Tacitus; single number answer, supported verbatim by 'sexcenta milia fuisse accepimus'. Indirect statement governed by accepit ('accepimus' marks the reported figure). Closed-book number fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Civilis haud porrecto agmine, sed cuneis adstitit: Batavi Cugernique in dextro, laeva ac propiora flumini Transrhenani tenuere.
question: Quis dux barbarorum aciem cuneis instruxit, cuius in dextro cornu Batavi steterunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which leader of the barbarians drew up his battle line in wedges, with the Batavi standing on his right wing, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Iulius Civilis, leader of the Batavian revolt against Rome. Anchored to the Batavi (named on his right wing) + Tacitus; single named leader, supported verbatim by 'Civilis ... cuneis adstitit: Batavi Cugernique in dextro'. Closed-book: Civilis is the famous leader of the Batavian revolt (AD 69-70); Book 5 names him simply 'Civilis' (full name Iulius Civilis in the earlier books).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Multa luce revecti hostes captivis navibus, praetoriam triremem flumine Lupia donum Veledae traxere.
question: Cui Germani praetoriam triremem captam, flumine Lupia subvectam, dono dederunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: To whom did the Germans give the captured praetorian trireme, brought up the river Lippe, as a gift, according to Tacitus?
derivation: The captured flagship dragged up the Lupia (Lippe) as a gift for the prophetess Veleda. Anchored to the Germans + the trireme; single named person in the dative, supported verbatim by 'praetoriam triremem flumine Lupia donum Veledae traxere'. Closed-book: Veleda, the Bructeran seeress (cf. Germania 8), is a well-known figure.
